CALENDERS

Pages 22-22

CALENDERS. See CALENDERS. KALENDS, or Calends, in the Roman chronology, the first day of every month.—The word is formed from καλεῖν, I call or proclaim; because, before the publication of the Roman fasti, it was one of the offices of the pontifices to watch the appearance of the new moon, and give notice thereof to the rex sacrificulus; upon which a sacrifice being offered, the pontiff summoned the people together in the Capitol, and there with a loud voice proclaimed the number of kalends, or the day whereon the nones would be; which he did by repeating this formula as often as there were days of kalends, Calo Juno Novella. Whence the name calende was given thereto, from calo, calare. This is the account given by Varro. Others derive the appellation hence, That the people being convened on this day, the pontifex called or proclaimed the several feasts or holidays in the month; a custom which continued no longer than the year of Rome 450, when C. Flavius, the curule aedile, ordered the fasti or kalendar to be set up in public places, that everybody might know the differences of times, and the return of the festivals. The kalends were reckoned backwards, or in a retrograde order. Thus, v. e. the first of May being the kalends of May; the last or the 30th of April was the pridie kalendarii, or second of the kalends of May; the 29th of April, the third of the kalends, or before the kalends; and so back to the 1st, where the ides commence; which are likewise numbered invertedly to the fifth, where the nones begin; which are numbered after the same manner to the first day of the month, which is the kalends of April. See IDES, and NONES. The rules of computation by kalends are included in the following verses: Prima dies mensis cujusque est dicta kalendae: Sex Maius nonas, October, Julius, et Mars; Quator ad reliqui: habet idus quilibet octo. Inde dies religiosi omnes die effe kalendas; Quas retro numerans dices a mensi sequente. To find the day of the kalends answering to any day of the month we are in; see how many days there are yet remaining of the month, and to that number add two: for example, suppose it the 22nd day of April; it is then the 10th of the kalends of May. For April contains 30 days: and 22 taken from 30, there remain 8; to which two being added, the sum is 10. The reason of adding two is, because the last day of the month is called secundo kalendas, the last but one tertio kalendas, &c. The Roman writers themselves are at a loss for the reason of this absurd and whimsical manner of computing the days of the month: yet it is still kept up in the Roman chancery; and by some authors, out of a vain affectation of learning, preferred to the common, more natural, and easy manner. Kalends are also used in church history to denote conferences anciently held by the clergy of each deanery, on the first day of every month, concerning their duty and conduct, especially in what related to the imposition of penance. Kalends of January, in Roman antiquity, was a solemn festival consecrated to Juno and Janus; wherein the Romans offered vows and sacrifices to those deities, and exchanged presents among themselves as a token of friendship. It was only a melancholy day to debtors, who were then obliged to pay their interests, &c. Hence Horace calls it tristis kalende; Lib. I. Serm. Sat. 3. KALI, the specific name of a plant which yields the substance also called kali or alkali. See SALSOLA. KALISH, a province of Lower Poland, with the title of a palatinate. It is bounded on the west by the palatinates of Bosnia, on the east by that of Syrad, on the north by Regal Prussia, and on the south by Silesia. Kalish is the capital town. Kalish, a town of Lower Poland, and capital of a palatinate of the same name, where the Jesuits had a magnificent college. It is seated on the river Przna, in a morass, which renders it difficult of access. E. Long, 18°. N. Lat. 52°. 20'. KALMIA, a genus of plants, belonging to the decidaria class, and in the natural method ranking under the 18th order, Bicornes. See BOTANY Index. KALMUCS, a tribe of Tartars, called also Eluths, inhabiting the larger half of what the Europeans call Western Tartary. Their territory extends from the Caspian sea, and the river Yalt or Ural, in 72 degrees of longitude from Ferro, to Mount Altay, in 110 degrees, and from the 40th to the 52nd degree of north latitude;

CALENDERS. See CALENDERS. KALENDS, or Calends, in the Roman chronology, the first day of every month.—The word is formed from καλεῖν, I call or proclaim; because, before the publication of the Roman fasti, it was one of the offices of the pontifices to watch the appearance of the new moon, and give notice thereof to the rex sacrificulus; upon which a sacrifice being offered, the pontiff summoned the people together in the Capitol, and there with a loud voice proclaimed the number of kalends, or the day whereon the nones would be; which he did by repeating this formula as often as there were days of kalends, Calo Juno Novella. Whence the name calende was given thereto, from calo, calare. This is the account given by Varro. Others derive the appellation hence, That the people being convened on this day, the pontifex called or proclaimed the several feasts or holidays in the month; a custom which continued no longer than the year of Rome 450, when C. Flavius, the curule aedile, ordered the fasti or

CONCERNING HIS RESIDENCE IN THE UNIVERSITY AND THE

Pages 331-336

g his residence in the university and the means by which he was there supported, his two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> biographers contradict each other; so that these are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of which we cannot write with certainty. According to Sir John Hawkins, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his continuance at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> is divisible into two periods: Mr Bofwell represents it as only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, with the usual <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> vacation. Sir John says, that he was supported at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> by Mr Andrew Corbet in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of assistant in the studies of his son: Mr Bofwell affirms us, that though he was promised pecuniary aid by Mr Corbet, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> was not in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> fulfilled. We should be inclined to adopt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>'s account of this transaction, were it not palpably inconsistent with itself. He says, that the two young men were entered in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; that Corbet <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the college two years; and yet that Johnson was driven home in little more than one year, because by the removal of Corbet he was deprived of his pension. A story, of which one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> contradicts the other, cannot wholly be true. Sir John adds, that "meeting with another source, the bounty, as it is supposed, of some one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more of the members of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Lichfield, he returned to college, and made up the whole of his residence in the university about three years." Mr Bofwell has told us nothing but that Johnson, though his father was unable to support him, continued three years in college, and was then driven from it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> poverty. These gentlemen differ likewise in their accounts of Johnson's tutors. Sir John Hawkins says that he had two, Mr Jordan and Dr Adams. Mr Bofwell affirms that Dr Adams could not be his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>, because Jordan did not quit the college till 1731; the year in the autumn of which Johnson himself was compelled to leave Oxford. Yet the same author represents Dr Adams as saying, "I was Johnson's nominal tutor, but he was above my mark;" a speech of which it is not easy to discover the meaning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was not Johnson's duty to attend Adams's lectures. In most colleges we believe there are two tutors in different departments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and therefore it is not improbable that Jordan and Adams may have been tutors to Johnson at the same time, the one in languages, the other in science. Jordan was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> abilities, that though his pupil loved him for the goodness of his heart, he would often risk the payment of a small fine, rather than attend his lectures; nor was he studious to conceal the reason of his absence. Upon occasion of one such impossession, he said, "Sir, you have foisted me twopence for non-attendance at a lecture not worth a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>." For some transgression or absence his tutor imposed upon him as a Christmas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the task of translating into Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> Pope's *Messian*; which being shown to the author of the original, was read and returned with this encomium, "The writer of this poem <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> leave it a question for posterity, whether his or mine be the original." The particular course of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> while in college, and during the vacation which he passed at home, cannot be traced. That at this period he read much, we have his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in what he afterwards told the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> was never regular, and at all times he thought more than he read. He informed Mr Bofwell, that what he read *folly* at Oxford was Greek, and that the study of which he was most fond was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>. It was in the year 1731 that Johnson left the university without a degree; and as his father, who died in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> of that year, had suffered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> misfortunes in trade, he was driven out a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and excluded from the regular modes of profit and prosperity. Having therefore no only a profession but the means of subsistence to seek, he accepted, in the month of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1732, an invitation to the office of under-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a free school at Market <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSWORTH">Bosworth</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>: but not knowing, as he said, whether it was more disagreeable for him to teach or for the boys to learn the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-rules, and being likewise disgusted at the treatment which he received from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the school, he relinquished in a few months a situation which he ever afterwards recollected with horror. Being thus again without any fixed employment, and with very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in his pocket, he translated *Lobo's voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>*, for the trifling sum, it is said, of five guineas, which he received from a bookeller in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>. Johnson. Birmingham. This was the first attempt which it is certain he made to procure pecuniary assistance by means of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>; and it must have held forth very little encouragement to his commencing author by profession. In 1735, being then in his 26th year, he married Mrs Porter, the widow of a mercer in Birmingham; whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> was almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> his; whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> form, according to Garrick and others, had never been captivating; and whose fortune amounted to hardly 800l. That she had a superiority of understanding and talents is extremely probable, both because she certainly inspired him with a more than ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and because she was herself so delighted with the charms of his conversation as to overlook his external disadvantages, which were many and great. He now set up a private academy; for which purpose he hired a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> well situated near his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; but his name having then nothing of that celebrity which afterwards commanded the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and respect of mankind, this undertaking did not succeed. The only pupils who are known to have been placed under his care, were the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Garrick, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> George Garrick, and a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of fortune whose name was Offely. He kept his academy only a year and a half; and it was during that time that he constructed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> and wrote a great part of his tragedy of Irene. The respectable character of his parents and his own merit had secured him a kind reception in the best families at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>; and he was particularly distinguished by Mr Walmley <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, a man of great worth and of very extensive and various erudition. That gentleman, upon hearing part of Irene read, thought so highly of Johnson's abilities as a dramatic writer, that he advised him by all means to finish the tragedy and produce it on the stage. To men of genius the stage holds forth temptations almost irresistible. The profits arising from a tragedy, including the representation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of it, and the connections which it sometimes enables the author to form, were in Johnson's imagination ineffinable. Flattered, it may be supposed, with these hopes, he set out some time in the year 1737 with his pupil David Garrick for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, leaving Mrs Johnson to take care of the house and the wreck of her fortune. The two adventurers carried with them from Mr Walmley an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> recommendation to the reverend Mr Collon, then master of an academy, and afterwards Lucasian professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but from that gentleman it does not appear that Johnson found either protection or encouragement. How he spent his time upon his first going to London is not particularly known. His tragedy was refused by the managers of that day; and for some years the Gentleman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> seems to have been his principal resource for employment and support. To enumerate his various communications to that far-famed miscellany, would extend this article beyond the limits which we can afford. Suffice it to say, that his connection with Cave the proprietor became very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>; that he wrote prefaces, essays, reviews of books, and poems; and that he was occasionally employed in correcting the papers written by other correspondents. When the complaints of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> against the administration of Sir Robert Walpole became loud, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> was made, February 13, 1742-3, to remove him from his majesty's councils forever, Johnson was pitched upon by Cave to write what was in the Magazine intitled Debates in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">Senate</a> of Lilliput, but was understood to be the speeches of the most eminent members in both houses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. These orations, which induced Voltaire to compare British with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> eloquence, were hastily sketched by Johnson while he was not yet 32 years old, while he was little acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, while he was struggling, not for distinction but for existence. Perhaps in none of his writings has he given a more conspicuous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of a mind prompt and vigorous almost beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>: for they were compiled from scanty notes taken by illiterate persons employed to attend in both houses; and sometimes he had nothing communicated to him but the names of the several speakers, and the part which they took in the debate. His separate publications which at this time attracted the greatest notice were, "London, a Poem in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Juvenal's third Satire;" "Marmor Norfolcense," or an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on an ancient prophetical Inscription in Monkfish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHYME">Rhyme</a>, lately discovered near Lynne in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>;" and "A complete Vindication of the Licencers of the Stage from the malicious and scandalous allegations of Mr Brook author of Gutavus Vasa." The poem, which was published in 1738 by Doddery, is universally known and admired as the most spirited instance in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of ancient sentiments adapted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> topics. Pope, who then filled the poetical throne without a rival, being informed that the author's name was Johnson, and that he was an obscure person, replied, "he will soon be dethroned." The other two pamphlets, which were published in 1739, are filled with keen satire on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; and though Sir John Hawkins has thought fit to declare that they display neither learning nor <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, Pope was of a different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; for in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of his preserved by Mr Boswell, he says, that "the whole of the Norfolk prophecy is very humorous." Mrs Johnson, who went to London soon after her husband, now lived sometimes in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and sometimes in another, sometimes in the city and sometimes at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>: but Johnson himself was oftener to be found at St John's Gate, where the Gentleman's Magazine was published, than in his own lodgings. It was there that he became acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">Savage</a>, with whom he was induced, probably by the similarity of their circumstances, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> a very close friendship; and such were their extreme necessities, that they have often wandered whole nights in the street for want of money to procure them a lodging. In one of these nocturnal rambles, when their distress was almost incredible, so far were they from being depressed by their situation, that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> spirits and brimful of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a>, they traversed St James's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a> for several hours, inveighed against the minister; and, as Johnson said in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of himself, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, and all such patriots, "resolved that they would stand by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>!" In 1744, he published the life of his unfortunate companion; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which, had he never written anything else, would have placed him very high. high in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of authors (a). His narrative is remarkably smooth and well disposed; his observations are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, and his reflections disclose the most recesses of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart. In 1749, when Drury-lane <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was opened under the management of Garrick, Johnson wrote a prologue for the occasion; which for just dramatic criticism on the whole range of the English stage, as well as for poetical excellence, is confessedly unrivalled. But this year is, in his life, distinguished as the epoch when his arduous and important work, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of the English Language, was announced to the world by the publication of its plan or prospectus, addressed to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Chesterfield. From that nobleman Johnson was certainly led to expect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> and encouragement; and it seems to be equally certain that his lordship expected, when the book should be published, to be honoured with the dedication. The expectations of both were disappointed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Chesterfield, after seeing the lexicographer once or twice, suffered him to be repulsed from his door; but afterwards thinking to conciliate him when the work was upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> of publication, he wrote two papers in "The World," warmly recommending it to the public. This artifice was seen through; and Johnson, in very polite language, rejected his lordship's advances, letting him know, that he was unwilling the public should consider him as owing to a patron that which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> had enabled him to do for himself. This great and laborious work its author expected to complete in three years; but he was certainly employed upon it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; for we know that it was begun in 1747, and the last sheet was sent to the press in the end of the year 1754. When we consider the nature of the undertaking, it is indeed astonishing that it was finished so soon, since it was written, as he says, "with little assistance of the learned, and without any patronage of the great; nor in the soft obscurities of retirement, or under the shelter of academic bowers, but amidst inconvenience and distraction, in sickness and in sorrow." The sorrow, to which he here alludes, is probably that which he felt for the loss of his wife, who died on the 11th of March O.S. 1752, the loss of whom he continued to lament as long as he lived. The Dictionary did not occupy his whole time: for while he was pushing it forward, he fitted his tragedy for the stage; wrote the lives of several eminent men for the Gentleman's Magazine; published an Imitation of the 10th Satire of Juvenal, entitled "The Vanity of human Wishes;" and began and finished "The Rambler." This last work is so well-known, that it is hardly necessary to say that it was a periodical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, published twice a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, from the 20th of March 1750 to the 14th of March 1752 inclusive: but to give our readers some notion of the vigour and promptitude of the author's mind, it may not be improper to observe, that notwithstanding the severity of his other labours, all the affluence which he received does not amount to five papers; and that many of the most masterly of those unequalled essays were written on the spur of the occasion, and never seen entire by the author till they returned to him from the press. Soon after the Rambler was concluded, Dr Hawkesworth projected "The Adventurer" upon a similar plan; and by the affluence of friends he was enabled to carry it on with almost equal merit. For a short time, indeed, it was the most popular work of the two; and the papers with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> T, which are confessedly the most splendid in the whole collection, are now known to have been communicated by Johnson, who received for each the sum of two guineas. This was double the price for which he sold sermons to such clergymen as either would not or could not compose their own discourses; and of sermon-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> he seems to have made a kind of trade. Though he had exhausted, during the time that he was employed on the Dictionary, more than the sum for which the bookellers had bargained for the copy; yet by means of the Rambler, Adventurer, sermons, and other productions of his pen, he now found himself in greater affluence than he had ever been before; and as the powers of his mind, distended by long and severe exercise, required relaxation to restore them to their proper tone, he appears to have done little or nothing from the closing of the Adventurer till the year 1756, when he submitted to the office of reviewer in the Literary Magazine. Of his reviews by far the most valuable is that of Soame Jenyns's "Free Inquiry into the Nature and Origin of Evil." Never were wit and metaphysical acuteness more closely united than in that criticism, which exposes the weaknesses and holds up to contempt the reasonings of those vain mortals, who presumptuously attempt to grasp the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of existence, and to form plans of conduct for the Creator of the universe. But the furnishing of magazines, reviews, and even newspapers with literary intelligence, and authors of books with dedications and prefaces, was considered as an employment unworthy of Johnson. It was therefore propounded by the bookellers that he should give a new edition of the dramas of Shakespeare; a work which he had projected many years before, and of which he had published a specimen which was commended by Warburton. When one of his friends expressed a hope that this employment would furnish him with amusement and add to his fame, he replied, "I look upon it as I did upon the Dictionary; it is all work; and my inducement to it is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> or desire of fame, but the want of money, which is the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to writing that I know of." He issued proposals, however, of considerable length; in which he showed that he knew perfectly what a variety of research such an undertaking required: but his indolence prevented him from pursuing it with diligence, and it was not published till many years afterwards. On the 15th of April 1758 he began a new periodical paper entitled "The Idler," which came out every Saturday. (a) From the merit of this work Mr Boswell has endeavoured to detract, by insinuating, that the person called Richard Savage was an impostor, and not the son of the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a> and the countess of Macclesfield. See our account of SAVAGE. Johnson. Saturday in a weekly newspaper, called "the Universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, or Weekly Gazette," published by Newberry. Of these essays, which were continued till the 5th of April 1760, many were written as hastily as an ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>; and one in particular composed at Oxford was begun only half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> before the departure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> which carried it to London. About this time he had the offer of a living, of which he might have rendered himself capable by entering into orders. It was a rectory in a pleasant country, of such yearly value as would have been an object to one in much better circumstances; but sensible, as it is supposed, of the severity of his temper, he declined it, saying, "I have not the requisites for the office, and I cannot in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> shear the flock which I am unable to feed." In the month of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1759 his mother died at the great age of 90; an event which deeply affected him, and gave birth to the first Idler, in which he laments, that "the life which made his own life pleasant was at an end, and that the gate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was shut upon his prospects." Soon afterwards he wrote his "Rasselas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of Abyssinia;" that with the profits he might defray the expense of his mother's funeral, and pay some debts which he had left. He told a friend, that he received for the copy 100l. and 25l. more when it came to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition; that he wrote it in the evenings of one week, sent it to the press in portions as it was written, and had never since read it over. Hitherto, notwithstanding his various publications, he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and obliged to provide by his labour for the wants of the day that was passing over him; but having been early in 1762 represented to the king as a very learned and good man without any certain provision, his majesty was pleased to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> him a pension, which Lord Bute, then first minister, assured him "was not given for anything which he was to do, but for what he had already done." A fixed annuity of three hundred pounds, if it diminished his distress, increased his indolence; for as he constantly avowed that he had no other motive for writing than to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> money, as he had now what was abundantly sufficient for all his purposes, as he delighted in conversation, and was visited and admired by the witty, the elegant, and the learned, very little of his time was past in solitary study. Solitude was indeed his aversion; and that he might avoid it as much as possible, Sir Joshua Reynolds and he, in 1764, instituted a club, which existed long without a name, but was afterwards known by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Literary Club. It consisted of some of the most enlightened men of the age, who met at the Turk's Head in Gerard-street, Soho, one evening in every week at seven, and till a late hour enjoyed "the feast of reason and the flow of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>." In 1765, when Johnson was more than usually oppressed with constitutional melancholy, he was fortunately introduced into the family of Mr Thrale, one of the most eminent brewers in England, and member of parliament for the borough of Southwark: and it is but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to acknowledge, that to the affluence which Mr and Mrs Thrale gave him, to the shelter which their house afforded him for 16 or 17 years, and to the pains which they took to soothe or repel his uneasy fancies, the public is probably indebted for some of the most masterly as well as most popular works which he ever produced. At length, in the October of this year, he gave to the world his edition of Shakespeare, which is chiefly valuable for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, where the excellencies and defects of that immortal bard are displayed with such judgement, as must please every man whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is not regulated by the standard of fashion or national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>. In 1767 he was honoured by a private conversation with the king in the library at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s house; and two years afterwards, upon the establishment of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, &c. he was nominated professor of ancient literature; an office merely honorary, and conferred on him, as is supposed, at the recommendation of his friend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. In the variety of subjects on which he had hitherto exercised his pen, he had forborne, since the administration of Sir Robert Walpole, to meddle with the disputes of contending factions; but having seen with indignation the methods which, in the business of Mr Wilkes, were taken to work upon the populace, he published in 1770 a pamphlet, entitled "The False Alarm;" in which he alerts, and labours to prove by a variety of arguments founded on precedents, that the expulsion of a member of the house of commons is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a>, and that no such calamity as the subversion of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was to be feared from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> warranted by usage, which is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of parliament. Whatever may be thought of the principles maintained in this publication, it unquestionably contains much wit and much argument, expressed in the author's best style of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>; and yet it is known to have been written between eight o'clock on Wednesday night and twelve o'clock on the Thursday night, when it was read to Mr Thrale upon his coming from the house of commons. In 1771 he published another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> pamphlet, entitled, "Thoughts on the late transactions respecting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALKLAND">Falkland</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>;" in which he attacked Junius; and he ever afterwards delighted himself with the thought of having destroyed that able writer, whom he certainly surpassed in nervous language and pointed ridicule. In 1773 he visited with Mr Botwell some of the most considerable of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> or Western Islands of Scotland, and published an account of his journey in a volume which abounds in extensive philosophical views of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, ingenious sentiments, and lively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, but which offended many persons by the violent attack which it made on the authenticity of the poems attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>. For the degree of offence that was taken, the book can hardly be thought to contain a sufficient reason: if the antiquity of these poems be yet doubted, it is owing more to the conduct of their editor than to the violence of Johnson. In 1774, the parliament being dissolved, he addressed to the electors of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> a pamphlet, entitled "The Patriot;" of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> them from imposition, and teach them to distinguish true from false patriotism. In 1775 he published "<a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">Taxation</a> no tyranny;" in answer to the resolutions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of the American <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a>. In this performance his admirer Mr Botwell cannot, he says, perceive that ability of argument or that felicity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> for which on other occasions Johnson was so eminent. This is a singular criticism. To the alluded principle principle upon which the reasoning of the pamphlet rests many have objected, and perhaps their objections are well founded; but if it be admitted that "the supreme power of every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> has the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of requiring from all its subjects such contributions as are necessary to the public safety or public prosperity," it will be found a very difficult task to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the chain of arguments by which it is proved that the British parliament had a right to tax the Americans. As to the expression of the pamphlet, the reader, who adopts the maxim recorded in the "Journal of a tour to the Hebrides," that a controversialist "ought not to strike soft in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>," must acknowledge that it is uncommonly happy, and that the whole performance is one of the most brilliant as well as most correct pieces of composition that ever fell from the pen of its author. These essays drew upon him numerous attacks, all of which he heartily despised; for though it has been supposed that "A letter addressed to Dr Samuel Johnson occasioned by his political publications" gave him great uneasiness, the contrary is manifest, from his having, after the appearance of that letter, collected them into a volume with the title of "Political Tracts by the author of the Rambler." In 1765 Trinity College <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> had created him LL.D., by diploma, and he now received the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> from the university of Oxford; an honour with which, though he did not boast of it, he was highly gratified. In 1777 he was induced, by a call of a very extraordinary nature, to exercise that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> which in him was obedient to every call. Dr William Dodd, a clergyman, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of death for the crime of forgery, found means to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> Johnson in his behalf, and procured from him two of the most energetic compositions of that kind ever seen; the one a petition from himself to the king, the other a like address from his wife to the queen. These petitions failed of success. The principal bookellers in London having determined to publish a body of English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, Johnson was prevailed upon to write the lives of the poets, and give a character of the works of each. This task he undertook with alacrity, and executed it in such a manner as must convince every competent reader, that as a biographer and a critic, no nation can produce his equal. The work was published in ten small volumes, of which the first four came abroad 1778, and the others in 1781. While the world in general was filled with admiration of the stupendous powers of that man, who at the age of seventy-two, and labouring under a complication of diseases, could produce a work which displays so much genius and so much learning, there were narrow circles in which prejudice and resentment were fostered, and whence attacks of different sorts issued against him. These gave him not the smallest disturbance. When told of the feeble, though shrill, outcry that had been raised, he said—"Sir, I considered myself as entrusted with a certain portion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. I have given my opinion sincerely: let them show where they think me wrong." He had hardly begun to reap the laurels gained by this performance, when death deprived him of Mr Thrale, in whose house he had enjoyed the most comfortable hours of his life; but it abated not in Johnson that care for the interests of those whom his friend had left behind him, which he thought himself bound to cherish, both in duty as one of the executors of his will, and from the nobler principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. On this account, his visits to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STREATHAM">Streatham</a>, Mr Thrale's villa, were for some time after his death regularly made on Monday and prolonged till Saturday, as they had been during his life; but they soon became less and less frequent, and he studiously avoided the mention of the place or the family. Mrs Thrale, now Piozzi, says indeed, that "it grew extremely perplexing and difficult to live in the house with him when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of it was no more; because his dislikes grew capricious, and he could scarce bear to have any body come to the house whom it was absolutely necessary for her to see." The person whom she thought it most necessary for her to see may perhaps be guessed at without any superior share of sagacity; and if these were the visits which Johnson could bear, we are so far from thinking his dislikes capricious, though they may have been perplexing, that if he had acted otherwise, we should have blamed him for want of gratitude to the friend whose "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> for fifteen years had never been turned upon him but with respect or benignity." About the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1783 his constitution sustained a feverish shock than it had ever before felt, by a stroke of the palsy; so sudden and so violent, that it awakened him out of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and rendered him for a short time speechless. As usual, his recourse under this affliction was to piety, which in him was constant, sincere, and fervent. He tried to repeat the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> first in English, then in Latin, and afterwards in Greek; but succeeded only in the last attempt; immediately after which he was again deprived of the power of articulation. From this alarming attack he recovered with wonderful quickness, but it left behind it some preludes of an hydropic affection; and he was soon afterwards seized with a spasmodic asthma of such violence that he was confined to the house in great pain, while his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> increased, notwithstanding all the efforts of the most eminent physicians in London and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. He had, however, such an interval of ease as enabled him, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> 1784 to visit his friends at Oxford, Litchfield, and Athbourne in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> being introduced one day as the topic of conversation when he was in the house of Dr Adams, Johnson said, "If you join the Papists externally, they will not interrogate you strictly as to your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in their tenets. No reasoning Papist believes every article of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. There is one side on which a good man might be persuaded to embrace it. A good man of a timorous disposition, in great doubt of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> with God, and pretty credulous, might be glad of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> where there are so many helps to go to heaven. I would be a Papist if I could. I have fear enough; but an obstinate rationality prevents me. I shall never be a Papist unless on the near approach of death, of which I have very great terror." His constant dread of death was indeed so great, that it astonished all who had access to know the piety of his mind and the virtues of his life. Attempts have been made to account for it in various ways; but doubts that is the true account which is given in the Olla Podrida, by an elegant and pious writer, who now adorns a high station in the church of England. "That he should not be conscious of the abilities with which Providence had blessed him was impossible. He felt his own powers; he felt what he was capable of having performed; and he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> how little, comparatively speaking, he had performed. Hence his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> on the near prospect of the account to be made, viewed through the medium of constitutional and morbid melancholy, which often excluded from his sight the bright beams of divine mercy." This, however, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> only while death was approaching from some distance. From the time that he was certain it was near, all his fears were calmed; and he died on the 13th of December 1784, full of resignation, strengthened by faith, and joyful in hope. For a just character of this great man our limits afford not room: we must therefore content ourselves with laying before our readers a very short sketch. His stature was tall, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> were large, his strength was more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> in early life had been greater than such a form gave reason to expect: but he was subject to an infirmity of the convulsive kind, resembling the distemper called St Vitus's dance; and he had the seeds of many diseases found in his constitution, that a short time before his death he declared that he hardly remembered to have passed one day wholly free from pain. He possessed very extraordinary powers of understanding; which were much cultivated by reading, and still more by meditation and reflection. His <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was remarkably retentive, his imagination uncommonly vigorous, and his judgment keen and penetrating. He read with great rapidity, retained with wonderful exactness what he so easily collected, and possessed the power of reducing to order and system the scattered hints on any subject which he had gathered from different books. It would not perhaps be safe to claim for him the highest place, among his contemporaries, in any single department of literature; but, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> one of his own expressions, he brought more mind to every subject, and had a greater variety of knowledge ready for all occasions, than any other man that could be easily named.—Though prone to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, he was in all other respects to remarkably incredulous, that Hogarth said while Johnston firmly believed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, he seemed determined to believe nothing but the Bible. Of the importance of religion he had a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and his zeal for its interests were always awake, so that profaneness of every kind was abashed in his presence.—The same energy which was displayed in his literary productions, was exhibited also in his conversation, which was various, striking, and instructive: like the sage in Raffelsas, he spoke, and attention watched his lips; he reasoned, and conviction closed his periods: when he pleaded, he could be the greatest sophist that ever contended in the lists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a>; and perhaps no man ever equalled him in nervous and pointed repartees. His veracity, from the most trivial to the most solemn occasions, was strict even to severity: he scorned to embellish a story with fictitious circumstances; for what is not a representation of reality, he used to say, is not worthy of our attention. As his purse and his house were ever open to the indigent, so was his heart tender to those who wanted relief, and his soul was susceptible of gratitude and every kind <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>. He had a roughness in his manner which subdued the fancy and terrified the meek: but it was only in his manner; for no man was more loved than Johnston by those who knew him; and his works will be read with veneration for their author as long as the language in which they are written shall be understood.

HYPOGLOSSI EXTERNI

Pages 25-25
or MAJORIS, in Anatomy, the ninth pair of nerves, called also linguales and gustatorii. See Anatomy. HYPOGLOTTIS or HYPOGLOSSIS, (composed of ἴνο under, and γλῶττα tongue), in Anatomy, is a name given to two glands of the tongue. There are four large glands of the tongue; two of them called hypoglottides, situated under it, near the venae ranulares: one on each side of the tongue. They serve to secrete a kind of feros matter of the nature of saliva, which is discharged into the mouth by little ducts near the gums.

HYPOGLOTTIS

Pages 25-25
or Hypoglossis, in Medicine, denotes an inflammation or ulceration under the tongue; called also ranula.

HYPOPYON

Pages 25-25

in Medicine, a collection of purulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> under the corner of the eye.

HYPOSCENIUM

Pages 25-25

in antiquity, a partition under the pulpit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> logeum of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, appointed for the music.

HYPOSTASIS

Pages 25-25

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, literally signifying substance, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subsistence; used in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> for person.—The word is Greek, ὑποστάσις; compounded of ὑπό under, and σώζω, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a>, exist; "I stand, I exist," q. d. sub sistentia. Thus we hold, that there is but one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or essence in God, but three hypostases or persons. The term hypostasis is of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> standing in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. St Cyril repeats it several times, as also the phrase union according to hypostasis. The first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it occurs is in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from that father to Nectarius, where he uses it instead of προσώπου, the word we <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> render person, which did not seem expressive enough. "The philosophers (says St Cyril) have allowed three hypostases: They have extended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a> to three hypostases: They have even sometimes used the word trinity: And nothing was wanting but to have admitted the consubstantiality of the three hypostases, to show the unity of the divine nature, exclusive of all triplicity in respect of distinction of nature, and not to hold it necessary to conceive any respective inferiority of hypostases." This term occasioned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> differences in the ancient church; first among the Greeks, and afterwards also among the Latins. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, hypostasis was defined to denote the same with essence or substance; so that it was hereby to say that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was of a different hypostasis from the Father; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> altered its meaning. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> they were under of expressing themselves strongly against the Sabellians, the Greeks made choice of the word hypostasis, and the Latins of persona; which change proved the occasion of endless disagreement. The phrase τρεῖς ἐνώπιον, used by the Greeks, scandalized the Latins, whose usual way of rendering ὑποστάσις in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> was by ἀποδιάνυσις. The barrenness of the Latin tongue in theological phrases, allowed them but one word for the two Greek ones, ἐνώπιον and ὑποστάσις; and thus disabled them from distinguishing essence from hypostasis. For which reason they chose rather to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the term τρεῖς περιστάσεις, and τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις.—An end was put to logomachias, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> held at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> about the year 362, at which St Athanasius assented; from which time the Latins made no great scruple of saying τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις, nor the Greeks of three persons.

HYPOTHECA

Pages 25-25

in the Civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, an obligation, whereby the effects of a debtor are made over to his creditor, to secure his debt. The word comes from the Greek ὑπόθεκα, a thing subject to some obligation; of the verb ὑποθέκω, suppose, "I am rejected;" of ὑπό under, and ἔχω pono, "I put." As the hypotheca is an engagement procured on purpose for the security of the creditor, various means have been made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to secure to him the benefit of the convention. The use of the pawn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pledge is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, which is almost the same thing with the hypotheca; all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> consisting in this, that the pledge is put into the creditor's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; whereas, in a simple hypotheca, the thing remained in the possession of the debtor. It was found more easy and commodious to engage an estate by a civil covenant than by an actual delivery: accordingly the expedient was first practised among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and from them the Romans borrowed both the name and the thing; only the Greeks, the better to prevent frauds, used to fix some visible mark on the thing, that the public might know it was hypothecate or mortgaged by the proprietor; but the Romans, looking on such advertisements as injurious to the debtor, forbade the use of them. The Roman lawyers distinguished four kinds of hypothecas: the conventional, which was with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> and consent of both parties; the legal, which was appointed by law, and for that reason called tacit; the praetor's pledge, when by the flight or non-appearing of the debtor, the creditor was put in possession of his effects; and the judiciary, when the creditor was put in possession by virtue of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The conventional hypotheca is subdivided into general and special. The hypotheca is general, when all the debtor's effects, both present and future, are engaged to the creditor. It is special, when limited to one or more particular things. For the tacit hypotheca, the civilians reckon no less than twenty-five different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> thereof.

HYPOTHENUSE

Pages 25-25

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, the longest side of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-angled triangle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which subtends the right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>.

HYPOTHESIS

Pages 25-26

in Physics, &c., denotes a kind of system laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from our own imagination, whereby to account for some phenomenon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Thus we have hypotheses to account for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, for gravity, for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a>, for the deluge, &c. The real and scientific causes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> things generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> very deep; observation and experiment, the proper means of arriving at them, are in most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> extremely slow, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind is very impatient; hence we are frequently driven to feign or invent something that may seem like the cause, and which is calculated to answer the several phenomena, so that it may possibly be the true cause. Philosophers are divided as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of such fictions or hypotheses, which are much less current now than they were formerly. The latest and best writers are for excluding hypotheses, and standing wholly on observation and experiment. Whatever is not deduced from phenomena, says Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, is an hypothesis; and hypotheses, whether metaphysical, or physical, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>, or of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> qualities, have no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. The Cartesians take upon them to suppose what affections in the primary particles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> they please; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> what figures, what magnitudes, what motions, and what situations, they find for their purpose. They also feign certain unseen, unknown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and endue them with the most arbitrary properties; give them a subtilty which enables them to pervade the pores of all bodies, and make them agitated with the most unaccountable motions. But is not this to set aside the real <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of things, and to substitute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> in their place? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a> is scarce attainable even by the surest observations; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fanciful conjectures ever come at it? They who found their speculations on hypotheses, even though they argue from them regularly, according to the strictest laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, may be said to compose an elegant and artful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>; but it is still only a fable. HYPOTHESIS is more particularly applied in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> to the several systems of the heavens; or the different ways in which different astronomers have supposed the heavenly bodies to be ranged, moved, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> hypotheses are the Ptolemaic, Copernican, and Tychoonic. The Copernican is now become so current, and is so well warranted by observation, that the retainers thereto hold it injurious to call it an hypothesis. See ASTRONOMY. HYPOTIPOSIS. See ORATORY, No. 91.

HYPOTRACHELION

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is used for a little frieze in the Tuscan and Doric <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, between the astragal and annulets; called also the colerin and gorgerin. The word is applied by four authors in a more general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, to the neck of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its capital below the astragal.

HYPOXIS

Pages 26-26

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 10th order Coronarie. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

HYPSISTARI

Pages 26-26

(formed from ὑψίς "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>"), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the fourth century; thus called from the profession they made of worshipping the most high God. The doctrine of the Hypsistarians was an assemblage of Paganism, Judaism, and Christianity. They adored the most high God with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; but they also revered fire and lamps with the heathens; and observed the Sabbath, and the distinction of clean and unclean things with the Jews. The Hypsistari bore a near resemblance to the Euchites, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>.

HYRCANIA

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Lydia, in the campus Hyrcanus, near Thyatira; so called from colonists brought from Hyrcania, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> lying to the south of the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The people called Hyrcani Macedones, because a mixed people (Pliny).—Another Hyrcania, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the country called Hyrcania. Thought to be the Tape of Strabo, the Syrinx of Polybius, the Zeudracarta of Arrian, and the Alasac of Isidorus Characenus.—A third, a strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Judea, built by Hyrcanus. HYSSOP. See HYSSOPUS. Hedge-Hyssop. See GRATIOLA.

HYSSOPUS

Pages 26-26

hyssop, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">MATERIA MEDICA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

HYSTERIC AFFECTION

Pages 26-26
or Passion, (formed of ἡρπα "womb"); a disease in women, called also suffocation of the womb, and vulgarly fits of the mother. It is a spasmodico-convulsive affection of the nervous system, proceeding from the womb; for the symptoms and cure of which, see MEDICINE.

HYSTERON PROTERON

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the hyperbaton, wherein the proper order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> is so <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> which should naturally come first is placed last: as in this of Terence, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALET">Valet</a> et vivit, for vivit et valet; and in the following of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Moriatur, in media arma ruamus, for In media arma ruamus, Moriatur.

HYSTRIX

Pages 26-27
or Porcupine, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of glires. See MAMMALIA Index. I, or i, the ninth letter and third vowel of the alphabet, is pronounced by throwing the breath suddenly against the palate, as it comes out of the larynx, with a small hollowing of the tongue, and nearly the same opening of the lips as in pronouncing a or e. Its sound varies: in some words it is long, as high, mind, &c.; in others short, as bid, hid, sin, &c.; in others, again, it is pronounced like y, as in collier, onion, &c.; and in a few, it finds like ee, as in machine, magasina, &c. No English word ends in i, e being either added to it, or else the i turned into y. But besides the vowel, there is the jod consonant; which, because of its different pronunciation, has likewise a different form, thus J, j. In English, it has the soft sound of g; nor is used, but when g is required before vowels, where g is usually hard: thus we say, jack, jet, join, &c. instead of gack, get, goin, &c., which would be contrary to the genius of the English language. I, used as a numeral, signifies one, and stands for so many units as it is repeated times; thus I, one; II, two; III, three, &c.; and when put before a higher numeral, it subtracts itself, as IV, four, IX, nine, &c. But, when put after it, so many are added to the higher numeral as there are I's added: thus VI is 5+1, or six; VII, 5+2, or seven; VIII, 5+3, or eight. The ancient Romans likewise used IO for 500, CIO for 1000, CCIO for 5000, CCCIO for 10,000. Farther than this, as Pliny observes, they did not go in their notation; but, when necessary repeated the last number, as CCCICOO, CCCICOO, for 200,000; CCCICOO, CCCICOO, CCCICOO, for 300,000; and so on. The ancients sometimes changed i into u; decimus for decimius; maximus for maximus, &c. According to Plato, the vowel i is proper to express delicate but humble things, as in this verse in Virgil which abounds in i's, and is generally admired: Accipiant inimicum imbreem, rimisque satiarent. I, used as an abbreviation, is often substituted for the whole word Jesus, of which it is the first letter.

IAMBIC

Pages 33-33

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, so called from its consisting either wholly, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IAMBUS">iambus</a>'s. See IAMBUS. Ruddiman makes two kinds of iambic, viz. dimeter and trimeter; the former containing four feet, and the latter six. And as to the variety of their feet, they consist wholly of iambus's, as in the two following verses of Horace: Dimeter. \[ \text{Dim. Iam.} \] Trimeter. \[ \text{<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">Trim</a>. Suis} \] Or, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DACTYLUS">dactylus</a>, spondeus, anapaetus, and sometimes tribrachys, obtain in the odd places; and the tribrachys also in the even places, excepting the last.—Examples of all which may be seen in Horace; as, Dimeter. \[ \text{Canida trahavit dapes} \] Trimeter. \[ \text{Quo quid fecit, si ruat, lacu cur dexterae?} \]

IAMBUS

Pages 33-33

in the Greek and Latin prosody, a poetical foot, consisting of a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> followed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> one; as in \[ \text{Syllaba longa brevi subiecta vocatur iambus, as Horace expresses it;} \] who also calls the iambus a swift, rapid foot, pes citus. The word, according to some, took its rise from Iambus, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECHO">Echo</a>, who invented this foot; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, perhaps, who only used sharp biting expressions to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, when afflicted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Proserpine. Others rather derive it from the Greek ἰάμβος, νενευμένος "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>;" or from ἰάμβος maledictus, "i rail, or revile;" because the verses composed of iambus's were at first only used in satire.

ICE-HOUSE

Pages 59-60

a repository for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months. The aspect of ice-houses should be towards the east <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> south-east, for the advantage of the morning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to expel the damp <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as that is more pernicious than warmth; for which reason trees in the vicinity of an ice-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> tend to its disadvantage. The best <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> for an ice-house to be made in is chalk, as it conveys away the waste <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> without any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> drain; next to that, loose flinty <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or gravelly soil. Its situation should be on the side of a hill, for the advantage of entering the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, Plate CCLXXXVIII. To construct an ice-house, first choose a proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at a convenient distance from the dwelling-house or houses it is to serve; dig a cavity (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> for one family, of the dimensions specified in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>) of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> cone, sinking the bottom concave, to form a reservoir for the waste water till it can drain off; if the soil requires it, cut a drain to a considerable distance, or so far as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> come out at the side of the hill, or into a well, to make it communicate with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, and in that drain form a flink or air-trap, marked l, by sinking the drain so much lower in that place as it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and bring a partition from the top an inch or more into the water, which will consequently be in the trap; and will keep the well air-tight. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">Work</a> up a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of brick piers to receive a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>-wheel, to be laid with its convex side upwards to receive the ice; lay hurdles and straw upon the wheel, which will let the melted ice drain through, and serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. The sides and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> of the cone are to be <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches thick—the sides to be done in screened brickwork, i.e., without <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and wrought at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the work: the filling in behind should be with gravel, loose <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, or brick-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATS">bats</a>, that the water which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> through the sides may the more easily escape into the well. The doors of the ice-house should be made as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as possible, and bundles of straw placed always before the inner door to keep out the air. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of the parts referred to by the letters.— a The line first dug out. b The brick circumference of the cell. c The diminution of the cell downwards. d The lesser diameter of the cell. e The cart-wheel or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOISTS">joists</a> and hurdles. f The piers to receive the wheel or floor. g The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> receptacle for straw. h The inner pallage, i the first entrance, k the outer door, pallages having a separate door each. l An air trap. m The well. n The profile of the piers. o The ice filled in. p The height of the cone. q The dome worked in two half brick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. r The arched pallage. s The door-ways inserted in the walls. t The floor of the pallage. u An aperture through which the ice may be put into the cell; this must be covered next the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the dome, and then filled in with earth. v The sloping door, against which the straw should be laid. The ice when to be put in should be collected during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, broken into small pieces, and rammed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> hard in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of not more than a foot, in order to make it one complete body; the care in putting it in, and well ramming it, tends much to its preservation. In a season when ice is not to be had in sufficient quantities, snow may be substituted. Ice may be preserved in a dry place under ground, by covering it well with chaff, straw, or reeds. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is made of chaff in some places of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to preserve ice: the ice-house for this purpose need only be a deep hole dug in the ground on the side of a hill, from the bottom of which they can easily carry out a drain, to let out the water which is separated at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> from the ice, that it may not melt and spoil the raft. If the ground is tolerably dry, they do not line the sides with anything, but leave them naked, and only make a covering of thatch over the top of the hole: this pit they fill either with pure snow, or else with ice taken from the purest and clearest water; because they do not use it as we do in England, to let the bottles in, but really mix it with the wine. They first cover the bottom of the hole with chaff, and then lay the ice, not letting it anywhere touch the sides, but ramming in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of chaff all the way between: they thus carry on the filling to the top, and then cover the surface with chaff; and in this manner it will keep as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as they please. When they take any of it out for use, they wrap the lump up in chaff, and it may then be carried to any distant place without waste or melting. It appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of Professor Beckman, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Inventions, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> from the earliest ages were acquainted with the method of preserving snow for the purpose of cooling liquors in summer. "This practice," (he observes), is mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>*; and proofs of it are so numerous in *Proverbs, the works of the Greeks and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, that it is unnecessary for me to quote them, especially as they have been collected by others. How the repositories for keeping it were constructed, we are not expressly told; but it is probable that the snow was preserved in pits or trenches. "When Alexander the Great besieged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Petra, he caused 30 trenches to be dug, and filled with snow, which was covered with oak branches; and which kept in that manner for a long time. Plutarch says, that a covering of chaff and coarse cloth is sufficient; and at present a like method is pursued in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. Where the snow has been collected in a deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, some grats or green sods, covered with dung from the sheep ICE sheep pens, is thrown over it; and under these it is so well preserved, that the whole summer through it is sent the distance of 60 Spanish (nearly 180 English) miles to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>. "When the ancients, therefore, wished to have cooling liquors, they either drank the melted snow, or put some of it in their wine; or they placed jars filled with wine in the snow, and suffered it to cool there as long as they thought proper.
