That ice was also preserved for the like purpose, is probable from the testimony of various authors; but it appears not to have been used to much in warm countries as in the northern. Even at present snow is employed in Italy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and Portugal; but in Perfin ice. I have never anywhere found an account of Grecian or Roman ice-houses. By the writers on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> they are not mentioned." Ice-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, a name given by sailors to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ice collected into one huge <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, and floating about upon the seas near or within the Polar circles. —Many of these fluctuating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> are met with on the coasts of Spitzbergen, to the great danger of the shipping employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> fishery. In the midst of those tremendous masses navigators have been arrested and frozen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In this manner the brave Sir Hugh Willoughby perished with all his crew in 1553; and in the year 1773, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Mulgrave, after every effort which the most finished seaman could make to accomplish the end of his voyage, was caught in the ice, and was near experiencing the same unhappy fate. See the account at large in Phipps's Voyage to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Pole. As there described, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, divested of the horror from the eventful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of change, was the most beautiful and picturesque.—Two large ships becalmed in a vast basin, surrounded on all sides by islands of various forms: the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> clear: the sun gliding the circumambient ice, which was low, smooth, and even; covered with snow, excepting where the pools of water on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the surface appeared crystaline with the young ice: the small space of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> they were confined in perfectly smooth. After fruitless attempts to force a way through the fields of ice, their limits were perpetually contracted by its closing; till at length it belet each vessel till they became immovably fixed. The smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of surface was soon lost: the pressure of the pieces of ice, by the violence of the swell, caused them to pack: fragment rose upon fragment, till they were in many places higher than the main-yard. The movements of the ships were tremendous and involuntary, in conjunction with the surrounding ice, actuated by the currents. The water shoaled to 14 fathoms. The grounding of the ice or of the ships would have been equally fatal: The force of the ice might have crushed them to atoms, or have lifted them out of the water and overflown them, or have left them suspended on the summits of the pieces of ice at a tremendous height, exposed to the fury of the winds; or to the risk of being dashed to pieces by the failure of their frozen deck. An attempt was made to cut a passage through the ice; after a perseverance worthy of Britons, it proved fruitless. The commander, at all times <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of himself, directed the boats to be made ready to be hauled over the ice, till they arrived at navigable water (a task alone of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days), and in them to make their voyage to England. The boats were drawn progressively three whole days. At length a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> sprung up, the ice separated sufficiently to yield to the pressure of the full-laded ships, which, after labouring against the resisting fields of ice, arrived on the 10th of August in the harbour of Smeeringberg, at the west end of Spitzbergen, between it and Hackluyt's Headland. The forms assumed by the ice in this chilling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> are extremely pleasing to even the most incurious eye. The surface of that which is congealed from the sea water (for we must allow it two origins) is flat and even, hard, opake, resembling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and incapable of being slid on, like the British ice. The greater pieces, or fields, are many leagues in length: the lesser are the meadows of the seas, on which these animals at times frolic by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the lesser pieces is as rapid as the currents: the greater, which are sometimes 200 leagues long, and 60 or 80 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, move slow and majestically; often fix for a time, immoveable by the power of the ocean, and then produce near the horizon that bright white appearance called the blink. The approximation of two great fields produces a most singular phenomenon: it forces the lesser (if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> can be applied to pieces of several acres <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>) out of the water, and adds them to their surface; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and often a third succeeds; so that the whole forms an aggregate of a tremendous height. These float in the sea like so many rugged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and are sometimes 500 or 600 yards thick; but the far greater part is concealed beneath the water. These are continually increased in height by the freezing of the spray of the sea, or of the melting of the snow, which falls on them. Those which remain in this frozen climate receive continual growth; others are gradually wafted by the northern winds into southern latitudes, and melt by degrees, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the sun, till they waft away, or disappear in the boundless element. The collision of the great fields of ice, in high latitudes, is often attended with a noise that for a time takes away the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of hearing anything else; and the lesser with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> of unpealable horror. The water which dashes against the mountainous ice freezes into an infinite variety of forms; and gives the voyager ideal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, streets, churches, steeples, and every shape which imagination can frame. ICE-PLANT. See MESEMBRYANTHEMUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

ICEBERGS

Pages 60-63

are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bodies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> filling the valleys between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in northern latitudes. Among the most remarkable are those of the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Spitzbergen (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">GREENLAND</a>, no. 10.) They are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, but at considerable distances from each other; each fills the valleys for tracts unknown in a region totally inaccessible in the internal parts. The glaciers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> seem contemptible to these; but present often a similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> into some lower valley. The last exhibits over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> a front 300 feet high, emulating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; cataracts of melted snow precipitate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> various parts, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spiring mountains, streaked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, bound the sides, and rise crag above crag, as far as eye can reach in the background. See Plate CCLXXVIII. At times immense fragments <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> off, and tumble into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, with a most alarming dashings. A piece of this vivid green substance has fallen, and grounded in 24 fathoms water, and spired above the surface 50 feet. Simi- Phipps's Voyage, lar. lar icebergs are frequent in all the Arctic regions; and to their lapses is owing the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> mountainous ice which infests those seas.—Frosts sports wonderfully with these icebergs, and gives them majestic as well as other most singular forms. Males have been seen assuming the shape of a Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with arched windows and doors, and all the rich drapery of that style, composed of what an Arabian tale would scarcely dare to relate, of crystal of the richest sapphire blue; tables with one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more feet; and often immense flat-roofed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, like those of Luxor on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, supported by round transparent columns of cerulean hue, float by the astonished spectator. These icebergs are the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of ages, and receive annually additional height by the falling of snows and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, which often instantly freezes, and more than repairs the loss occasioned by the influence of the melting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>.

ICELAND

Pages 63-69

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> lying in the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, between 63 and 68 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between 10 and 26 degrees of west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; its greatest length being about 700 miles, and its breadth 390. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> lying partly within the frigid zone, and being liable to be surrounded with vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> which come from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLAR_SEAS">polar seas</a>, is, on account of the coldness of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, very inhospitable; but much so for other reasons. It is exceedingly subject to earthquakes; and so full of volcanoes, that the little part of it which appears fit for the habitation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> seems almost totally laid waste by them. The best account that hath yet appeared of the island of Iceland is in a late publication, intitled "Letters on Iceland, &c. written by Uno Von Troil, D.D. first chaplain to his Swedish majesty." This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> sailed from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1772, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with Mr Banks, Dr Solander, and Dr James Lind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, in a ship for which 100l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> was paid every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. After visiting the Western isles of Scotland, they arrived on the 28th of August at Iceland; where they call <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> at Bessafelladr <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bessafelladr, lying in about 64° 6' N. Lat. in the western part of the island. The country had to them the most dismal appearance that can be conceived. "Imagine to yourself (says Dr Troil) a country, which from one end to the other presents to your view only barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, whose summits are covered with eternal snow, and between them fields divided by vitrified cliffs, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and sharp <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> seem to vie with each other to deprive you of the sight of a little grass which scantily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> up among them. These same dreary rocks likewise conceal the few scattered habitations of the natives, and nowhere a single tree appears which might afford shelter to friendship and innocence. The prospect before us, though not pleasing, was uncommon and surprising. Whatever presented itself to our view bore the marks of devastation; and our eyes, accustomed to behold the pleasing coasts of England, now <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> nothing but the vestiges of the operation of a fire, Heaven knows how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>!" The climate of Iceland, however, is not unwholesome, or naturally subject to excessive colds, notwithstanding its northerly situation. There have been instances indeed of Fahrenheit's thermometer sinking to 24° below the freezing point in winter, and rising to 102° in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Since the year 1749, observations have been made on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and the result of these observations hath been unfavourable, as the coldness of the climate is thought to be on the increase, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> the country is in danger of becoming unfit for the habitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Wood, which formerly grew in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities all over the island, cannot now be raised. Even the hardy firs of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> cannot be reared in this island. They seemed indeed to thrive till they were about two feet high; but then their tops withered, and they ceased to grow. This is owing chiefly to the storms and hurricanes which frequently happen in the months of May and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and which are very unfavourable to vegetation of every kind. In 1772, Governor Thodal sowed a little barley, which grew very briskly; but a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before it was to be reaped, a violent storm so effectually destroyed it, that only a few grains were found scattered about. Besides these violent winds, this island lies under another disadvantage, owing to the floating ice already mentioned, with which the coasts are often beset. This ice comes on by degrees, always with an easterly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and frequently in such quantities as to fill up all the gulfs on the north-west side of the island, and even covers the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> as far as the eye can reach; it also sometimes drives to other shores. It generally comes in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, and goes away in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. Sometimes it only reaches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> in April; and, remaining there for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time, does an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of mischief. It consists partly of mountains of ice, said to be sometimes 60 fathoms in height; and partly of field ice, which is neither so thick nor so much dreaded. Sometimes these enormous masses are grounded in shoal-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and in these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> they remain for many months, nay years, undisturbed, chilling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> for a great way round. When many such bulky and lofty ice-masses are floating together, the wood which is often found drifting between them, is so much chafed, and pressed with such violence together, that it sometimes takes fire; which circumstance has occasioned fabulous accounts of the ice being in flames. In 1753 and 1754, this ice occasioned such a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, that horses and sheep dropped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> dead by reason of it, as well as for want of food; horses were observed to feed upon dead cattle, and the sheep ate off each other's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. In 1755, towards the end of the month of May, the waters were frozen over in one night to the thickness of an inch and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. In 1756, on the 26th of June, snow fell to the depth of a yard, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> falling through the months of July and August. In the year following it froze very hard towards the end of May and beginning of June, in the south part of the island, which occasioned a great scarcity of grass. These frosts are generally followed by a famine, many examples of which are to be found in the Icelandic chronicles. Besides these calamities, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bears annually arrive with the ice, which commit great ravages among the sheep. The Icelanders attempt to destroy these intruders as soon as they get sight of them. Sometimes they assemble together, and drive them back to the ice, with which they often float off again. For want of firearms, they are obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> spears on these occasions. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> also encourages the destruction of these animals, Iceland. by paying a premium of 10 dollars for every bear that is killed, and purchasing the skin of him who killed it. Notwithstanding this dismal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, however, taken from Von Troil's letters, some tracts of ground, in high cultivation, are mentioned as being covered by the great eruption of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> in 1783. It is possible, therefore, that the above may have been somewhat exaggerated. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> are seldom heard in Iceland, except in the neighbourhood of volcanoes. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> Borealis is very frequent and strong. It most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> appears in dry weather; though there are not wanting instances of its being seen before or after <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, or even during the time of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> halo, which prognosticates bad weather, is likewise very frequent here; as are also parhelions, which appear from one to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in number at a time. These parhelions are observed chiefly at the approach of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> ice, which an intense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a> has produced, and the frozen vapours fill the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIRE_BALLS">Fire-balls</a>, sometimes round and sometimes oval, are observed, and a kind of ignis fatuus which attaches itself to men and beasts; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a> are also frequently mentioned in their chronicles. This last circumstance deserves the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of astronomers. Iceland, besides all the inconveniences already mentioned, has two very terrible ones, called by the natives ferida and finafloki: the name of the first imports large pieces of a mountain tumbling down and destroying the lands and houses which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> at the foot of it: this happened in 1554, when a whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> was ruined, and thirteen people buried alive. The other word signifies the effects of a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of snow, which covers the top of the mountains, rolling down in immense masses, and doing a great deal of damage: of this there was an instance in 1669, during the night, when two farms were buried, with all their inhabitants and cattle. This last accident Iceland has in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with all very mountainous countries, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. "Iceland abounds with hot and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> springs, some of which spout up into the air to a surprising height. All the jets d'eau which have been contrived with so much art, and at such an enormous expense, cannot by any means be compared with these wonders of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in Iceland. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER_WORKS">water-works</a> at Herrenhausen throw up a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of water of half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a yard in circumference to a height of about 70 feet; those at the Winterkette at Cassel throw it up, but in a much thinner column, 130 feet; and the jet d'eau at St Cloud, which is thought the greatest of all the French water-works, casts up a thin column 80 feet into the air; but some springs in Iceland pour forth columns of water several feet in thickness to the height of many fathoms; and many affirm of several hundred feet. "These springs are unequal in their degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; but we have observed none under 188 degrees of Fahrenheit's thermometer; in some it is 192, 193, 212, and in one small vein of water 213 degrees. From some the water flows gently, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is then called laug, "a bath;" from others it spouts with a great noise, and is then called Huer, or kitter. It is very common for some of these spouting springs to Iceland. cole up, and others to appear in their stead. All Iceland. these hot waters have an incrusting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, so that we very commonly find the exterior surface from whence it bursts forth covered with a kind of rind, which almost resembles chafed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and which we at first took for lime, but which was afterwards found by Mr Bergman to be of a filaceous or flinty nature. In some places the water tastes of sulphur, in others not; but when drank as soon as it is cold, tastes like common boiled water. The inhabitants use it at particular times for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>; and were they to adopt proper regulations, it might be of still greater use. Victuals may also be boiled in it, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> held over its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> becomes sweet; owing, most probably, to the excessive heat of the water, as the same effect is produced by boiling it a long time over the fire. They have begun to make <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> by boiling sea water over it, which when it is refined, is very pure and good. The cows which drink this hot water yield a great deal of milk. Egbert Olafsen relates, that the water does not become turbid when alkali is thrown into it, nor does it change the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of syrup of violets. Horrebow affirms, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you fill a bottle at one of the spouting springs, the water <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> boil over two or three times while the spring throws forth its water; and if corked too soon, the bottle will burst. "Among the many hot springs to be met with in Iceland, several bear the name of geyser: the following is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the most remarkable of that name, named from Hecla, near a farm called Haukadul. Here a poet would have an opportunity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> whatever nature has of beautiful and terrible, united in one picture, by delineating this surprising phenomenon. Refuse to yourself a large field, where you see on one side, at a great distance, high mountains covered with ice, whose summits are generally wrapped in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, so that their sharp and unequal points become invisible. This loss, however, is compensated by a certain wind, which causes the clouds to sink, and cover the mountain itself, when its summit appears as it were to rest on the clouds. On the other side Hecla is seen, with its three points covered with ice, rising above the clouds, and, with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> which ascends from it, forming other clouds at some distance from the real ones: and on another side is a ridge of high rocks, at the foot of which boiling water from time to time issues forth; and further on extends a marsh of about three English miles in circumference, where are 40 or 50 boiling springs, from which a vapour ascends to a prodigious height.—In the midst of these is the greatest spring geyser, which deserves a more exact and particular account. In travelling to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, about an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from the river, from which the ridge of rocks still divided us, we hear a loud roaring noise, like the rushing of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> precipitating itself from stupendous rocks. We asked our guide what it meant; he answered, it was geyser roaring; and we soon saw with our naked eyes what before seemed almost incredible. "The depth of the opening or pipe from which the water gushes cannot well be determined; for sometimes the water sunk down several fathoms, and some seconds passed before a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> which was thrown into the aperture reached the surface of the water. The opening itself was perfectly round, and 19 feet in diameter, meter, and terminated in a basin 59 feet in diameter. Both the pipe and the basin were covered with a rough halastic rind, which had been formed by the force of the water; the outermost border of the basin is nine feet and an inch higher than the pipe itself. The water here spouted several times a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, but always by fits, and after certain intervals. The people who lived in the neighbourhood told us, that they rose higher in cold and bad weather than at other times; and Egbert Olafsen and several others affirm, that it has spouted to the height of 60 fathoms. Most probably they guessed only by the eye, and on that account their calculation may be a little extravagant; and indeed it is to be doubted whether the water was ever thrown up so high, though probably it sometimes mounts higher than when we observed it. The method we took to observe the height was as follows. Every one in company wrote down, at each time that the water spouted, how high it appeared to him to be thrown, and we afterwards chose the medium. The first column marks the spoutings of the water, in the order in which they followed one another; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the time when these effusions happened; the third, the height to which the water rose; and the last, how long each spouting of water contained. | No | Time | Height | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">Duration</a> | |----|--------|--------|----------| | 1 | At VI 42 m. | 30 feet | 0 20 seconds | | 2 | 51 | 6 | 0 20 | | 3 | VII 16 | 6 | 0 10 | | 4 | 31 | 12 | 0 15 | | 5 | 51 | 60 | 0 6 | | 6 | VIII 17 | 24 | 0 30 | | 7 | 29 | 18 | 0 40 | | 8 | 36 | 12 | 0 40 | The pipe was now for the first time full of water, which ran slowly into the basin. | No | Time | Height | Duration | |----|--------|--------|----------| | 9 | IX 25 | 48 | 1 10 | | 10 | X 16 | 24 | 1 00 | "At 35 minutes after twelve we heard, as it were, three discharges of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> under ground, which made it shake: the water flowed over immediately, but instantly sunk again. At eight minutes after two, the water flowed over the border of the basin. At 15 minutes after three, we again heard several subterranean noises, though not so strong as before. At 43 minutes after four, the water flowed over very strongly during the space of a minute. In five minutes after, we heard many loud subterranean discharges, not only near the spring, but also from the neighbouring ridge of rocks, where the water spouted. At 51 minutes after six, the fountain spouted up to the height of 92 feet, and continued to do so for four minutes. After this great effort, it sunk down very low into the pipe, and was entirely quiet during several minutes; but soon began to bubble again: it was not, however, thrown up into the air, but only to the top of the pipe. "The force of the vapours which throw up these waters is excessive: it not only prevents the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> which are thrown into the opening from sinking, but even throws them up to a very great height, together with the water. When the basin was full, we placed ourselves before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in such a manner that we could see our shadows in the water; when every one observed round the shadow of his own head (though not round that of the heads of others), a circle of almost the same colours which compose the rainbow, and round this another bright circle. This most probably proceeded from the vapours exhaling from the water. "Not far from this place, another spring at the foot of the neighbouring ridge of rocks spouted water to the height of one or two yards each time. The opening through which this water issued was not so wide as the other: we imagined it possible to stop up the hole entirely by throwing large stones into it, and even flattered ourselves that our attempts had succeeded: but, to our astonishment, the water gushed forth in a very violent manner. We hastened to the pipe, and found all the stones thrown aside, and the water playing freely through its former channel. In these large springs the waters were hot in the highest degree, and tasted a little of sulphur; but in other respects it was pure and clear. In the smaller springs of the neighbourhood the water was tainted: in some, it was as muddy as that of a clay-pit: in others, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> as milk; and in some few, as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> as blood. "Iceland abounds with pillars of basaltic Account of the lower sort of people imagine have been piled upon the basaltic each other by the giants, who made use of supernatural force to effect it. They have generally from three to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sides; and are from four to six feet in thickness, and from 12 to 16 yards in length, without any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> divisions. But sometimes they are only from six inches to one foot in height, and they are then very regular, inasmuch that they are sometimes made use of for windows and door-panes. In some places they only peep out here and there among the lava, or more frequently among the tufa; in other places they are quite overthrown, and pieces of broken pillars only make their appearance. Sometimes they extend without interruption for two or three miles in length. In one mountain they have a singular appearance: on the top the pillars lie horizontally, in the middle they are sloping; the lowest are perfectly perpendicular; and in some parts they are bent into a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the Iceland basaltic seems to be the same with that of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFA">Staffa</a>; though in some it is more porous, and inclines to a gray. Some we observed which were of a blackish gray, and composed of several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>. Another time we observed a kind of porous glassy stone, consequently a lava, which was so indistinctly divided, that we were for some time at a loss to determine whether it was basaltic or not, though at last we all agreed that it was. "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> ore is found in some parts of the island, and that beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> ore called malachites. Horrebows speaks of native silver. A stratum of sulphur is found near Myvatu from nine inches to two feet in thickness; partly of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour, and partly of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>. Immediately over the sulphur is a blue <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; above that a vitriolic and aluminoous one; and beneath the sulphur a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a>. "At what time the island of Iceland was first peopled <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of is uncertain. An English colony indeed is said to the island have been settled there in the beginning of the fifth century." Iceland. century; but of this there are not sufficient proofs. There is, however, reason to suppose that the English and Irish were acquainted with this country under another name, long before the arrival of the Norwegians; for the celebrated Bede gives a pretty accurate description of the island. But of the original inhabitants we cannot pretend to say anything, as the Iceland chronicles go no farther back than the arrival of the Norwegians. What they relate is to the following purpose. Naddodd, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>, was driven on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Iceland in 861, and named the country Snio-land, "Snow-land," on account of the great quantities of snow with which he perceived the mountains covered. He did not remain there long; but on his return extolled the country to such a degree, that one Gardar Suaforson, an enterprising Swede, was encouraged by his account to go in search of it in 864. He failed quite round the island, and gave it the name of Gardaðholmur, or Gardar's island. Having remained in Iceland during the winter, he returned in the spring to Norway, where he described the newly-discovered island as a pleasant well-wooded country. This excited a desire in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLOKE">Floke</a>, another Swede, reputed the greatest navigator of his time, to undertake a voyage thither. As the compass was then unknown, he took three ravens on board to employ them on the discovery. By the way he visited his friends at Ferro; and having failed farther to the northward, he let fly one of his ravens, which returned to Ferro. Some time after, he dispatched the second, which returned to the ship again, as he could find no land. The last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> proved more successful; the third raven took his flight to Iceland, where the ship arrived a few days after. Floke stayed here the whole winter with his company; and, because he found a great deal of floating ice on the north side, he gave the country the name of Iceland, which it has ever since retained. When they returned to Norway in the following spring, Floke, and those that had been with him, made a very different description of the country. Floke described it as a wretched place; while one of his companions, named Thorulfr, praised it so highly, that he affirmed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> dropped from every plant; which extravagant commendation procured him the name of Thorulfr-sjór, or Butter-Thorulfr. From this time there are no accounts of any voyages to Iceland, till Ingolfur and his friend Leifr undertook one in 874. They spent the winter on the island, and determined to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there for the future. Ingolfur returned to Norway, to provide whatever might be necessary for the comfortable establishment of a colony, and Leifr in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time went to assist in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in England. After an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of four years, they again met in Iceland, the one bringing with him a considerable number of people, with the necessary tools and instruments for making the country habitable; and the other imported his acquired treasures. After this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> many people went there to settle; and, in the space of 60 years, the whole island was inhabited. The tyranny of Harold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Norway contributed not a little to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Iceland; and so great was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> of his subjects, that he was at last obliged to issue an order, that no one should sail from Norway to Iceland without paying four ounces of fine silver to the king. Besides the Norwegians, new colonies arrived from different nations, between whom wars soon commenced; and the Icelandic histories are full of the accounts of their battles. To prevent these conflicts for the future, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> was chosen in 928, upon whom great powers were conferred. This man was the speaker in all their public deliberations; pronounced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> in difficult and intricate cases; decided all disputes; and published new laws, after they had been received and approved of by the people at large; but he had no power to make laws without the approbation and consent of the rest. He therefore assembled the chiefs whenever the circumstances seemed to require it; and after they had deliberated among themselves, he represented the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the majority to the people, whose silent assent was necessary before it could be considered as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. His authority among the chiefs and leaders, however, was inconsiderable, as he was chosen by them and retained his place no longer than while he preserved their confidence. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> did not prove sufficient to restrain the turbulent spirit of the Icelanders. They openly waged war with each other; and, by their intestine conflicts, so weakened all parties, that the whole became at last a prey to a few arbitrary and enterprising men; who, as is too generally the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, wantonly abused their power to the oppression of their countrymen, and the disgrace of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. Notwithstanding these troubles, however, the Icelanders remained free from a foreign yoke till 1261; when the greatest part of them put themselves under the protection of Hakon, king of Norway, promising to pay him tribute upon certain conditions agreed on between them; and the rest followed their example in 1264. Afterwards, Iceland, together with Norway, became subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. For a long time the care of the island was committed to a governor, who commonly went there once a year; though, according to his instructions, he ought to have resided in Iceland. As the country suffered incredibly through the absence of its governors, it was resolved a few years ago that they should reside there, and have their seat at Belfeldið, one of the old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> domains. He has under him a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, two laymen, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, and 21 fylkemenn, or magistrates who superintend small districts; and almost everything is decided according to the laws of Denmark. At the first settlement of the Norwegians in Iceland, they lived in the same manner as they had done in their own country, namely, by war and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>. Their situation with regard to the kings of Norway, however, soon obliged them to apply to other states, in order to learn as much of the knowledge of government and politics as was necessary to preserve their colony from subjugation to a foreign yoke. For this purpose they often sailed to Norway, Denmark, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, England, and Scotland. The travellers, at their return, were obliged to give an account to their chiefs of the state of those kingdoms through which they passed. For this reason, history, and what related to science, was held in high repute as long as the republican form of government lasted; and the great number of histories to be met with in the country, show at least the desire of the Icelanders to be instructed. To secure themselves, therefore, against their powerful neighbours, they were obliged to enlarge their historical knowledge. They likewise took great pains in studying perfectly their own laws, for the maintenance and protection of their internal security. Thus Iceland, at a time when <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and obduracy overwhelmed the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, was enabled to produce a considerable number of poets and historians. When the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> was introduced, about the end of the 10th century, more were found conversant in the law than could have been expected, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the country, and the number of its inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a> was followed among them; but they devoted their attention considerably more to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, which has since entirely ceased. Two things have principally contributed towards producing a great change both in their character and way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, viz., the progress of the Christian religion, and their subjection first to Norway, and afterwards to Denmark. For if religion, on one side, commanded them to desist from their ravages and warlike expeditions; the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> power, on the other, deprived them of the necessary forces for the execution of them; and, since this time, we find no farther traces of their heroic deeds, except those which are preserved in their hillories. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Icelanders apply themselves to fishing and breeding of cattle. They are middle-sized and well made, though not very strong; and the women are in general ill-featured. Vices are much less common among them, than in other parts where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> have corrupted the morals of the people. Though their poverty disables them from imitating the hospitality of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> in all respects, yet they continue to show their inclination to it: they cheerfully give away the little they have to spare, and express the utmost joy and satisfaction if you are pleased with their gift. They are uncommonly obliging and faithful, and extremely attached to government. They are very zealous in their religion. An Icelander never passes a river or any other dangerous place, without previously taking off his hat, and imploring the divine protection; and he is always thankful for the protection of the Deity when he has passed the danger in safety. They have an inexplicable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to their native country, and are nowhere so happy. An Icelander therefore rarely settles in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, though ever such advantageous terms should be offered him. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, we cannot ascribe any great indolence or ingenuity to these people. They work on in the way to which they have all along been accustomed, without thinking of improvements. They are not cheerful in conversation, but simple and credulous; and have no aversion against a bottle, if they can find an opportunity. When they meet together, their chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a> consists in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> their history. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> makes the beginning, and the rest continue in their turns when he is tired. Some of them know these stories by heart; others have them in print, and others in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Besides this, they are great players at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESS">chess</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, but only for their amusement, since they never play for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; which, however, seems to have been formerly in use among them; since by one of their old laws, a fine is imposed upon those who play for money. The modern Icelanders have made very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in their dress from what was formerly in use. Their dress is as follows: The men all wear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> shirt next to the skin, with a short jacket, and a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of wide breeches over it. When they travel, another short coat is put over all. The whole is made of coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cloth, called wadmal; but some wear clothes of a white colour. On their head they wear large three-cornered <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, and on the feet Iceland shoes and worsted stockings. Some of them indeed have shoes from Copenhagen; but, as they are rather too dear for them, they generally make their own shoes, sometimes of the hide of oxen, but more frequently of sheep's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. They make them by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> piece of leather, rather wider than the length of the foot; this they sew up at the toes and behind at the heel, and tie it on with leather thongs. These shoes are convenient enough where the country is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>; but it would be very difficult for us who are not accustomed to walk with them amongst the rocks and stones, though the Icelanders do it with great ease. The women are likewise dressed in black wadmal. They wear a bodice over their shifts, which are sewed up at the bottom; and above this a jacket laced before with long narrow sleeves reaching down to the wrists. In the opening on the side of the sleeve, they have buttons of chased silver, with a plate fixed to each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>; on which the lover, when he buys them in order to present them to his mistress, takes care to have his name engraved along with hers. At the top of the jacket a little black collar is fixed, of about three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, of velvet or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and frequently trimmed with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. The petticoat is likewise of wadmal, and reaches down to the ankles. Round the top of it is a girdle of silver or some other metal, to which they fasten the apron, which is also of wadmal, and ornamented at top with buttons of chased silver. Over all this they wear an upper dress nearly resembling that of the Swedish peasants; with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that it is wider at bottom: this is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> at the neck and wrists, and a hand's-breadth shorter than the petticoat. It is adorned with a facing down to the bottom, which looks like cut velvet, and is generally woven by the Icelandic women. On their fingers they wear gold, silver, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> rings. Their head-dress consists of several cloths wrapped round the head almost as high again as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. It is tied fast with a handkerchief, and serves more for warmth than ornament. Girls are not allowed to wear this head-dress till they are marriageable. At their weddings they are adorned in a very particular manner; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> wears, close to the face, round her head-dress, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of silver gilt. She has two chains round her neck, one of which hangs down very low before, and the other rests on her shoulders. Besides these, she wears a lesser chain, from whence generally hangs a little heart, which may be opened to put some kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a> in it. This dress is worn by all the Icelandic women without exception: only with this difference, that the poorer sort have it of coarse wadmal, with ornaments of brass; and those that are in easier circumstances have it of broad cloth, with silver ornaments gilt. The houses of the Icelanders are very indifferent, but the worst are said to be on the south side of the island. In some parts they are built of drift-wood, in others of lava, almost in the same manner as the stone-walls we make for inclosures, with moss stuffed between the pieces of lava. In some parts the walls are wainscotted on the inside. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is covered with sods, laid over rafting, or sometimes over the ribs of whales; the walls are about three yards high, and the entrance somewhat lower. Instead of glass, the windows are made of the chorion and amnios of sheep, or the membranes which surround the womb of the ewe. These are stretched on a hoop, and laid over a hole in the roof. In the poorer sort of houses they employ for the windows the inner membrane of the stomach of animals, which is less transparent than the others. As the island of Iceland produces no kind of grain, the inhabitants of consequence have no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> but what is imported; and which being too dear for common use, is reserved for weddings and other entertainments. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of their viands is taken from Troil's Letters. 1. Flour of fjalgras, (lichen flandicus), or rock-grass. The plant is first washed, and then cut into small pieces by some; though the greater number dry it by fire or in the sun, then put it into a bag in which it is well beaten, and lastly work it into flour by stamping. 2. Flour of komfygr, (polygonum biflorum), is prepared in the same manner, as well as the two other sorts of wild corn melur (arundo arenaria, and arundo foliolum latericium convolutus), by separating it from the chaff, pounding, and lastly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> it. 3. Surt finoer, (four butter). The Icelanders seldom make use of fresh or salt butter, but let it grow four before they eat it. In this manner it may be kept for 20 years, or even longer; and the Icelanders look upon it as more wholesome and palatable than the butter used among other nations. It is reckoned better the older it grows; and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of it then is valued as much as two of fresh butter. 4. String, or whey boiled to the consistence of sour milk, and preserved for the winter. 5. Fish of all kinds, both dried in the sun and in the air, and either salted or frozen. Those prepared in the last manner are preferred by many. 6. Mjölk, or whey boiled to cheese, which is very good. But the art of making other kinds of good cheese is lost, though some tolerably palatable is sold in the east quarter of Iceland. 7. Beina flriug, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and cartilages of beef and mutton, and likewise bones of cod, boiled in whey till they are quite dissolved; they are then left to ferment, and are eaten with milk. 8. Skyr. The curds from which the whey is squeezed are preserved in casks or other vessels; they are sometimes mixed with black crow-berries or juniper-berries, and are likewise eaten with new milk. 9. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYRA">Syra</a>. is four whey kept in casks, and left to ferment; which, however, is not reckoned fit for use till a year old. 10. Blunda, is a liquor made of water, to which a twelfth part of syra is added. In winter, it is mixed with the juice of thyme and of the black crow-berries. 11. They likewise eat many vegetables, some of which grow wild, and some are cultivated; also shell-fish and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a>. The Icelanders in general eat three meals a-day, at seven in the morning, two in the afternoon, and nine at night. In the morning and evening they commonly eat curds mixed with new milk, and sometimes with juniper or crow-berries. In some parts, they also have porridge made of rock-grass, which is very palatable, or curdled milk boiled till it becomes of a red colour, or new milk boiled a long time. At dinner, the food consists of dried fish, with plenty of sour butter; they also sometimes eat fresh fish, and, when possible, a little bread and cheese with them. It is reported by some, that they do not eat any fish till it is quite rotten; this report perhaps proceeds from their being fond of it when a little tainted: they however frequently eat fish which is quite fresh, though, in the same manner as the rest of their food, often without salt. The common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a> is milk, either warm from the cow or cold, and sometimes boiled: they likewise use butter-milk with or without water. On the coasts they generally drink blanda and sour milk; which is sold after it is skimmed at two fifths of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIXDOLLAR">rixdollar</a> per cask: some likewise send for beer from Copenhagen, and some brew their own. A few of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants also have claret and coffee. The common people sometimes drink a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, which they make from the leaves of the dryas octopetala, and the veronica officinalis. On the coasts the men employ themselves in fishing, both summer and winter. On their return home, many, when they have drawn and cleaned their fish, they give them to their wives, whose care it is to dry them. In the winter, when the inclemency of the weather prevents them from fishing, they are obliged to take care of their cattle, and spin wool. In summer, they mow the grass, dig turf, provide <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, go in search of sheep and goats that were gone astray, and kill cattle. They prepare leather with the spiraea ulmaria instead of bark. Some few work in gold and silver; and others are instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, in which they are tolerable proficient. The women prepare the fish, take care of the cattle, manage the milk and wool, sew, spin, and gather eggs and down. When they work in the evening, they use, instead of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>-glass, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> with a wick made of epilobium dipt in train <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which is contrived to burn four, six, or eight hours. Among the common people of Iceland, time is not reckoned by the course of the sun, but by the work they have done, and which is prescribed by law. According to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, a man is to mow as much hay in one day as grows on 30 fathoms of manured <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, or 40 fathoms of land which has not been manured; or he is to dig 700 pieces of turf eight feet long and three broad. If as much snow falls as reaches to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s bellies, a man is required daily to clear a piece of ground sufficient for 100 sheep. A woman is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> together as much hay as three men can mow, or to weave three yards of wadmal a-day. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> of a man are fixed at four dollars and 12 yards of wadmal; and those of a woman at two dollars and five yards of wadmal. When men are sent a-fishing out of the country, there is allowed to each man, by law, from the 25th of September to the 14th of May, six pounds of butter, and 18 pounds of dried fish every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. This may seem to be too great an allowance; but it must be remembered that they have nothing else to live upon. When they are at home, and can get milk, &c., every man receives only five pounds of dried fish and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a pound of butter a-week.

ICHOR

Pages 72-73

properly signifies a thin watery humour like serum; but is sometimes used for a thicker kind flowing from ulcers, called also fæcer.

ICHTHYOCOLLA

Pages 73-75

Isinglass, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> from the fish known by the name of hæso. See Aceti- PENSER. The word is Greek, formed of ἰχθύς fish, and κόλλα <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>.—The method of making isinglass was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a secret in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Ruffians; but hath lately been discovered, and the following account of it published by Humphrey Jackson, Esq., in the 63d volume of the Philo- lophical Transactions. "All authors who have hitherto delivered pro- cesses for making ichthyocolla, fish-glue, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> isinglass, have greatly mistaken both its constituent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and preparation. "To prove this assertion, it may not be improper to recite what Pomet says upon the subject, as he appears to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> author whom the rest have copied. After describing the fish, and referring to a cut engrav- ed from an original in his custody, he says: 'As to the manner of making the isinglass, the finev parts of the fish are boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> till all of them be dissolved that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> dissolve; then the gluey liquor is strained, and set to cool. Being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, the fat is carefully taken off, and the liquor itself boiled to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> consistence, then cut to pieces, and made into a twist, bent in form of a cres- cent, as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> fold; then hung upon a string, and carefully dried.' "From this account, it might be rationally con- cluded, that every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fish which contained gelatinous principles would yield isinglass; and this parity of reasoning seems to have given rise to the halting con- clusions of those who strenuously vouch for the extrac- tion of isinglass from sturgeon; but as that fish is easily procurable, the negligence of ascertaining the fact by ex- periment seems inexcusable. "In my first attempt to discover the constituent parts and manufacture of isinglass, relying too much up- on the authority of some chemical authors whose veraci- ty I had experienced in many other instances, I found myself constantly disappointed. Glue, not isinglass, was the result of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>; and although, in the same view, a journey to Russia proved fruitless, yet a steady perseverance in the research proved not only successful as to this object, but, in the pursuit, to discover a resi- nous matter plentifully procurable in the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, which has been found by ample <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to answer fis- hur purposes. It is now no longer a secret, that our (a) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> are stocked with immense quantities of fish, said to be the same species with those in Muscovy, and yielding the finest isin- glasses; the fisheries whereof, under due encouragement would doubtless supply all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> with this valuable article. "No <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is necessary to the production of isinglass, neither is the matter dissolved for this purpose; for, (a) As the lakes of North America <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> nearly in the same latitude with the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, particularly Lake Su- perior, which is said to be of greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, it was conjectured they might abound with the same sorts of fish; and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of public advertisements distributed in various parts of North America, offering premiums for the sounds of sturgeon and other fish, for the purpose of making isinglass, several specimens of fine isinglass, the produce of fish taken in these parts, have been lately sent to England, with proper attestations as to the unlimited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> which may be procured. for, as the continuity of its fibres would be destroyed by solution, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> would become brittle in drying, and snap short asunder, which is always the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with glue, but never with isinglass. The latter, indeed, may be resolved into glue with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water; but its <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> re-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> would be found impracticable afterwards, and a fibrous texture is one of the most distinguishing characteristics of genuine isinglass. "A due consideration that an imperfect solution of isinglass, called fining by the brewers, possessed a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of clarifying malt-liquors, induced me to attempt its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> in cold subacid menstruums. One ounce and a half of good isinglass, steeped a few days in a gallon of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> beer, was converted into good fining, of a remarkably thick consistence: the same quantity of glue, under similar treatment, yielded only a mucilaginous liquor, resembling diluted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water, which, instead of clarifying beer, increased both its tenacity and turbidity, and communicated other properties in no respect corresponding with those of genuine fining. On commixing three spoonfuls of the solution of isinglass with a gallon of malt liquor, in a tall cylindrical glass, a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of curdly masses became presently formed, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of the particles of isinglass and the feculencies of the beer, which, increasing in magnitude and specific gravity, arranged themselves accordingly and fell in a combined state to the bottom, through the well-known laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>; for, in this case, there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> attraction, as some have imagined, which bears the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with what frequently occurs in chemical decompositions. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> what is commercially termed long or short flaked isinglass be steeped a few hours in fair cold water, the entwisted membranes will expand, and reassume their original beautiful (b) hue, and, by a dexterous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, may be perfectly unfolded. By this simple operation, we find that isinglass is nothing more than certain membranous parts of fishes, divested of their native mucosity, rolled and twisted into the forms above-mentioned, and dried in open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. "The founds, or air-bladders, of fresh water fish in general, are preferred for this purpose, as being the most transparent, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, delicate substances. These constitute the finest sorts of isinglass; those called book and ordinary flake are made of the intestines, and probably of the peritoneum of the fish. The belluga yields the greatest quantity, as being the largest and most plentiful fish in the Mucovoy rivers; but the founds of all fresh-water fish yield, more or less, fine isinglass, particularly the smaller sorts, found in prodigious quantities in the Caspian sea, and several hundred miles beyond Afracan, in the Wolga, Yaik, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a>, and even as far as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, where it is called kle or klo by the natives, which implies a glutinous matter; it is the basis of the Russian glue, which is preferred to all other kinds for its strength. "The founds, which yield the finer isinglass, consist of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> fibres, and are easily rent longitudinally; but the ordinary sorts are found composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> membranes, whose fibres <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> each other obliquely, resembling the coats of a bladder: hence the former are more readily pervaded and divided with subacid liquors; but the latter, through a peculiar kind of interwoven texture, are with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty torn asunder, and long resist the power of the same menstruum; yet, when duly resolved, are found to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> with equal energy in clarifying liquors. "Izinglass receives its different shapes in the following manner: "The parts of which it is composed, particularly the founds, are taken from the fish while sweet and fresh, slit open, washed from their slimy folder, deprived of every thin membrane which envelopes the found, and then exposed to stiffen a little in the air. In this state, they are formed into rolls about the thickness of a finger, and in length according to the intended size of the staple: a thin membrane is generally selected for the centre of the roll, round which the rest are folded alternately, and about half an inch of each extremity of the roll is turned inwards. The due dimensions being thus obtained, the two ends of what is called florit flake are pinned together with a small wooden peg; the middle of the roll is then pressed a little downwards, which gives it the resemblance of a heart-shape; and thus it is laid on boards, or hung up in the air to dry. The founds, which compose the long-flake, are longer than the former; but the operator lengthens this sort at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, by interfolding the ends of one or more pieces of the found with each other. The extremities are fastened with a peg, like the former; but the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the roll is bent more considerably downwards, and, in order to preserve the shape of the three obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> thus formed, a piece of round stick, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch diameter, is fastened in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with small wooden pegs, in the same manner as the ends. In this state, it is permitted to dry long enough to retain its form, when the pegs and sticks are taken out, and the drying completed; lastly, the pieces of isinglass are colligated in rows, by running pack-thread through the peg-holes, for convenience of package and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. "The membranes of the book fort, being thick and refractory, will not admit a similar formation with the preceding; the pieces, therefore, after their sides are folded inwardly, are bent in the centre, in such manner that the opposite sides resemble the cover of a book, from whence its name; a peg being run across the middle, fastens the sides together, and thus it is dried like the former. This fort is interleaved, and the pegs run across the ends, the better to prevent its unfolding. "That called cake-isinglass is formed of the bits and fragments of the staple sorts, put into a flat metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, with a very little water, and heated just enough to make the parts cohere like a pancake when it is dried; but frequently it is overheated, and such pieces, as before observed, are useless in the business of fining. Experience has taught the consumers to reject them. (b) If the transparent isinglass be held in certain positions to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, it frequently exhibits beautiful prismatic colours. "Ifinglaf is best made in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> gives it a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, deprives it of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and impairs its gelatinous principles; its fashionable forms are unnecessary, and frequently injurious to its native qualities. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to find oily putrid matter, and exuviae of insects, between the implicated membranes, which, through the inattention of the cellarman, often contaminate wines and malt-liquors in the act of clarification. These peculiar shapes might probably be introduced originally with a view to conceal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> the real substance of ifinglaf, and preserve the monopoly; but, as the mark is now taken off, it cannot be doubted to answer every purpose more effectually in its native state, without any subsequent manufacture whatever, especially to the principal consumers, who hence will be enabled to procure sufficient supply from the British colonies. Until this laudable end can be fully accomplished, and as a species of ifinglaf, more easily producible from the marine fisheries, may probably be more immediately encouraged, it may be manufactured as follows: "The founds of cod and ling bear great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> with those of the acipenser genus of Linnaeus and Arvedi; and are in general so well known as to require no particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. The Newfoundland and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> fishermen split open the fish as soon as taken, and throw the back-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> with the founds annexed, in a heap; but previous to incipient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, the founds are cut out, washed from their flimes, and salted for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> out the founds, the intercostal parts are left behind, which are much the best; the Iceland fishermen are so sensible of this, that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the bone upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> with a thick stick, till the pockets, as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> them, come out easily, and thus preserve the found entire. If the founds have been cured with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, that must be dissolved by steeping them in water before they are prepared for ifinglaf; the fresh found must then be laid upon a block of wood, whose surface is a little elliptical, to the end of which a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> is nailed, and with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> the membranes on each side of the found must be scraped off. The knife is rubbed upon the brush occasionally, to clear its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; the pockets are cut open with scissors, and perfectly cleansed of the mucous matter with a coarse cloth; the founds are afterwards washed a few minutes in lime-water in order to absorb their oily principle, and finally in clear water. They are then laid upon nets to dry in the air; but if intended to resemble the foreign ifinglaf, the founds of cod will only admit of that called book, but those of ling both shapes. The thicker the founds are, the better the ifinglaf, colour excepted; but that is immaterial to the brewer, who is its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> consumer. "This ifinglaf resolves into fining, like the other sorts, in subacid liquors, as stale beer, cyder, old hock, &c., and in equal quantities produces similar effects upon turbid liquors, except that it falls speedier and closer to the bottom of the vessel, as may be demonstrated in tall cylindrical glasses; but foreign ifinglaf retains the consistency of fining preferably in warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, owing to the greater tenacity of its native mucilage. "Vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> are, in every respect, best adapted to fining: the mineral acids are too corrosive, and even infalubrious, in common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a>. "It is remarkable, that, during the conversion of ifinglaf into fining, the acidity of the menstruum seems greatly diminished, at least to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; not on account of any alkaline property in the ifinglaf, probably, but by its enveloping the acid particles. It is likewise reducible into jelly with alkaline liquors, which indeed are solvents of all animal matters; even cold lime-water dissolves it into a pulpy mass.
