Notwithstanding this is inadmissible as fining, on account of the menstruum, it produces admirable effects in other respects: for, on commixture with compositions of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, lime, &c., for ornamenting walls exposed to vicissitudes of weather, it adds firmness and permanency to the cement; and if common brick-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> be worked up with this jelly, it soon becomes almost as hard as the brick itself; but, for this purpose, it is more commodiously prepared, by dissolving it in cold water, acidulated with vitriolic acid; in which case, the acid quits the jelly, and forms with the lime a felicitous mass, while, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the jelly being deprived in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of its moisture, through the formation of an indissoluble concrete amongst its parts, soon dries, and hardens into a firm body; whence its superior strength and durability are easily comprehended. "It has long been a prevalent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that sturgeon, on account of its cartilaginous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, would yield great quantities of ifinglaf; but, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, no part of this fish, except the inner coat of the found, promised the least success. This being full of rugae, adheres so firmly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> membrane, which is useless, that the labour of separating them supercedes the advantage. The intestines, however, which in the larger fish extend several yards in length, being cleansed from their mucus, and dried, were found surprisingly strong and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, resembling cords made with the intestines of other animals, commonly called catgut, and, from some trials, promised superior advantages when applied to mechanic operations." Ifinglaf is sometimes used in medicine; and may be given in a thin acrimonious state of the juices, after the same manner as the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> and mucilages, regard being had to their different disposition to putrefaction.

IDOMENEUS

Pages 139-139

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, succeeded his father <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a> on the throne of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. He accompanied the Greeks to the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with a fleet of 90 ships. During this celebrated war he rendered himself famous by his valour, and slaughtered many of the enemy. At his return from the Trojan war, he made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> in a dangerous tempest, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he escaped from the fury of the seas and storms, he would offer to the god whatever living creature first presented itself to his eye on the Cretan shore. This was no other than his son, who came to congratulate his father upon his safe return. Idomeneus performed his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to the god; and the inhumanity and ruthlessness of this sacrifice rendered him so odious in the eyes of his subjects, that he left Crete, and migrated in quest of a settlement. He came to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and founded a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, which he called Salentum. He died in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, after he had had the satisfaction of seeing his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> flourish and his subjects happy. According to the Greek scholiast of Lycophron, v. 1217, Idomeneus, during his absence in the Trojan war, intrusted the management of his kingdom to Leucos, to whom he promised his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Clitihere in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> at his return. Leucos at first governed with moderation, but he was persuaded by Nauplius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Euboea to put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> Meda the wife of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, with her daughter Clitihere, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the kingdom. After these violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> he strengthened himself on the throne of Crete, and Idomeneus at his return found it impossible to expel the usurper. IDUMÆA. See Edom.

IDYLLION

Pages 139-139

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, is only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of the word EIDOS, and properly signifies any poem of moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, without considering the subject. But as the collection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>'s poems were called Idyllia, and the pastoral pieces being by far the best in that collection, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Idyllion seems to be now appropriated to pastoral pieces. JEARS <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> GEERS, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, an assemblage of tackles, by which the lower yards of a ship are hoisted along the mast to their usual station, or lowered from thence as occasion requires: the former of which operations is called swaying, and the latter striking. JEBUSÆI, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> ancient peoples of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, descendants of Jebufl, Canaan's son; so warlike and brave, as to have stood their ground, especially in Jebus, afterwards called <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Judges i. 21. 1 Sam. v. 6.

IERNUS

Pages 423-423
or IERNUS (Ptolemy), a river in the south-west of Ireland. Now called the Maire, or Kenmare, running from east to west, in the province of Munster.

IGLAW

Pages 175-175

a considerable and populous town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, where they have a manufactory of good cloth, and excellent beer. It is seated on the river Iglia, 40 miles west of Brin, and 62 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 42. N. Lat. 47. 8.

IGNATIA

Pages 175-175

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNATIUS_LOYOLA">IGNATIUS Loyola</a>, (canonized), the founder of the well-known order of the Jesuits, was born at the castle of Loyola, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>, 1491; and became first page to Ferdinand V. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and then an officer in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. In this last capacity, he signalized himself by his valour; and was wounded in both legs at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAMPLONA">Pamplona</a>, in 1521. To this circumstance the Jesuits owe their origin; for, while he was under cure of his wound, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of the Saints was put into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, which determined him to forsake the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> profession. His first devout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> was to dedicate himself to the blest virgin as her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>; he then went a pilgrimage to the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>; and on his return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his theological studies in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Spain, though he was then 33 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. After this he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and in France laid the foundation of this new order, the institutes of which he presented to Pope Paul III., who made many objections to them, but at last in 1540 confirmed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. The founder died in 1555, and left his disciples two famous books; 1. Spiritual exercises; 2. Constitutions <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rules of the order. But it must be remembered, that though these avowed institutes contain many privileges obnoxious to the welfare of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, the most diabolical are contained in the private rules, intitled Monita secreta, which were not discovered till towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the last century; and most writers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> these, and even the Constitutions, to Laynez, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> general of the order.

IGNATIUS

Pages 175-177

St., surnamed Theophrytus, one of the apostolical fathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and educated under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> and evangelist St John, and intimately acquainted with some other of the apostles, especially St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul. Being fully instructed in the doctrines of Christianity, he was, for his eminent parts and piety, ordained by St John, and confirmed about the year 67 bishop of Antioch, by the two apostles, who first planted Christianity in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, where the disciples also were first called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Antioch was then not only the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Syria, but a city the most famous and renowned of any in the east, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> seat of the Roman emperors, as well as of the viceroys and governors. In this important seat he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to sit somewhat above 40 years, both an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and safeguard of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, till the year 107, when Trajan the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, flushed with a victory which he had lately obtained over the Scythians and Daci, about the ninth year of his reign, came to Antioch to make preparations for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Parthians and Armenians. He entered the city with the pomp and solemnities of a triumph; and, as his first care usually was about the concerns of religion, he began presently to inquire into that affair. Christianity had by this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> made such a progress, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> grew jealous and uneasy at it. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, therefore, had already commenced a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> against the Christians in other parts of the empire, which he now resolved to carry on here. However, as he was naturally of a mild Ignatius, mild disposition, though he ordered the laws to be put in force against them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> convicted, yet he forbade them to be sought after. In this state of affairs, Ignatius, thinking it more prudent to go himself than stay to be sent for, of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> presented himself to the emperor; and, it is said, there palled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and particular discourse between them, wherein the emperor expressing a surprise how he dared to transgress the laws, the bishop took the opportunity to assert his own innocence, and to explain and vindicate his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and freedom. The issue of this was, that he was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into prison, and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> passed upon him, That, being incurably overrun with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, he should be carried bound by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to Rome, and there thrown as a prey to wild beasts. He was first conducted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, a port of Syria, at about 16 miles distance, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were Paul and Barnabas set sail for Cyprus. Arriving at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, he went to visit Polycarp bishop of that place, and was himself visited by the clergy of the Asian churches round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In return for that kindness, he wrote letters to several churches, as the Ephesians, Magnesians, and Trallians, besides the Romans, for their instruction and establishment in the faith; one of these was addressed to the Christians at Rome, to acquaint them with his present state, and passionate desire not to be hindered in the course of martyrdom which he was now hastening to accomplish. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, a little impatient of their stay, set sail with him for Troas, a noted city of the lesser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, not far from the ruins of old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; where, at his arrival, he was much refreshed with the news he received of the persecution ceasing in the church of Antioch: hither also several churches sent their messengers to pay their respects to him; and hence too he dispatched two epistles, one to the church of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, and the other to that of Smyrna; and, together with this last, as Eusebius relates, he wrote privately to Polycarp, recommending to him the care and instruction of the church of Antioch. From Troas they sailed to Neapolis, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>; thence to Philippi, a Roman colony, where they were entertained with all imaginable kindness and courtesy, and conducted forwards on their journey, passing on foot through Macedonia and Epirus, till they came to Epidamnum, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>; where again taking shipping, they sailed through the Adriatic, and arrived at Rhegium, a port-town in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; directing their course thence through the Tyrrhenian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to Puteoli, whence Ignatius desired to proceed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, ambitious to trace the same way by which St Paul went to Rome: but this wish was not complied with; and, after a stay of 24 hours, a prosperous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> quickly carried them to the Roman port, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> harbour and station for their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, built near Oria, at the mouth of the Tyber, about 16 miles from Rome; whither the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> longed to come, as much desirous to be at the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, as his keepers, weary of their voyage, were to be at the end of their journey. The Christians at Rome, daily expecting his arrival, were come out to meet and entertain him, and accordingly received him with a mixture of joy and sorrow; but when some of them intimated, that possibly the populace might be taken off from desiring his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he expressed a pious indignation, intreating them to cast no rubs in his way, nor do anything that might hinder him; now he was hastening to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. There are many such expressions as this in his epistle to the Romans, which plainly show that he was highly ambitious of the crown of martyrdom. Yet it does not appear that he rashly sought <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> provoked danger. Among other expressions of his ardour for suffering, he said, that the wild beasts had feared and refused to touch some that had been thrown to them, which he hoped would not happen to him. Being conducted to Rome, he was presented to the prefect, and the emperor's letters probably delivered concerning him. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> before his martyrdom was spent in prayers for the peace and prosperity of the church. That his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> might be the more pompous and public, one of their solemn festivals, the time of their Saturnalia, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it when they celebrated their Sigillaria, was pitched on for his execution; at which time it was their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to entertain the people with the bloody conflicts of gladiators, and the hunting and fighting with wild beasts. Accordingly, on the 13th kal. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 20, he was brought out into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, and the lions being let loose upon him, quickly dispatched their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, leaving nothing but a few of the hardest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. These remains were gathered up by two deacons who had been the companions of his journey; and being transported to Antioch, were interred in the cemetery, without the gate that leads to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAPHNE">Daphne</a>; whence, by the command of the emperor Theodore, they were removed with great pomp and solemnity to the Tycheon, a temple within the city, dedicated to the public genius of it, but now consecrated to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the martyr. St Ignatius stands at the head of those Antinicene fathers, who have occasionally delivered their opinions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of Christ, whom he calls the Son of God, and his eternal world. He is also reckoned the great champion of the doctrine of the episcopal order, as distinct and superior to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> and deacon. And one, the most important, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his writings respects the authenticity of the Holy Scriptures, which he frequently alludes to, in the very expressions as they stand at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>.—Archbishop Usher's edition of his works, printed in 1647, is thought the best; yet there is a farther edition extant at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, where, beside the best notes, there are the dissertations of Usher and Pearson. St Ignatius's Bean, the fruit of a plant. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNATIA">Ignatia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. IGNIS-fatuo, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, supposed to be of an electric <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, appearing frequently in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, marshy places, and near stagnating waters. It was formerly thought, and is still by the superstitious believed, to have something ominous in its nature, and to prefigure death and other misfortunes. There have been instances of people being decoyed by these lights into marshy places, where they have perished; whence the names of Ignis-fatuo, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">Will</a>-with-a-wisp, and Jack-with-a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a>, as if this appearance was an evil spirit which took delight in doing mischief. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNITION">Ignition</a> of that kind. For a further account of the nature and properties of the ignis-fatua, see <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a> Index.

IGNITION

Pages 177-177

properly signifies the setting fire to any substance; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is sometimes limited to that kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> which is not accompanied with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, such as that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, cinders, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substances. The effects of ignition, according to the old chemical doctrine, are first to dissipate what is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a> of the ignited substance, after which it is reduced to ashes. Vitrification next follows; and lastly, the substance is totally dissipated in vapour. All these effects, however, depend on the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; for in vacuo the phlogiston of any substance cannot be dissipated. Neither can a body which is totally destitute of phlogiston be ignited in such a manner as those which are not deprived of it: for as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the phlogiston remains, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is kept up in the body by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> air upon it; but when the phlogiston is totally gone, the air always destroys, instead of augmenting, the heat. But for the explanation of the phenomena of ignition, according to the views of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, see IGNITION, Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

IGNOBILES

Pages 177-177

amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was the designation of such persons as had no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of using pictures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>. See Jus Imaginis.

IGNOMINIA

Pages 177-177

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, whereby the offender suffered public shame, either by virtue of the praetor's edict, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by order of the censor. This punishment, besides the scandal, deprived the party of the privilege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> any offices, and almost all other liberties of a Roman citizen.

IGNORAMUS

Pages 177-177

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a word properly used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> inquest empannelled in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> of causes criminal and public, and written upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> whereby any crime is offered to their consideration, when, as they dislike their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> as defective <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> too weak to make good the presentment; the effect of which word so written is, that all farther inquiry upon that party for that fault is thereby stopped, and he delivered without farther answer. It hath a resemblance with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, where the judges, when they absolved a person accused, did write A. upon a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> provided for that purpose, i.e. absolvimus; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they judged him guilty, they wrote C. i.e. condemnamus; if they found the cause difficult and doubtful, they wrote N. L. i.e. non liquet.

IGNORANCE

Pages 177-177
or mistake, in Law, a defect of will, whereby a person is excused from the guilt of a crime, when, intending to do a lawful act, he does that which is unlawful. For here the deed and the will acting separately, there is not that conjunction between them which is necessary to form a criminal act. But this must be an ignorance or mistake of fact, and not an error in point of law. As if a man intending to kill a thief or house-breaker in his own house, by mistake kills one of his own family, this is no criminal action: but if a man thinks he has a right to kill a person excommunicated or outlawed wherever he meets him, and does so; this is wilful murder. For a mistake in point of law, which every person of discretion not only may, but is bound and presumed to know, is, in criminal cases, no sort of defence. Ignorantia juris quod quisque tenetur seire, nonimem executat, is as well the maxim of our own law as it was of the Roman.

IGUANA

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">Lacerta</a>. See Reptology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Mud Iguana, a species of fish. See Murena, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index.

IHROR

Pages 177-177

JOHOR, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jor, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> beyond the Ganges. It was taken by the Portuguese in 1603, who destroyed it, and carried off the cannon; but it has since been rebuilt, and was afterwards in possession of the Dutch. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 93. 55. N. Lat. 1. 15.

IKENILD STREET

Pages 179-180

one of the four famous ways which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> made in England, called Stratum Icenorum, because it began in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Iceni, who inhabited <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>. ILÀ, ILAY, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ilà, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> or Western isles of Scotland, lying to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURA">Jura</a>, from which it is separated by a narrow channel. It extends 24 miles in length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and is 18 in breadth from east to west. On the east side there are many lofty sterile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; but in the interior, and to the southward and westward, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is in good cultivation. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> of a bluish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> lying in the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, stretches almost through its whole length, and is now extensively employed for the purposes of manure. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">Marl</a>, which is also abundant, is applied to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">Lead</a>-ore has been dug out in several places, and at so early a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Danes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> harbour in Ilà is at Lochindaal, but there are several others which are safe and commodious. Here are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> well stored with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, eels, and salmon. In the centre is Loch Finlagan, about three miles in circuit, with the little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of that name in the middle. Here the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the isles once resided in all the pomp of royalty; but his palaces and offices are now in ruins. Instead of a throne, Macdonald stood on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, in which there was an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> made to receive his feet; here he was crowned and anointed by the bishop of Argyle and seven inferior priests, in presence of the chieftains. This stone still exists. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> (after the new lord had collected his kindred and vassals) was truly patriarchal. After putting on his armour, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, he took an oath to rule as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had done; that is, to govern as a father would his children; his people in return swore that they would pay the same obedience to him as children would to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. The dominions of this potentate, about the year 1586, consisted only of Ilay, Jura, Knapdale, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTYRE">Cantyre</a>; so reduced were they from what they had been before the deprivation of the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Rothes in the reign of James III. Near this is another little isle, where he assembled his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, "Ilan na Corlie," or "the isle of council;" where 13 judges constantly sat to decide differences among his subjects; and received for their trouble the 11th part of the value of the affair tried before them. In the first isle were buried the wives and children of the lords of the isles; but their own persons were deposited in the more sacred ground of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONA">Iona</a>. On the shores of the lake are some marks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of his Carnauch and Gilli-glashees, "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> of the isles;" the first signifying a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, the last a grim-looking fellow. The first were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-armed, and fought with darts and daggers; the last with sharp hatchets. These are the troops that Shakespeare alludes to, when he speaks of a Donald, who From the Western isles Of Kerns and Gallow-glashees was supplied. Besides those already mentioned, the lords had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and chapel at Laggan, on the south side of Lochindaal: a strong castle on a rock in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at Dunowall, at the south-east end of the country; for they made this isle their residence after their expulsion from that of Man in 1304.—There is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that while the isle of Man was part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the isles, the rents were for a time paid in this country: those in silver were paid on a rock, still called Creig-a-nisne, or "the rock of the silver rent;" the other, Creig-a-nairrid, or "the rock of rents in kind." These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> opposite to each other, at the mouth of a harbour on the south side of this isle. There are several forts built on the isles in fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> lakes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> caverns in different parts of the isle, which have been used occasionally as places of strength. The isle is divided into four parishes, viz. Kildalton, Killarow, Kilchoman, and Kilmenie. The produce is corn of different kinds; such as bear, which sometimes yields eleven fold; and oats six fold. Much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> is raised here, and about £2000. worth sold out of the isle in yarn, which might better be manufactured on the spot, to give employ to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> natives. Notwithstanding the excellency of the land, above £1000. worth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> is annually imported (a). Ale is frequently made in this isle of the young tops of heath, mixing two-thirds of that plant with one of malt, sometimes adding hops. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> relates, that this liquor was much used among the Piets; but when that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> was extirpated by the Scots, the secret of making it perished with them. Numbers of cattle are bred here, and about 1700 are annually exported at the (a) This might have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in the time of Pennant, from whom the above account is taken. It is not now, although the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> has increased to nearly 12,000. Ilà indeed enjoys the peculiar advantages of being not only a grazing but a corn country, and can thus afford a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of both <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of produce. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle now exported far exceeds that stated above by Pennant. the price of 50 shillings each. The island is often overcrowded, and numbers die in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> for want of fodder. None but milch-cows are housed; cattle of all other kinds, except the fiddle-horses, run out during winter. The number of inhabitants, when Ilay was visited by Pennant, is computed to have been between seven and eight thousand. About 700, says he, are employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and in the fishery; the rest are gentlemen-farmers, and subtenants or servants. The women spin. The servants are paid in kind; the sixth part of the crop. They have houses gratis; the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> gives them the seed for the first year, and lends them horses to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> annually the land annexed. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> of this island, as enumerated by Mr Pennant*, are dogs, weasels, otters, and hares: the last small, dark-coloured, and bad runners. The birds are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, peregrine falcons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and a very few ptarmigans. Red-breasted goosanders breed on the shore among the loofe <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, wild geese in the moors, and herons in the island in Loch-guirm. The fish are plaice, fineardab, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> dabs, mullets, balan, lump-fish, black goby, greater dragonet, and that rare fish the lepadogaiter of M. Gouan. Vipers swarm in the heath; the natives retain the vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of their stinging with their forked tongues (b); that a sword on which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> has fallen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> in water like a red-hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and that a poultice of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> ordure is an infallible cure for the bite. In this island, Mr Pennant informs us, several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> diversions and superstitions are still preserved: the last indeed are almost extinct, or at most lurk only amongst the very meanest of the people. The late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAKES">wakes</a> or funerals, like those of the Romans, were attended with sports, and dramatic entertainments composed of many parts, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> often changed their dresses suitably to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. The subject of the drama was historical, and preserved by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.—The power of fascination is as strongly believed here as it was by the shepherds of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in times of old. Nescio quis teneros oculis milii fascinat agnos? But here the power of the evil eye affects more the milch-cows than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the good housewife perceives the effect of the malicious on any of her kine, she takes as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> as she can drain from the enchanted herd (for the witch <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> leaves very little). She then boils it with certain herbs, and adds to them flints and untempered <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>; after that she secures the door, and invokes the three sacred persons. This puts the witch into such an agony, that she comes willing-willing to the house, begs to be admitted, to obtain relief by touching the powerful pot: the good woman then makes her terms; the witch restores the milk to the cattle, and in return is freed from her pains. But sometimes, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the trouble of those charms (for it may happen that the disorder may arise from other causes than an evil-eye), the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> is made by immersing in milk a certain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, and if the cows are supernaturally affected, it instantly distils blood. The unsuccessful lover revenges himself on his happy rival by charms potent as those of the shepherd Alpheibaeus, and exactly similar: Nettle tribus nodis ternor, Amarylli, colorer: Nette, Amarylli, modo. Donald takes three threads of different hues, and ties three knots on each, three times imprecating the most cruel disappointments on the nuptial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>: but the bridegroom, to avert the harm, stands at the altar with an untied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>, and puts a sixpence beneath his foot. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> furnishes very few materials for the great events or revolutions of Ilay. It seems to have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a seat of empire, probably jointly with the Isle of Man, as being most conveniently situated for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the rest of the Hebrides; for Crovan the Norwegian, after his conquest of that island in 1066, retired and finished his days in Ilay. There are more Danish or Norwegian names of places in this island than any other; almost all the present farms derive their titles from them; such as Peribus, Torridale, Torribolfe, and the like. On the retreat of the Danes it became the seat of their successors the lords of the illes; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, after their power was broken, in the reign of James III. in their descendants the Macdonalds, who held or ought to have held it from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. It was in the possession of a Sir James Macdonald, in the year 1598, the same who won the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Traill-dhruinard. His power gave umbrage to James VI. who directed the lord of Macleod, Cameron of Lochiel, and the Macneiles of Barra, to support the Macleans in another invasion. The rival parties met near the hill of Benbigger, east of Kilbarrow; a fierce engagement ensued, and the Macdonalds were defeated and almost entirely cut off. Sir James escaped to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; but returned in 1620, was pardoned, received a pension, and died the same year at Glasgow; and in him expired the last of the great Macdonalds. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, irritated by the disturbances raised by private wars waged between these and other clans, refused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> made by his predecessor, and transferred it to Sir John Campbell of Calder, who held it on paying an annual feu-duty of five hundred pounds <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, which is paid to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The island was granted to Sir John as a reward for his undertaking the conquest; but the family considered it as a dear acquisition, by the loss of many gallant followers, and by the expenses incurred in support of it.

ILCHESTER

Pages 180-181

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in England, situated on the river Yeo, 129 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is so called, because it once had a castle, and stands on the river Ivel. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, as appears by the Roman coins which are sometimes dug up. It is likewise evident, from the ruins and from two towers on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, that it was once a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> place, and encompassed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall. It also had several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches, though now but one. It is governed by two bailiffs, who with the twelve burgesses are lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>. In the reign of Edward III. the assizes for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> were fixed here, which have since been held (b) This vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> is by no means limited to the natives of Ilay. held alternately at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a>, and Bridgewater. The knights of the shire are always chosen here, and it is the place for the county courts and jail. On the latter is its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> dependence, and therefore it cannot be very polite. It is noted for being the birth-place of Roger the famous Friar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>. Ilchester is an earldom in the Fox family.

ILDEFONSO

Pages 181-182

Sr., a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, distant about two miles from Segovia. It was erected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> V. in the midst of a solitary wood, and in the bosom of steep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It is chiefly remarkable for its gardens. There is nothing magnificent in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, particularly in its exterior appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> on the side of the garden is of the Corinthian order, and not destitute of elegance. Here are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s apartments, which look upon a parterre surrounded with vases and marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and a cascade which, for the richness of its decorations, may be compared with the finest of the kind. The purity and clearness of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is indeed incomparable. Philip V. could not, in this respect, be better served by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. From the mountains which thine the palace descend several rivulets, which supply the reservoirs. These waters answer the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> purpose of supplying numerous fountains, and of diffusing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and verdure through the magnificent gardens, the sight of which alone is a sufficient recompense for a journey into Spain. They are on the inside a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in circumference. The inequality of the ground affords every moment new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> alleys answer to different summits of neighbouring mountains; and one in particular produces the most agreeable effect. It is terminated at one end by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> front of the palace. From this point are seen, at one view, five fountains, ornamented with elegant groups, rising into an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, above which appear the summits of lofty mountains. The most elevated of these groups is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a> fastened to a rock. When seen at a little distance it is perhaps defective, because the rock appears too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> by the side of the monster which threatens Andromeda; and of Perseus, by whom it is attacked; but the whole contributes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the view. The most remarkable of the five groups is that of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. "Genius (says M. Bourgoanne) prefixed at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and in the choice of the situation; the deity of the ocean appears erect, surrounded by the marine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. His attitude, his threatening countenance, and the manner of holding his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>, announce that he has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> imposed silence on the mutinous waves; and the calm which reigns in the basin, defended from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> by the triple wall of verdure by which it is surrounded, seems to indicate that he has not issued his commands in vain. Often have I seated myself, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, by the side of this silent water, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of the verdant foliage, nor ever did I fail to recollect the famous Quos Ego? "There are other fountains worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the curious; such as that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>, where the limpid heaves, some perpendicularly, and others in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the horde throats of the Lycian peasants, half transformed into frogs, and spouting them forth in such abundance, that the statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> disappears under the wide mantle of liquid crystal; that also of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> in the bath, fur- Vol. XI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. Ildelfonso, fenced by thick shades. Some hollows, overshadowed by arching trees, seem to be the abodes of the Naiades. Disturb them not by indireet loquacity, but silently admire and meditate. "It is impossible, however, not to go to the source of these waters; let us follow the meandering of their course, and observe the winding paths which there terminate, after appearing and disappearing at intervals through the copse. Let us listen to the bubbling of the rivulets which from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time escape from our sight, and hasten to the rendezvous assigned them by the descendants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. They formerly lost themselves in the valleys, where they quenched the thirst of their humble inhabitants, but are now consecrated to the pleasures of kings. Ascending the back of the pyramidal mountain, behind which their source is concealed, we arrive at the wall which confines a part of them in the garden, and which was hidden by the trees; nothing, however, ought here to recall to mind exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. Woods, waters, and the majestic solitude of mountains, which are at a distance from the tumult of courts and cities, are the property of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.—Beyond this wall, which forms the exterior enclosure of the gardens, is an empty and flat ground, where the infant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Louis, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the king, chose a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which he consecrated to cultivation. Farther on, the mountain becomes more steep, and is covered with trees to its summit. Let us now return; as we seek amusement and not fatigue. We <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> follow the course of the waters, they descend in bubbling streams from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the gardens to the other. In their course, in one place they water the feet of the trees, in others they crook an alley to nourish more slowly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of a parterre. From the basin of Andromeda they run between two rows of trees in the form of a canal, the too sudden inclination of which is taken off by cascades and windings. They receive and carry with them from the gardens the rivulets; which after having played amongst the gods and nymphs, and moistened the throats of the swans, tritons, and lions, humbly descend under ground, and run on into the bosom of the neighbouring meadows, where they fulfill purposes less brilliant but more useful. "We must not quit these magnificent gardens without stopping at a place which appears to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> much, but produces not any very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> effect. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the eight alleys, Plaza de las ocho calles. In the centre is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of Pandora, the only one which is of whitened <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, all the others are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> painted of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Eight alleys answer to this centre, and each is terminated by a fountain. Plots of verdure fill up the intervals between the alleys, and each has an altar under a portico of white marble by the side of a basin sacred to some god or goddess. These eight altars, placed at equal distances, and decorated among other jets-d'eau, have two which rise in the form of tapers on each side of their divinities. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> regularity displeased Philip V., who a little before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, when visiting the gardens, made some severe reproaches to the inventor upon the subject. Philip had not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of completely enjoying what he had created; death surprized him when the works he had begun were but half finished. The undertaking was however the most expensive one of his reign. The finances of Spain, so deranged under the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, (thanks to the wife calculations of Orry, to the subsidies of France, and still more to the courageous efforts of the faithful Castilians) would have been sufficient for three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and ruinous wars, and for all the operations of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> which Philip V. had conquered and formed anew, as well as to have resettled the flocks of ambition and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> intrigue; but they sunk beneath the expensive efforts of magnificence." It is singular that the castle and gardens of St Ildefonso should have cost about 45,000,000 of piastras, precisely the sum in which Philip died indebted. This enormous expense will appear credible, when it is known that the situation of the royal palace was at the beginning of this century the sloping top of a pile of rocks; that it was necessary to dig and hew out the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and in several places to level the rock; to cut out of its sides a paillage for a hundred different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, to carry vegetative <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to every place in which it was intended to facilitate cultivation for fertility, and to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> a mine to clear a paillage to the roots of the numerous trees which are there planted. All these efforts were crowned with success. In the orchards, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-gardens, and parterres, there are but few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, espaliers, or plants, which do not thrive; but the trees, naturally of a lofty growth, and which consequently must strike their roots deep into the earth, already prove the insufficiency of art when it attempts to struggle against nature. Many of them languish with withered trunks, and with difficulty keep life in their almost naked branches. Every year it is necessary to call in the aid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> to make new beds for those which are to supply their place; and none of them are covered with that tufted foliage which belongs only to those that grow in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. In a word, there are in the groves of St Ildefonso, marble statues, basins, cascades, limpid waters, verdure, and delightful prospects, everything but that which would be more charming than all the rest, thick shades. The court of Spain comes hither annually during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the dog-days. It arrives towards the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and returns at the beginning of October. The situation of St Ildefonso, upon the declivity of the mountains which separate the two Castiles, and fronting a vast plain where there is no obstacle to the paillage of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> wind, renders this abode delightful in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The mornings and evenings of the hottest days are agreeably cool. Yet as this palace is upwards of 20 leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, and half of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> which leads to it crosses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> tops of mountains, extremely steep in many places, it is much more agreeable to the lovers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> and solitude than to others.

ILERDA

Pages 182-182

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Ilargentes; situated on an eminence between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Sicoris and Cinga: An unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, often besieged, and often taken, because lying exposed to the incursions from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>; and under Gallienus it was destroyed by the Germans. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LERIDA">Lerida</a>, in Catalonia, on the river Segra.

ILFRACOMB

Pages 182-183

ILFRACOMB, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, almost opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWANSEA">Swansea</a> in Glamorganshire, 186 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a populous, rich, trading sea-port, especially with herrings in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>-channel; noted for maintaining constant lights to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the sailors; for its convenience of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and repairing ships; and for the safe shelter ships from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> find here, when it is extremely dangerous for them to run into the mouth of the Taw, which they call Barnstaple-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and this is one reason why the Barnstaple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> do so much of their business at this port. The harbour, with its quay, warp-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-house, pilot-boats, and tow-boats, were formerly maintained at the expense of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>; and then it had a quay <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pier 850 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; but by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and the violence of the sea all went to decay; to remedy which, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> passed an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in 1731, for both repairing and enlarging the piers, harbour, &c. It is governed by a mayor, bailiffs, &c. and consists chiefly of one street of scattered houses almost a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> long. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, containing several tythings and manors.

ILIAC PASSION

Pages 183-183

a violent and dangerous kind of colic; called also volvulus, miserere mei, and chordophae. It takes its name from the intestine ilion, on account of its being usually affected in this distemper; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perhaps from the Greek verb ἰλιος, "to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> or twist;" whence also it is the Latins call it volvulus. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ILIAD

Pages 183-183

the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> epic poem, the first and finest of those composed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. The poet's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in the Iliad was to show the Greeks, who were divided into several little states, how much it was their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to preserve a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and good understanding among themselves; for which end he sets before them the calamities that befell their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> from the wrath of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, and his misunderstanding with Agamemnon; and the advantages that afterwards accrued to them from their union. The Iliad is divided into 24 books <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rhapsodies, which are marked with the letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>.

ILICICUM

Pages 183-183

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decidua clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ILIUM

Pages 183-183

ILION, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ilios, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a name for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, but most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used by the poets, and distinguished by the epithet Vetus; at a greater distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> than what was afterwards called Ilium Novum, and thought to be the Ilionium Pagus of Strabo. New or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Ilium was a village nearer the sea, with a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>; where Alexander, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANICUS">Granicus</a>, offered gifts, and called it a city, which he ordered to be enlarged. His orders were executed by Lytimachus, who encompassed it with a wall of 40 stadia. It was afterwards adorned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who granted it immunities as to their mother-city. From this city the Ilias of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> takes its name, containing an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> carried on between the Greeks and Trojans on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> of Helen; a variety of disasters being the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, gave rise to the proverb Ilias Malorum.

ILKUCH

Pages 183-183

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>, remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. It is seated in a barren and mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20° 0. N. Lat. 50° 26'.

ILLECEBRUM

Pages 183-183

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 12th order, Holoraceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ILLINOIS

Pages 183-183

a people of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, inhabiting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> lying near a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake of the same name (called also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICHIGAN">Michigan</a>), formed by the river St Lawrence. The country is fertile; and the people plant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, on which they chiefly subsist. They are civil, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, lively, and robust; and are much less cruel in their dispositions than the other Indian nations. They are, however, said to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIBERTINES">libertines</a>, and to marry a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of wives; but some of their villages have embraced Christianity.

ILLISSUS

Pages 183-183

a river running to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; which, with the Eridanus running on the west side, falls below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Sacred to the mules, called Iliares; on whose <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> their altar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSTRATION">lustration</a> in the less <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> was usually performed.

ILLUMINATI

Pages 183-183

the name of a secret <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> order, in Germany and other countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, whose professed object, it is said, was to propagate the purest principles of virtue; but whose real views were to subvert every established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and delivering mankind from the necessary and salutary restraints of civil society, to bring them to an imaginary state of freedom and independence. Of this order much has been said, and much has been written; but that a society has existed, regularly organized in the way this has been represented, working in secret, and, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, possessing such extensive power and influence, no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> whatever has been adduced. The thing indeed seems impossible. See MASONS, Free.

ILLUMINATING

Pages 183-185

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, anciently much practised for illustrating and adorning books. Besides the writers of books, there were artists whose profession was to ornament and paint <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, who were called illuminators; the writers of books first finished their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, and the illuminators embellished them with ornamented letters and paintings. We frequently find blanks left in manuscripts for the illuminators, which were never filled up. Some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manuscripts are gilt and burnished in a style superior to later times. Their colours were excellent, and their skill in preparing them must have been very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. The practice of introducing ornaments, drawings, emblematical figures, and even portraits, into manuscripts, is of great antiquity. Varro wrote the lives of 700 illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, which he enriched with their portraits, as Pliny attests in his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> (lib. xxxv. chap. 2.). Pomponius Atticus, the friend of Cicero, was the author of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the actions of the great men amongst the Romans, which he ornamented with their portraits, as appears in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by Cornelius Nepos (chap. 18.). But these works have not been transmitted to posterity. There are, however, many precious documents remaining, which exhibit the advancement and decline of the arts in different ages and countries. These ineffable paintings and illuminations display the manners, customs, habits <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>, civil, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, weapons and instruments of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, utensils and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; they are of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in illustrating many important facts relative Illuminative to the history of the times in which they were executed. In these treasures of antiquity are preserved a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of specimens of Grecian and Roman art, which were executed before the arts and sciences fell into neglect and contempt. The manuscripts containing these specimens form a valuable part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>, Cottonian, and Harleian libraries, as also those in the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> in England, the Vatican at Rome, the imperial at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, the royal at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, St Mark's at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, and many others. A very ancient MS. of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, which was in the Cottonian library, and almost destroyed by a fire in 1734, contained 250 curious paintings in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> colours. Twenty-one fragments, which escaped the fire, are engraved by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of antiquarians of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Several specimens of curious paintings also appear in Lambecius's catalogue of the imperial library at Vienna, particularly in vol. iii., where 48 drawings of nearly equal antiquity with those in the Cottonian library are engraved; and several others may be found in various catalogues of the Italian libraries. The drawings in the Vatican <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> made in the fourth century, before the arts were entirely neglected, illustrate the different subjects treated of by the Roman poet. A miniature <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> is prefixed to each of the gospels brought over to England by St Augustin in the 6th century, which is preserved in the library of Corpus Christi <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; in the compartments of those drawings are depicted representations of several transactions in each gospel. The curious drawings, and elaborate ornaments in St Cuthbert's gospels made by St Ethelwald, and now in the Cottonian library, exhibit a striking specimen of the state of the arts in England in the 7th century. The same may be observed with respect to the drawings in the ancient copy of the four gospels preserved in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>, and those in the Codex Ruthwonthianus in the Bodleian library at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. The life of St Paul the hermit, now remaining in Corpus Christi college, Cambridge, (G. 2.), affords an example of the style of drawing and ornamenting letters in England in the 8th century; and the copy of Prudentius's Physiognomia in the Cottonian library (Cleop. c. 8.) exhibits the style of drawing in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the 9th century. Of the 10th century there are Roman drawings of a singular kind in the Harleian library (No. 2820). Nos. 2820, 1802, and 432, in the same library, contain specimens of ornamented letters, which are to be found in Irish MSS. from the 12th to the 14th century. Cadmon's Poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">Paraphrase</a> of the book of Genesis, written in the 11th century, which is preserved amongst F. Junius's MSS. in the Bodleian library, exhibits many specimens of utensils, weapons, instruments of music, and implements of husbandry used by the Anglo-Saxons. The like may be seen in extracts from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in the Cottonian library (Claud. B. 4.). The manuscript copy of Terence in the Bodleian library (D. 17.) displays the dresses, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a>, &c. worn by comedians in the 12th century, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not earlier. The very elegant Psalter in the library of Trinity college, Cambridge, exhibits specimens of the art of drawing in England in the same century. The Virgil in the Lambeth library of the 13th century (No. 471.), written in Italy, shows both by the drawings and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, that the Italians produced works much inferior to ours at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The copy of the Apocalypse in the same library (No. 259.), contains a curious example of the manner of painting in the 14th century.—The beautiful paintings in the history of the latter part of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Richard II. in the Harleian library (No. 1349.), afford curious specimens of manners and customs, both civil and military, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 14th and in the beginning of the 15th century; as does No. 2278. in the same library.—Many other instances might be produced; but those who desire farther information may consult Strutt's Regal and Ecclesiastical Antiquities, 4to, and his Horda-Angel-cymyn lately published in 3 vols. This art was much practised by the clergy, and even by some in the highest stations in the church.
