The saints and prophets of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> were sensible of this; and our Saviour, in the gospel, has strongly inculcated, that they are not outward and corporeal pollutions which render us unacceptable to God, but such inward pollutions as infect the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and are violations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>.

IMPUTATION

Pages 195-195

in general, the charging something to the account of one which belonged to another; thus, the affections of original sin maintain, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>'s sin is imputed to all his posterity. In the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the righteousness and merits of Christ are imputed to true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>.

INACCESSIBLE

Pages 195-195

something that cannot be approached, by reason of intervening obstructions, as a river, rock, &c. It is chiefly used in speaking of heights and distances. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">MENSURATION</a>.

INACHUS

Pages 195-195

founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, 1856 B.C. See ARGOS.

INALIENABLE

Pages 195-195

that which cannot be legally alienated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> made over to another; thus the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, the revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the estates of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, &c. are inalienable, otherwise than with a reserve of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>.

INANIMATE

Pages 195-195

a body that has either lost its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that is not of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> capable of having any.

INANITION

Pages 195-195

among physicians, denotes the state of the stomach when empty, in opposition to repletion.

INAUGURATION

Pages 196-196

the coronation of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, or the consecration of a prelate: so called from the ceremonies used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, when they were received into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of augurs.

INCA

Pages 196-196
or YNCA, a name given by the natives of Peru to their kings and the princes of the blood. Pedro de Cieca, in his Chronicles of Peru, gives the origin of the incas; and says, that that country was, for a long time, the theatre of all manner of crimes, of war, diffusion, and the most dreadful disorders, till at last two brothers appeared, one of whom was called Mangocapa; of this person the Peruvians relate many wonderful stories. He built the city of Cuzco, made laws, established order and harmony by his wise regulations; and he and his descendants took the name of inca, which signifies king or great lord. These incas became so powerful, that they rendered themselves masters of all the country from Patto to Chili, and from the river Maule on the south to the river Augafmago on the north; these two rivers forming the bounds of their empire, which extended above thirteen hundred leagues in length. They enjoyed till the divisions between Inca Guascar and Atabalipa; which the Spaniards laying hold of, made themselves masters of the country, and destroyed the empire of the incas. See PERU.

INCAMERATION

Pages 196-196

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> of Rome, for the uniting of lands, revenues, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, to the pope's domain.

INCANTATION

Pages 196-196

denotes certain ceremonies, accompanied with a formula of words, and supposed to be capable of raising devils, spirits, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">Charm</a>, &c.

INCAPACITY

Pages 196-196

in the canon-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is of two kinds: 1. The want of a dispensation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, for legitimation in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a>, and the like: this renders the provision of a benefice void in its original. 2. Crimes and heinous offences, which annul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> at first valid.

INCARNATION

Pages 196-196

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby the Son of God assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the mystery by which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, the eternal word, was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in order to accomplish the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. The era used among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, whence they <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> their years, is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the incarnation, that is, of Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> in the virgin's womb. This era was first established by Dionysius Exiguus, about the beginning of the fifth century, till which time the era of Diocletian had been in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Some time after this, it was considered, that the years of a man's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were not numbered from the time of his conception, but from that of his birth: which occasioned them to postpone the beginning of this era for the space of one year, retaining the cycle of Dionysius entire in every thing else. At Rome they reckon their years from the incarnation or birth of Christ, that is, from the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has obtained from the year 1431. In France, and several other countries, they also reckon from the incarnation; but then they differ from each other in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the incarnation, fixing it, after the primitive manner, not to the day of the birth, but conception of our Saviour; though the Florentines retain the day of the birth, and begin their year from Christmas. INCARNATION (formed from in and caro "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>") in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, signifies the healing and filling up of ulcers and wounds with new flesh. See SURGERY.

INCARNATIVES

Pages 196-196

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, medicines which were supposed to assist <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in filling up wounds <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ulcers with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>.

INCENDIARY

Pages 196-196

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is applied to one who is guilty of maliciously setting fire to another's dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and all outhouses that are parcel thereof, though not contiguous to it, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, as barns and stables. A bare intent or attempt to do this, by actually setting fire to a house, unless it absolutely burns, does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of incendii et combusti. But the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> and consuming of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is sufficient; though the fire be afterwards extinguished. It must also be a malicious burning; otherwise it is only a trespass. This offence is called arson in our law. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, criminals of this kind were to be burnt. Qui aedes, acervumque frumenti juxta domum posuisse scierit, prudenteque dolo malo combusturit, vinculo igni necatur. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of arson was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxon laws and by the Gothic constitutions: and in the reign of Edward I. incendiaries were burnt to death. The stat. 8 Hen. VI. c. 6. made the wilful burning of houses, under special circumstances, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; but it was reduced to felony by the general acts of Edward VI. and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. This offence was denied the benefit of clergy by 21 Hen. VIII. c. 1., which statute was repealed by 1 Edw. VI. c. 12.; and arson was held to be out of clergy, with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, by inference from the stat. 4 and 5 P. and M. c. 4., which expressly denied it to the accesorify; though now it is expressly denied to the principal also, by 9 Geo. I. c. 22.

INCENSE

Pages 196-197
or FRANKINCENSE, in the Materia Medica, &c. a dry resinous substance, known among authors by the names THUS and OLIBANUM. Incense is a rich perfume, with which the Pagans and the Roman Catholics still perfume their temples, altars, &c.—The word comes from the Latin incensum, q. d. burnt; as taking the effect for the thing itself. The burning of incense made part of the daily service of the ancient Jewish church. The priests drew lots to know who should offer it: the destined person took a large silver dish, in which was a censer full of incense; and being accompanied by another priest carrying some live coals from the altar, went into the temple. There, in order to give notice to the people, they struck upon an instrument of brass placed between the temple and the altar; and being returned to the altar, he who brought the fire left it there, and went away. Then the offerer of incense having said a prayer or two, waited the signal, which was the burning of the holocaust; immediately upon which he set fire to the incense, the whole multitude continuing all Inceptive all the time in prayer. The quantity of incense offered each day was half a pound in the morning and as much at night. One reason of this continual burning of incense might be, that the multitude of victims that were continually offered up, would have made the temple smell like a slaughter-house, and consequently have inspired the comers rather with disgust and aversion, than awe and reverence, had it not been overpowered by the agreeable fragrance of those perfumes.

INCEPTIVE

Pages 197-197

a word used by Dr Wallis to express such moments, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> first principles, which, though of no magnitude themselves, are yet capable of producing such as are. Thus a point has no magnitude itself, but is inceptive of a line which it produces by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. So a line, though it have no breadth, is yet inceptive of breadth; that is, it is capable, by its motion, of producing a surface which has breadth, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INCEST">incest</a>, the crime of venereal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> between persons who are related in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> wherein <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> is prohibited by the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that marriage ought to be permitted between kinsfolks, to the end that the affection so necessary in marriage might be heightened by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> tie: yet the rules of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> have formerly extended this prohibition even to the seventh degree; but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> has now brought it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the third or fourth degree. Most nations look on incest with horror, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> alone excepted. In the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings of those countries we meet with instances of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s marrying the sister; the reason was, because they thought it too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to join in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with their own subjects, and still more so to have married into any foreign family. incest Spiritual, a crime committed in like manner between persons who have a spiritual alliance by means of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>. Spiritual incest is also understood of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEFICIARY">beneficiary</a>, who enjoys both the mother and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>; that is, holds two benefices, the one whereof depends upon the collation of the other. Such a spiritual incest renders both the one and the other of these benefices vacant.

INCH

Pages 197-197

a word prefixed to the names of different places in Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Inchcolm <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Columba, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Columba, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> situated in the frith of Forth in Scotland, and famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. See FORTH. This monastery was founded about 1123, by Alexander I, on the following occasion. In passing the frith of Forth he was overtaken with a violent storm, which drove him to this island, where he met with the most hospitable reception from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> hermit, then residing here in the chapel of St Columba, who, for the three days that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> remained there tempest-bound, entertained him with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of his cow, and a few shell-fish. His majesty, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the danger he had escaped, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to the saint to whom he attributed his safety, vowed some token of respect; Inchcolm accordingly founded here a monastery of Augustines, and dedicated it to St Columba. Allan de Mortimer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABERDOUR">Aberdour</a>, who attended Edw. III., in his Scotch expedition, bestowed half of those lands on the monks of this island, for the privilege of a family <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The buildings made in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the piety of Alexander were very considerable. There are still to be seen a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> tower belonging to the church, the ruins of the church, and of several other buildings. The wealth of this place in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Edward III. proved so strong a temptation to his fleet, then lying in the Forth, as to suppress all the horror of sacrilege and respect to the sanctity of the inhabitants. The English landed, and spared not even the furniture more immediately consecrated to divine worship. But due vengeance overtook them; for in a storm which instantly followed, many of them perished; those who escaped, struck with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the judgment, vowed to make ample recompense to the injured saint. The tempest ceased; and they made the promised atonement.—The Danish monument, figured by Sir Robert Sibbald, lies on the south-east side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, on a rising ground. It is of a rigid form, and the surface ornamented with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>-like figures. At each end is the representation of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> head. Inch Keith, a small island situated in the same frith, midway between the port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGHORN">Kinghorn</a> on the opposite shore. See FORTH. This island is said to derive its name from the gallant Keith who so greatly signalized himself by his valour in 1016, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRY">Barry</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, against the Danes; after which he received in reward the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> of Keith, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>, and this little isle. In 1549 the English fleet, sent by Edward VI., to assist the lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>-dowager, landed, and began to fortify this island, of the importance of which they grew sensible after their neglect of securing the port of Leith, so lately in their power. They left here five companies to cover the workmen under the command of Cotterel; but their operations were soon interrupted by M. Deffe, general of the French auxiliaries, who took the place, after a gallant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the English. The Scots kept possession for some years; but at last the fortifications were destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, to prevent it from being of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the former. The French gave it the name of L'isle des chevaux, from its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of soon fattening horses. In 1497, by order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, all venereal patients in the neighbourhood of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> were transported there to prevent their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> from spreading, ne quid detrimenti respublica caperet. A <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>, which must prove highly beneficial to the shipping which frequent the Forth, was erected in 1835. Inch Garvie, a small island, also lying in the frith of Forth, near <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEENSFERRY">Queensferry</a>. See FORTH. INCHANTMENT. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">WITCHCRAFT</a>.

INCHOATIVE

Pages 197-198

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying the beginning of a thing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; the same with what is otherwise called inceptive. INCHOATIVE verbs denote, according to Priscian and other grammarians, verbs that are characterized by the termination <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INCIDENCE">Incidence</a> termination feco or fecor, added to their primitives: as augefco from augeo, calcefco from caleo, dulcefco from dulcis, irafco from ira, &c.

INCIDENCE

Pages 198-198

denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in which one body strikes on another. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">OPTICS</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">MECHANICS</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">Angle</a> of INCIDENT. See ANGLE.

INCIDENT

Pages 198-198

in a poem, is an episode, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, joined to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> action, or depending on it. A good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> is to be full of agreeable incidents, which divert the spectators, and form the intrigue. The poet ought always to make choice of such incidents as are susceptible of ornament suitable to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of his poem. The variety of incidents well conducted makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of an heroic poem, which ought always to take in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of incidents to suspend the catastrophe, that would otherwise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out too soon.

INCINERATION

Pages 198-198

(derived from in, and cinis, "ashes,") in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of any substance into ashes by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>.

INCISIVE

Pages 198-198

an appellation given to whatever cuts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> divides: thus, the fore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are called dentes incisivi, or cutters; and medicines of an attenuating <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, incidents, or incitive medicines.

INCLINATION

Pages 198-198

is a word frequently used by mathematicians, and signifies the mutual approach, tendency, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> leaning of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> or two planes towards each other, so as to make an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>.

INCLINED PLANE

Pages 198-198

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, one that makes an oblique <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the horizon. See MECHANICS.

INCOGNITO

Pages 198-198
or INCOG, is applied to a person who is in any place where he would not be known: but it is more particularly applied to princes, or great men, who enter towns, or walk the streets, without their ordinary train or the usual marks of their distinction and quality. INCORPORABLE CLOTH. See ASBESTOS, MINERALOGY Index. On this Cronstedt observes, that the natural store of the asbestos is in proportion to their economical use, both being very inconsiderable. It is an old tradition (says he), that in former ages they made clothes of the fibrous asbestos, which is said to be composed by the word buffer; but it is not very probable, since if one may conclude from some trifles now made of it, as bags, ribbons, and other things, such a dress could neither have an agreeable appearance, nor be of any conveniency or advantage. It is more probable that the Scythians dressed their dead bodies which were to be burned, in a cloth manufactured of this stone; and this perhaps has occasioned the above fable. M. Magellan confirms this opinion of Cronstedt's, and informs us that some of the Romans also inclosed dead bodies in cloth of this kind. In the year 1756 or 1757 he tells us, that he saw a large piece of asbestos cloth found in a stone tomb, with the ashes of a Roman, as appeared by the epitaph. It was kept, with the tomb also, if our author remembers rightly, in the right-hand wing of the Vatican library at Rome. The under-librarian, in order to show that it was combustible, lighted a candle, and let some drops of wax fall on the cloth, which he set on fire with a candle in his presence without any detriment to the cloth. Its texture was coarse, but much finer than he could have expected.

INCOMMENSURABLE

Pages 198-198

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, used where two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, when compared to each other, have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, how small soever, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> exactly measure them both. And in general, two quantities are said to be incommensurable, when no third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> can be found that is an aliquot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of both. INCOMMENSURABLE Numbers, are such as have no common divisor that will divide them both equally.

INCOMPATIBLE

Pages 198-198

that which cannot subsist with another without destroying it; thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> are incompatible in the same subject, the strongest overcoming and expelling the weakest.

INCONTINENCE

Pages 198-198

in Medicine, signifies an inability in any of the organs to retain what should not be discharged without the concurrence of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. It is most frequently applied to an involuntary discharge of urine. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

INCORPORABLE

Pages 198-198

something that cannot be burnt <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> consumed by fire. See ASBESTOS.

INCORPORATE

Pages 198-198

[spiritual] a thing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> substance, which has no body. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is incorporeal, and may subsist independent of the body. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>.

INCORPORATION

Pages 198-198

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of dry substances to the confluence of a paste, by the admixture of some fluid: thus pills, boles, &c., are made by incorporation.

INCORRUPTIBLE

Pages 198-198

that which cannot be corrupted. Thus spiritual substances, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> souls, &c., and thus also, glass, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, &c., may be called incorruptible.

INCORRUPTIBLES

Pages 198-198

INCORRUPTIBLES, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which sprang out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUTYCHIANS">Eutychians</a>.—Their distinguishing tenet was, that the body of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was incorruptible; by which they meant, that after and from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> wherein he was formed in the womb of his holy mother, he was not susceptible of any change <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>; not even of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and innocent passions, as of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, thirst, &c., so that he ate

INCRASSATING

Pages 198-199

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, &c., the rendering of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> thicker by the mixture of other substances less fluid, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of the thinner parts.

INCUBATION

Pages 199-199

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of a hen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other fowl, brooding on her eggs. See HATCHING.

INCUBUS

Pages 199-199

Night-mare, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> consisting in an oppression of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, so very violent, that the patient cannot speak <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even breathe. The word is derived from the Latin incubare, to "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>" on any thing and press it; the Greeks call it ἐπικάλυψις, q.d. fallator, "leaper," or one that rushes on a person. In this disease the senses are not quite lost, but drowned, and astonished, as is the understanding and imagination; so that the patient seems to think some huge <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> thrown on him, ready to strangle him. Children are very liable to this distemper; so are fat people, and men of much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and application of mind; by reason the stomach in all these finds some difficulty in digestion.

INCUMBENT

Pages 199-199

a clerk <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> minister who is resident on his benefice; he is called incumbent, because he does, or at least ought to, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> his whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> to discharge the cure of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. INCURATION of the Rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> out of a rectilinear straight course, occasioned by refraction. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">OPTICS</a>.

INCUS

Pages 199-199

in Anatomy, a bone of the internal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, somewhat resembling one of the anterior dentes molares. See ANATOMY, No. 141.

INDEFEASIBLE

Pages 199-199

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> for what cannot be defeated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> made void; as an indefeasible estate of inheritance, &c. Indefeasible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> to the Throne. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">HEREDITARY</a> RIGHT.

INDEFINITE

Pages 199-199

that which has no certain bounds, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind cannot affix any. Indefinite, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, is understood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRONOUNS">pronouns</a>, verbs, participles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, &c., which are left in an uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and not fixed to any particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, thing, or other circumstance.

INDEMNITY

Pages 199-199

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the saving harmlesse; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to secure one from all damage and danger that may ensue from any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>.

INDENTED

Pages 199-199

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is when the outline of an ordinary is notched like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>.

INDENTURE

Pages 199-199

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> which compiles some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> between two at least; being indented at top, answerable to another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which has the same contents. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">DEED</a>.

INDEPENDENTS

Pages 199-258

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> so called Independents, from their maintaining that each <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, which meets in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for public worship, is a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, has sufficient power to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> and perform every thing relating to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> within itself, and is in no respect subject <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> accountable to other churches. The Independents, like every other Christian sect, derive their own origin from the practice of the apostles in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the first churches; but they were unknown in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times till they arose in England during the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a> established by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in the churches of her dominions, the vestments worn by the clergy in the celebration of divine worship, the book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, and above all the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> used in the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, were very offensive to many of her subjects, who during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of the former reign had taken refuge among the Protestants of Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. Those men thought that the church of England resembled, in too many particulars, the antichristian church of Rome; and they called perpetually for a more thorough reformation and a purer worship. From this circumstance they were stigmatized by their adversaries with the general name of Puritans, as the followers of Novatian (A) had been in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church. Elizabeth was not disposed to comply with their demands; and it is difficult to say what might have been the issue of the contest, had the Puritans been united among themselves in sentiments, views, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> was quite otherwise. That <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body, composed of persons of different ranks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, opinions, and intentions, and unanimous in nothing but in their antipathy to the forms of doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> that were established by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, was all of a sudden divided into a variety of sects. Of these the most famous was that which was formed about the year 1581 by Robert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> infirmating in his manners, but unsteady and inconsistent in his views and notions of men and things. See Brown. This innovator differed not in point of doctrine either from the church of England, or from the rest of the Puritans; but he had formed notions then new and singular concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the church and the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> government. He was for dividing the whole body of the faithful into separate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> or congregations; and maintained, that such a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons as could be contained in an ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of worship ought to be considered as a church, and enjoy all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges that are competent to an ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. These small societies he pronounced independent jure divino, and entirely exempt from the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, in whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> had placed the reins of spiritual government; and also from that of presbyteries. (A) The followers of Novatian were called Puritans, because they would not communicate with the Catholic church, under pretence that her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> was polluted by admitting those to the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> who through infirmity had sacrificed to idols in times of persecution. These unhappy men were not received by the church till after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>. The Novatians would not receive them at all, however long their penance, or however sincere their sorrow, for their sin. In other respects, the ancient Puritans were, like the English, orthodox in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and of irreproachable morals. and synods, which the Puritans regarded as the supreme visible sources of ecclesiastical authority. He also maintained, that the power of governing each congregation resided in the people; and that each member had an equal share in this government, and an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to order matters for the good of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Hence all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> both of doctrine and discipline were submitted to the discussion of the whole congregation; and whatever was supported by a majority of voices passed into a law. It was the congregation also that elected certain of the brethren to the office of pastors, to perform the duty of public instruction, and the several branches of divine worship; reserving, however, to themselves the power of dismissing these ministers, and reducing them to the condition of private members, whenever they should think such a change conducive to the spiritual advantage of the community. It is likewise to be observed, that the right of the pastors to preach was by no means of an exclusive nature, or peculiar to them alone; since any member that thought proper to exhort or instruct the brethren, was abundantly indulged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of prophesying to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. Accordingly, when the ordinary teacher or pastor had finished his discourse, all the other brethren were permitted to communicate in public their sentiments and illustrations upon any useful or edifying subject. The zeal with which Brown and his associates maintained and propagated these notions was in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> intemperate and extravagant. He affirmed, that all communion was to be broken off with those religious societies that were founded upon a different <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> from his; and treated, more especially the church of England, as a spurious church, whose ministers were unlawfully ordained, whose discipline was popish and antichristian, and whose sacraments and institutions were destitute of all efficacy and virtue. The sect of this hot-headed innovator, not being able to endure the severe treatment which their own violence had brought upon them from an administration that was not distinguished by its mildness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, retired into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, and founded churches at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLEBURG">Middleburg</a> in Zeeland, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; but their establishments were neither <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> nor lasting. Their founder returned into England; and having renounced his principles of separation, took orders in the established church, and obtained a benefice. The Puritan exiles, whom he thus abandoned, disagreed among themselves, were split into parties, and their affairs declined from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to day. This engaged the wiser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them to mitigate the severity of their founder's plan, and to soften the rigour of his uncharitable decisions. The persons who had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> merit of bringing about this reformation was one of their pastors called John Robinson, a man who had much of the solemn piety of the times, and no inconsiderable portion of learning. This well-meaning reformer, perceiving the defects that reigned in the discipline of Brown, and in the spirit and temper of his followers, employed his zeal and diligence in correcting them, and in new-modelling the society in such a manner as to render it less odious to its adversaries, and less liable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> censure of those true Christians, who looked upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> as the end of the commandments. Hitherto the sect had been called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWNISTS">Brownists</a>; but Robinson having, in his Apology, affirmed, Cætum quemlibet particularis, effe totam, integram, et perfectam ecclesiam ex suis partibus constatentium immediatè et independenter (quod alias ecclesias) sub ipso Christo,—the sect was henceforth called Independents, of which the apologist was considered as the founder. The Independents were much more commendable than the Brownists. They surpassed them both in the moderation of their sentiments, and in the order of their discipline. They did not, like Brown, pour forth bitter and uncharitable invectives against the churches which were governed by rules entirely different from theirs, nor pronounce them on that account unworthy of the Christian name. On the contrary, though they considered their own form of ecclesiastical government as of divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, and as originally introduced by the authority of the apostles, nay by the apostles themselves; they yet had candour and charity enough to acknowledge, that true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and solid piety might flourish in those communities which were under the jurisdiction of bishops or the government of synods and presbyteries. This is put beyond all doubt by Robinson himself, who expresses his own private sentiments and those of his community in the following clear and precise words: "Profitemur <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORAM">coram</a> Deo et hominibus, adeo nosl consenire cum ecclesiis reformatis Belgicis in re religiosis, ut omnibus et singulis earumdem ecclesiarum fidei articulis, praet habentur in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONIA">harmonia</a> confessionalium fidei, parati simus subfervire. Ecclesias reformatas pro veris et genuinis habemus, cum ipsidem in sacris Dei communione profitemur, et quantum in nobis est, colimus." They were also much more attentive than the Brownists, in keeping on foot a regular ministry in their communities; for while the latter allowed promiscuously all ranks and orders of men to teach in public, the Independents had, and still have, a certain number of ministers, chosen respectively by the congregations where they are fixed; nor is any person among them permitted to speak in public, before he has submitted to a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of his capacity and talents, and been approved of by the heads of the congregation. This religious society still subsists, and has produced divines as eminent for learning, piety, and virtue, as any church in Christendom. It is now distinguished from the other Protestant communities chiefly by the two following circumstances. 1. The Independents reject the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all creeds and confessions drawn up by fallible men, requiring of their teachers no other test of orthodoxy than a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in the gospel of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, and their adherence to the Scriptures as the sole standard of faith and practice. 2. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> no virtue whatsoever to the rite of ordination, upon which some other churches lay so much stress; for the Independents declare, that the qualifications which constitute a regular minister of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, are, a firm belief in the gospel, a principle of sincere and unaffected piety, a competent stock of knowledge, a capacity for leading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and communicating instruction, a serious inclination to engage in the important employment of promoting the everlasting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of mankind, and ordinarily an invitation to the pastoral office from some particular society. Where these things concur, they consider a person as fitted and authorized for the discharge of every duty which belongs to the ministerial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>; and they believe that the imposition of the hands of bishops or presbyters would convey to him no powers or prerogatives of which he was not before possessed. When the reformers separated from the church of Rome, they drew up public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONFESSIONS_OF_FAITH">confessions of faith</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of religion, to which they demanded subscription from their respective followers. Their purpose in this was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against dangerous heresies, to ascertain the meaning of Scripture-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and, we doubt not, to promote the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. These were laudable ends; but of the means chosen for attaining them, the late Dr Taylor of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the Independent churches, and whose learning would have done <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to any church, expresses his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in the following indignant language: "How much soever the Christian world vaunteth these creeds and confessions, I confess, for my own part, that I have no opinion of them. But we are told that they were generally drawn up by the ablest divines. But what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> is there of this? Are divines in vogue and power <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the most knowing and upright? But granting that the reformers were in those days the ablest divines; the ablest divines educated in populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, notwithstanding any pretended learning, might comparatively be very weak and defective in scripture knowledge, which was a thing in a manner new to them. In times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> they might be men of eminence; and yet far short of being qualified to draw up and decide the true and precise rules of faith for all Christians. Yea, their very attempting to draw up, decide, and establish such rules of faith, is an incontestable evidence of their surprising ignorance and weakness. How could they be able divines, when they imposed upon the consciences of Christians their own decisions concerning gospel-faith and doctrine? Was not this in fact to teach and constrain Christians to depart from the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> principle of their religion, subjection and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to Christ, the only teacher and lawgiver? But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were able men, were they infallible? No: they publicly affirmed their own fallibility; and yet they acted as if they had been infallible, and could not be mistaken in prescribing faith and doctrine. But even if they were infallible, who gave them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to do what the Spirit of God had done already? Could the first reformers hope to deliver the truths of religion more fully and more clearly than the Spirit of God? Had they found out more apt expressions than had occurred to the Holy Spirit? The Son of God 'spake not of himself; but as the Father said unto him, so he spake,' (John xii. 50.). 'The Spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> spake not of himself; but whatsoever he heard, that he spake,' (John xvi. 13.). 'The things of God the apostles spake, not in the words which man's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth,' (1 Cor. ii. 13.). If the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> was thus handed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us from the Fountain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a> with so much care and exactness, both as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and words, by the Son of God, by the Spirit, and by the apostles, who were the ancient doctors and bishops? or who were the first reformers? or who were any synods or assemblies of divines, that they dared to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> Christian faith into their own invented forms, and impose it upon the minds of men in their own devised terms and expressions? Hath Christ given authority to all his ministers to the end of the world, to new-mould his doctrines by the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> learning whenever they think fit? or hath he delegated his power to any particular persons? Neither the one nor the other. His doctrines are not of such a ductile nature; but stand fixed, both as to matter and words, in the Scripture. And it is at any man's peril, who pretends to put them, as they are rules of faith, into any new dress or shape. I conclude, therefore, that the first reformers, and all councils, synods, and assemblies, who have met together to collect, determine, and decide, to prescribe and impose matters pertaining to Christian faith, have acted without any warrant from Christ, and therefore have invaded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of him who is the sole Prophet and Lawgiver to the church. Peace and unity, I know, is the pretended good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of those creeds and confessions. But as God never sanctified them for those ends, to all the world knows they have produced the contrary effects; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, and the spilling of whole seas of Christian blood for 1400 years together." Such sentiments as these are now maintained by Christians of various denominations; but they were first avowed by the Independents, to whom therefore the merit or demerit of bringing them to light properly belongs. Our readers <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> think differently of them according to their preconceived opinions; but it is not our province either to confirm or to confute them. They rise almost necessarily out of the independent scheme of congregational churches; and we could not suppress them without deviating from our fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of doing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to all religious parties, as well those from whom we differ as those with whom we agree. It ought not, however, to be rashly concluded, that the Independents of the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, merely because they reject the use of all creeds of human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, doubt or disbelieve the doctrines deemed orthodox in other churches. Their predecessors in the last century were thought to be more rigid Calvinists than the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a> themselves; as many of those may likewise be who in the present century admit not the confessions and formulas of the Calvinistic churches. They acknowledge as divine truth every doctrine contained in the Scriptures; but they think more necessary that scripture-doctrines are most properly expressed in simple scripture-language; and the same spirit of religious liberty, which makes them reject the authority of bishops and synods in matters of discipline, makes them reject the same authority in matters of faith. In either case, to call any man or body of men their masters, would, in their opinion, be a violation of the divine law, since "one is their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, even Christ, and they are all brethren." In support of their scheme of congregational churches, their arguments observe, that the word ἐκκλησία, which we translate church, is always used in Scripture to signify either a single congregation, or the place where a single congregation meets. Thus that unlawful assembly at Ephesus gathered together against Paul by the craftsmen, is called ἐκκλησία, a church, (Acts xix. 32, 39, 41.). The word, however, is generally applied to a more sacred rule; Independence, but still it signifies either the body assembling, or the place in which it assembles. The whole body of the disciples at Corinth is called the church, and spoken of as coming together into one place, (1 Cor. xiv. 23.) The place into which they came together we find likewise called a church; “where ye come together in the church—when ye come together into one place,” (1 Cor. xi. 18, 20.). Wherever there were more congregations than one, there were likewise more churches than one: Thus, “Let your women keep silence in the churches,” (1 Cor. xvi. 41.) The whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of Israel is indeed called a church, but it was no more than a single congregation; for it had but one place of public worship, viz., the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>, and afterwards the temple. The Catholic church of Christ, his holy nation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, is likewise a single congregation, having one place of worship, viz., heaven, where all the members assemble by faith and hold communion; and in which, when they shall all be fully gathered together, they will in fact be one glorious assembly. We find it called “the general assembly and church of the first-born, whose names are written in heaven.” Besides these, the Independent can find no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of a church in the New Testament; not a trace of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> or presbytery consisting of several congregations all subject to one jurisdiction. The number of disciples in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> was certainly great before they were dispersed by the persecution in which Paul bore so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> a part; yet they are never mentioned as forming distinct assemblies, but as one assembly meeting with its elders in one place; sometimes in the temple, sometimes in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>’s porch, and sometimes in an upper room. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>, the disciples who fled from Jerusalem, as they could no longer assemble in one place, are never called a church by themselves, or one church, but the churches of Judea, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, and Galilee, (Acts ix. 31. Gal. i. 22.) Whence the Independent concludes, that in Jerusalem the words church and congregation were of the same import; and if such was the case there, where the gospel was first preached, he thinks we may reasonably expect to find it so in other places. Thus when Paul on his journey calls the elders of the church of Ephesus to Mileto, he speaks to them as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> overseers of a single congregation: “Take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock, over which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers,” (Acts xx. 28.) Had the church at Ephesus consisted of different congregations united under such a jurisdiction as that of a modern presbytery, it would have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to say, “Take heed to yourselves, and to the flocks over which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers;” but this is a way of speaking of which the Independent finds not an instance in the whole New Testament. The sacred writers, when speaking of all the Christians in a nation or province, never call them the church of such a nation or province, but the churches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a> (Gal. i. 2.), the churches of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> (2 Cor. viii. 1), the churches of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> (1 Cor. xvi. 10.) On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, when speaking of the disciples in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> or town, who might ordinarily assemble in one place, they uniformly call them a church; saying, the church of Antioch, the church at Corinth, the church of Ephesus, and the like. In each of these churches or congregations there were elders or presbyters and deacons; and in every church congregation there seems to have been more than one elder, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> more than one. Thus we read (Acts xiv. 23.) of Paul and Barnabas ordaining elders in every church; and (Acts xix. 17) of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of elders in the church of Ephesus, who were exhorted to “feed the flock, and take heed to themselves and to the flock over which the Holy Ghost had made them overseers;” but of such elders as are to be found in modern presbyterian churches, who neither teach nor are apt to teach, the Independent finds no vestige in the Scriptures, nor in the earliest uninspired writers of the Christian church. The rule or government of this presbytery or eldership in a church is not their own, but Christ’s. They are not lords over God’s heritage, nor can they pretend to more power over the disciples than the apostles had. But when the administration of the apostles in the church of Jerusalem, and other churches where they acted as elders, is inquired into by an Independent, it does not appear to him that they did any thing of common concern to the church without the consent of the multitude; nay, it seems they thought it necessary to judge and determine in discipline in presence of the whole church (Acts vi. 6—xv. 29. 1 Cor. v. 1, 4, 5.) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">Excommunication</a> and abjuration were in the power of the church at Corinth, and not of the elders as distinct excommunicated from the congregation (1 Cor. v. 2 Cor. ii.) and abjurant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> indeed speaks of his delivering form unto Satan (1 Tim. i. 20.); but it is by no means clear the power of he did it by himself, and not after the manner pointed at each congregation, that the gift was given unto Timothy by putting on of his hands, that this was not done in the presbytery of a church, as in the other epistle we find it actually was. The trying and judging of false apostles was a matter of the first importance; but it was done by the elders with the flock at Ephesus (Rev. ii. 2. Acts xx. 28.) and that whole flock did in the days of Ignatius all partake of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>’s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, and pray together in one place. Even the power of binding and loosing, or the power of the keys, as (b) The evidence upon which this is said by Mr. Graf (for the whole of this reasoning is extracted from his works) is probably the following passage in the epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians: Εκ γεγενέσθαι μετὰ τῶν εὐαγγελισμῶν Ἀποστόλων, “For if the prayer of one or two be of such force as we are told, how much more prevalent must that be which is made by the bishop and the whole church? He then that does not come together into the same place with it, is proud, and hath condemned himself; for it is written, God refuseth the proud. Let us therefore respect the bishop, that we may be the servants of God.” as it has been called, was by our Saviour conferred not upon a particular order of disciples, but upon the church: "If thy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother. But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of one or two witnesses every word may be established. And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican. Verily I say unto you, whatsoever ye shall bind on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, shall be bound," &c. (St Mat. xviii. 15, 16, 17, 18.). It is not said, if he shall neglect to hear the one or two, tell it to the elders of the church; far less can it be meant that the offended person should tell the cause of his offence to all the disciples in a presbytery or diocese consisting of many congregations: but he is required to tell it to that particular church or congregation to which they both belong; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of that assembly, pronounced by its elders, is in a very solemn manner declared to be <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a>, from which there lies no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to any jurisdiction on earth. With respect to the constituting of elders in any church or congregation, the Independent reasons in the following manner: The officers of Christ's appointment are either ordinary and permanent in the church, or they were extraordinary and peculiar to the planting of Christianity. The extraordinary were those who were employed in laying the plan of the gospel churches, and in publishing the New Testament revelation. Such were the apostles, the chosen witnesses of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>; such were the prophets inspired by the Holy Ghost for explaining infallibly the Old Testament by the things written in the New; and such were the evangelists, the apostles ministers. These can be succeeded by none in that which was peculiar to them, because their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was completed by themselves. But they are succeeded in all that was not peculiar to them by elders and deacons, the only two ordinary and permanent orders of ministers in the church. We have already seen, that it belongs to the office of the elder to feed the flock of Christ: and the only question to be settled is, how men are ordinarily called to that office? for about the office of the deacon there is little or no dispute. No man now can pretend to be so called of God to the ministry of the word as the apostles and other inspired elders were, whom he chose to be the publishers of his revealed truth, and to whose mission he bore witness in an extraordinary manner. But what the apostles were to those who had the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> from their mouths, that their writings are to us; and therefore no man can lawfully pretend a call from God to make any addition to those writings, so neither can any man pretend to be lawfully called to the ministry of the word already written but in the manner which that word directs. Now there is nothing of which the New Testament speaks more clearly than of the characters of those who should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the office of elders in the church, and of the actual exercise of that office. The former are graphically drawn in the epistles to Timothy and Titus; and the latter is minutely described in Paul's discourse to the Ephesian elders, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s exhortation to elders, and our Lord's commission to those ministers, with whom he promised to be always present even unto the end of the world. It is not competent for any man or body of men to add to, or diminish from, the description of a gospel minister given in these places, so as to insist upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of any qualification which is not there mentioned, or to dispense with any qualification as needless which is there required. Neither has Jesus Christ, Arguments the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> to the church, given to any mind against the elders or people any power or right whatsoever to call, ordain, elect, or ordain, to that office any person who is not qualified according to the description given in his law; nor has he given any power or right to reject the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of them who are so qualified, and who desire the office of a bishop or elder. Let a man have hands laid upon him by such as could prove an uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> by imposition of hands from the apostles; let him be set apart to that office by a company of ministers themselves, the most conformable to the scripture character, and let him be chosen by the most holy people on earth; yet if he answer not the New Testament description of a minister, he is not called of God to that office, and is no minister of Christ, but is indeed running unclean. No form of ordination can pretend to such a clear foundation in the New Testament as the description of the persons who should be elders of the church; and the laying on of hands, whether by bishops or presbyters, is of no more importance in the mission of a minister of Christ, than the waving of one's hand in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> or the putting of it into his bosom; for now when the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> has ceased, it is obvious that such a rite, by whomsoever performed, can convey no powers, whether ordinary or extraordinary. Indeed it appears to have been sometimes used, even in the apostolic age, without any such intention. When Paul and Barnabas were separated to the particular employment of going out to the Gentiles, the prophets and teachers at Antioch "prayed and laid their hands on them:" But did this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> confer upon the two apostles any new power or authority to act as ministers of Christ? Did the imposition of hands make those shining lights of the gospel one whit better qualified than they were before to convert and baptize the nations, to feed the flock of God, to teach, rebuke, or exhort, with all long-suffering and doctrine. It cannot be pretended. Paul and Barnabas had undoubtedly received the Holy Ghost before they came to Antioch; and as they were apostles, they were of course authorized to discharge all the functions of the inferior and ordinary ministers of the gospel. In a word, whoever in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and conversation is conformable to the character which the inspired writers give of a bishop or elder, and is likewise qualified by his "mightiness in the scripture" to discharge the duties of that office, is fully authorized to administer the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's supper, to teach, and even exhort, and rebuke, with all long-suffering and docility; and has all the call and mission which the Lord now gives to any man; whilst he who wants the qualifications mentioned, has not God's call, whatever he may have, nor any authority to preach the gospel of Christ, or to dispense the ordinances of his religion. From this view of the Independent principles, which is faithfully taken from their own writers, it appears, that, according to them, even the election of a congregation... The first catalogues of this kind were made by the inquisitors; and these were afterwards approved by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, after some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> was made in them by way of retrenchment or addition. Thus an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of heretical books being formed, it was confirmed by a bull of Clement VIII. in 1593, and printed with several introductory rules; by the fourth of which, the use of the Scriptures in the vulgar tongue is forbidden to all persons without a particular licence; and by the tenth rule it is ordained, that no book shall be printed at Rome without the approbation of the Pope's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, or some person delegated by the Pope; nor in any other places, unless allowed by the bishop of the diocese, or some person deputed by him, or by the inquisitor of heretical pravity. The Trent index being thus published, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> ordered another to be printed at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, in 1571, with considerable enlargements. Another index was published in Spain 1584; a copy of which was snatched out of the fire when the English plundered <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>. Afterwards there were several expurgatory indexes printed at Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and particularly in Spain. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">INDIA</a>. See Hindostan.—By the name of India the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> understood only the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, on this side the Ganges, and the peninsula beyond it, having little or no knowledge of the countries which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> farther to the eastward; though by the moderns all those vast tracts from the eastern parts of the Persian empire to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, are confounded under the general name of East Indies. Even the ancients, though originally they were acquainted only with the western parts of Hindoostan, gradually extended the name of India over the other countries they discovered to the eastward; so that probably they would have involved all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> in the same general designation, had they been as well acquainted with them as the moderns are. By whom these countries were originally peopled, is a question which in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> will never be resolved. Certain it is, that some works in these parts display marks of astonishing skill and power in the inhabitants, such as the images in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Elephanta; the rocking <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of immense <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, yet so nicely balanced that a man can move them with his hand; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a>, &c. These stupendous works are by Mr Bryant attributed to the Cuthites or Babylonians, the first distinct nation in the world, and who of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> must for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> have possessed in a manner the sovereignty of the whole earth; and it can by no means appear improbable, that the subjects of Nimrod, the beginning of whose kingdom was in Shinar, might extend themselves eastward, and thus fill the fertile regions of the east with inhabitants, without thinking it worth while for a long time to meddle with the less mild and rich countries to the westward. Thus why the would be formed that great and for some time influential Indians and other countries; so that the western nations knew not ignorant of even of the existence of the Indians but by obscure one another report; while the latter, ignorant of their own origin, invented a thousand idle tales concerning the antiquity of their nation, which some of the moderns have been credulous enough to believe and regard as facts. The first among the western nations who distinguished ed themselves by their application to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and who were of consequence likely to discover these distant nations, were the Egyptians and Phenicians. The former, however, soon lost their inclination for naval affairs, and held all seafaring people in detestation as profane persons; though the extensive conquests of Scelotris, if we can believe them, must have in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> supplied this defect. Without regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of his people against <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs, he is said to have fitted out a fleet of 400 sail in the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA">Red <a </a>class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which conquered all the countries lying along the Erythrean sea (a) to India; while the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> led by himself marched through Asia, and subdued all the countries to the Ganges; after which he crossed that river, and advanced to the eastern ocean. Great disputes have been carried on with respect to this conqueror, and the famous expedition just now related; but the learned Dr Robertson, in his Disquisition concerning ancient India, declares himself in doubt whether any such expedition ever was made, for the following reasons. 1. Few historical facts seem to be better established than that of the aversion the Egyptians entertained to seafaring people and naval affairs; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> considers it as impossible even for the most powerful monarch to change in a few years a national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> confirmed by time and sanctified by religion.
