Accordingly I took some of the more finking kinds of paper, and common paper made damp as for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>; and had the satisfaction to find, that neither the oily nor the simple gummy mixtures spread upon them so much as might have been expected, and that the characters were as fixed as could be desired, for they could not be washed out without rubbing off part of the substance of the paper itself. "All these inks must be now and then stirred or shaken during the time of use, to mix up the black powder, which settles by degrees to the bottom: those with oil must be well shaken also, though not used, once a-day, or at least once in three or four days, to keep the oil united with the water and gum; for, if once the oil separates, which it is apt to do by standing at rest for some days, it can no longer be mixed with the thin fluid by any agitation. But though this imperfect union of the ingredients renders these inks less fit for general use than those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> employed, I apprehend there are many occasions in which these kinds of inconveniences will not be thought to counterbalance the advantage of having writings which we may be assured will be as lasting as the paper they are written upon. And indeed the inconvenience may be in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> obviated by using cotton in the inkstand, which, imbibing the fluid, prevents the separation of the black powder diffused through it. "All the inks, however, made on the principle we are now speaking of, can be discharged by washing, unless the paper admits them to sink into its substance. The ancients were not insensible of this imperfection; and sometimes endeavoured to obviate it, according to Pliny, by using vinegar instead of water, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERING">tempering</a> the mixture of lamp-black and gum. I tried vinegar, and found it to be of some advantage, not as giving any improvement to the cement, but by promoting the sinking of the matter into the paper. As this washing out of the ink may be prevented by using a kind of paper easy enough to be procured, it is scarce to be considered as an imperfection; and indeed, on other kinds of paper, it is an imperfection only so far as it may give occasion to fraud, for none of these inks are in danger of being otherwise discharged than by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. The vitriolic inks themselves, and those of printed books and copperplates, are all dischargeable; nor can it be expected of the ink-maker to render writings secure from frauds. "But a further improvement may yet be made, namely, that of uniting the ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> inks together; or using the common vitriolic ink instead of water, for tempering the ancient mixture of gum and lamp-black. By this method it should seem that the writings would have all the durability of those of former times, with all the advantage that results from the vitriolic ink fixing itself in the paper. Even where the common vitriolic mixture is depended on for the ink, it may in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> be improved by a small addition of the ancient composition, or of the common Indian ink which answers the same purpose: when the vitriolic ink is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a>, and flows so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> from the pen, that the fine strokes, on first writing, are scarcely visible, the addition of a little Indian ink is the readiest means of giving it the due blackness. By this admixture it may be presumed also that the vitriolic ink will be made more durable, the Indian ink in some measure covering it, and defending it from the action of the air. In all cases, where Indian ink or other similar compositions are employed, cotton should be used in the inkstand, as already mentioned, to prevent the settling of the black powder." Since the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of printing much less attention than formerly has been paid to the making of ink, so that now the art seems to be in a great measure lost. This will appear from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of some ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> with the writings of modern times. It being of the utmost importance, however, that public records, wills, and other valuable papers, which cannot admit of being printed, should be written with ink of a durable quality, this inattention seems to have been very culpable, and a restoration of the method of making writing ink a very valuable acquisition. "The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> (says Mr Attle) of paying greater attention to this matter may readily be seen, by comparing the rolls and records that have been written from the 15th century to the end of the 17th, with the writings we have remaining of various writings from the 5th to the 12th centuries. Notwithstanding the superior antiquity of the latter, they are in excellent preservation; but we frequently find the former, though of more modern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>, so much defaced that they are scarcely legible." Our author agrees with Dr Lewis in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that that the ancient inks were composed of foot or ivory black instead of the galls, copperas, and gums, which form the composition of ours. Besides their black inks, however, the ancients used various other colours, as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, purple, &c. Green ink was frequently used in Latin manuscripts, especially in the latter ages; and it was frequently employed in signatures by the guardians of the Greek emperors till their wards were of age. Blue or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> ink was seldom used except in manuscripts; but (says Mr Attle) "the yellow has not been much in use, as far as we can learn, these 600 years." Some kinds of characters, particularly the metallic, were burnished. Wax was used by the Latins and Greeks as a varnish, but especially by the former, and particularly in the 9th century. It continued a long time in vogue. A treatise upon inks was published by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Canliarius professor of medicine at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; of which an edition was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1660. It is divided into six parts. The first treats of inks made from pyrites, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; the second of such as are made from metals and calces; the third from foot and vitriol; the fourth of the different kinds of inks used by the librarii or book-writers, by printers, and engravers; likewise of staining or writing upon marble, flucco, or scaliola, and of encatolic modes of writing; also of liquids for painting or colouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> or woollen cloth; restoring inks that had been decayed by time; together with many methods of effacing writing, restoring decayed paper, and different modes of secret writing. The fifth treats of writing inks made in different countries from gums, woods, the juices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, &c., as well as of different kinds of varnishes. The sixth treats of the different methods of extracting vitriol, and the chemical uses of it. Weckerus de Secretis, a treatise printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1612, contains a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of curious particulars concerning ink. He gives also receipts for making gold and silver inks, composed both with these metals and without them; directions for making inks for secret writing, and for defacing them; though in this last part there are many particulars bordering too much on the marvellous. In the Philosophical Transactions for 1787, Dr Blagden gives some account of a method of restoring decayed inks so as to render them legible. His experiments originated from a conversation with Mr Attle already quoted, on the question whether the inks make eight or ten centuries ago, and which are found to have preserved their colour very well, were made of the same materials now employed or not? In order to decide the question, Mr Attle furnished the doctor with several manuscripts on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a> from the 9th to the 15th centuries inclusively. Some of these were still very black; others of different shades, from a deep yellowish brown to a very pale yellow, in some parts to faint that it could scarcely be seen. This was tried with simple and phlogisticated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, the mineral acids, and infusion of galls. From these experiments it appeared that the ink anciently employed was of the same nature as at present: the letters turned of a reddish or yellowish brown with alkalies became pale, and were at length obliterated by the dilute mineral acids. The drop of acid liquor, which had been put upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, changed to a deep blue or green on the addition of phlogisticated alkalies; with an infusion of galls, in some cases the letters acquired a deep tinge, in others a slight one. "Hence says the doctor it is evident, that one of the ingredients was iron, which there is no reason to doubt was joined with the vitriolic acid; and the colour of the more perfect MSS. which in some was a deep black, and in others a purplish black, together with the restitution of that colour in those which had lost it by the infusion of galls, sufficiently proved that another of the ingredients was astringent matter, which from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> appears to have been that of galls. No trace of a black pigment of any sort was discovered; the drop of acid, which had completely extracted a letter, appearing of an uniform pale and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> colour, without an atom of black powder, or other extraneous matter floating in it." As this account differs very materially from the former extracted from Mr Attle's writings, so the reason given for the continuance of the colour differs so little. This, according to Dr Blagden, "seems to depend very much on a better preparation of the material upon which the writing was made, namely the parchment or vellum; the blackest letters being generally those which had sunk into it the deepest. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of effervescence was commonly to be perceived when acids were in contact with the surface of these old vellums. I was led, however, to suspect, that the ancient inks contained rather a less proportion of iron than the more modern; for, in general, the tinge of colour produced by the phlogisticated alkali in the acid laid upon them, seemed less deep; which, however, might depend in part upon the length of time they have been kept; and perhaps more gum was used in them, or they were walked over with some kind of varnish, though not such as gave any glofs." Among the specimens with which our author was favoured by Mr Attle, there was one which differed very materially from the rest. It was said to be a manuscript of the 15th century: the letters were of a full engraving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, angular without any fine strokes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and very black. None of the chemical solvents above mentioned seemed to produce any effect. Most of them seemed rather to make the letters blacker, probably by cleaning the surface; and the acids, after having been rubbed strongly upon the letters, did not strike any deeper tinge with the phlogisticated alkali. Nothing could obliterate these but what took off part of the vellum; when small rolls of a dirty matter were to be perceived. "It is therefore unquestionable (says the doctor) that no iron was used in this ink; and, from its resistance to the chemical solvents, as well as a certain clotted appearance in the letters when examined closely, and in some places a slight degree of glofs, I have little doubt that they were formed of a footy or carbonaceous powder and oil, probably something like our present printers' ink; and am not without suspicion that they were actually printed." On examining this MS. more fully, our author was convinced that it was really a part of a very ancient printed book. In considering the methods of restoring the legibility of decayed writings, our author observes, that perhaps one of the best may be to join phlogisticated alkali with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of iron which remains; because causè the precipitate formed by these two substances greatly exceeds that of the iron alone. On this subject Dr Blagden disagrees with Mr Bergmann; but to bring the matter to a test, the following experiments were made. 1. The phlogisticated alkali was rubbed in different quantities upon the bare writing. This, in general, produced little effect; though, in a few instances, it gave a bluish tinge to the letters, and increased their intensity; "probably (says the doctor) where something of an acid nature had contributed to the diminution of their colour." 2. By adding, besides the alkali, a dilute mineral acid to the writing, our author found his expectations fully answered; the letters then changing quickly to a very deep and beautiful blue. It is but of little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> whether the acid or phlogisticated alkali be first added; though upon farther consideration the doctor inclined to begin with the alkali. The reason is, that when the alkali is first put on, the colour seems to spread less, and thus not to hurt the legibility of the writing so much as would otherwise be done. His method is to spread the alkali thin over the writing with a feather, then to touch it as gently as possible upon or nearly over the letters with the diluted acid by means of a feather or bit of stick cut to a blunt point. The moment that the acid liquor is applied, the letters turn to a fine blue, beyond comparison stronger than the original trace of the letter; and by applying a bit of blotting-paper to soak up the superfluous liquid, we may in a great measure avoid the staining of the parchment: for it is this superfluous liquor which, absorbing part of the colouring matter from the letters, becomes a dye to whatever it touches. Care ought, however, to be taken not to allow the blotting paper to come in contact with the letters, because the colouring matter may easily be rubbed off while soft and wet. Any one of the three mineral acids will answer the purpose effectually. Dr Blagden commonly uses the marine. But whichever of the three is used, it ought to be diluted so far as not to be in danger of corroding the parchment; after which the degree of strength seems not to be a matter of great nicety. Another method of restoring the legibility of old writings is by wetting them with an infusion of galls in white wine: but this is subject to the same inconvenience with the former, and is besides less efficacious. The doctor is of opinion that the acid of the galls by itself would be better for the purpose than the infusion of the whole substance of them; and he thinks also that a preferable kind of phlogisticated alkali might be prepared either by purifying the common kind from iron as much as possible, or by making use of the volatile alkali instead of the fixed. Mr Aftle mentions a method of restoring the legibility of decayed writings; but says that it ought not to be hazarded lest a suspicion of deceit should arise. A method has been proposed of preventing ink from decaying by washing over the paper to be written upon with the colouring matter of Prussian blue, which will not deprave it in colour, or any other respect. By writing upon it with common ink afterwards, a ground of Prussian blue is formed under every stroke; and this remains strong after the black has been decayed by the weather, or destroyed by acids. Thus the ink will bear a larger proportion of vitriol at first, and will have the advantage of looking blacker when first written. Indian Ink, a valuable black for water-colours, brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and other parts of the East Indies, sometimes in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rolls, but more commonly in small quadrangular cakes, and generally marked with Chinese characters. Dr Lewis, from experiments made on this substance, hath shown that it is composed of fine lamp-black and animal glue: and accordingly, for the preparation of it, he desires us to mix the lamp-black with as much melted glue as is sufficient to give it a tenacity proper for being made into cakes; and these when dry, he tells us, answered as well as those imported from the East Indies, both with regard to the colour and the freedom of working. Ivory black, and other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> blacks, levigated to a great degree of fineness, answered as well as the lamp-black; but in the flake in which ivory-black is commonly sold, it proved much too gritty, and separated too hastily from the water. Printing Ink, is totally different from Indian ink, or that made use of in writing. It is an oily composition, of the consistence of an ointment: the method of preparing it was long kept a secret by those whose employment it was to make it, and who were interested in concealing it; and even yet is but imperfectly known. The properties of good printing ink are, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> clean and easily, without daubing the types, or tearing the paper; to have a fine black colour; to wash easily off the types; to dry soon; and to preserve its colour, without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> brown. This last, which is a most necessary property, is effectually obtained by setting fire to the oil with which the printing ink is made for a few moments, and then extinguishing it by covering the vessel (a). It is made to wash easily off the types, by using <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> as an ingredient; and its working clean depends on its having a proper degree of strength, which is given by a certain addition of rosin. A good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, however, depends on the proportion of the ingredients to each other; for if too much soap is added, the ink will work very foul, and daub the types to a great degree. The same thing will happen from using too much black, at the same time that both the soap and black hinder the ink from drying; while too much oil and rosin tear the paper, and hinder it from washing off.—The following receipt has been found to make printing ink of a tolerable good quality. "Take a Scots pint of linseed oil, and set it over a pretty brisk fire in an iron or copper vessel capable of holding three or four times as much. When it boils strongly, and emits a thick <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, kindle it with a piece of paper, and immediately take the vessel off the fire. Let the oil burn for about a minute; then extinguish it by covering the vessel; after it has grown (a) This is mentioned by Dr Lewis in his Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a> of Arts; but he seems not to have been acquainted with the method of giving it the other necessary properties. grown pretty cool, add two pounds of black rosin, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of hard soap cut into thin slices. If the oil is very hot when the soap is added, almost the whole mixture will run over the vessel. The mixture is then to be set again over the fire; and when the ingredients are thoroughly melted, a pound of lampblack, previously put through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> sieve, is to be stirred into it. The whole ought then to be ground on a marble <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or in a levigating mill. Though the above receipt is greatly superior to any that hath been hitherto published, all of which are capitally deficient in not mentioning the necessary ingredients of rosin and soap; yet it must be acknowledged, that ink made in this manner is inferior in point of colour, and is likewise more apt to daub the types and make an indistinct <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, than such as is prepared by some of those who make the manufacture of this commodity their employment; so that either a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in the proportion of the ingredients, a nicety in the mixture, or some additional ingredient, seems necessary to bring it to the requisite perfection. **Ink for the rolling Press**, is made of lintseed oil burnt in the same manner as that for common printing ink, and then mixed with Frankfort black, and finely ground. There are no certain proportions which can be determined in this kind of ink; every workman adding oil or black to his ink as he thinks proper, in order to make it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>.—Some, however, mix a portion of common boiled oil, which has never been burnt; but this must necessarily be a bad practice, as such oil is apt to go through the paper; a fault very common in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, especially if the paper is not very thick. No soap is added; because the ink is not cleared off from the copperplates with alkaline ley as in common printing, but with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> dipped in oil. Ink is also an appellation given to any coloured liquor used in writing. Different kinds of these inks may be prepared by the directions given under the article **Colour-Making**. **Sympathetic Ink**, a liquor with which a person may write, and yet nothing appear on the paper after it is dry, till some means are used, as holding the paper to the fire, rubbing it over with some other liquor, &c. These kinds of ink may be divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> classes, with respect to the means used to make them visible; viz. 1. Such as become visible by puffing another liquor over them, or by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> them to the vapour of that liquor. 2. Those that do not appear so long as they are kept <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, but soon become visible on being exposed to the air. 3. Such as appear by freezing or setting some very fine powder of any colour over them. 4. Those which become visible by being exposed to the fire. 5. Such as become visible by heat, but disappear again by cold or the moisture of the air. 6. Those which become visible by being wetted with water. 7. Such as appear of various colours. I. The first class contains four kinds of ink, viz. solutions of lead, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, gold, and green vitriol, or sulphate of iron. The first two become visible by the contact of sulphurous liquids or fumes. For the first, a solution of common sugar of lead in water answers very well. With this solution write with a clean pen, and the writing when dry will be totally invisible; but if it be wetted with a solution of bepar sulphuris, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>, dissolved by means of quicklime; or exposed to the strong vapours of these solutions, the writing will appear of a brown colour, more or less deep according to the strength of the sulphurous fume. By the same means the solution of nitrate of bismuth will appear of a deep black. The sympathetic ink prepared from gold depends on the property by which that metal precipitates from its solvent on the addition of a solution of tin. Write with a solution of gold in nitro-muriatic acid, and let the paper dry gently in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; nothing will appear for the first seven or eight hours. Dip a pencil in the solution of tin, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> it lightly over the invisible characters, they will immediately appear, of a purple colour. Characters written with a solution of green vitriol, will likewise be invisible when the paper is dry; but if wetted with an infusion of galls, they will immediately appear as if written with common ink. If, instead of this infusion, a solution of an alkaline prussiate be used, the writing will appear of a deep blue. II. To the second class belong the solutions of all those metals which are apt to attract <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> from the air, such as lead, bismuth, silver, &c. The sympathetic ink of gold already mentioned belongs also to this class; for if the characters written with it are long exposed to the air, they become by degrees of a deep violet colour, nearly approaching to black. In like manner, characters written with a solution of nitrate of silver are invisible when newly dried, but being exposed to the sun, appear of a gray colour like slate. To this class also belong solutions of sugar of lead, nitrates of copper and of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, acetate of iron, and muriate of tin. Each of these has a particular colour when exposed to the air; but they corrode the paper. III. The third class of sympathetic inks contains such liquids as have some kind of glutinous viscoity, and at the same time are long in drying; by which means, though the eye cannot discern the characters written with them upon paper, the powders strewed upon them immediately adhere, and thus make the writing become visible. Of this kind are urine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, the juices of some vegetables, weak solutions of the deliquescent salts, &c. IV. This class, comprehending all those that become visible by being exposed to the fire, is very extensive, as it contains all those colourless liquids in which the matter dissolved is capable of being reduced, or of reducing the paper, into a sort of charcoal by a small heat. Sulphuric acid diluted with as much water as will prevent it from corroding the paper makes a good ink of this kind. Letters written with this fluid are invisible when dry, but instantly on being held near the fire appear as black as if written with the finest ink. Juice of lemons or onions, a solution of sal-ammoniac, green vitriol, &c. answer the same purpose. V. The fifth class comprehends only a solution of muriate of cobalt; for the properties of which, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No. 1668, p. 627. VI. This class comprehends such inks as become visible when characters written with them are wetted with water. They are made of all such substances as deposit a copious sediment when mixed with water, dissolving only imperfectly in that fluid. Of this kind are Ink-stones are dried <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, sugar of lead, vitriol, &c. We have therefore only to write with a strong solution of these salts upon paper, and the characters will be invisible when dry; but when we apply water, the small portion of dried <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> cannot again be dissolved in the water. Hence the insoluble part becomes visible on the paper, and shows the characters written in white, gray, brown, or any other colour which the precipitate affumes. VII. Characters may be made to appear of a fine crimson, purple, or yellow, by writing on paper with solution of muriate of tin, and then paling over it a pencil dipped in a decoction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>-wood, logwood, yellow wood, &c. Ink Stones, a kind of small round stones, of a white, red, gray, yellow, or black colour, containing a quantity of native martial vitriol, whence they derive the property of making ink, and from thence their name. They are almost entirely soluble in water, and besides their other ingredients, contain also a portion of copper and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>.

INLAND

Pages 289-289

a name for any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> at a distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Inland <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>. See Canal and (Inland) Navigation. Inland Trade, that kind of trade carried on between the different parts of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, whether over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by means of inland navigation. Inlaying. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENEERING">Veneering</a>, Mosaic, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARQUETRY">Marquetry</a>. Inleased, in our old writers, signifies entangled or ensnared. It is used in the champion's oath. Inlisting, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. See Listing. Inmates, such persons as are admitted for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, to live in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or cottage with another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in different rooms, but going in at the same door; being usually supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and not able to maintain a whole house themselves. These are inquirable in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-leet.—No owner or occupier of a cottage shall suffer any inmates therein, or more families than one to inhabit there, on pain of forfeiting 10s. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the leet.

INN

Pages 289-290

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> appointed for the entertainment and relief of travellers. Inns are licensed and regulated by justices of the peace, who oblige the landlord to enter into recognizances for keeping good order. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a person who keeps a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> inn, refuses to receive a traveller into his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> as a guest, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to find him victuals and lodging on his tendering a reasonable price for them, he is liable to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of damages, and may be indicted and fined at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> of all commodities sold by innkeepers, according to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> laws, may be inflicted; and innkeepers not selling their hay, oats, beans, &c., and all manner of victuals, at reasonable prices, without taking anything for litter, may be fined and imprisoned, &c. by 21 Jac. I. c. 21. Where an innkeeper harbours thieves, persons of infamous character, or suffers any disorders in his house, or sets up a new inn where there is no need of one, to the hinderance of ancient and well governed inns, he is indictable and fineable; and by statute, such inn may be suppressed. Action upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> lies against any innkeeper, if a theft be committed on his guest by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the inn, or any other person not belonging to the guest; though it is otherwise where the guest is not a traveller, but one of the same town or village, for there the innkeeper is not chargeable; nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of a private tavern answerable for a robbery committed on his guest; it is said, that even though the travelling guest does not deliver his goods, &c., into the innkeeper's possession, yet if they are stolen, he is chargeable. An innkeeper is not answerable for anything out of his inn, but only for such as are within it; yet, where he of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> puts the guest's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to graze, and the horse is stolen, he is answerable, he not having the guest's orders for putting such horse to graze. The innkeeper may justify the stopping of the horse, or other thing of his guest, for his reckoning, and may retain the same till it be paid. Where a person brings his horse to an inn, and leaves him in the stable, the innkeeper may detain him till such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as the owner pays for his keeping; and if the horse eats out as much as he is worth, after a reasonable appraisement made, he may sell the horse and pay himself; but when a guest brings several horses to an inn, and afterwards takes them all away except one, this horse so left may not be sold for payment of the debt for the others; for every horse is to be sold, only to make satisfaction for what is due for his own meat. Inns. Our colleges of municipal or common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> professors and students, are called inns: the old English word for houses of noblemen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and others of extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, being of the same signification with the French word hotels. Inns of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> are so called, as some think, because the students there are to serve and attend the courts of judicature; or else, because anciently these colleges received none but the sons of noblemen, and better sort of gentlemen, who were here to be qualified to serve the king in his court; as Fortescue affirms. And, in his time, he says, there were about 2000 students in the inns of court and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, all of whom were filii nobilium, or gentlemen born. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has gradually fallen into disuse; so that in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> does not reckon above 1000 students, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> at present is very considerably less; for which Judge Blackstone assigns the following reasons. 1. Because the inns of chancery, being now almost totally filled by the inferior branches of the profession, are neither commodious nor proper for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of gentlemen of any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; so that there are very rarely any young students entered at the inns of chancery. 2. Because in the inns of court all sorts of regimen and academical superintendence, either with regard to morals or studies, are found impracticable, and therefore entirely neglected. Lastly, because persons of birth and fortune, after having finished their usual courses at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, have seldom leisure or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> sufficient to enter upon a new scheme of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at a new place of instruction; wherefore few gentlemen now resort to the inns of court, but such for whom the knowledge of practice is absolutely necessary in such as are intended for the profession. Our inns of court, justly famed for the production of men of learning in the law, are governed by masters, principals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCHERS">benchers</a>, stewards, and other officers; and have public halls for exercises, readings, &c., which which the students are obliged to attend and perform for a certain number of years, before they can be admitted to plead at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. These <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> have not, however, any judicial authority over their members; but instead of this they have certain orders among themselves, which have by consent the force of laws. For <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> offences persons are only excommunicated, or put out of commons; for greater, they lose their chambers, and are expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; and when once expelled out of one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, they are never received by any of the others. The gentlemen in these societies may be divided into benchers, outer-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRISTERS">barristers</a>, inner-barristers, and students. The four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inns of court, are the Inner Temple and Middle Temple, heretofore the dwelling of the Knights <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPLARS">Templars</a>, purchased by some professors of the common law about 300 years ago; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn and Gray's Inn, anciently belonging to the earls of Lincoln and Gray. The other inns are the two Sergeants Inns. Inns of Chancery were probably so called, because anciently inhabited by such clerks as chiefly studied the forming of writs, which regularly belonged to the curitors, who are officers of chancery. The first of these is Thavies Inn, begun in the reign of Edward III. and since purchased by the society of Lincoln's Inn. Beside this, we have New Inn, Symond's Inn, Clement's Inn, Clifford's Inn, anciently the house of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clifford; Staple Inn, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of the staple; Lion's Inn, anciently a common inn with the sign of the lion; Furnival's Inn, and Bernard's Inn. These were heretofore preparatory colleges for younger students; and many were entered here, before they were admitted into the inns of court. Now they are mostly taken up by attorneys, solicitors, &c. They all belong to some of the inns of court, who formerly used to send yearly some of their barristers to read to them.

INNATE IDEAS

Pages 290-290

those supposed to be stamped on the mind, from the first moment of its existence, and which it constantly brings into the world with it: a doctrine which Mr Locke has taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to refute. INNERKEITHING. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERKEITHING">INVERKEITHING</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INNERLOCHY">INNERLOCHY</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERLOCHY">INVERLOCHY</a> and FORT-WILLIAM. INNIS. See Inch.

INNISCLOCHRAN

Pages 290-290
or the STONEY ISLAND, an island in Lough Ree, in the river Shannon, between the counties of Westmeath and Roscommon, at which place a monastery was founded by St Dermond, about the beginning of the 6th century.

INNISFALLEN

Pages 290-290

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILLARNEY">Killarney</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>: in it are the ruins of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, founded by St Finian, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> saint of these parts, and to him the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Aghadoe is also dedicated. The remains of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> are very extensive, its situation romantic and retired. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of religious houses, the possessions of this abbey were granted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Robert Collam. The island contains about 12 acres, is agreeably wooded, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fruit-trees. St Finian flourished about the middle of the 6th century; he was surnamed in Irish Lobhar, his father's name was Conail the son of Eochaidh; descended from Kian the son of Alld, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Munster. There was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> kept in this abbey, which is frequently cited by Sir J. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">Ware</a> and other antiquaries under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Annals of Innisfallen. They contain a sketch of universal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the world to the year 430 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thereabouts, but from thence the annalist has amply enough prosecuted the affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to his own times. He lived to the year 1215. Sir J. Ware had a copy of them, whereof there is an imperfect transcript among the MSS. of the library of Trinity-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. They were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to the year 1320. Bishop Nicholas, in his Irish historical library, informs us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Chandos had a complete copy of them down to 1320 in his possession. These annals tell us, that in the year 1180, the abbey, which had at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver and richest goods of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> deposited in it, as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of greatest security, was plundered by Mildwin son of Daniel O'Donoghue, as was also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Ardert, and many persons were slain in the very cemetery by the MacCarthys; but God, as it is laid in this chronicle, punished this impiety by the untimely end of some of the authors of it.

INNISHANNON

Pages 290-290

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, 134 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANDON">Bandon</a>, and six miles from Kinfaile. The river is navigable to Collier's quay, about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> below the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. On the west side of the town is a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. This place was formerly walled, and of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, as appears by the foundations of several castles and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> buildings discovered in it. The town of Innishannon, together with its ferry, were granted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRY">Barry</a> by Henry V. by letters patent, anno 1412.

INNISHIRKAN

Pages 290-290

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> situated between <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Clear island and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALTIMORE">Baltimore</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>. In this island stood the castle of Dunelong, possessed by the O'Driscolls, which was surrendered after the defeat of the Spaniards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Hervey on 23rd Feb. 1602. There was afterwards a regular fortification erected on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island, which was garrisoned in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but it has been for several years dismantled; about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> to the south are the remains of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, founded 1460, for Franciscans, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> O'Driscoll. This island has very good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and is vastly preferable to that of Cape Clear island. To the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Innishirkan island lies Hare island, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fruitful spot; and near it are four small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called the Schemes: also along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, in the following order from east to west, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a> island, containing 100 acres; Castle island, containing 119 acres; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> island, containing 316 acres; and west of all these is a small spot called Goat island. All these islands, together with the adjacent coast, produce large crops of fine English barley.

INNISKILLING INNISKILLING

Pages 290-291

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Fermanagh and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, lying between three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. It is about 24 miles east of Bal- lyhannon, and 79 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> giving <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of vicount to the family of Cole. Its inhabitants distinguished themselves in several considerable engagements in the wars of Ireland at the revolution, out of which a regiment of dragoons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the title of the Inniskillers, was mostly formed. They form the 6th regiment of dragoons in the British <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>.

INNISPAIL

Pages 290-290

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> names of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, so denominated from Bheal, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> among the ancient inhabitants of the British isles. Innispail has been erroneously translated the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">Destiny</a>, as Bheal was sometimes taken for Fate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>.

INNOCENT'S DAY

Pages 291-291

a festival of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, observed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 28, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the massacre of the innocent children by the command of Herod <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Judea. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; and Jews, No. 24 par. ult. The Greek church in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDAR">kalendar</a>, and the Abyssinians of Ethiopia in their offices, commemorate 14,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> on this occasion.

INNUENDO

Pages 291-291

is a word frequently used in writs, declarations, and pleadings, to ascertain a person <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thing which was named, but left doubtful, before; as, he (innuendo the plaintiff) did so and so: mention being before made of another person.—In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> conversation or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, an innuendo denotes an oblique hint or distant reference, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and positive <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>.

INO

Pages 291-291

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONIA">Harmonia</a>, who nursed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. She married Athamas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thesbes, after he had divorced Nephele, by whom he had two children Phryxus and Helle. Ino became mother of Melicerta and Learchus; and soon conceived an implacable hatred against the children of Nephele, because they were to ascend the throne in preference to her own. Phryxus and Helle were informed of Ino's machinations, and they escaped to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> ram. Juno, jealous of Ino's prosperity, resolved to disturb her peace; and more particularly because she was of the descendants of her greatest enemy, Venus. Tiphione was sent by order of Juno to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Athamas; and she filled the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> with such fury, that Athamas taking Ino to be a hones and her children whelps, pursued her and dashed her son Learchus against a wall. Ino escaped from the fury of her husband; and from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock she threw herself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with Melicerta in her arms. The gods pitied her fate; and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> made her a sea deity, which was afterwards called Leucothoe. Melicerta became also a sea god, known by the name of Palemon.

INOA

Pages 291-291

festivals in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Ino, celebrated yearly with sports and sacrifices at Corinth. An anniversary sacrifice was also offered to Ino at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, where she was first worshipped under the name of Leucothoe.—Another in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the same. It was usual at the celebration to throw cakes of flour into a pond, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they sunk were prelages of prosperity, but if they swam on the surface of the waters they were inauspicious and very unlucky.

INOCARPUS

Pages 291-291

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the deciduous class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

INOCULATION

Pages 291-293

in a physical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used for the transplantation of dippers from one subject to another, particularly for the cagraftment of the smallpox; which, though of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the eastern countries, is but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> practice among us, at least under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of art. It is well observed by the baron Dimsdale, that accident hath furnished the art of medicine with many valuable hints, and some of its greatest improvements have been received from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and barbarism. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is remarkably exemplified in the practice of inoculation of the smallpox: but to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the British physicians, they measured not the value of this practice by the means of its origin, but by its real importance and utility; they patronized a barbarous discovery with no less zeal and affection than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it had been their own. Indeed the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> might be said to have adopted the practice; for the greatest encouragement it by becoming examples, and the wisest were determined by the general event of the method. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which the art of inoculating for the smallpox was first formed, are equally unknown. Accident probably gave rise to it. Pylarini says, that among the Turks it was not attended to except amongst the meaner sort. Dr Ruffel informs us in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. lviii. p. 142, that no mention is made of it by any of the ancient Arabian medical writers that are known in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and the physicians who are natives in and about <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> assert, that nothing is to be found regarding it in any of those of a more modern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>. He farther says, that he engaged some of his learned Turkish friends to make inquiry; but they did not discover any thing on this subject of inoculation either in the writings of physicians, historians, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> poets. Until the beginning of the 18th century, all the accounts we have of inoculating the smallpox are merely traditional. The silence on this subject, observed amongst writers in the countries where the practice obtained, Dr Ruffel supposes, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, to be owing to the physicians there never countenancing or engaging in it. It is also remarkable, that before Pylarini's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in 1701, nor yet for several years after, this practice is not noticed by any of the most inquisitive travellers. On this Dr Ruffel very justly observes, that customs, the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in distant countries, are often the least apt to attract the observation of travellers, who, engaged in other pursuits, must be indebted to accident for the knowledge of such things as the natives seldom talk of, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that they are known to all the world. The first accounts we have in the learned world concerning inoculation, are from two Italian physicians, viz. Pylarini and Timoni, whose letters on the subject may be seen in the Phil. Trans. abridged, vol. v. p. 370, &c. The first is dated A.D. 1701; the next is dated A.D. 1713. Whether our inquiries are extended abroad or confined to our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, inoculation hath been practised under one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> or other time immemorial; in Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and its adjacent isles we have well authenticated accounts, extending farther backward than any from the continent. Dr Williams of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAVERFORDWEST">Haverfordwest</a>, who wrote upon inoculation in 1725, proves, that it had been practised in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, though in a form somewhat different, time out of mind. Mr Wright, a surgeon, Inoculation in the same place, says, that buying the smallpox is both a common practice, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> standing in that neighbourhood. He says, that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKESHIRE">Pembrokeshire</a> there are two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> villages near the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILFORD">Milford</a>, more famous for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> than any other, viz. St Ithmael's and Marloes. The old inhabitants of these villages say, that it hath been a common practice; and that one William Allen of St Ithmael's, who in 1722 was 90 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, declared to some persons of good sense and integrity, that this practice was used all his time; that he well remembered his mother telling him, that it was a common practice all her time, and that she got the smallpox that way; so that at least we go back 160 years or more. In the Highlands of Scotland and some of the adjacent isles, Dr Alexander Monro senior informs us, that the custom through ages past hath been, to put their children to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> with those who laboured under a favourable smallpox, and to tie worsted threads about their children's wrists, after having drawn them through variolous pustules. According to the result of Dr Ruffell's inquiries, the Arabians assert, that the inoculation of the smallpox has been the common custom of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and that they have no doubt of its being as ancient as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> itself. It is remarkable, that buying the smallpox is the name universally applied in all countries to the method of procuring the disease: it is true that there are other terms; but in Wales and Arabia, as well as many other countries, this is the usual appellation. From the sameness of the name, and the little diversity observable in the manner of performing the operation, it is probable that the practice of inoculation in these countries was originally derived from the same source. From its extensive spread, it is probably of great antiquity too. In the year 1717, Lady <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Wortley Montague, wife of the English <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> at Constantinople, had her son inoculated there at the age of five years; he had but few pustules, and soon recovered. In April 1721, inoculation was successfully tried on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> condemned criminals in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, by permission of his majesty. In 1722, Lady Mary Wortley Montague had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of five years old inoculated in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; soon after which, the children of the royal family that had not had the smallpox were inoculated with success; then followed some of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and the practice soon prevailed. And here we date the commencement of inoculation under the direction of art. From the example of the royal family in England, the practice was adopted in Germany, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and its adjacent countries. After Mr Maitland had succeeded with those he had inoculated in and about London, he introduced the practice into Scotland in the year 1726. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> soon followed the example of the British. Russia lately engaged one of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> promoters and improvers of this art. And now there are not many countries that do not more or less practise it. Different Modes of Inoculation. The practice of inoculation having obtained in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world, it may be grateful, at least to curiosity, to have a general account of the different modes that are and have been adopted in that practice. Inoculation with the blood of variolous patients hath been tried without effect; the variolous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> only produces the variolous disease. The application of the variolous matter takes place in a sensible part only; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of the virus is such, that the smallest atom, though imperceptible to any of our senses, conveys the disease as well as the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. Hence the most obvious method is the prick of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> or the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCET">lancet</a> dipped in the matter of a variolous pustule. Cotton or thread is used, that is previously rubbed with powdered variolous scabs; this thread is drawn with a needle through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTIS">cutis</a>, but not left in. This is the method in some parts of the East Indies. The Indians <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the thread on the outside of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, between any of the fingers, or between the forefinger and thumb. The Thesalian women inoculate in the forehead and chin. Some abrade the scarf-skin, and rub in the powdered dry scabs which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the pustules of patients with the smallpox. Many of the Greek women make an oblique puncture with a needle, on the middle of the top of the forehead, on each cheek, the chin, each metacarpus, and each metatarsus; then drop in each a little of the pus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> taken warm from a patient, and brought in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>'s bosom. Others in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> make several little wounds with a needle in one, two, or more places, in the skin, till some drops of blood exude; then the operator pours a drop of warm pus fresh from a pustule, and mixes it with the blood as it issues out; then the wound is covered by some with a bandage, by others with half a walnut shell placed with its concave side over each orifice. The Chinese convey a pellet of variolated cotton, with the addition of a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, into the nostrils of the patient; they collect dry pustules, and keep them in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> bottle well corked; and when they inoculate, they mix a grain of musk with three or four grains of the dry scales, and roll them in cotton. This method may be called inodoration. About <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, in the East Indies, the person who intends to be inoculated, having found a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> where there is a good fort of the smallpox, goes to the bed of the sick person, if he is old enough; or if a child, to one of his relations, and speaks to him as follows: "I am come to buy the smallpox." The answer is, "Buy if you please." A sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is accordingly given, and one, three, or four pustules, for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> must always be odd, and not exceeding five, extracted whole, and full of matter. These are immediately rubbed on the skin of the outside of the hand between the forefinger and the thumb; and this suffices to produce the disease. The same custom obtains in Algiers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and other countries. Very similar to the custom among the people about Bengal, &c., is that in Arabia, where on some flethly part they make several punctures with a needle imbued in variolous matter, taken from a pustule of a favourable kind. Here they buy the smallpox too, as follows: the child to be inoculated carries a few raisins, dates, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-plums, or such like; and showing them to the child from whom the matter is to be taken, asks how many pocks he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> give in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>? The bargain being made, they proceed to the operation; but this buying, though still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, is not thought necessary. necessary to the success of the operation. The Arabs say that any flabby part is proper; but generally they infert the matter between the fore-finger and thumb on the outside of the hand. The Georgians infert the matter on the fore-arm. The Armenians introduce the matter on the two thighs. In Wales the practice may be termed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INFRACTION">infraction</a> of the smallpox. There some of the dry pustules are procured by purchase, and are rubbed hard upon the naked arm or leg.

INQUISITION

Pages 293-294

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, a tribunal in several Roman Catholic countries, erected by the popes for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of heretics. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> was founded in the 12th century by Father Dominic and his followers, who were sent by Pope Innocent III. with orders to excite the Catholic princes and people to extirpate heretics, to search into their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and to transmit a faithful account thereof to Rome. Hence they were called inquisitors; and this gave birth to the formidable tribunal of the inquisition, which was received in all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the dominions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and the Low Countries. This diabolical tribunal takes cognizance of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, Judaism, Mahometanism, sodomy, and polygamy; and the people stand in so much fear of it, that parents deliver up their children, husbands their wives, and masters their servants, to its officers, without daring in the least to murmur. The prisoners are kept for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, till they themselves turn their own accusers, and declare the cause of their imprisonment; for they are neither told their crime nor confronted with witnesses. As soon as they are imprisoned, their friends go into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>, and speak of them as dead, not daring to solicit their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, lest they should be brought in as accomplices. When there is no shadow of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against the pretended criminal, he is discharged, after suffering the most cruel tortures, a tedious and dreadful imprisonment, and the loss of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his effects. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> against the prisoners is pronounced publicly, and with extraordinary solemnity. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, they erect a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> capable of holding 3000 persons; in which they <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> a rich altar, and raise seats on each side in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. There the prisoners are placed; and over against them is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, whither they are called, one by one, to hear their doom, from one of the inquisitors. These unhappy people know what they are to suffer by the clothes they wear that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Those who appear in their own clothes are discharged upon payment of a fine; those who have a santo benito, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> strict <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> coat without sleeves, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with St. Andrew's crofs, have their lives, but forfeit all their effects: those who have the resemblance of flames made of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>, sewed upon their santo benito, without any crofs, are pardoned, but threatened to be burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> ever they relapse: but those who, besides these flames, have on their santo benito their own <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, surrounded with figures of devils, are condemned to expire in the flames. The inquisitors, who are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, do not pronounce the sentence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but form and read an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, in which they say, that the criminal being convicted of such a crime, by his own confession, is with much reluctance delivered to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> power to be punished according to his demerits: and this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> they give to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> judges who at- tend at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side of the altar, who immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> sentence. For the conclusion of this horrid <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, see Act of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>.

INSCRIBED

Pages 294-294

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is said to be inscribed in another, when all its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> touch the side <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> planes of the other figure.

INSCRIPTION

Pages 294-294

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> affixed to any thing, to give some farther knowledge of it, or to tran- mit some important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> to posterity. Antiquaries are very curious in examining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> found on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and other monuments of antiquity. Sanchoniathon, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a>, as it is said, with Gideon, drew most of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> whereof his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is composed from inscriptions which he found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and on columns, both among the Heathens and the Hebrews. It appears, indeed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> engraved upon pillars the principles of sciences, as well as the history of the world. Those mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> show, that this was the first way of instructing people, and of transmitting histories and sciences to posterity. This is confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> in his Hippias; wherein he says, that Pittistratus engraved on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-pillars precepts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>- ful for husbandmen. Pliny affirms us, that the first public monuments were made of plates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>; and that the treaties of confederacy concluded be- tween the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and the Jews were written upon plates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; that (says he) the Jews might have something to put them in mind of the peace and con- federacy concluded with the Romans. The Greeks and Romans were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dealers in inscriptions, and were extremely fond of being mentioned in them: and hence it is, that we find so many in those countries of ancient learning, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> volumes have been com- posed, as the collection of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GRUTER">Gruter</a>, &c. Since Gruter's collection, Th. Reinfeius has compiled another huge volume of inscriptions. M. Fabrety published ano- ther volume at Rome in 1669, wherein he has correc- ted abundance of errors which had escaped Gruter, Rei- nfeius, and other antiquaries, &c. and added a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inscriptions omitted by them.—Since all these, Grevis has published a complete collection of inscriptions, in three vols. folio.

INSCRUTABLE

Pages 294-294

UNSEARCHABLE, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, is usually understood of the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and the judgments of God, which cannot be found out, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> into which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> reason cannot penetrate. Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>. See Academy.

INSECTS

Pages 294-297

INSECTA, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a smaller sort of animals, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed to be exanguious; and distinguished by certain incisions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in- dentings in their bodies. The word is originally La- tin, formed of in, and feco "I cut;" the reason of which is, that in some of this tribe, as ants, the body seems to be cut or divided into two; or because the bodies of many, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, caterpillars, &c. are com- posed of different circles, or rings, which are a sort of incision. See Entomology. Noxious Insects; Means of destroying them, or pre- venting their Increase. The following remedies we find collected in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> for Octo- ber 1790.—Of those substances which have been gen- erally observed to be efficacious in driving away or in destroying insects, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, and its various preparations, may be reckoned one of the most generally useful. Sulphur is also useful. Oils of all kinds have been of- ten and deservedly recommended. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a> is not less remarkable for its utility. Of the application of these in order. 1. Mercury is known to kill or drive away <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body; and it may probably be of equal ef- ficacy in ridding other animals of their insects.
