For instance, sheep having a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of mercurial ointment rubbed on their skins, on the sides, between the fore-legs and the body, it may kill or drive away the insect peculiar to them. Sulphur is recommended to be added to the mercurial ointment. Thus not only the insect peculiar to them, but also the fleas, may be cured: See the Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for the Encourage- ment of Arts, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, vol. vii. viii. p. 90. In the Transactions of the same society, vol. vi. vi. p. 59. Mr. Alway directed that, in the winter, the walls, frames, &c. of his green and hot-houses should be well washed with the following mixture: Take of corrosive subli- mate mercury four ounces, and dissolve it in two gal- lons of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. These houses had been greatly infested with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> spiders and ants. After having been washed with the above mixture, neither were to be seen next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. This wash may be used on old garden-walls, and to the roots of fruit-trees infested with insects, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> made weaker. It may destroy the tender leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, though not the roots. This wash <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> effectual- ly destroy all disagreeable insects the bugs, and all other insects of a tender cuticle; and it will not in the least hurt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-furniture or hangings. Care must be taken, that the wash be applied into every cre- vice or folding of the furniture with a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. It will sometimes be necessary to repeat the wash, as some of the ova of bugs may remain concealed, not- withstanding the utmost care. Some of the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> were much infested with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ants, which greatly hurt the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes. The remedy was, to dissolve corrosive sublimate mer- cury in rum, in the proportion of two drams to a pint of spirits. This solution was poured on dry powdered sugar; and when the sugar was dried, it was laid in the paths of the ants. They ate it, and were destroyed. Might not this practice be imitated, by laying sugar thus prepared on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> or pieces of thin boards near the roots of fruit-trees infested by insects, espe- cially when the fruit is ripening? The papers or boards might be taken in during the night, or when it rained. The sugar should be coloured with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, or other substance, thereby to mark it as a substance to be avoided by curious idlers. 2. We are informed that a person in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a> em- ployed brimstone in the following manner. Having cleared all round the roots of trees infested with cater- pillars or other insects, he threw some flour of brim- <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> round the roots, and covered it with a thin sprinkling of fine mould, that it might not be blown away by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, yet so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> might operate through, and cause the brimstone to fumigate. Thus he destroyed the caterpillars. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> he found sufficient for 200 trees. In that hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> the sun may Insects may perhaps have that effect; but it scarcely will in this. He also employed sulphur in the following manner to drive insects from tall trees. He split the end of a pole, and put in the slit some matches, let them on fire, and held them under the parts of the trees chiefly affected. A pole thus armed, he found, would answer for three or four trees. Brimstone thus mixed with damp straw, and set on fire, for instance, in hop-ground infested with the fly, might be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to drive away the fly. The itch is supposed to proceed from a very small insect which nettles under the skin, and proceeds no farther into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; and is therefore attended with no dangerous consequences. Brimstone made into an ointment with hogs-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> is a sure remedy. Sheep are liable to an eruption on the skin, known by the name of the scab. The brimstone, when added to the mercurial ointment recommended for that disorder in the Transactions of the Society for the Encouragement of Arts, vol. vii. p. 90, might perhaps render the application more efficacious and less dangerous. 3. The natives of hot countries are taught by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that an unctuous covering on their bodies prevents the bites of mosquitoes and all gnats. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> inhabitants in such countries are not sufficiently careful in preventing the least stagnant water near their dwellings, in which the mosquitoes are bred; even in the waste water thrown out they are produced. Dr Franklin, by a careful <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to this circumstance, guarded his family in Philadelphia from such insects: one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> seeing a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of mosquitoes in his library, he found on inquiry, that one of his servants had taken the cover off a tub placed near his window for receiving <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-water. On such an occasion the remedy is easy, viz. shutting the room up for the day, so that the mosquitoes cannot come at any water, in which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they die. Though this caution may seem trifling to us who live in a mild climate, it is far otherwise in hot countries. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">Oil</a> being known to be most efficacious in destroying insects, may not the use of it be extended to the destruction of worms in the bowels of horses, where they may occasion the violent pain they seem sometimes to suffer? If the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> was for some time kept fasting, and a large quantity of oil, suppose a pint, was given, if worms are the cause, the oil may in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> kill them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">Flowers</a>, leaves, and fruit, on plants, are known to be devoured by caterpillars. These are destroyed by oils, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the lateral pores by which they breathe. For this purpose it is advised, that, on the approach of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, a cloth dipped in train oil be laid on such parts of the tree in which there is the least appearance of them. We are informed in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Society of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, that oil of turpentine, when applied to animals which were covered with insects, destroyed the insects without hurting the animal. The author tried it on several trees, mixed with fine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> so as to incorporate them well, then adding water, still stirring them carefully till the whole was brought to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fluidity. In this mixture he dipped branches of fruit-trees on which there were insects, and hereby destroyed not only the eggs but also the insects, without hurting the leaves. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> may be got off by washing, or the first heavy shower. From these experiments the author thinks, that oil of turpentine may with equal efficacy be employed for killing various kinds of lice on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals. We are informed, in the Transactions of the Society for the Encouragement of Arts, vol. v. p. 45, that Mr Winter, among other experiments on turnip-feed, steeped the seed 24 hours in a sufficient quantity of train oil. He then drained the oil from the feed, which he mixed with a quantity of fine sifted earth, and immediately sowed it in drills. When the plants began to appear on the surface, the ground was fown with foot. He found that feed steeped in lintseed oil answered equally well. The turnips the least injured by the fly were those that grew from seed steeped as above, which grew so luxuriantly as to produce rough leaves several days <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the most flourishing of any of his other experiments, and were the better enabled to withstand the fly's attack. The leaves of these turnips were of a darker green, and appeared twice as thick in bulk and luxuriancy than the other turnips, and were a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> larger. The seed was drilled an inch and a half deep, and at a foot distance in the rows. Train oil is apt to kill the leaves of plants which have been injured by insects, but lintseed oil has not that effect, though equally destructive to the insects. The train oil seems to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> both as an oil, and by its disagreeable smell it prevents insects approaching it. In this respect it may be successfully used to prevent field mice or other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> preying on acorns, chestnuts, or other seeds steeped in it before they are fown. When thus giving directions for preventing the fly on turnips, a late experiment should be mentioned, by the disclosing of which a person gained a considerable reward. His secret was, running a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a> over the ground early in the morning, while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> remained on the ground, on the first appearance of the fly. The dew entangled the flies so much, that they could not make their escape, and were therefore crushed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. As the roller may leave the surface of the earth too hard, some very properly advise to fix some boughs of elder in a gate or hurdle, to be drawn over the field; and if the boughs had been before fumigated with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of tobacco, or tincture of saltpeter, the success would be the surer. The most certain method of preventing the hurt done by the fly is to raise the plants in a nursery, and at a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> to transplant them, being carried to the ground in a wheel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">barrow</a> filled with manure softened with water so as to admit the plants. This method will secure their more speedy growth. In the nursery the attack of the fly may be prevented by sprinkling foot or quicklime on the ground. The utility of transplanting turnips is evident by the practice of transplanting the turnip-rooted cabbage. They who are discouraged from this practice by the expense attending it, do not reflect that the hoeing is prevented, and the plants grow the better, being fed in fresh earth. 3. Before proceeding to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the use of the last means mentioned, viz. tobacco, for destroying insects in turnips, it may be proper to mention an experiment made by Mr Green, of her majesty's flower-garden at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEW">Kew</a>. He contrived a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of bellows, similar to that employed in recovering people seemingly drowned. It has Insects have a cavity in the nozzle, in which some tobacco is put, with a live coal over it. The bellows being then worked, the tobacco is set on fire, and the smoke is directed to any particular spot. A lady was fond of having the mokrofe in her dressing-room, but was prevented having it on account of the green insects which constantly adhere to that plant. To remedy this inconvenience, Mr Green had a box made large enough to contain a pot in which a plant of the mokrofe grew. In one end of the box was a hole, to admit the nozzle of the bellows; the bellows was worked, and the smoke was received into the box. When the tobacco was consumed, the nozzle was withdrawn, and a cork being put into the hole, the box thus remained till morning, when the insects were all laid dead on the earth. Being swept off, the plant was in a state fit for a dressing-room. Many plants thus infected with insects may be too large, or otherwise so placed as not to be put into a box. In this case it occurred to the writer of these observations, that being sprinkled with an infusion of tobacco in water might in some degree answer the same purpose. On <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> he found it answered, and he thus freed other plants of their insects. He also used it on trees of easy access with advantage. Train oil is so inimical to tender plants or leaves, that it destroys them if insects have in the least hurt them; whereas the infusion, instead of killing the leaves, promoted a fresh vegetation. Fruit trees often become the prey of insects. Those against a wall, or in espaliers, being easily come at, much of the mischief may be prevented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the leaves so soon as they are observed to be curled; for then fresh eggs are laid on them, probably by butterflies. If sprinkled with the infusion of tobacco, it will prevent their coming to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. After the fruit is formed, the infusion must not be used, lest the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell may remain. The fellifers are then the proper remedies, which ladies may employ as amusement, and may thereby prevent fruit to their friends of their own preserving. A lye of the ash of plants sprinkled on the leaves may have a good effect, as also on other pot-herbs, which are often the prey of caterpillars. As many insects, besides those bred on the leaves or in the walls, may destroy the fruit, the sugar with the corrosive sublimate, as already described, may be laid in the way of other insects, to which it will prove a speedy death. Diligent inspection into their retreats is the most certain means of preventing the loss sustained by snails. Ants are prevented rising up the trees, by laying round the roots powdered chalk, or any other substance which by entangling their feet prevents their crawling it. Care should be taken to destroy their nests everywhere near the garden. Hops are now become an article of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, that it deserves our particular attention. Early in its growth, when the vines begin to ascend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> fly preys on its leaves, frequently in such numbers as, by destroying the leaves, to interrupt the vegetation, much of the food of plants being absorbed by the leaves. The infusion of tobacco destroys them, or at least drives them away so effectually, that a plant almost totally stripped of its leaves has put out fresh leaves after the use of it. If care be not taken, they will again <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the fresh leaves. As the flies lodge on the lower side of the leaves, they are protected from storms of rain, and therefore the infusion must be driven upwards by a forcing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>. As it is said that the expense of tobacco is too great, perhaps lime-water, or even water by itself, driven strongly against the leaves, might drive them away. The labour attending such experiments in a large plantation discourages others, without reflecting, that, if such means are used early, the flies may more easily be got rid of. Free ventilation is undoubtedly beneficial to all plants; and hence perhaps the particular advantages of drilling corn in rows a little distant. If alleys somewhat larger than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> were made in the plantations of hops, there might be sufficient spaces left where the alleys <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> one another to admit of setting damp straw, or other materials mixed with brimstone, foot, &c., on fire. Smoke itself is said to prevent the fly; and if it, it will still act more powerfully when mixed with such materials. It has been observed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, that the hops grow naturally among heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> or fragments of rocks. They therefore advise to cover the ground round their roots with stones, which will prevent the insects laying their eggs near the roots in the ground, where they lay them to be protected during the winter. The stones will also preserve moisture at the roots during the summer. A rope cannot be drawn across a plantation of hops, as it can across a field of corn, in case of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILDEW">mildew</a>. Here water to wash off the clammy juice that entices and feeds insects seems to be the only remedy. The plantation being well ventilated, may at least prevent the frequency of it. The forcing pump will most effectually wash off this exudation. Cruelty to Insects. It does not appear upon what principle of reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> it is, that mankind have founded their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> over the lives of every creature that is placed in a subordinate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of being to themselves. Whatever claim they may have in right of food and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-<a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> (to which ought we to add the purposes of the naturalist, explained above?) did they extend their privilege no farther than those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> would reasonably carry them, numberless beings might enjoy their lives in peace, who are now hurried out of them by the most wanton and unnecessary cruelties. It is surely difficult to discover why it should be thought less inhuman to crush to death a harmless insect, whose single offence is that he eats that food which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has prepared for his sustenance, than it would be were we to kill any bulky creature for the same reason. There are few tempers so hardened to the impressions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, as not to shudder at the thought of the latter; and yet the former is universally practised without the least check of compassion. This seems to arise from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of supposing, that every creature is really in itself contemptible, which happens to be clothed with a body infinitely disproportionate to our own, not considering that great and little are merely relative terms. But the inimitable Shakespeare would teach us, that --- the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> beetle that we <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> upon, In corporal suff'rance, feels a pang as great As when a giant dies. And indeed there is every reason to believe that the sensations of many insects are as exquisite as those of creatures of far more enlarged dimensions, perhaps even more... more so. The milipede, for instance, rolls itself round upon the slightest touch, and the snail draws in its horns upon the least approach of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Are not these the strongest indications of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>? and is it any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of ours, that we are not therefore induced to treat them with a more sympathizing tenderness? Montaigne remarks, that there is a certain claim of kindness and benevolence which every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of creatures has a right to from us. It is to be regretted that this general maxim is not more attended to in the affair of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and pressed home upon tender minds in its full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and latitude. We are far, indeed, from thinking, that the early delight which children discover in tormenting flies, &c., is a mark of any innate cruelty of temper, because this turn may be accounted for on other principles; and it is entertaining unworthy notions of the Deity, to suppose he forms mankind with a propensity to the most detestable of all dispositions: but most certainly, by being unrestrained in sports of this kind, they may acquire by habit what they never would have learned from nature, and grow up into a confirmed inattention to every kind of suffering but their own. Accordingly the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of judicature at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> thought an instance of this sort not below its cognizance, and punished a boy for putting out the eyes of a poor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> that had unhappily fallen into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. It might be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, therefore, it should seem, in order to awaken as early as possible in children an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of humanity, to give them a view of several sorts of insects as they may be magnified by the assistance of glasses, and to show them that the same evident marks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and goodness prevail in the formation of the minutest insect, as in that of the most enormous Leviathan: that they are equally furnished with whatever is necessary, not only to the preservation, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of their beings in that state of existence which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> has assigned them; in a word, that the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of their respective organs distinctly proclaims them the objects of the divine benevolence, and therefore that they justly ought to be so of ours.

INSERTION

Pages 297-297

in Anatomy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> conjunction of the vessels, tendons, fibres, and membranes of the body with some other parts.

INSINUATION

Pages 297-297

* denotes a cunning and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> way of creeping into any person's favour. **INSINUATION of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">Will</a>**, among civilians, is the first production of it, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the leaving it with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, in order to its probate. See WILL.

INSIPID

Pages 297-297

TASTELESS, that which has nothing in it pungent enough to affect the palate, tongue, &c., and to occasion that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> we call **tasting**.

INSITION

Pages 297-297

INSITIO, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, denotes the same with engraving; viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of inserting and uniting a cyon, bud, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, in the substance of the stock.

INSOLATION

Pages 297-297

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a method of preparing certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, drugs, &c. by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays; either to dry, to mature, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to sharpen them; as is done in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, figs, &c.—The word comes from the Latin verb *infloare*, which is used by Pliny and Columella, and signifies to expose to the sun.

INSOLVENT

Pages 297-297

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to such persons as have not wherewithal to pay their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> debts. A person dying, and not leaving estate sufficient to discharge these, is said to die insolvent. **<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">Trial</a> by INSPECTION**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">EXAMINATION</a>**, is when, for the greater expedition of a cause, in some point or issue, being either the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> question, or arising collaterally out of it, but being evidently the object of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, upon the testimony of their own senses, shall decide the point in dispute. For, where the affirmative or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> of a question is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of such obvious determination, it is not thought necessary to summon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> to decide it; who are properly called in to inform the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> of the court of dubious facts; and therefore, when the fact, from its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, must be evident to the court either from ocular demonstration or other irrefragable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, there the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> departs from its usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, the verdict of 12 men, and relies on the judgment of the court alone. As in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> to reverse a fine for non-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the cognizor, or to set aside a flatute or recognition entered into by an infant; here, and in other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of the like sort, a writ shall issue to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, commanding him that he constrain the said party to appear, that it may be ascertained by the view of his body by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s justices, whether he be of full age or not: *Ut per spectum corporis sui confolare poterit jucitarii nostris, si praedictus an sit plene aetatis necne*. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, however, the court has, upon inspection, any doubt of the age of the party (as may frequently be the case), it may proceed to take proofs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; and, particularly may examine the infant himself upon an oath of *voir dire, veritatem dicere*; that is, to make true answers to such questions as the court shall demand of him; or the court may examine his mother, his godfather, or the like.

INSPECTOR

Pages 297-297

a person to whom the care and conduct of any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is committed.

INSPECTORS

Pages 297-297

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, were such persons as examined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and value of lands and effects, in order to the adjusting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proportioning taxes and impositions to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s estate. The Jews also have an officer, in their synagogue, whom they call *inspector*, *māḥzen*. His business consists principally in inspecting or overlooking the prayers and lections, in preparing and showing them to the reader, and in standing by him to see he reads <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he makes mistakes, he is to correct him.

INSPIRATION

Pages 297-298

among divines, &c., implies the conveying of certain extraordinary and supernatural notices <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> motions into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; or it denotes any supernatural influence of God upon the mind of a rational creature, whereby he is formed to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of intellectual improvements, to which he could not, or would not, in fact have attained in his present circumstances, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> way. Thus the prophets are said to have spoken by divine inspiration. Some authors reduce the inspiration of the sacred writers to a particular care of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, which prevented anything they had said from failing or coming to nought; maintaining, that they never were really inspired either with knowledge or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. According to M. Simon, inspiration is no more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Holy Spirit, which never permitted the sacred writers to be mistaken. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the inspiration of the Holy Holy Spirit regards only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, not the style or words; and this seems to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in with M. Simon's doctrine of direction. Theological writers have enumerated several kinds of inspiration; such as an inspiration of superintendency, in which God does so influence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the mind of any person, as to keep him more secure from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in some various and complex discourse, than he would have been merely by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his natural faculties; plenary superintendent inspiration, which excludes any mixture of error at all from the performance so superintended; inspiration of elevation, where the faculties <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in a regular, and, as it seems, in a common manner, yet are raised to an extraordinary degree, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> shall, upon the whole, have more of the true sublime or pathetic, than natural genius could have given; and inspiration of suggestion, when the use of the faculties is superseeded, and God does, as it were, speak directly to the mind, making such discoveries to it as it could not otherwise have obtained, and dictating the very words in which such discoveries are to be communicated, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are designed as a message to others. It is generally allowed that the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> was written by a superintendent inspiration; for without this the discourses and doctrines of Christ could not have been faithfully recorded by the evangelists and apostles; nor could they have assumed the authority of speaking the words of Christ, and evinced this authority by the actual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of miraculous powers: and besides, the sacred writings bear many obvious internal marks of their divine original, in the excellence of their doctrines, the spirituality and elevation of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, the majesty and simplicity of their style, the agreement of their various parts, and their efficacy on mankind; to which may be added, that there has been in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, from its earliest ages, a constant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that the sacred books were written by the extraordinary assistance of the Spirit, which must at least amount to superintendent inspiration. But it has been controverted whether this inspiration extended to every minute circumstance in their writings, so as to be in the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> plenary. Jerome, Grotius, Erasmus, Epiphanes, and many others, maintain that it was not; whilst others contend, that the emphatical manner in which our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> speaks of the agency of the Spirit upon them, and in which they themselves speak of their own writings, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> justify our believing that their inspiration was plenary, unless there be very convincing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> brought on the other side to prove that it was not: and if we allow, it is said, that there were some errors in the New Testament, as it came from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the apostles, there may be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> danger of subverting the main purpose and design of it; since there will be endless room to debate the importance both of facts and doctrines. Among the Heathens, the priests and priestesses were said to be divinely inspired, when they gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>.—The poets also laid claim to it; and to this end they always invoked <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> at the beginning of any great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Inspiration, in Physic, is understood of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is admitted within the lungs; in which sense, inspiration is a branch of respiration, and stands opposed to Exspiration. This admission of the air depends immediately on its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> or elasticity, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the cavity of the breast is enlarged by the elevation of the thorax and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, and particularly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the diaphragm downwards; so that the air does not enter the lungs, because they are dilated; but those dilate, because the air enters within them. Nor is it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of the breast which draws in the air, as is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> thought, though this is a condition absolutely necessary to inspiration; but an actual intrusion of the air into the lungs. See Respiration. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSPISSATING">Inspissating</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, an operation whereby a liquor is brought to a thicker consistence, by evaporating the thinner parts. Innsbruck, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, in the circle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Tyrol, received its name from the river Inn, which runs by it. It has a noble castle or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, formerly the residence of the archdukes of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Austria, with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> where they are buried. The houses, though built in the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, are rather handsome; and the streets, though narrow, are remarkably well paved. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this city the inhabitants can <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> but little confidence in their fortifications, which are very trifling. They seem rather to depend on the natural advantages of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; which appear indeed to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, so perfectly inaccessible to any enemy, that even the great Gustavus Adolphus, after having overrun with his victorious arms the other parts of Germany, could never make any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon this. It is seated in a pleasant valley, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 27. N. Lat. 47. 10. Installation, the act of giving visible possession of an order, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, or office, by placing in the proper seat. See Installment. Instalment, a settling or instituting any person in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The word is derived from the Latin in, and statum, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for a seat in church, in the choir, or a seat or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, &c. Though Vossius is of opinion the word is of German origin. Instalment is chiefly used for the induction of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, prebendary, or other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a>, into the possession of his stall, or proper seat, in the cathedral church to which he belongs. This is sometimes also called installation. Instalment is likewise used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, whereby the knights of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a> are placed in their rank, in the chapel of St George at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>. Instant, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> in which we perceive no succession; or it is that which takes up the time only of one idea in our minds. Instauration, the re-establishment, or restoration of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, a church, or the like, to its former state. The word is by some derived from the old Latin inflaurum, which signified the "stock" of things necessary for the tillage and managing of grounds; as cattle, tools, harness, &c. But the word inflaurum is only of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>: inflauratio is of much greater antiquity, and by some derived from inflatus, "like," as importing a thing's being brought

INSTINCT

Pages 298-309

in the manege, is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s hind leg, which reaches from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAM">ham</a> to the pastern-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">Definition</a>. INSTINCT, a certain power <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disposition of mind, by which, independent of all instruction or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, without deliberation, and without having any end in view, animals are unerringly directed to do spontaneously (a) whatever is necessary for the preservation of the individual or the continuation of the kind. Such in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the instinct of sucking exerted immediately after birth; and such in the inferior <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> is the instinct by which insects invariably deposit their eggs in situations most favourable for hatching and affording nourishment to their future progeny. These operations are necessary for the preservation of the individual and the continuation of the kind; but neither the infant nor the insect knows that they are necessary: they both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> without having any end in view, and act uniformly without instruction and without experience. The actions of the inferior animals are generally directed by instinct; those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> by reason. This at least is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with respect to men in a state of civilization: in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> state they are probably little less the slaves of instinct than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> themselves. Concerning human instincts, indeed, philosophers differ widely in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; some maintaining that man is endowed with a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of instincts than any species of brutes; whilst others deny that in human <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> there is any power or propensity at all which can properly be called instinctive. This diversity of opinion may easily be traced to its source. There are not many original thinkers in the world. The greater part even of those who are called philosophers, implicitly adopt the opinions of certain matters whose authority they deem sufficient to supply the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of argument; and having chosen their respective guides, each maintains with zeal what his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> taught, or is supposed to have taught. When Locke so successfully attacked the doctrine of innate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and innate principles of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, he was thought by many to have overturned at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> all innate principles whatever; to have divested the human mind of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, affection, and instinct; and to have left in it nothing but the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and intellect. Such, we are persuaded, was not his intention; nor is there anything in his immortal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which, when interpreted with candour, appears to have such a tendency. In our opinion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Human Understanding has been very generally misinterpreted. Much of its merit, however, was soon discovered; and mankind, finding <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> disfigured by the barbarous jargon of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and built upon a few self-evident principles, implicitly embraced every opinion advanced, or which they supposed to be advanced, by the illustrious author; especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that opinion was contrary to any part of the scholastic system which had so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been employed to perplex the understanding and to veil absurdity. Hence arose many philosophers of eminence both at home and abroad; who maintained, as they imagined, upon the principles of Locke, that in the human mind there are no instincts, but that every thing which had been usually called by that name is resolvable into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. This doctrine was attacked by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a>, who introduced into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of mind, as faculties derived from nature, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, a sense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and a sense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; and these he considered as the tests of speculative truth and moral rectitude. His lordship's principles were in part adopted by Mr Hutcheson of Glasgow, who published a system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a>, founded upon a sense or instinct, to which he gave the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral sense</a>; and the undoubted merit of his work procured him many followers. Men generally run from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> to another. It being now discovered, or at least supposed, that the human mind is endowed with instinctive principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of philosophers soon afterwards arose, who maintained with much vehemence that it is likewise endowed with instinctive principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>; and who built a system of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, if such it may be called, upon a number of innate, distinct, and independent senses. The rise of this sect is well known. Berkeley and Hume had adopted Locke's doctrine reflecting the origin of our ideas; and had thence deduced consequences supposed to be dangerous in themselves, but which, it was thought, could not be denied without refusing the principles from which they were inferred. The foundation of the instinctive system being thus laid, the system itself was rapidly carried to a height far beyond what seems to have been the intention of its excellent author; and reason was well nigh banished from the regions of philosophy. For such a proceeding it is not difficult to assign the cause. The instinctive scheme requires much less labour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> than the systems of Locke and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; for upon the principles of it, when carried to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, every phenomenon in human nature is thought to be sufficiently accounted for, by supposing it. (a) As nothing is of greater importance in the philosophy of mind than accurate definitions, it may not be improper to observe, that through the whole of this article the word spontaneous is to be taken in the sense in which it is used in the following extracts from Hales's Origin of Mankind: "Many analogical motions in animals, though I cannot call them voluntary, yet I see them spontaneous: I have reason to conclude, that these are not simply <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>." "The sagacities and instincts of brutes, the spontaneousness of many of their motions, are not explicable, without supposing some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> determinate power connected to and inherent in their spirits, of a higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> than the bare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> modification of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>." If this be attended to, our definition of instinct <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found perfectly consonant to that which has been given by the author of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Metaphysic. "Instinct (he says) is a determination given by Almighty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> to the mind of the brute, to act in such or such a way, upon such or such an occasion, without intelligence; without knowledge of good or ill, and without knowing for what end or purpose he acts." In the effect of a particular instinct implanted in the mind for that very purpose. Hence in some popular works of philosophy we have a detail of so many distinct internal senses, that it requires no small strength of memory to retain their very names: besides the moral sense, we have the sense of beauty, the sense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, the sense of honour, the hoarding sense, and a thousand others which it is needless here to mention. This new system, which converts the philosophy of mind into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, or rather into a collection of facts and anecdotes, though it has made a rapid progress, is not yet universally received. It has been opposed by many speculative men, and by none with greater skill than Dr Priestley; who maintains, with the earliest admirers of Locke, that we have from nature no innate sense of truth, nor any instinctive principle of action; that even the action of sucking in new-born <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> is to be accounted for upon principles of mechanism; and that the desire of the senses is merely association. Whilst men, eminent for candour as well as for science, have thus been disputing the limits between instinct and reason in the human mind, and endeavouring to ascertain the actions which result from each, two writers of name, treating of that subject, have lately advanced opinions, which, if admitted as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, must render the dispute henceforth ridiculous, and put an end forever to all moral inquiries. Mr Smellie, in a work which he calls The Philosophy of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural History</a>, affirms, that between instinctive and rational motives no distinction exists, but that the reasoning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> itself is the necessary result of instinct; and Dr Reid, in his Essays on the Active Powers of Man, by attributing to instinct the action of breathing, seems to confound that principle with mere mechanism. That reason, instinct, and mechanism, are all essentially different from one another, has hitherto been universally allowed; and it appears not to be a talk of much difficulty to point out in what respect each of them differs from the other two. Actions performed with a view to accomplish a certain end are called rational actions, and the end in view is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to their performance. Instinctive actions have a cause, viz. the internal impulse by which they are spontaneously performed; but they cannot be said to have a motive, because they are not done with any view to consequences. Actions automatic have likewise a cause; but that cause is not internal impulse, but mere mechanism, by which they are performed without any spontaneity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. Thus, a man gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> in order to relieve a person from want; he performs a grateful action as a duty incumbent on him; and he fights for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in order to repel its enemies. Each of these actions is performed from a motive, and therefore they are all rational actions. An infant is impelled to suck the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, but he knows not that it is necessary for his preservation; a couple of young savages go together, for the first time, without any view to offspring or any determinate idea of enjoyment. These actions have no motive, and therefore are not rational; but as they are performed by a spontaneous exertion of the agents, they are not to be attributed to mere mechanism; they are therefore instinctive actions. A man breathes without any motive, without any spontaneous exertion of his own, and that as well when he is asleep as when he is awake. The action of breathing therefore is neither rational nor instinctive, but merely automatic or mechanical. All this seems to be very plain. To talk of the motives of actions performed by instinct, in an argument intended to prove that between reason and instinct there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, is either to beg the question or to pervert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. If the author of the Philosophy of Natural History chooses to call the impulse which prompts the infant to suck by the name of motive, he only uses an English word improperly; if it be his intention to affirm that such a motive is not totally and essentially different from that which prompts a man to give charity or to fight for his country, he affirms what all mankind know to be false (B). Having thus ascertained what we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> by instinct, we shall now proceed to inquire, Whether or not there be any instinctive principles in man? But in order to proceed upon sure grounds, it will be proper to consider, in the first place, such actions of the inferior animals as are generally allowed to be instinctive: for an attempt has lately been made to prove, that even these actions are the offspring of reason influenced by motives; and that instinct, as we have defined it, is a mere imaginary principle, which has no existence either in man or brute. (B) The author of Ancient Metaphysics, whose learned work contains more good sense on this subject than any other book which we have seen, thus distinguishes between reason and instinct: "With respect to the mere animal, it is evident, that he pursues nothing but what is conducive either to the preservation of the animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or to the continuation of the kind. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the object which the intellectual mind pursues, is the fair and the handsome; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> consists in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of these. And though it pursue also what is useful and profitable for the being and well-being of the animal life, yet it is for the sake, not of the animal life itself, but of the το χαράς or beautiful; which therefore is the ultimate object of its pursuit in all things. "Another material difference in practice betwixt the animal and intellectual mind is, that every action of intellect proceeds from an opinion formed concerning what is good or ill, beautiful or the contrary, in the action. When we do so, we are said to act from will, which is always determined by some opinion formed of the kind I have mentioned: whereas, when we act from mere appetite or inclination, without deliberation or opinion formed, we act as the brute does always; for he has no will, but is prompted to action by natural impulse, or ἐγκίνησις, as the Greeks call it. "A third very material difference is, that intellect, in all its operations, proposes ends, and devises means to accomplish these ends; whereas the instinct of the brute proceeds without consideration either of ends or means." It has been said that caterpillars, when shaken off a tree in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, instantly turn round towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> and climb up, though they had never formerly been on the surface of the ground. This is a striking instance of instinct. On the tree, and not upon the ground, the caterpillar finds its food. If therefore it did not turn and climb up the trunk it would inevitably perish; but surely the caterpillar knows not that such an exertion is necessary to its preservation; and therefore it acts not from motives, but from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> impulse. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">bee</a> and the beaver are endowed with an instinct which has the appearance of foresight. They build magazines, and fill them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; but the foresight is not theirs. Neither bees nor beavers know anything of futurity. The solitary wasp digs holes in the sand, in each of which she deposits an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. Though she certainly knows not that an animal is to proceed from that egg, and fill its cells, if possible, that this animal must be nourished with other animals, she collects a few small green <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, which she rolls up in a circular form, and fixes in the hole in such a manner that they cannot move. When the wasp-worm is hatched, it is simply stored with the food which nature has destined for its support. The green worms are devoured in succession; and the number deposited is exactly proportioned to the time necessary for the growth and transformation of the wasp-worm into a fly; when it issues from the hole, and is capable of procuring its own nourishment. This instinct of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>-wasp is the more remarkable, that she feeds not upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> herself. Birds of the same species, unless when restrained by peculiar circumstances, uniformly build their nests of the same materials, and in the same form and situation, though they inhabit very different climates; and the form and situation are always exactly suited to their nature, and calculated to afford them shelter and protection. When danger, or any other circumstance peculiar to certain countries, renders a deviation from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> form or situation of nests necessary, that deviation is made in an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and in the very same manner, by all the birds of one species; and it is never found to extend beyond the limits of the country where alone it can serve any good purpose. When removed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> from their eggs, birds return to them with haste and anxiety, and shift them so as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> them equally; and it is worthy of observation, that their haste to return is always in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. But do birds reason, and all of the same species reason, equally well, upon the nature and extent of danger, and upon the means by which it can best be avoided? Have birds any notion of equality, or do they know that heat is necessary for incubation? No: in all these operations men recognize the intentions of nature; but they are hid from the animals themselves, and therefore cannot operate upon them as motives. Of the instinct of animals we shall give one instance more in the elegant and perspicuous language of Dr. Reid. "Every manufacturing art among men (says that able writer) was invented by some man, improved by others, and brought to perfection by time and experience. Men learn to work in it by long practice, which produces a habit. The arts of men vary in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and in every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and are found only in those men who have been taught them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of animals differ from those of men in many striking particulars. No animal of the species can claim the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; no animal ever introduced any new improvement, or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from the former practice; every one of the species has equal skill from the beginning, without teaching, without experience, and without habit; every one has its art by a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. I do not mean that it is inspired with the principles or rules of the art, but with the ability of working in it to perfection, without any knowledge of its principles, rules, or end. The work of every animal is indeed like the works of nature, perfect in its kind, and can bear the most critical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the mechanic or the mathematician; of which a honeycomb is a striking instance. "Bees, it is well known, construct their combs with remarkable cells on both sides, fit both for holding their storeable in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and for rearing their young. There are in them only three possible figures of the cells, which can make them all equal and similar, without any useless surfaces. These are the equilateral triangle, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and the regular hexagon. Of the three, the hexagon is the most proper, both for convenience and strength. Bees, as if they knew this, make their cells regular hexagons. As the combs have cells on both sides, the cells may either be exactly opposite, having partition against partition, or the bottoms of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> may rest upon the partitions between the cells on the other side, which will serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTRESS">buttress</a> to strengthen it. The last way is the best for strength; accordingly the bottom of each cell rests against the point where three partitions meet on the other side, which gives it all the strength possible. The bottom of a cell may either be one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, perpendicular to the side partitions; or it may be composed of several planes, meeting in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> in the middle point. It is only in one of these two ways that all the cells can be similar without losing room. And, for the same intention, the planes, of which the bottom is composed, if there be more than one, must be three in number, and neither more nor fewer. It has been demonstrated, that by making the bottoms of the cells to consist of three planes meeting in a point, there is a saving of material and labour no way inconsiderable. The bees, as if acquainted with these principles of solid <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, follow them most accurately; the bottom of each cell being composed of three planes, which make obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the side partitions and with one another, and meet in a point in the middle of the bottom; the three angles of this bottom being supported by three partitions on the other side of the comb, and the point of it by the common intersection of these three partitions. One instance more of the mathematical skill displayed in the structure of a honeycomb deserves to be mentioned. It is a curious mathematical problem, at what precise angle the three planes which compose the bottom of a cell ought to meet, in order to make the greatest possible saving of material and labour. This is one of those problems belonging to the higher parts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, which are called problems of maxima and minima. The celebrated Mr. Laurin resolved it by a fluxionary calculation, which is to be found in the Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and determined precisely the angle required. Upon the most exact <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> which the subject could admit, he he afterwards found, that it is the very angle in which the three planes in the bottom of the cell of a honeycomb do actually meet. "Shall we ask here, Who taught the bees the properties of solids, and to resolve problems of maxima and minima? If a honeycomb were a work of human art, every man of common sense would conclude, without hesitation, that he who invented the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> must have understood the principles on which it was constructed. We need not say that bees know none of these things. They work most geometrically without any knowledge of geometry; somewhat like a child, who by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the handle of an organ makes good music without any knowledge of music. The art is not in the child, but in him who made the organ. In like manner, when a bee makes its combs so geometrically, the geometry is not in the bee, but in that great Geometrician who made the bee, and made all things in number, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>." We have given a full detail of the structure of a honeycomb, because it is an effect of instinct which cannot be confounded with the operations of reason. The author of *The Natural History of Animals*, justly offended with that theory which treats of instinctive motives, which represents the human mind as a bundle of instincts, and of which the object seems to be to degrade mankind to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of brutes, has very laudably exerted his endeavours to detect its weaknesses, and to expose it to contempt. But in avoiding one extreme, he seems to have run into the other; and whilst he maintains the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of his own species, he almost raises the brutes to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of men. "It is better (he says) to share our rights with others than to be entirely deprived of them." This is certainly true; and no good man will hesitate to prefer his theory to that of his antagonist; but we see no necessity for adopting either; the phenomena may be accounted for without degrading reason to the level of instinct, or elevating instinct to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of reason. We shall readily allow to Locke (c), that some of the inferior animals seem to have perceptions of particular truths, and within very narrow limits the faculty of reason; but we see no ground to suppose that their souls; but natural operations are performed with a view to convey their consequences; and therefore cannot persuade ourselves, from their conduct, that these operations are the result of a train of reasoning in the mind of the animal. He acknowledges indeed, that their reasoning and thinking powers are remarkably deficient when compared with those of men; that they cannot take so full (c) "For if they have any ideas at all, and are not mere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, as some would have them, we cannot deny them to have some reason. It seems as evident to me, that some of them do, in certain instances, reason, as that they have senses; but it is only in particular ideas, just as they received them from the senses. They are the best of them tied up within those narrow bounds, and have not, as I think, the faculty to enlarge them by any kind of abstraction." *Essay on Human Understanding*, Book ii, chap. xi. This is in part a just observation, and serves to account for many phenomena which later writers have derived from instinct. The author of *The Philosophy of Natural History* had "a cat that frequented a closet, the door of which was fastened by a common <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> latch. A window was situated near the door. When the door was shut, the cat gave herself no uneasiness. As soon as she tired of her confinement, she mounted on the sole of the window, and with her paw dexterously lifted the latch and came out." This practice, which we are told <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for years, must have been the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of what Locke calls reasoning in particular ideas. It could not be the effect of instinct; for instinct is adapted only to a state of nature, in which cats have neither latches to lift nor doors to open; and as it is not said that the animal attempted to lift the latches of other doors, we are not authorized to infer that this particular action was the consequence of reasoning in ideas enlarged by abstraction: the cat had repeatedly seen one door opened by an exertion which she was capable of imitating. Yet that animals have no power of enlarging their ideas, is a position, of the truth of which, though it is advanced by Locke, we are by no means confident. It is well known that crows feed upon several kinds of shell-fish when within their reach; and that they contrive to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the shell by raising the fish to a great height, and letting it drop upon a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or a rock. This may perhaps be considered as pure instinct directing the animal to the proper means of acquiring its food. But what is to be thought of the following fact, which was communicated to us by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> whose veracity is unquestioned, and who, being totally unacquainted with the theories of philosophers, has of course no favourite <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> to support? In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the year 1791, a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of crows made their nest in a tree, of which there are several planted round his garden; and in his morning-walks he had often been amused by witnessing furious combats between them and a cat. One morning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> raged more fiercely than usual, till at last the cat gave way and took shelter under a hedge, as if to wait a more favourable opportunity of retreating to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. The crows continued for a short time to make a threatening noise; but perceiving that on the ground they could do nothing more than threaten, one of them lifted a stone from the middle of the garden and perched it on a tree planted in the hedge, where she sat watching the motions of the enemy of her young. As the cat crept along under the hedge, the crow accompanied her by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> from branch to branch and from tree to tree; and when at last she ventured to quit her hiding-place, the crow, leaving the tree, and hovering over her in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, let the stone drop from on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> on her back. That the crow on this occasion reasoned, is self-evident; and it seems to be little less evident, that the ideas employed in her reasoning were enlarged beyond those which she had received from her senses. By her senses, she may have perceived, that the shell of a fish is broken by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; but could her senses inform her, that a cat would be wounded or driven off the field by the fall of a stone? No: from the effect of the one fall preserved in her memory, she must have inferred the other by her power of reasoning. a review of the past, nor look forward with so penetrating an eye to the future; that they do not accumulate observation upon observation, or add the experience of one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to that of another; that their manners do not vary nor their customs fluctuate like ours; and that their arts always remain the same, without degeneracy and without improvement. "The crow (he observes) always builds its nest in the same way; every hen treats her young with the same measure of affection; even the dog, the horse, and the furtiveous elephant, seem to act rather mechanically than with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. From such hasty observations as these, it has been inferred (he says), that the brutes are directed in their actions by some mysterious influence, which impels them to employ their powers unintentionally in performing actions beneficial to themselves, and suitable to their nature and circumstances." And are these observations indeed hasty? And is this inference ill founded? To us the matter appears quite otherwise. If the arts of brutes and other animals have always remained the same without degeneracy, and without improvement; and if they be at the same time the result of reasoning, they must either be so perfect that they cannot be improved, or so imperfect that they cannot degenerate. That the structure of a honeycomb is imperfect, no man has ever imagined. We have seen, that, as far as we are capable of discerning the end which it is intended to serve, it is the most perfect structure possible: and therefore, if it be the result of the reasoning of the bee, the author must retract his assertion reflecting the extent of the reasoning and thinking powers of inferior animals; and instead of saying that they are remarkably deficient when compared with those of men, affirm that they are infinitely more perfect. No human art has yet arrived at such perfection as that it might not be improved; no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> has ever built a town, or constructed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, which he could mathematically demonstrate to be of the very best possible form for the end intended, and so absolutely perfect as to be incapable of improvement. But the same author proceeds to affirm, that "the laws of analogical reasoning do not justify the idea that the brutes act, on any occasion, absolutely without design." Nay, he says, it seems more probable, "that the inferior animals, even in those instances in which we cannot distinguish the motives which actuate them, or the views with which they proceed, yet act with design, and extend their views, if not a great way, yet at least a certain length forward; than that they can be upon any occasion, such as in rearing of their young, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> nests, &c., actuated merely by feeling, or overruled by some mysterious influence, under which they are nothing but insensible instruments." This last phrase is ambiguous. If by insensible instruments it be meant that the brutes are considered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for instinct as mere machines without the faculties of sensation and spontaneity, the author is combating a phantom of his own creation; for we believe an opinion so absurd is not now maintained by any man, (see BRUTE.) But if by insensible instruments be meant such instruments as act spontaneously without being conscious of the end to which their actions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, he appears not only to be egregiously mistaken in his conjecture reflecting the design of brutes, but also to have advanced an hypothesis contradictory and inconsistent. If it be true, that the inferior animals act with de Maintaining-sign, even in those instances in which we cannot distinguished, and distinguish their motives, their views may indeed exist but a little way when compared with infinity; but certainly they extend farther than ours; for there is no useless work of man constructed with such skill, but that, after it is finished, another man of equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> will be able to distinguish the general design of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. But if the inferior animals, on all occasions, act with design, we should be glad to know the design of the bees in forming the cells of their combs in the manner which we have so largely described. Do these little animals indeed know that a comb, consisting on both sides of hexagonal cells, with the bottom of each composed of several planes meeting in a certain solid angle, and so formed as that the bottom of a cell on the one side shall rest upon the partitions between the cells on the other side, is in all respects the most proper both for holding their stores of honey and for rearing their young? And do they likewise know, that its excellence arises from the precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and position of the cells, by which there is a very considerable saving of labour and materials, whilst the comb at the same time has the greatest possible strength, and the greatest possible capacity?
