Bodies may be reduced into their integument parts by trituration or grinding, limation or filing, solution, amalgamation, &c. See GRINDING. INTEGRAL Calculus, in the new analysis, is the reverse of the differential calculus, and is the finding of the integral from a given differential; being similar to the inverse method of fluxions. See FLUXIONS.

INTEGUMENTS

Pages 314-314

in Anatomy, denote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> coverings which invest the body; as the cuticle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTIS">cutis</a>, &c. See ANATOMY. INTEGUMENT is also extended to the particular membranes which invest certain parts of the body; as the coats <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tunics of the eye.

INTELLECT

Pages 314-314

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used among philosophers, to signify that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> usually called the understanding. See LOGIC and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>.

INTENDANT

Pages 314-315

one who has the conduct, inspection, and management of any thing. See SUPERINTENDANT. This is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> frequent among the French: they have intendants of the marine, who are officers in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-ports, Intendant ports, whose business it is to take care the ordinances and regulations relating to sea affairs be observed; intendants of the finances, who have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the revenues; intendants of provinces, who are appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> to take care of the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, policy, and finances in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>; also intendants of buildings, of houses, &c.

INTENDMENT

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the intention, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> true meaning, of a person or thing which frequently supplies what is not fully expressed; but though the intent of parties in deeds and contracts is much regarded by the law, yet it cannot take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> against the rules of law. INTENDMENT of Crimes; this, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> where the intention is proved by circumstances, is punishable in the same manner as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was put in execution. So, if a person enter a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the night-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, with an intent to commit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGLARY">burglary</a>, it is felony; also, an assault, with an intent to commit a robbery on the highway is made felony, and punished with transportation, 7 Geo. II. c. 21.

INTENT

Pages 315-315

in the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies to begin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> commence, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>.

INTENTION

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, denotes an exertion of the intellectual faculties with more than ordinary vigour; when the mind with earnestness fixes its view on any idea, considers it on all sides, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be called off by any solicitation.

INTERAMNA

Pages 315-315
or Interamnia Pretutianorum (Ptolemy); a town in the territory of the Pretutiani, a part of the Picenum. Now Teramo, in the Abruzzo of Naples. E. Long. 15. N. Lat. 42. 40.

INTERANNA

Pages 315-315

a town and colony of the Volsci in Latium, on the confines of Samnium, at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Liris and Melpis; and for distinction sake called Livinara. The town is now in ruins.

INTERCALARY

Pages 315-315

an appellation given to the odd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> inserted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>-year; which was so called from calo, calare, "to proclaim," it being proclaimed by the priests with a loud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>.

INTERCATIA

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Vaccei in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. Here Scipio Aemilianus flew a champion of the barbarians in single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>; and was the first who mounted the wall in taking the town. It was situated to the south-east of Asturica; now said to be in ruins.

INTERCESSION

Pages 315-315

was used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of a tribune of the people, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, by which he inhibited the acts of other magistrates; or even, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the tribunes, the decrees of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. Veto was the solemn word used by the tribunes when they inhibited any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the senate or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> proposed to the people. The general law of these intercessions was, that any magistrate might inhibit the acts of his equal or inferior; but the tribunes had the sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of controlling the acts of every other magistrate, yet could not be controlled themselves by any.

INTERCESSOR

Pages 315-315

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> heretofore applied to such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> as, during the vacancy of a see, administered the bishopric, till a successor to the deceased bishop had been elected. The third <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> calls these intervenors.

INTERCOLUMNIATION

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, denotes the space between two columns, which is always to be proportioned to the height and bulk of the columns.

INTERCOSTAL

Pages 315-315

in Anatomy, an appellation given to such muscles, nerves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, and veins, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between the ribs.

INTERDICT

Pages 315-315

an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> censure, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome forbids the performance of divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, town, &c. This censure has been frequently executed in France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Germany; and in the year 1170, Pope Alexander III. put all England under an interdict, forbidding the clergy to perform any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of divine service, except baptising of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, taking confessions, and giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a> to dying penitents. But this censure being liable to the ill consequences of promoting libertinism and a neglect of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, the succeeding popes have very seldom made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it. There was also an interdict of persons, who were deprived of the benefit of attending on divine service. Particular persons were also anciently interdicted of fire and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which signified a banishment for some particular offence; by their censure no person was allowed to receive them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> allow them fire or water; and being thus wholly deprived of the two necessary elements of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, they were doubtless under a kind of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

INTEREST

Pages 315-317

is the premium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid for the loan or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of other money. Many good and learned men have in former times very much perplexed themselves and other people by raising doubts about the legality of interest in furo conscientiae. It may not be amiss here to inquire upon what grounds this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> does really stand. The enemies to interest in general make no distinction between that and usury, holding any increase of money to be indefensibly usurious. And this they ground as well on the prohibition of it by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Moses among the Jews, as also upon what is laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, That money is naturally barren; and to make it breed money is preposterous, and a perversion of the end of its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, which was only to serve the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, and not of increase. Hence the school-divines have branded the practice of taking interest, as being contrary to the divine law both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and revealed; and the canon law has prohibited the taking any the least increase for the loan of money as a mortal sin. But, in answer to this, it may be observed, that the Mosaic precept was clearly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>, and not a moral, precept. It only prohibited the Jews from taking usury from their brethren the Jews; but in express words permitted them to take it of a stranger: which proves that the taking of moderate usury, or a reward for the use, for so the word signifies, is not malum in se, since it was allowed where any but an Israelite was concerned. And as to Aristotle's reason, deduced from the natural barrenness of money, the same may with equal force be alleged of houles, which never breed houles; and twenty other things, which nobody doubts it is lawful to make profit of, by letting them to hire. And though money was originally used only for the purposes of exchange, yet the laws of any state may be well justified in permitting it to be turned to the purposes of profit, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the convenience of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> (the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> end for which money was invented) shall require it. And that the allowance of moderate interest tends greatly to the benefit of the public, especially in a trading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear from that generally acknowledged principle, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> cannot subsist without mutual and extensive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. Unless money therefore can be borrowed, trade cannot be carried on; and if no premium were allowed for the hire of money, few persons would care to lend it; or at least the rate of borrowing at a short warning (which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of commerce) would be entirely at an end. Thus, in the dark ages of monkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and civil tyranny, when interest was laid under a total <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERDICT">interdict</a>, commerce was also at its lowest ebb, and fell entirely into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>: but when men's minds began to be more enlarged, when true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> revived, commerce grew again into credit; and again introduced with itself its inseparable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, the doctrine of loans upon interest. And, really, considered abstractedly from this its use, since all other conveniences of life may be either bought or hired, but money can only be hired, there seems no greater impropriety in taking a recompense or price for the hire of this, than of any other convenience. If one borrow tools to employ in a beneficial trade, it is but equitable that the lender should have a proportion of the gains. To demand an exorbitant price is equally contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, for the loan of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, or the loan of a sum of money: but a reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> for the temporary inconvenience which the owner may feel by the want of it, and for the hazard of his losing it entirely, is not more immoral in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> than it is in the other. And indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> prohibition of lending upon any, even moderate interest, introduces the very inconvenience which it seems meant to remedy. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of individuals will make borrowing unavoidable. Without some profit by law, there will be but few lenders; and those principally bad men, who will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through the law, and take a profit; and then will endeavour to indemnify themselves from the danger of the penalty, by making that profit exorbitant. Thus, while all degrees of profit were discomfited, we find more complaints of usury, and more flagrant instances of oppression, than in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times when money may be easily had at a low interest. A <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> distinction must therefore be made between a moderate and exorbitant profit; to the former of which we usually give the name of interest, to the latter the truly odious appellation of usury: the former is necessary in every civil state; if it were but to exclude the latter, which ought never to be tolerated in any well regulated society.—For, as the whole of this matter is well summed up by Grotius, "if the compensation allowed by law does not exceed the proportion of the hazard run, or the want felt, by the loan, its allowance is neither repugnant to the revealed nor to the natural law: but if it exceeds those bounds, it is then oppressive usury; and though the municipal laws may give it impunity, they never can make it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>." We see, that the exorbitance or moderation of interest, for the money <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a>, depends upon two circumstances; the inconvenience of parting with it for the present, and the hazard of losing it entirely. The inconvenience to individual lenders can never be estimated by laws; the rate therefore of general interest must depend upon the usual of general inconvenience. This results entirely from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of specie or current money in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>: for, the more specie there is circulating in any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, the greater superfluity there will be, beyond what is necessary to carry on the business of exchange and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> concerns of life. In every nation, or public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, there is a certain quantity of money thus necessary; which a person well skilled in political <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> might perhaps calculate as exactly as a private banker can the demand for running cash in his own shop: all above this necessary quantity may be spared, or lent, without much inconvenience to the respective leaders; and the greater this national superfluity is, the more numerous will be the lenders, and the lower ought the rate of the national interest to be; but where there is not enough, or barely enough, circulating cash to answer the ordinary uses of the public, interest will be proportionably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; for lenders will be but few, as few can submit to the inconvenience of lending. So also the hazard of an entire loss has its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in the regulation of interest: hence, the better the security, the lower will the interest be; the rate of interest being generally in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> ratio, formed out of the inconvenience and the hazard. And as, if there were no inconvenience, there should be no interest but what is equivalent to the hazard; so, if there were no hazard, there ought to be no interest, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> only what arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> inconvenience of lending. Thus, if the quantity of specie in a nation be such, that the general inconvenience of lending for a year is computed to amount to three per cent, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that has money by him will perhaps lend it upon good personal security at five per cent, allowing two for the hazard run; he will lend it upon landed security, or mortgage, at four per cent, the hazard being proportionably less; but he will lend it to the state, on the maintenance of which all his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> depends, at three per cent, the hazard being none at all. But sometimes the hazard may be greater than the rate of interest allowed by law will compensate. And this gives rise to the practice, 1. Of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTTOMRY">bottomry</a>, or respondentia. 2. Of policies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a>. See BOTTOMRY, and INSURANCE. Upon the two principles of inconvenience and hazard, compared together, different nations have at different times established different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> of interest. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> allowed centumlinea, one per cent. monthly, or twelve per cent. per annum, to be taken for common loans; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> reduced it to trientes, or one-third of the as or centumlinea, that is four per cent.; but allowed higher interest to be taken of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, because there the hazard was greater. So too Grotius informs us, that in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> the rate of interest was then eight per cent. in common loans, but twelve to merchants. Our law establishes one standard for all alike, where the pledge or security itself is not put in jeopardy; left, under the general pretence of vague and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> hazards, a door should be opened to fraud and usury; leaving specific hazards to be provided against by specific insurances, or by loans upon respondebuntia or bottomry. But as to the rate of legal interest, it has varied and decreased for 200 years past, according as the quantity of specie in the kingdom has increased by accretions of trade, the introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-credit, and other circumstances. The statute 37 Hen. VIII. c. 9., confirmed interest to ten per cent. and so did the statute 13 Eliz. c. 8. But as, through the encouragements given in her reign to commerce, the nation grew more wealthy; so, under her successor, the statute 21 Jac. I. c. 17., reduced it to eight per cent.; as did the statute 12 Car. II. c. 13., to six; and lastly, by the statute 12 Ann. stat. 2. c. 16., it was brought down to five per cent. yearly, which is now the extremity of legal interest that can be taken. But yet, if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> which carries interest be made in a foreign country, our courts will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the payment of interest according to the law of that country in which the contract was made. Thus Irish, American, Turkish, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> interest, have been allowed in our courts to the amount of even 12 per cent. For the moderation or exorbitance of interest depends upon local circumstances; and the refusal to enforce such contracts would put a stop to all foreign trade. And, by stat. 14 Geo. III. c. 79., all mortgages and other securities upon estates or other property in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> or the plantations, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> interest not exceeding five per cent. shall be legal; though executed in the kingdom of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>: unless the money lent shall be known at the time to exceed the value of the thing in pledge; in which case also, to prevent usurious contracts at home under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of such foreign securities, the borrower shall forfeit treble the sum so borrowed. For the method of computing interest, see Arithmetic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. iv. p. 645; and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, sect. xx. p. 658.

INTERIM

Pages 317-317

a name given to a formulary, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> kind of confession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, obtruded upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. when he had defeated their forces; so called because it was only to take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the interim (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>) till a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> should have decided all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in dispute between the Protestants and Romanists. It retained most of the doctrines and ceremonies of the Romanists, excepting that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, which was allowed to the clergy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> under both kinds. Most of the Protestants rejected it. There were two other interims; one of Leipic, the other of Franconia.

INTERJECTION

Pages 317-317

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, an indeclinable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of speech, signifying some pallion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> of the mind. See Grammar.

INTERLOCUTOR

Pages 317-317

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the decision <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> judgment of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> is passed and extracted.

INTERLOCUTORY DECREES

Pages 317-317

in English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. In a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact be strongly controverted, the fact is usually directed to be tried at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at the affizes, upon a feigned issue. If a question of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> law arises in the course of a cause, it is the practice of the court of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> to refer it to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the judges of the court of king's bench, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> stated for that purpose. In such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, interlocutory decrees or orders are made. INTERLOCUTORY judgments are such as are given in the middle of a cause, upon some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>, proceeding on default, which is only intermediate, and does not finally determine or complete the suit. But the interlocutory judgments most usually spoken of, are those incomplete judgments, whereby the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the plaintiff is established, but the quantum of damages sustained by him is not ascertained, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. In such a case a writ of inquiry issues to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, who summons a jury, inquires of the damages, and returns to the court the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> so taken, whereupon the plaintiff's attorney taxes costs, and signs <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> judgment. INTERLOCUTORY Order, that which decides not the cause, but only settles some intervening matter relating to the cause. As where an order is made in chancery, for the plaintiff to have an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>, to quit possession till the hearing of the cause; this order, not being final, is called interlocutory.

INTERLOPERS

Pages 317-317

are properly those who, without due authority, hinder the trade of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> corporation lawfully established, by dealing in the same way.

INTERLUDE

Pages 317-317

an entertainment exhibited on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> between the acts of a play, to amuse the spectators while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> take breath and shift their dress, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to give <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for changing the scenes and decorations. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tragedy, the chorus sung the interludes, to show the intervals between the acts. Interludes, among us, usually consist of songs, dances, feats of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, concerts of music, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and Horace give it for a rule, that the interludes should consist of songs built on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts of the drama: but since the chorus has been laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, dancers, buffoons, &c. ordinarily furnish the interludes.

INTERMENT

Pages 317-321

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of interring, i.e. burying <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> laying a deceased person in the ground. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> asserted, that it was more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> to assist the dead than the living. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, in his Republic, does not forget, amongst other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, that which concerns the dead. Cicero establishes three kinds of justice; the first respects the gods, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the manes or dead, and the third men. These principles seem to be drawn from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and they appear at least to be necessary for the support of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, since at all times civilized nations have taken care to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead, and to pay their last respects to them. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">BURIAL</a>. We find in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> several traces of the respect which the Indians, the Egyptians, and the Syrians entertained for the dead. The Syrians embalmed their bodies with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, aloes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, wax, bitumen, and resinous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>; they dried them also with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of the fir and the pine tree. The Egyptians preserved theirs with the resin of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, with aromatic spices, and with salt. These people often kept such mummies, or at least their effigies, in their houses; and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> entertainments they were introduced, that by reciting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> actions of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> they might be better excited to virtue. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNERAL_RITES">FUNERAL <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">RITES</a>. The Greeks, at first, had probably not the same veneration for the dead as the Egyptians. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEDOCLES">Empedocles</a>, therefore, in the eighty-fourth Olympiad, restored to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> Pontia, a woman of Argirgentum, who was about to be interred. But this people, in proportion as they grew civilized, becoming more enlightened, perceived the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of establishing laws for the protection of the dead. At <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> required that no person should be interred before the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and in the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> a funeral did not take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> till the fifth or seventh. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> appeared to have breathed his last, his body was generally washed by his nearest relations, with warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mixed with wine. They afterwards anointed it with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; and covered it with a dress <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the Egyptians. This dress was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> at Messina, Athens, and in the greater part of the cities of Greece, where the dead body was crowned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> it was of a purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and the body was surrounded with olive leaves. The body was afterwards laid upon a couch in the entry of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where it remained till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the funeral. At the magnificent obsequies with which Alexander honoured Hephaestion, the body was not burned until the tenth day. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in the infancy of their empire, paid as little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to their dead as the Greeks had done. Acilius Aviola having fallen into a lethargic fit, was supposed to be dead; he was therefore carried to the funeral pile; the fire was lighted up; and though he cried out he was still alive, he perished for want of speedy assistance. The praetor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMIA">Lamia</a> met with the same fate. Tubero, who had been praetor, was saved from the funeral pile. Aesclepiades a physician, who lived in the time of Pompey the Great, about one hundred and twenty years before the Christian era, returning from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-house, observed near the walls of Rome a grand convoy and a crowd of people, who were in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> afflicting at a funeral, and showing every exterior sign of the deepest grief. Having asked what was the occasion of this concourse, no one made any reply. He therefore approached the pretended dead body; and imagining that he perceived signs of life in it, he ordered the bystanders to take away the flambeaux, to extinguish the fire, and to pull <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the funeral pile. A kind of murmur on this arose throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. Some said that they ought to believe the physician, while others turned both him and his profession into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>. The relations, however, yielded at length to the remonstrances of Aesclepiades; they consented to defer the obsequies for a little; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, the restoration of the pretended dead person to life. It appears that these examples, and several others of the like nature, induced the Romans to delay funerals longer, and to enact laws to prevent precipitate interments. At Rome, after allowing a sufficient time for mourning, the nearest relation generally closed the eyes of the deceased; and the body was bathed with warm water, either to render it fitter for being anointed with oil, or to reanimate the principle of life, which might remain suspended without manifesting itself. Proofs were afterwards made, to discover whether the person was really dead, which were often repeated during the time that the body remained exposed; for there were persons appointed to visit the dead, and to prove their situation. On the second day, after the body had been washed a second time, it was anointed with oil and balm. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">Luxury</a> increased to such a pitch in the choice of foreign perfumes for this purpose, that under the consulship of Licinius Cratius and Julius Caesar, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> forbade any perfumes to be used except such as were the production of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. On the third day the body was clothed according to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and condition. The robe called the praetexta was put upon magistrates, and a purple robe upon consuls; for conquerors, who had merited triumphal honours, this robe was of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> tissue. For other Romans it was white, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> for the lower classes of the people. These dresses were often prepared at a distance, by the mothers and wives of persons still in life. On the fourth day the body was placed on a couch, and exposed in the vestibule of the house, with the visage turned towards the entrance, and the feet near the door; in this situation it remained till the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. Near the couch were lighted wax-tapers, a small box in which perfumes were burnt, and a vessel full of water for purification, with which those who approached the body befriended themselves. An old man, belonging to those who furnished everything necessary for funerals, sat near the deceased, with some domestics clothed in black. On the eighth day the funeral rites were performed; but to prevent the body from corrupting before that time, salt, wax, the resinous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> of the cedar, myrrh, honey, balm, gypsum, lime, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASPHALTITES">asphaltites</a> or bitumen of Judea, and several other substances, were employed. The body was carried to the pile with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> uncovered, unless wounds or the nature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> had rendered it loathsome and disgusting. In such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a mask was used, made of a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>; which has given rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of funera larvata, used in some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors. This was the last method of concealment which Nero made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, after having caused Germanicus to be poisoned; for the effect of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> had become very sensible by livid spots and the blackness of the body; but a shower of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> happening to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, it washed the plaster entirely away, and thus the horrid crime of fratricide was discovered. The Turks have, at all times, been accustomed to wash the bodies of their dead before interment; and as their ablutions are complete, and no part of the body escapes the attention of those who assist at such melancholy ceremonies, they can easily perceive whether Interment one be really dead or alive, by examining, among other methods of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, whether the sphincter ani has lost its power of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this muscle remains still contracted, they warm the body, and endeavour to recall it to life; otherwise, after having washed it with water and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, they wipe it with linen cloths, wash it again with rose-water and aromatic substances, cover it with a rich dress, put upon its head a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> ornamented with flowers, and extend it upon a carpet placed in the vestibule or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> at the entrance of the house. In the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> the dead were washed and then anointed; the body was wrapped up in linen, or clothed in a dress of more or less value according to circumstances, and it was not interred until after being exposed and kept some days in the house. The custom of clothing the dead is preserved in France only for princes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>. In other countries, more or less care is taken to prevent sudden interments. At <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, there are people appointed to inspect all dead bodies. Their duty consists in examining whether the person be really dead, and whether one died naturally or by violence. In the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, as well as at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, it is usual not to bury the dead till three days have expired. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, people carry their precautions much farther, and delay the funeral's longer. And in England bodies generally remain unburied three or four days. Premature Interment. Notwithstanding the customs above recited; still, in many places, and on many occasions in all places, too much precipitation attends this last office; or if not precipitation, a neglect of due precautions in regard to the body. In general, indeed, the most improper treatment that can be imagined is adopted, and many a person made to descend into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> before he has sighed his last breath. The histories related by Hildanus, by Camerarius, by Horilius, by Macrobius in his Somnium Scipionis, by Plato in his Republic, by Valerius Maximus, and by a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors, leave us no doubt respecting the dangers and misconduct of such precipitation. It must appear astonishing that the attention of mankind has been after all so little raised by an idea the most terrible that can be conceived on this side of eternity. If nature recoils from the idea of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, with what horror must she start at the thought of death anticipated, precipitated by inattention—a return of life in darkness, dilution, and despair—then death repeated under agonies unspeakable! To revive nailed up in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>! The brain can scarce sustain the reflection in our coolest safest moments. According to present usage, as soon as the semblance of death appears, the chamber of the sick is deserted by friends, relatives, and physicians; and the apparently dead, though frequently living, body, is committed to the management of an ignorant and unfeeling nurse, whose care extends no farther than laying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> straight, and securing her accustomed perquisites. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-clothes are immediately removed, and the body is exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. This, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, must extinguish any spark of life that may remain, and which, by a different treatment, might have been kindled into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>; or it may only continue to refresh it, and the unhappy person afterwards revive amidst the horrors of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the end of a weak life and interment; the commencement of death, is so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a>, and the uncertainty of the signs of the latter is so well established both by ancient and modern authors who have turned their attention to that important object, that we can scarcely suppose undertakers capable of distinguishing an apparent from a real death. Animals which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> during winter show no signs of life; in this case, circulation is only suspended: but were it annihilated, the vital spirit does not so easily lose its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> as the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> of the body; and the principle of life, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> survives the appearance of death, may re-animate a body in which the action of all the organs seems to be at an end. But how difficult is it to determine whether this principle may not be revived? It has been found impossible to recall to life some animals suffocated by mephitic vapours, though they appeared less affected than others who have revived. Coldness, heaviness of the body, a leaden livid colour, with a yellowness in the visage, are all very uncertain signs: Mr Zimmerman observed them all upon the body of a criminal, who fainted through the dread of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> which he had merited. He was shaken, dragged about, and turned in the same manner as dead bodies are, without the least signs of respiration; and yet at the end of 24 hours he was recalled to life by means of volatile alkali. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a>-office at Dijon, named Colinet, was supposed to be dead, and the news of this event was spread through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. One of his friends, who was desirous of seeing him at the moment when he was about to be buried, having looked at him for a considerable time, thought he perceived some remains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> in the muscles of the face. He therefore made an attempt to bring him to life by spirituous liquors, in which he succeeded; and this director enjoyed afterwards for a long time that life which he owed to his friend. This remarkable circumstance was much like those of Empedocles and Asclepiades. These instances would perhaps be more frequent, were men of skill and abilities called in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of sudden death, in which people of ordinary knowledge are often deceived by false appearances. A man may fall into a syncope, and may remain in that condition three or even eight days. People in this situation have been known to come to life when deposited among the dead. A body belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> appeared to have breathed its last; he was carried into the hall where the dead were exposed, and was wrapped up in a piece of canvas. Some time after, recovering from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a>, he recollected the place in which he had been deposited, and crawling towards the door knocked against it with his foot. This noise was luckily heard by the sentinel, who soon perceiving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the canvas called for assistance. The youth was immediately conveyed to a warm bed, and soon perfectly recovered. Had his body been confined by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> bandages or ligatures, he would not have been able, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, to make himself be heard: his unavailing efforts would have made him again fall into a syncope, and he would have been thus buried alive. We must not be astonished that the servants of an hospital should take a syncope for a real death, since, even the most enlightened people have fallen into errors of Dr John Schmid relates, that a young girl, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, after being afflicted for some weeks with a violent cough, was all of a sudden freed from this troublesome malady, and appeared to be in perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. But some days after, while playing with her companions, this child fell down in an instant as if struck by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. A death-like pallor was diffused over her face and arms; she had no apparent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were sunk, and she showed no signs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> when shaken or pinched. A physician, who was called, and who believed her to be dead, in compliance with the repeated and pressing request of her parents, attempted, though without any hopes, to recall her to life; and at length, after several vain efforts, he made the soles of her feet be firmly rubbed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> dipped in strong pickle. At the end of three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> she was observed to sigh; she was then made to swallow some spirituous liquor; and she was soon after restored to life, much to the joy of her disconsolate parents.—A certain man having undertaken a journey, in order to see his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, on his arrival at his house found him dead. This news affected him so much, that it brought on a most dreadful syncope, and he himself was supposed to be in the like situation. After the usual means had been employed to recall him to life, it was agreed that his body should be dissected, to discover the cause of so sudden a death; but the supposed dead person overhearing this proposal, opened his eyes, started up, and immediately betook himself to his heels.—<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Espanola, prime minister to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II., was not so fortunate; for we read in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Amelot de la Houllai, that he put his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> with which he was opened in order to be embalmed. In short, almost every one knows that Vesalius, the father of anatomy, having been sent for to open a woman subject to hysterics, who was supposed to be dead, he perceived, on making the first incision, by her motion and cries, that she was still alive; that this circumstance rendered him so odious, that he was obliged to fly; and that he was so much affected by it, that he died soon after.—On this occasion, we cannot forbear to add an event more recent, but no less melancholy. The abbe Prevost, so well known by his writings and the singularities of his life, was seized with a fit of the apoplexy, in the forest of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANTILLY">Chantilly</a>, on the 23d of October 1763. His body was carried to the nearest village, and the officers of justice were proceeding to open it, when a cry which he sent forth affrightened all the assistants, and convinced the surgeon that the abbe was not dead; but it was too late to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> him, as he had already received the mortal wound. Even in old age, when life seems to have been gradually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> to a close, the appearances of death are often fallacious. A lady in Cornwall, more than 80 years of age, who had been a considerable time declining, took to her bed, and in a few days seemingly expired in the morning. As she had often desired not to be buried till she had been two days dead, her request was to have been regularly complied with by her relations. All that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> her looked upon her as dead, and the report was current through the whole place; nay, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the town actually wrote to his friend in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Scilly that she was decease. But one of those who were paying the last kind office of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> to her remains, perceived some warmth about the Interm. middle of the back; and acquainting her friends with it, they applied a mirror to her mouth; but, after repeated trials, could not observe it in the least alarmed; her under jaw was likewise fallen, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> phrase is; and, in short, she had every appearance of a dead person. All this time she had not been stripped or dried; but the windows were opened, as is usual in the chambers of the deceased. In the evening the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> seemed to increase, and at length she was perceived to breathe. In short, not only the ordinary signs are very uncertain, but we may say the same of the stiffness of the limbs, which may be convulsive; of the dilation of the pupil of the eye, which may proceed from the same cause; of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, which may equally attack some parts of a living body; and of several others. Haller, convinced of the uncertainty of all these signs, proposes a new one, which he considers as infallible. "If the person (says he) be still in life, the mouth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> immediately shut of itself, because the contraction of the muscles of the jaw will awaken their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a>." The jaw, however, may be deprived of its irritability though a man may not be dead. Life is preserved a long time in the passage of the intestines. The sign pointed out by Dr Fothergill appears to deserve more attention: "If the air blown into the mouth (says this physician) passes freely through all the alimentary channel, it affords a strong presumption that the irritability of the internal sphincters is destroyed, and consequently that life is at an end." These signs, which deserve to be confirmed by new experiments, are doubtless not known to undertakers. The difficulty of distinguishing a person apparently dead from one who is really so, has, in all countries where bodies have been interred too precipitately, rendered it necessary for the law to assist humanity. Of several regulations made on this subject, we shall quote only a few of the most recent; such as those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAS">Arras</a> in 1772; of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> in 1774; of the grand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> in 1775; of the fenechauffee of Sivrai, in Poitou, in 1777; and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a> in the same year. To give an idea of the rest, it will be sufficient to relate only that of Tuscany. By this edict, the grand duke forbids the precipitate interment of persons who die suddenly. He orders the magistrates of health to be informed, that physicians and surgeons may examine the body; that they may use every endeavour to recall it to life, if possible, or to discover the cause of its death; and that they shall make a report of their procedure to a certain tribunal. On this occasion, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of health orders the dead not to be covered until the moment they are about to be buried, except so far as decency requires; observing always that the body be not closely confined, and that nothing may compress the jugular veins and the carotid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>. He forbids people to be interred according to the ancient method; and requires that the arms and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> should be left extended, and that they should not be folded or placed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-wise upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. He forbids, above all, to press the jaws one against the other; or to fill the mouth and nostrils with cotton, or other stuffing. Lastly, he recommends not to cover the visage with any kind of cloth until the body is deposited in its coffin. We shall conclude this article by adjoining, from Dr Hawes's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">Address</a> to the Public on this subject, a few of the cases in which this fallacious appearance of death is most likely to happen, together with the respective modes of treatment which he recommends. In apoplectic and fainting fits, and in those arising from any violent agitation of mind, and also when opium or spirituous liquors have been taken in too great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, there is reason to believe that the appearance of death has been frequently mistaken for the reality. In these cases, the means recommended by the Humane Society for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">Recovery</a> of Drowned Persons should be persevered in for several hours; and bleeding, which in similar circumstances has sometimes proved pernicious, should be used with great caution. (See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROWNING">DROWNING</a>.) In the two latter instances it will be highly expedient, with a view of counteracting the soporific effects of opium and spirits, to convey into the stomach, by a proper tube, a solution of tartar emetic, and by various other means to excite vomiting. From the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of children carried off by convulsions, and the certainty arising from undoubted facts, that some who have in appearance died from that cause have been recovered; there is the greatest reason for concluding, that many, in consequence of this disease, have been prematurely numbered among the dead; and that the fond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, by neglecting the means of recalling life, has often been the guiltless executioner of her own offspring. To prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of such dreadful mistakes, no child, whose life has been apparently extinguished by convulsions, should be confined to the grave till the means of recovery above recommended in apoplexies, &c., have been tried; and, if possible, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of some skilful practitioner of medicine, who may vary them as circumstances shall require. When fevers arise in weak habits, or when the cure of them has been principally attempted by means of depletion, the consequent debility is often very great, and the patient sometimes sinks into a state which bears so close an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to that of death, that there is reason to suspect it has too often deceived the bystanders, and induced them to send for the undertaker when they should have had recourse to the succours of medicine. In such cases, volatiles, eau de luce for example, should be applied to the nose, rubbed on the temples, and sprinkled often about the bed; hot flannels, moistened with a strong solution of camphorated spirit, may likewise be applied over the breast, and renewed every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an hour; and as soon as the patient is able to swallow, a teaspoonful of the strongest cordial should be given every five minutes. The same methods may also be used with propriety in the smallpox when the pustules sink, and death apparently ensues; and likewise in any other acute diseases, when the vital functions are suspended from a similar case.

INTERMITTENT

Pages 321-321
or INTERMITTING, Fever; such fevers as go off and soon return again, in opposition to those which are continual. See MEDICINE Index.

INTERPOLATION

Pages 321-321

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, is used for finding an intermediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the series being given. This method was first invented by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIGGS">Briggs</a>, and applied by him to the calculation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a>, &c. See ALGEBRA.

INTERPOSITION

Pages 321-321

the situation of a body between two others, so as to hide them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prevent their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. The eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is occasioned by an interposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> between the sun and us; and that of the moon by the interposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> between the sun and moon. See ECLIPSE.

INTERPRETER

Pages 321-321

a person who explains the thoughts, words, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> writings, of some other, which before were unintelligible.—The word interpretes, according to Ifidore, is composed of the preposition inter, and partes, as signifying a person in the middle betwixt two parties, to make them mutually understand each other's thoughts; others derive it from inter, and pret, i.e. sidehelper; q.d. a person who serves as security between two others who do not understand one another. There have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> debates about interpreting Scripture. The Romanists contend, that it belongs absolutely to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>: adding, that where the is silent, reason may be consulted; but where it speaks, reason is to be disregarded. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> generally allow reason the sovereign judge, or interpreter; though some among them have a strong regard to synods, and others to the authority of the primitive fathers. Lastly, others have recourse to the Spirit within every person to interpret for them; which is what Bochart calls anabaptisi, or pneumatici.

INTERREGNUM

Pages 321-321

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> during which the throne is vacant in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> kingdoms; for in such as are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, like ours, there is no such thing as an interregnum.

INTERREX

Pages 321-321

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> who governs during an interregnum. This magistrate was established in old Rome, and was almost as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> itself; after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> there was an interregnum of a year, during which the senators were each interrex in their turn, five days a-piece. After the establishment of consuls and a commonwealth, though there were no kings, yet the name and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of interrex was still preserved: for, when the magistrates were absent, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> there was any irregularity in their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, or they had abdicated, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a> could not be held; provided they were unwilling to create a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, they made an interrex, whose office and authority was to last five days; after which they made another. To the interrex was delegated all the regal and consular authority, and he performed all their functions. He assembled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, held comitia or courts, and took care that the election of magistrates was according to rules. Indeed at first it was not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the interrex to hold comitia, at least we have no instance of it in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The patricians alone had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of electing an interrex; but this office fell with the republic, when the emperors made themselves masters of every thing.

INTERROGATION

Pages 322-322

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, is a point which serves to distinguish such parts of a discourse, where the author speaks as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were asking questions. Its form is this (?).

INTERROGATORIES

Pages 322-322

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, are particular questions demanded of witnesses brought in to be examined in a cause, especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. And these interrogatories must be exhibited by the parties in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> on each side; which are either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> for the party that produces them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>, on behalf of the adverse party; and generally both plaintiff and defendant may exhibit direct, and counter or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> interrogatories. They are to be pertinent, and only to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> necessary; and either drawn or perused by counsel, and to be signed by them.

INTERSCENDENT

Pages 322-322

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, is applied to quantities, when the exponents of their powers are radical quantities. Thus, \(x^{1/2}, x^{1/3}\), &c., are interescendent quantities.

INTERSECTION

Pages 322-322

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> of one line, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, by another; or the point or line wherein two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, or two planes, cut each other. The mutual intersection of two planes is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line. The centre of a circle is in the intersection of two diameters. The central point of a regular or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of four sides, is the point of intersection of the two diagonals. The equinoxes happen when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is in the intersections of the equator and ecliptic. INTERSPINALE. See ANATOMY, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

INTERVAL

Pages 322-322

in Music. The distance between any given <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and another, strictly speaking, is neither measured by any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> standard of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; but either by immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by computing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the numbers of vibrations produced by two or more sonorous bodies, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of sounding, during the same given <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. As the vibrations are slower and fewer during the same instant, for example, the sound is proportionally lower or graver; on the contrary, as during the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the vibrations increase in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and velocity, the sounds are proportionably higher or more acute. An interval in music, therefore, is properly the difference between the number of vibrations produced by one sonorous body of a certain magnitude and texture, and of those produced by another of a different magnitude and texture in the same time. Intervals are divided into consonant and dissonant. A consonant interval is that whose extremes, or whose highest and lowest sounds, when simultaneously heard, coalesce in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, and produce an agreeable sensation called by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames a tertium quid. A dissonant interval, on the contrary, is that whose extremes, simultaneously heard, far from coalescing in the ear, and producing one agreeable sensation, are each of them plainly distinguished from the other, produce a grating effect upon the senses, and repel each other with an irreconcilable hostility. In proportion as the vibrations of different sonorous bodies, or of the same sonorous body in different modes, more or less frequently coincide during the same given time, the chords are more or less consonant. When these vibrations never coincide at all in the same given time, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> is consummate, and consequently the interval absolutely dissonant. But, for a full account of these, see MUSIC.

INTESTATE

Pages 322-322

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a person that dies without making a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>.

INTESTINA

Pages 322-322

in the Linnean System, one of the orders of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

INTESTINES

Pages 322-322

Intestina, in Anatomy, the guts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bowels; those hollow, membranous, cylindrical parts, extended from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> orifice of the stomach to the anus; by which the chyle is conveyed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACTEALS">lacteals</a>, and the excrements are voided. See ANATOMY, No. 93.

INTONATION

Pages 322-322

in Music, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of sounding the notes in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other given order of musical tones. Intonation may be either true or false, either too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or too low, either too sharp or too flat; and then this word intonation, attended with an epithet, must be understood concerning the manner of performing the notes. In executing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, to form the sounds, and preserve the intervals as they are marked with justness and accuracy, is no inconsiderable difficulty, and scarcely practicable, but by the affluence of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> idea, to which, as to their ultimate test, these sounds and intervals must be referred: these common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> are those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> in which the performer is engaged; and from the word tone, which is sometimes used in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> almost identical with that of the key, the word intonation may perhaps be derived. It may also be deduced from the word diatonic, as in that scale it is most frequently conversant; a scale which appears most convenient and most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to the voice. We feel more difficulty in our intonation of such intervals as are greater or lesser than those of the diatonic order; because, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the glottis and vocal organs are modified by gradations too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; or too complex, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>.

INTRENCHMENT

Pages 322-322

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> that fortifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> against an enemy who attacks. It is generally taken for a ditch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trench with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>. Intrenchments are sometimes made of fascines with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> thrown over them, of gabions, hogheads, or bags filled with earth, to cover the men from the enemy's fire.

INTRIGUE

Pages 322-323

an assemblage of events <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circumstances, occurring in an affair, and perplexing the persons concerned in it. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it is used to signify the nodus or plot of a play or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>; or that point wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are most embarrassed through Intrigue through the artifice and opposition of certain persons, or the unfortunate falling out of certain accidents and circumstances. In tragedy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, or an epic poem, there are always two designs. The first and principal is that of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of the piece; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> contains the designs of all those who oppose him. These opposite causes produce opposite effects, to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, the efforts of the hero for the execution of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and the efforts of those who thwart it. As these causes and designs are the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, so these efforts are the middle, and there form a knot or difficulty which we call the intrigue, that makes the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the poem. It lasts as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the mind of the reader or hearer is suspended about the event of those opposite efforts: the solution or catastrophe commences when the knot begins to unravel, and the difficulties and doubts begin to clear up. The intrigue of the Iliad is twofold. The first comprehends three days fighting in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>' absence, and consists on the one side in the resistance of Agamemnon and the Greeks, and on the other in the inexorable temper of Achilles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a> unravels this intrigue, and makes the beginning of a second. Achilles resolves to be revenged, but Hector opposes his design; and this forms the second intrigue, which is the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. In the Æneid there are also two intrigues. The first is taken up in the voyage and landing of Æneas in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; the second is his establishment there: the opposition he met with from Juno in both these undertakings forms the intrigue. As to the choice of the intrigue, and the manner of unravelling it, it is certain they ought both to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> naturally from the ground and subject of the poem. Boëthius gives us three manners of forming the intrigue of a poem: the first is that already mentioned; the second is taken from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> and design of the poet; in the third the intrigue is so laid, as that the solution follows from it of course.

INTRINSIC

Pages 323-323

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to the real and genuine values and properties, &c., of any thing, in opposition to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRINSIC">extrinsic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apparent values.

INTUITION

Pages 323-323

among logicians, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby the mind perceives the agreement <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disagreement of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, immediately by themselves, without the intervention of any other; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the mind perceives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> as the eye does the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, only by being directed towards it.
