See LOGIC, No. 25, 27. INTUITIVE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, is that which results from INTUITION. Dr Campbell distinguishes different sorts of intuitive evidence; one resulting purely from intuition, or that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> which others have called intuition; another kind arising from consciousness; and a third sort from that now named faculty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">Sense</a>, which this ingenious writer, as well as several others, contends to be a distinct original source of knowledge; whilst others refer its supposed office to the intuitive power of the understanding.

INULA

Pages 326-326

ELECAMPEAE; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

INUNDATAE

Pages 326-326

the name of the 15th order in Linnaeus's fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method; consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which grow in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>, p. 309.

INUNDATION

Pages 326-326

a sudden overflowing of the dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> by the waters of the ocean, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rains.

INVALID

Pages 323-323

a person wounded, maimed, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disabled for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. At Chelsea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> are magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">Hospitals</a>, or rather colleges, built for the reception and accommodation of invalids, or foldiers and seamen worn out in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. We have also twenty independent companies of invalids, dispersed in the several forts and garrisons. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the same kind, called les Invalides, which is accounted one of the finest buildings in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>.

INVENTION

Pages 323-323

denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of finding anything new, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even the thing thus found. Thus we say, the invention of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, &c. The alcove is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> invention owing to the Moors. The Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders, are of a Greek invention; the Tuscan and Composite of Latin invention. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> Almeloveen has written an Onomasticum of inventions; wherein are shown, in an alphabetical order, the names of the inventors, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, &c., where they are made. Pancrillus has a treatise of old inventions that are lost, and new ones that have been made; Polydore <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> has also published eight books of the inventors of things, De Inventoribus Rerum. Invention is also used for the finding of a thing hidden. The Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> celebrates a feast on the 4th of May, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Invention of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a>. Invention is also used for subtlety of mind, or something peculiar to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s genius, which leads him to a discovery of things new; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say, a man of invention. Invention, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, is the choice which the painter makes of the objects that are to enter the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of his piece. See PAINTING. Invention, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, is applied to whatever the poet adds to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the subject he has chosen; as well as to the new turn he gives it. See POETRY. Invention, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, signifies the finding out and choosing of certain arguments which the orator is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for the proving or illustrating his point, moving the passions or conciliating the minds of his hearers. Invention, according to Cicero, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of oratory: he wrote four books De Inventione, whereof we have but two remaining. See ORATORY.

INVENTORY

Pages 323-324

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a catalogue <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHEDULE">schedule</a> orderly made, of all the deceased person's goods and chattels at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, with their value appraised by indifferent persons, which every executor or administrator is obliged to exhibit to the ordinary at such time as he shall appoint. By 21 Hen. VIII, c. v. executors and administrators are are to deliver in upon oath to the ordinary, indented inventories, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is to remain with the ordinary, and the other part with the executor or administrator; this is required for the benefit of the creditors and legatees, that the executor or administrator may not conceal any part of the personal estate from them. The statute ordains, that the inventory shall be exhibited within three months after the person's decease; yet it may be done afterwards; for the ordinary may dispense with the time, and even with its being ever exhibited, as in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the creditors are paid, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> is executed.

INVERARY

Pages 324-324

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> town of Argyllshire, in Scotland, pleasantly situated on a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> formed by the junction of the river Ary with Loch-fyne, where the latter is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in width and 60 fathoms in depth. Here is a castle, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seat of the dukes of Argyll, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Campbells. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of a quadrangular form, with a round tower at each corner; and in the middle rises a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> one glazed on every side to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to the staircase and galleries, which has from without rather a heavy appearance. This castle is built of a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> ollaris brought from the other side of Loch-fyne; and is of the same kind with that found in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is built. The founder of the castle, the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> Archibald, also formed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of an entire new town, upon a commodious elegant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, becoming the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Argyllshire, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> most admirably situated for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. The town hath been rebuilt agreeable to the original design; and the inhabitants are well lodged in houses of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, lime, and flate. They are fully employed in arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and plentifully supplied in the produce of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> around Inverary is extensive beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, and admirably variegated; every crevice, glen, and mountain, displaying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. The value of the immense wood at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, for the various purposes of bark, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, forges, paling, furniture, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and ship building, is thus estimated by Mr Knox: "Some of the beech are from 9 to 12 feet in circumference, and the pines from 6 to 9; but these being comparatively few, we shall state the medium girth of 2,000,000 trees planted within these last hundred years, at 3 feet, and the medium value at 4s. which produces 400,000l.; and this, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, upon grounds unfit for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, being chiefly composed of hills and rock." One of these hills rises immediately from the house a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, and is clothed to the summit with a thick wood of vigorous ornamental trees. On this summit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> point Archibald duke of Argyle built a Gothic tower, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, where he sometimes amused himself. The ascent by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> seems to be half a mile, and the perpendicular height about 800 feet.

INVERBERVIE

Pages 324-324
or Bervie, a town of Scotland, in Kincardineshire or the Mearns, and a royal borough, 13 miles north-east from Montrose. It lies between two small hills, which terminate in high cliffs towards the sea; it is but a small place, the inhabitants of which are chiefly employed in making thread.

INVERKEITHING

Pages 324-324

a town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Fife, situated on the northern shore of the frith of Forth, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 15'. N. Lat. 56° 5'. It was much favoured by William, who granted its first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. He extended its liberties considerably, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. it became a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence. The Moubrays had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> possessions here, which were forfeited in the reign of Robert II. The Franciscans had a convent in this town; and, according to Sir Robert Sibbald, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> had another. This town has a considerable trade in coal and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>.

INVERLOCHY

Pages 324-324

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle in the neighbourhood of Fort-William in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERNESS_SHIRE"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>-shire. It is adorned with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> round towers; and, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, seems to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the English in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Edward I. who laid large fines on the Scotch barons for the purpose of erecting new castles. The largest of these towers is called Cumins's. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to these ruins, Inverlochy, according to Boece, had been a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, a most opulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, remarkable for the vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of French and Spaniards, probably on account of trade. It was also a seat of the kings of Scotland, for here Atholus in the year 790 signed (as is reported) the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> offensive and defensive between himself and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. In after-times it was utterly destroyed by the Danes, and never again restored. In the neighbourhood of this place were fought two fierce battles, one between Donald Balloch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to Alexander <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the illes, who with a great power invaded Lochaber in the year 1427: he was met by the earls of Mar and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAITHNESS">Caithness</a>; the last was slain, and their forces totally defeated. Balloch returned to the illes with vast booty. Here also the Campbells under the marquis of Argyll, were in February 1645, defeated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>. Fifteen hundred fell in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and in the pursuit, with the loss only of three to the royalists.

INVERNESS

Pages 324-326
capital of a county of the same name in Scotland, is a parliament-town, finely seated on the river Nevis, over which there is a stone bridge of seven arches, in W. Long. 4°. N. Lat. 57° 36'. It is large, well built, and very populous, being the most northerly town of any note in Britain. As there are always regular troops in its neighbourhood, there is a great air of politeness, a plentiful market, and more money and business stirring than could have been expected in such a remote part of the island. The country in the neighbourhood is remarkably well cultivated; and its produce clearly shows that the soil and climate are not defective. The salmon-fishery in the Nevis is very considerable, and is let to London fishmongers. Some branches both of the woollen, linen, and hemp manufacture, are also carried on here; and, in consequence of the excellent military roads, there is a great proportion of inland trade. But besides all this, Inverness is a port with 20 creeks dependent upon it, part on the Murray frith to the east, and part on the north of the town, reaching even the fourth border of the county of Caithness. Inverness has several good schools; and an academy was erected some years ago on an extensive and liberal plan. The inhabitants speak the Erse and English language promiscuously. On an eminence near the town are the remains of a castle, where, according to some historians, the famous Macbeth murdered Duncan his royal guest. Inverness-Shire, Inverness-Shire, a county of Scotland, bounded on the north by Ross-shire; on the east by the shires of Nairne, Murray, and Aberdeen; on the south, by those of Perth and Argyle; and on the west, by the Atlantic ocean. Its extent from north to south is above 50 miles; from east to west about 80.—The northern part of this county is very mountainous and barren. In the district of Glenelg are seen the ruins of several ancient circular buildings, similar to those in the Western Isles, Sutherland, and Ross-shires; concerning the uses of which antiquarians are not agreed. In their outward appearance, they are round and tapering like glass-houses. In the heart of the wall, which is perpendicular within, there are horizontal galleries going quite round and connected by stairs. These ascend toward the top, which is open. They are all built of stone, without lime or mortar of any kind. They have no opening outward, except the doors and the top; but there are several in the inside, as windows to the galleries. From Bernera barracks, in this district, proceeds the military road to Inverness. This county is nearly divided by water, so that by means of the Caledonian canal uniting Loch Ness, Loch Oich, Loch Lochy, and Lochiel or Loch Eil, a communication will be opened between the eastern and western seas. This great undertaking is now (1807) going forward. In this tract, Fort George, Fort Augustus, and Fort William, form what is called the Chain of Forts across the island. By means of Fort George on the east, all entrance up the strait towards Inverness is prevented; Fort Augustus curbs the inhabitants midway; and Fort William is a check to any attempts in the west. Detachments are made from all these garrisons to Inverness, Bernera barracks opposite to the Isle of Skye, and Castle Duart in the Isle of Mull. The river Ness, upon which the capital of the shire is situated, is the outlet of the great lake called Loch Ness. This beautiful lake is 22 miles in length, and for the most part one in breadth. It is screened on the north-west by the lofty mountains of Urquhart and Meall-fourvonny, and bordered with coppices of birch and oak. The adjacent hills are adorned with many extensive forests of pine; which afford shelter to the cattle, and are the retreat of flags and deer. There is much cultivation and improvements on the banks of Loch Ness; and the pasture-grounds in the neighbouring valleys are excellent.—From the south, the river Fyers descends towards this lake. Over this river there is built a stupendous bridge, on two opposite rocks; the top of the arch is above 100 feet from the level of the water. A little below the bridge is the celebrated Fall of Fyers, where a great body of water darts through a narrow gap between two rocks, then falls over a vast precipice into the bottom of the chasm, where the foam rises and fills the air like a great cloud of smoke. Loch Oich is a narrow lake, stretching about four miles from east to west. It is adorned with some small wooded islands, and is surrounded with ancient trees. Near this is the family seat of Glenary, surrounded by natural woods of full grown fir, which extend nine or ten miles along the banks of the river Gary. The waters of Loch Oich flow through Loch Ness into the eastern sea.—Loch Lochy transmits its waters in an opposite direction, this being the highest part of the vast flat tract that here stretches from sea to sea. This extensive lake is above ten miles in length, and from one to two in breadth. From the west, the waters of Loch Arrok descend into this lake. Out of it runs the river Lochy, which about a mile below its issue from the lake receives the Spean, a considerable river, over which there is a magnificent bridge, built by General Wade, about two miles above the place where it falls into the Lochy. These united streams traversing the plains of Lochaber, after a course of five or six miles, fall into Loch Eil. A few miles to the south-east of Loch Lochy is Glenroy or King's Vale. The north-east end of this valley opens on Loch Spey. A small river palisades along the bottom of the vale, accompanied by a modern road. On the declivity of the mountains, about a mile from the river, on either hand, are seen several parallel roads of great antiquity. On the north-west side, five of these roads run parallel and close by each other. On the opposite side are three other roads exactly similar. These roads are 30 feet broad, all perfectly horizontal, and extend eight or nine miles in length. Their delineation or use has baffled the conjectures of antiquaries.—Not far from Fort Augustus soars the pointed summit of Ben Nevis, which is esteemed the highest mountain in Britain, rising more than 4300 feet above the level of the sea.—In the districts of Moydart, Arisaig, Morer, and Knoydart, there are numerous bays and creeks, along the coast, many of which might be excellent fishing stations. The southern part of this county is very mountainous, and is supposed to be the most elevated ground in Scotland. From its numerous lakes many streams descend toward both seas. In the extensive district called Badenoch lies Loch Spey, the source of the great river Spey, which proceeding eastward with an increasing stream, enters the shire of Murray at Rothesmurchus, after having expanded into a fine lake. Not far from this is seen the lofty top of Cairngorm; a mountain celebrated for its beautiful rock-crystals of various tints. These are much esteemed by lapidaries; and some of them, having the lustre of fine gems, bring a very high price. Limestone, iron-ore, and some traces of different minerals, are found in the county, but no mines have yet been worked with much success. Its rivers and lakes afford abundance of salmon and trout. The extensive plains which surround the lakes are in general fertile; and the high grounds feed many sheep and black cattle, the rearing and selling of which forms the chief trade of the inhabitants.—By the present spirited exertions of the gentlemen in this populous county, the commerce and the industry of the inhabitants have of late been greatly increased; and to facilitate the communication with other parts, application has been made to parliament for leave to levy a tax on the proprietors of land for improving the roads and erecting bridges in this extensive shire. The commonalty in the high parts of the county and on the western shore speak Gaelic; but the people of fashion in Inverness and its vicinity use the English language, and pronounce it with remarkable propriety. INVERSE

Pages 326-326

is applied to a manner of working the rule of three. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">ARITHMETIC</a>, p. 13.

INVERSION

Pages 326-326

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, is where the words of a phrase are ranged in a manner not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> as they might be. For an instance: "Of all vices, the most abominable, and that which least becomes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>." Here is an inversion; the natural order being this: Impurity is the most abominable of all vices, and that which least becomes a man.—An inversion is not always disagreeable, but sometimes has a good effect.

INVERTED

Pages 326-326

in Music, is derived from the Latin preposition in, and vertere, "to turn any thing a contrary way." It signifies a change in the order of the notes which form a chord, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the parts which compose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>: which happens by substituting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, those founds which ought to have been in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; an operation not only rendered practicable, but greatly facilitated by the resemblance which one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> has to another in different octaves; whence we derive the power of exchanging one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> for another with so much propriety and success, or by substituting in the extremes those which ought to have occupied the middle station; and vice versa. See MUSIC.

INVESTIGATION

Pages 326-326

properly denotes the searching <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> finding out any thing by the traces or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> of the feet; whence mathematicians, schoolmen, and grammarians, come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in their respective researches. INVESTING a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">PLACE</a>, is when a general, having an intention to besiege it, detaches a body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to possess all the avenues; blocking up the garrison, and preventing relief from getting into the place, till the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> are got up to form the siege.

INVESTITURE

Pages 326-326

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEISIN">seisin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> possession. There was anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of ceremonies used upon investitures; as at first they were made by a certain form of words, and afterwards by such things as had the greatest resemblance to the thing to be transferred: thus, where lands were intended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, a turf, &c. was delivered by the grantor to the grantee. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, it was customary for princes to make investiture of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> benefices, by delivering to the person they had chosen a pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>.

INVICTED

Pages 323-323

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes a thing fluted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> furrowed. See HERALDRY.

INVICTIVE

Pages 323-323

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, differs from reproof, as the latter proceeds from a friend; and is intended for the good of the person reproved; whereas the invective is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of an enemy, and entirely designed to vex and give uneasiness to the person against whom it is directed.

INVISIBLE LADY

Pages 326-326

an amusing experiment in Acoustics, which was exhibited in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, first by a Frenchman, and afterwards by others; in which, from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, a lady who conversed, sung and played on musical instruments, seemed to be enclosed in a hollow metallic globe, of about a foot in diameter. See SCIENCE, Amusements of.

INVOCATION

Pages 327-327

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> at the beginning of a poem, wherein the poet calls for the assistance of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, particularly of his muse, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the deity of poetry.

INVOICE

Pages 327-327

an account in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of the particulars of merchandise, with their value, customs, charges, &c., transmitted by one merchant to another in a distant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

INVOLUCRUM

Pages 327-327

among botanists, expresses that sort of cup which surrounds a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> together, every one of which has beside this general cup its own particular perianthium. The involucrum consists of a multitude of little leaves disposed in a radiated manner. See CALYX.

INVOLUTION

Pages 327-327

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, the raising any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> from its root to any height <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> power assigned.—See ALGEBRA.

IO

Pages 327-327

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Inachus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> according to others of Julus or Piraeus, was priestess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>. Jupiter became enamoured of her; but Juno, jealous of his intrigues, discovered the object of his affection, and purified him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of Io. Jupiter changed his mistress into a beautiful heifer; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, who well knew the fraud, obtained from her husband the animal whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> she had condemned to bequeath. Juno commanded the hundred-eyed Argus to watch the heifer; but Jupiter, anxious for the situation of Io, sent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> to destroy Argus, and to restore her to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Io, freed from the vigilance of Argus, was now persecuted by Juno, who sent one of the Furies to torment her. She wandered over the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and crossed over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, till at last she stopped on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, still exposed to the unceasing torments of the Fury. Here the entreated Jupiter to restore her to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> form; and when the god had changed her from a heifer into a woman, she brought forth Epaphus. Afterwards she married Telegonus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> according to others; and she treated her subjects with such mildness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, that after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> she received divine honours, and was worshipped under the name of Isis. According to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Io was carried away by Phoenician <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, who wished to make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPRISALS">reprisals</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a> who had been stolen from them by the Greeks.

IOLAI

Pages 337-337

a festival at Thebes, the same as that call- ed Heraclia. It was instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> and his friend Iolas, who assisted him in conquering the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">hydra</a>. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> during several days, on the first of which were offered solemn sacrifices. The next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races and athletic exercises were exhibited. The following day was set apart for wrestling; the victors were crowned with garlands of myrtle generally used at funeral solemnities. They were sometimes rewarded with tripods of brals. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the exercises were exhibited was called Iolaium; where there were to be seen the monument of Amphitryon and the cenotaph of Iolas, who was buried in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>. These monu- ments were crowned with garlands and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on the day of the festival. Vol. XI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> I.

IOLAS OF IOLAS

Pages 337-337

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a son of Iphiclus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thessaly, who assisted <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> in conquering the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">hydra</a>, and burnt with a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the heads had been cut off, to prevent the growth of others. He was restored to his youth and vigour by Hebe, at the request of his friend Hercules. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after- wards Iolas assisted the Heraclidae against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURYSTHEUS">Eurystheus</a>, and killed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">Accord</a>- ing to Plutarch, Iolas had a monument in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, where lovers used to go and bind themselves by the most solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of fidelity, considering the place as sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and friendship. According to Diodorus and Pausanias, Iolas died and was buried in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, where he had gone to make a settlement at the head of the sons of Hercules by the 50 daughters of Thespius.

IONA

Pages 337-338

JONA, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ICHANAKILL, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>; a small, but celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, "once the luminary of the Caledonian regions (as Dr Johnson expresses it), whence savages clans and roving barbarians derived the benefits of knowledge and the blessings of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>." The name Iona is derived from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word signifying a dove, in allusion to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Columba, who landed here in 565. See COLUMBA.—It is said to have been a seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> before his arrival, when its name in Irish was Inis Drunach, or the "Druid Island." The druids being expelled or converted, he founded here a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> of canons regular, who till 716 differed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, in the observance of Easter and in the tonsure. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the island retained his name, and was called Icolmkill or "Columb's cell," now Icolmkill. The Danes dislodged the monks in the 9th century, and Cluniacs were the next order that settled here. This island, which belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Rothesay in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, is three miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: the east side is mostly flat; the middle rises into small hills; and the west side is very rude and rocky; the whole form- ing a singular mixture of rock and fertility.—There is in the island only one town, or rather village, con- sisting of about 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> houses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1798 amounted to about 330. Near the town is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Martyrs slain by the Danes. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> inclo- sure, bounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> dyke, and called Clachan Druimach, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> have been found, is supposed to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the Druids or rather the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cemetery of the townspeople. Beyond the town are the ruins of the nunnery of Austin cano- nesses, dedicated to St <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a>, and said to be founded by Columba: the church was 58 feet by 20, and the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is entire. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, covered deep with cow-dung, is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the last prioress, with her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> praying to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, and this inscrip- tion on the ledge: *Hic jacet domina <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> Donaldi Ferleti filia, quondam prioressa de Iona, qui <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBIT">obit</a> an's m° d° xii° ejus animam Altissimo commendamus*; and another <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>, *Hic jacet Mariota filia Iohan: Lauch- lain domini de.....*. A broad paved way leads hence to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>; and on this way is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome cros called Maclean's, the only one that remains of 360, which were demolished here at the Reformation. Rei- lig Oran, or the Burying-place of Oran, is the large inclosure where the kings of Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and of the isles, and their descendants, were buried in three several chapels. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the isles, who tra- velled over them 1549, and whose account has been copied by Buchanan, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> 1781, says, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on one of these chapels (or "tombs of slain formit like little chapels with ane braid gray marble or quhin slain on the gavil of ilk ane of the tombes," containing, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> says, the remains of 48 Scotch monarchs, from Fergus II. to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>; 16 of whom were pretended to be of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Alpin) was inscribed, *Tumulus regum Scotiae.* The next was inscribed, *Tumulus regum Hiberniae,* and contained four Irish monarchs: and the third, inscribed *Tumulus regum Norvegiae,* contained eight Norwegian princes, or viceroys of the Hebrides while they were subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>. Boetius says, that Fergus founded this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> for the burial-place of his successors, and caused an office to be composed for the funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. All that Mr Pennant could discover here were only certain slight remains, built in a ridged form and arched within, but the inscrip- tions lost. These were called *fornaire nan righ,* or "the ridge of the kings." Among these <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are to be seen only these two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> in the Gaelic or Erse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>: *Gros Domhail faid'ach,* i.e. "the cros of Donald Long- shanks," and that of *Urchuine o Guin,* and another inscribed *Hic jacent priores de Hy, Johannes, Hug- niut, Patricius,* in decrevis olim baccularius, qui obit an. Dom. millesimo quingentesimo.* About 300 inscrip- tions were collected here by Mr Sacheverel in 1688 and given to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Argyle, but afterwards lost in the troubles of the family. The place is in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>- ner filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>-stones, but so overgrown with weeds, that few or none are at present to be seen, far less any inscriptions read. Here also stands the chapel of St Oran, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> begun by Columba, which the evil spirits would not suffer to stand till some hu- man victim was buried alive; for which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> Oran offered himself, and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> grave-stone is near the door. In this chapel are tombs of several chiefs, &c. A little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of the door is the pedestal of a cros: on it are certain stones that seem to have been the supports of a tomb. Numbers who visit this island think it incumbent on them to turn each of these thrice round, according to the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. They are called *Glacha-braith,* for it is thought that the braith, or end of the world, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not arrive till the pe- daffal on which they stand is worn through. Origi- nally (says Mr Sacheverel) here were three noble globes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, placed on three stone bases, and these were turned round; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> ordered them and 60 croses to be thrown into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The present stones are probably substituted in place of these globes. The precinct of these tombs was held sacred, and en- joyed the privileges of a girth or sanctuary. These places of retreat were by the ancient Scotch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, not to shelter indiscriminately every offender, as was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in more bigoted times in Catholic countries; for here all atrocious criminals were excluded; and only the unfortunate delinquent, or the penitent sinner, was shielded from the instant stroke of rigorous ju- stice. A little to the north of this inclosure stands the cathedral, built in form of a cros, 115 feet long by 23, the transept 70 feet: the pillars of the choir have their capitals <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with scripture and other histories; and near the altar are the tombs of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOTS">bots</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>. A fragment remains of the altar- stone of white marble veined with gray. This church is ascribed to Maldwin in the 7th century; but the present structure is far too magnificent for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Most of the walls are built of red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">Nun</a>'s island in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. Two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> walls of a cov- ered way about 12 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and 10 wide, reach from the south-east corner to the sea. In the church-yard is a fine cros of a single piece of red granite, 14 feet high, 22 inches broad, and 10 inches thick. Near the south- east end is Mary's chapel. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> is behind the chapel; of which only a piece of the cloisters re- mains, and some sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> stones in a corner, on which contracts and alliances were made and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> sworn. East of it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>'s gardens and of- fices. North of this was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the bishop of the isles after the separation of Man from them. This see was endowed with 13 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; several of which were frequently taken away by the chieftains. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Soder, which some explained Soter, Zaling, "the name of Christ, or Soder, an imaginary town," is really de- rived from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> into the north- ern islands or Norderseys (i.e. all to the north of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">Ad</a>- namurchan point), and the Southern or Sudereys; which last being the most important, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Man retained both titles. Other ruins of monastic buildings and offices may be traced, as well as some druidical sepulchral remains. Several abbeys were derived from this, which with the island was governed by an abbot-prebiter, who had rule even over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. The place where Columba landed is a pebbly beach, where a heap of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> re- prefents the form of his ship. Near it is a hill with a circle of stones called *Cnoc-nar aingeal,* or "the hill of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>," with whom the saint held conference; and on Michaelmas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> the inhabitants coursed their horses round it, a remain of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of bringing them there to be blest. In former times, this island was the place where the archives of Scotland and many valuable old <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> were kept. Of these most are suppo- sed to have been destroyed by the Reformation; but many, it is said, were carried to the Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a> in France, and it is hoped some of them may still be recovered. In the island of Iona a schoolmaster is established; but there is no temple for worship, no instructor in religion, excepting the schoolmaster, unless it is visited by the parish minister from another island.

IONIA

Pages 342-342

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Æolia, on the west by the Ægean and Icarian seas, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, and on the east by Lydia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Caria. It was founded by colonies from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and particularly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, by the Ionians <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subjects of Ion. Ionia was divided into 12 small states, which formed a celebrated confederacy often mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. These 12 states were Priene, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>, Colophon, Clazomenae, Ephesus, Lebedos, Teos, Phocæa, Erythre, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, and the capitals of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a> and Chios. The inhabitants of Ionia built a temple which they called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> Ionium from the concourse of people that flocked there from every part of Ionia. After they had enjoyed for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> their freedom and independence, they were made tributary to the power of Lydia by Croesus. The Athenians assisted them to shake off the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> of the Asiatic monarchs; but they soon forgot their duty and relation to their mother-country, and joined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> when he invaded Greece. They were delivered from the Persian yoke by Alexander, and restored to their original independence. They were reduced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> Sylla. Ionia has been always celebrated for the salubrity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, the fruitfulness of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and the genius of its inhabitants. IONIC ORDER. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, No. 45. IONIC Dialect, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a manner of speaking peculiar to the people of Ionia. IONIC <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">SECT</a> was the first of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sects of philosophers; the others were the Italic and Eleatic. The founder of this sect was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THALES">Thales</a>, who, being a native of Miletus in Ionia, occasioned his followers to assume the appellation of Ionic: Thales was succeeded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAXIMANDER">Anaximander</a>, and he by Anaximenes, both of Miletus; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a> Clazomenius succeeded them, and removed his school from Asia to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> was his scholar. It was the distinguishing tenet of this sect, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> was the principle of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> things.

IONIUM MARE

Pages 342-342

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at the bottom of the Adriatic. It lies between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. That part of the Ægean sea which lies on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, is called the Sea of Ionia, and not the Ionian sea. According to some authors, the Ionian sea receives its name from Io, who swam across there after she had been metamorphosed into a heifer.

IPOMEA

Pages 344-344

QUAMOCLIT, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> SCARLET CONVOLVULUS; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandra clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 29th order, Campanaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

IPSWICH

Pages 344-344

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, in England, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 6. N. Lat. 52. 12. The name comes from the Saxon Cygefewick, that is, a town situated upon the Gyppen, now called Orwell. It had once 21 churches, but now has only 12. It was plundered by the Danes in 991, and afterwards besieged by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Stephen. It had charters and a mint in the reign of King John, but its last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> was from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. The remains of a wall and five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses are still to be seen. Though it is not in so flourishing a state as formerly when the harbour was more commodious, yet it is still a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> well built town. Besides the churches already mentioned, it has several meeting-houses, two chapels, a town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-chamber, a large market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> in the middle of it, a shire-hall for the county sessions, a library, several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, a free-school, a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river, stately flambles in the market-place built by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey, who was a native of the town and a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s son, and who also began to build a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> here on the ruins of a small college of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> canons, which still bears his name, though it was never finished. Here are also several almshouses, three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and a convenient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> and customhouse. By virtue of Charles II.'s charter, the town is governed by two bailiffs, a recorder, 12 portmen, of whom the bailiffs are two, a town-clerk, two coroners, and 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-council. The bailiffs and 4 of the portmen are justices of the peace. The town enjoys a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many privileges, as palling fines and recoveries, trying criminals, and even <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> and capital causes among themselves, settling the affix of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, wine, and beer. No freeman is obliged to serve on juries out of the town, or bear any office for the king, except that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, or to pay tolls or duties in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. They have an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> jurisdiction beyond Harwich on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and on both sides the Suffolk coast, by which they are entitled to all goods <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> on shore. The bailiffs even hold an admiralty-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> beyond Landguard-fort. By a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in King Edward III.'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it appears that the town had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-duties for all goods coming into Harwich-haven. They claim a right also to all waifs and strays, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the town are chiefly woollen and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth. It has still a considerable foreign trade. The tide rises pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and brings great ships irrefleble, within a small distance of the town. They export a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of corn to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and sometimes to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. Formerly, they had a great trade in shipbuilding; but that having declined, they now send great quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> to the king's yard at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>. It has several great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> for cattle, cheese, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>; and is admirably situated for the trade to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, because the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> that carries them out of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> carry them to Greenland. It is worth remarking, that it is one of the best places in England for persons in narrow circumstances, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> rent being easy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> cheap and plentiful, the passage by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to London, &c., convenient, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the place good. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of viscount, as well as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THETFORD">Thetford</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Grafton; and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.

IRASCIBLE

Pages 344-344

in the old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to an appetite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> and the other passions, which animate us against things difficult or odious, were supposed to reside. Of the eleven kinds of passions attributed to the soul, philosophers ascribe five to the irascible appetite; viz. wrath, boldness, fear, hope, and despair; the other six are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> on the concupiscible appetite, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, pain, desire, aversion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and hatred. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> divided the soul into three parts; the reasonable, irascible, and concupiscible parts. The two last, according to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, are the corporeal and mortal parts of the soul, which give rise to our passions. Plato fixes the seat of the irascible appetite in the heart; and of the concupiscible in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>; as the two sources of blood and spirits, which alone affect the mind.

IRELAND

Pages 344-375

one of the Britannic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, situated between the 5th and 10th degrees of west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between the 51st and 56th of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, extending in length about 300 miles, and about 150 in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is involved in so much obscurity, that it has been the object of contention among the antiquarians for upwards of a century and a half. The Irish historians pretend to very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. According to them, the island was first inhabited about 322 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. At Origin of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Partholansus the son of Scara landed in Mun-the Irish after the 14th of May with 1000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and some according women, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. This voyage he had undertaken on account of his having killed his father and mother in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The same historians inform us, that a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> broke out in Ireland during the reign of Partholansus, which had no existence when he came into the island, with many other particulars not worth mentioning; but the most surprising circumstance is, that about 300 years after the arrival of this Grecian colony, all of them perished by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, not a single person remaining to tell the fate of the rest; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is wonderful how the catastrophe should have been known. After the extinction of this first colony, Ireland remained a perfect wilderness for 30 years; when another colony arrived from the east, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of one Nemedius. He set sail from the Euxine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with 30 transports, each manned with 40 heroes; and Ireland, at last arrived on the coasts of Ireland, after a very tedious and strange <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. During his reign also many lakes were formed in the country, which had no existence before; the most material circumstance, however, was an unsuccessful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in which he was engaged with some African pirates, who in the end enslaved his people. The victors proved such inapplicable tyrants, that the Irish found themselves under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of quitting the island altogether. They embarked on board a fleet of 1150 ships, under the command of three grandsons of Nemedius, viz., Simon Breac, To Chath, and Briatan Maoil. The first returned to Greece, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sailed to the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and the third landed in the north of Scotland, and from him the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> is said to have taken its name, and the Welsh their origin. About 216 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Nemedius, the descendants of Simon Breac returned from Greece into Ireland. They were conducted by five princes of great reputation, who divided the island into five kingdoms, nearly equal in size. These kingdoms were called <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, Connacht, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a>, and Ulster; and the subjects of these kings are called by the Irish historians Firbolgs. The Firbolgs were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time expelled <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> totally subdued, after the loss of 100,000 men in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, by the Tuath de Dananns, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of necromancers, who came from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, and Achaia, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, from Denmark to Scotland, and from Scotland to Ireland. These necromancers were so completely skilled in their art, that they could even restore the dead to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and bring again into the field those warriors who had been slain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> before. They had also some curiosities which possessed a wonderful virtue. These were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, a spear, a cauldron, and a marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>; on which last were crowned first the kings of Ireland, and afterwards those of Scotland. But neither the powerful virtues of these Danish curiosities, nor the more powerful spells of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> art, were able to preserve the Tuath de Dananns from being subdued by the Gadelians when they invaded Ireland. The Gadelians were descended from one Gathelus, from whom they derived their name. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and intimately acquainted with Moses the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. His mother was Scotia, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>, by Niul the son of a Scythian monarch <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Nimrod. The Gadelians, called also Scots, from Scotia above-mentioned, conquered Ireland about 1300 B.C., under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a> and Heremon, two sons of Milesius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, from whom were descended all the kings of Ireland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the English conquest, and who are therefore styled by the Irish historians, princes of the Milesian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the Irish historians trace a gradual refinement of their countrymen from a state of the grossest barbarity, until a monarch, named Ollam Fodla, established a regular form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> seminary of learning, and instituted the Fer, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIENNIAL">triennial</a> convention of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> kings, priests, and poets, at Feamor or Tarah in Meath, for the establishment of laws and regulation of government. But whatever were the institutions of this monarch, it is acknowledged that they proved insufficient to withstand the wildness and disorder of the times. To Kinnab, one of his successors, the annalists give the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of reviving them, besides that of regulating Ulster, his family-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and adorning it with a stately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Eamannia near <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>. His immediate successor, called Hugony, is still more celebrated for advancing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of reformation. It seems, that from the earliest origin of the Irish nation, the island had been divided into the five provincial kingdoms above-mentioned, and four of these had been subject to the fifth, who was nominal monarch of the whole island. These four, however, proved such obstinate disturbers of the peace, that Hugony, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> their power, parcelled out the country into 25 dynasties, binding them by oath to accept no other monarch but one of his own family. This precaution proved ineffectual. Hugony himself died a violent death, and all his successors for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of ages were assassinated, scarcely with one exception. About 100 B.C. the pentarchal government was restored, and is said to have been succeeded by a considerable revolution in politics. The Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARDS">bards</a> had for many ages dispensed the laws, and the whole nation submitted to their decisions; but as their laws were exceedingly obscure, and could be interpreted only by themselves, they took occasion from thence to oppress the people, until at last they were in danger of being totally exterminated by a general insurrection. In this emergency they fled to Convocar-Mac-Nefia, the reigning monarch, who promised them his protection in case they reformed; but at the same time, in order to quiet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> complaints of his people, he employed the most eminent among them to compile an intelligible, equitable, and distinct, body of laws, which were received with the greatest joy, and dignified with the name of celestial decrees. These decisions seem to have produced but very little reformation among the people in general. We are now presented with a new series of barbarities, murders, factions, and anarchy; and in this disordered situation of affairs it was, according to the Irish historians, that the chieftain mentioned by Tacitus addressed himself to Agricola, and encouraged him to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> on Ireland. This scheme happened not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the views of the Roman general at that time, and therefore was not adopted; and so confident are these historians of the strength of their country even in its then disturbed state, that they treat the notion of its being subdued by a Roman legion and some auxiliaries (the force proposed to Agricola) as utterly extravagant; acquainting us at the same time, that the Irish were so far from dreading a Roman invasion, that they failed to the affluence of the Piets, and having made a successful incursion into South Britain, returned home with a considerable booty. In the same state of barbarity and confusion the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Ireland <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the introduction of Christianity by St Patrick, about the middle of the fifth century. This missionary, according to the adversaries of the Irish antiquity, first introduced letters into Ireland, and thus laid the foundations of a future civilization. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for that antiquity maintain, that the Irish had the knowledge of letters, and had made considerable progress in the arts, before the time of St Patrick: though they allow, that he introduced the Roman character, in which his copies of the Scripture and liturgies were written. To enter into the dispute would be contrary to our <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. It is sufficient to observe, that, excepting by some of the Irish themselves, the history already given is generally reckoned entirely fabulous, and thought to have been invented after the introduction of Christianity. An origin of the Irish nation has been found out much nearer than <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Greece, or Egypt; namely, the island of Britain, from whence it is now thought that Ireland was first peopled. A dispute hath arisen concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from whence the first emigrants from Britain set sail for Ireland. The honour of being the mother-country of the Irish hath been disputed between the North and South Britons. Mr Macpherson has argued strenuously for the former, and Mr Whitaker for the latter. For an account of their dispute, however, we must refer to the works of these gentlemen. Mr Whitaker claims the victory, and challenges himself the honour of being the first who clearly and truly demonstrated the origin of the Irish. The name of Ireland, according to Mr Whitaker, is obviously derived from the word *Iar* or *Eir*, which in the Celtic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies "west." This word was sometimes pronounced *Iver*, and *Hiver*; whence the names of *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">Iris</a>*, *Ierna*, *Juverna*, *Iverna*, *Hibernia*, and *Ireland*; by all of which it hath at some time or other been known. About 350 B.C., according to the same author, the Belgae crossed the channel, invaded Britain, and seized the whole extended line of the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. Numbers of the former inhabitants, who had gradually retired before the enemy, were obliged at last to take shipping on the western coast of England, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over into the uninhabited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Ireland. These were afterwards joined by another body of Britons driven out by the Belgae under Divitius, about 100 B.C. For two centuries and a half afterwards, these colonies were continually reinforced with fresh swarms from Britain; as the populousness of this island, and the vicinity of that, invited them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the one, or the bloody and successive wars in Britain during this period naturally induced them to relinquish the other: and the whole circuit of Ireland appears to have been completely peopled about 150 years after Christ: and as the inhabitants had all fled equally from the dominion of the Belgae, or for some other cause left their native country, they were distinguished among the Britons by one general and very apposite name, viz. that of *Scutes* or *Scots*, "the wanderers, or refugees." Mr Whitaker also informs us, "that in the times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Ireland was inhabited by 18 tribes; by one upon the northern and three on the southern shore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> upon the western, six on the eastern, and one in the centre. "Along the eastern coast, and the Vergilian or internal ocean, were ranged the Dumnii, the Voluntii, and the Eblani, the Caucii, the Menapii, and the Coriondii. The first inhabited a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the two counties of Antrim and Down, extending from Fair head, the most northerly extremity of the island, to Ifannum Promontorium, or the point of Ardglass haven, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Down; and, having the Logia or Lagan, which falls into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRICKFERGUS">Carrickfergus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, within their possessions, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNUM">Dunum</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol8.html#article-DOWNPATRICK">Downpatrick</a> for their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. The Voluntii possessed the coast from the point of that haven to the river Buvinda or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>, the remainder of Down, the breadth of Armagh, and all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUTH">Louth</a>; having the Vindurus or Carlingford river in their dominions, and the town of Laberus near the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVA">Deva</a> (Atherden in the county of Louth) for their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. And the Eblani reached from the Boyne to the Lebusius, Leuvi, or Liffy; residing in East Meath, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> county which is to the north of this river; and acknowledging <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDIOLANUM">Mediolanum</a>, Eblana, or Dublin, for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town. The Caucii spread from the Liffy to the Letrim, the Oboca of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; had the rest of Dublin county, and such parts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WICKLOW">Wicklow</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the north of the latter; and owned Dunum or Rath-Downe for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>.
