a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> touching Pamphylia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, rugged and mountainous, situated almost in Mount Taurus, and taking its name from Isaura; according to some, extending to the Mediterranean by a narrow slip. Stephanus, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, and Zofimus, make make no mention of places on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; though Pliny does, as also Strabo; but doubtful, whether they are places in Ilauria Proper, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in Pamphylia, or in Cilicia.

ISATIS

Pages 384-384

Woad; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetradymium clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 39th order, Siliqueae. One <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this plant, the tinctoria, yields a colouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>-Making and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">Dyeing</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Isatis, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a synonyme of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">canis</a> lagopus. See Canis, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index.

ISAURA

Pages 384-384
or Isaurus, in Ancient Geography, a strong city at Mount Taurus, in Isauria, twice demolished; first by Perdiccas, or rather by the inhabitants, who, through despair, destroyed themselves by fire rather than fall into the hands of the enemy; again by Servilius, who thence took the surname Isauricus. Strabo says there were two Isauras, the old and the new, but so near that other writers took them but for one.

ISCA DUMNIORUM

Pages 385-385

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 40'. Lat. 5° 44'. Called Caer-Isca in British, (Camden.) **ISCA Silurum**, in *Ancient Geography*, the station of the Legio II. Augusta, in Britain. Now <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERLEON">Caerleon</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, on the Uske.

ISCHALIS

Pages 385-385
or **ISCALIS**, in *Ancient Geography*, a town of the Belgae in Britain. Now Ilchester, in Somersetshire, on the river Ilt. **ISCHÆUM**, a genus of plants belonging to the polygamia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 4th order, Graminae. See Botany Index.

ISCHIA

Pages 385-385

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the same name, with a bishop's see and a strong fort. Both the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and fortresses stand upon a rock, which is joined to the island by a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; the rock is about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> furlongs in circumference. The city is like a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> of houses piled upon one another, which makes a very singular and striking appearance. At the end of the bridge next the city are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> gates, which open into a subterraneous passage, through which they enter the city. They are always guarded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who are natives of the island. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 55'. N. Lat. 40° 50'.

ISCHIUM

Pages 385-385

in Anatomy, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the pelvis. See Anatomy, No. 41.

ISCHURIA

Pages 385-385

*irrigua* (formed from *irge* "I stop," and *ger* "urine.") In *Plutus*, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> consisting in an entire suppression of urine. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ISCRATES

Pages 387-388

one of the greatest orators of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, 436 B.C. He was the son of Theodorus, who had enriched himself by making musical instruments, and gave his son a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Isocrates was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Prodicus, Gorgias, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> orators. He endeavoured at first to declaim in public, but without success; he therefore contented himself with instructing his scholars, and making private orations. He always showed great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and being informed of the loss of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cheronea, he abstained four days from eating, and died, aged 98. There are still extant 21 of his discourses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> orations, which are excellent performances, and have been translated from the Greek into Latin by Wolfius. Isocrates particularly excelled in the justness of his thoughts, and the elegance of his expressions. There are also <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> letters attributed to him.

ISELASTICS

Pages 385-385

a kind of games, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> combats, celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Roman emperors. The victor at these games had very considerable privileges conferred on him, after the example of Augustus and the Athenians, who did the like to conquerors at the Olympic, Pythian, and Isthmian games. They were crowned on the spot immediately after their victory, had pensions allowed them, were furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> at the public cost, and were carried in triumph to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

ISENACH

Pages 385-385

a town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, from whence one of the Saxon princes takes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in the neighbourhood. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 17'. N. Lat. 51° 0'.

ISENARTS

Pages 385-385
or **EISENARTS**, a considerable town of Germany, in Austria and in Stiria; famous for its iron mines. E. Long. 15° 25'. N. Lat. 46° 56'.

ISENBURG

Pages 385-385

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, with a handsome castle, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 14'. N. Lat. 50° 28'. The county belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Isengheim of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a>.

ISENGHEIN

Pages 385-385

a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality, seated on the river Mander, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 18'. N. Lat. 50° 44'.

ISERNIA

Pages 385-385

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Molise, with a bishop's see. It is seated at the foot of the Apennines, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 20'.

ISIAC TABLE

Pages 385-385

is one of the most considerable monuments of antiquity, discovered at Rome in 1525, and supposed by the various figures in bas relief upon it, to represent the feats of Isis, and other Egyptian deities. There have been various opinions as to the antiquity of this monument; some have supposed that it was engraved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the Egyptians worshipped the figures of men and women. Others, among whom is Bishop Warburton, apprehend, that it was made at Rome by persons attached to the worship of Isis. Dr Warburton considers it as one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> of the Egyptian monuments, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mixture of hieroglyphic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which it bears.

ISIACI

Pages 385-385

priests of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Isis.—Dioecorides tells us, that they bore a branch of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a> in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> instead of olive. They sung the praises of the goddess twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, viz. at the rising of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, when they opened her temple; after which they begged alms the rest of the day, and returning at night, repeated their orisons, and shut up the temple. Such was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and office of the isiaci; they never covered their feet with any thing but the thin bark of the plant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPYRUS">papyrus</a>, which occasioned Prudentius and others to say they went barefooted. They wore no garments but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, because Isis was the first who taught mankind the culture of this commodity.

ISIDORUS

Pages 385-385

called **DAMIATENSIS**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **PELUSIOTA**, from his living in a solitude near that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, was one of the most famous of all St Chrysostom's disciples, and flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> held in 421. We have 2012 of his epistles in five books. They are short, but well written, in Greek. The best edition is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in Greek and Latin, printed in 1638, in folio.

ISIGNI

Pages 385-385

a town of France, in Lower Normandy, with a small harbour, and well known on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> works, its cider, and its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 50'. N. Lat. 49° 20'. **ISINGLASS**. See **ICHTHYOCOLLA**.

ISIS

Pages 385-386

a celebrated deity of the Egyptians, daugh- ter of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Rhea, according to Diodorus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Some suppose her to be the same as Io, who was changed into a cow, and restored to her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, where she taught <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and governed the people with mildness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, for which reasons she received divine honours after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. According to some traditions mentioned by Plutarch, Isis married her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, and was pregnant by him even before she had left her mother's womb. These two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> deities, as some authors observe, comprehended all <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and all the gods of the heathens. Isis was the Venus of Cyprus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, the Cybele of the Phrygians, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, the Proserpine of Sicily, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, the Bellona of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, &c. Osiris and Isis reigned conjointly in Egypt; but the rebellion of Typhon, the brother of Osiris, proved fatal to this sovereign. The ox and the cow were the symbols of Osiris and Isis; because these deities, while on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, had diligently applied themselves to cultivating the earth. As Isis was supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, as Osiris the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, she was represented as holding a globe in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with a vessel full of ears of corn. The Egyptians believed that the yearly and regular inundations of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> proceeded from the abundant tears which Isis shed for the loss of Osiris, whom Typhon had basely murdered. The word *Isis*, according to some, signifies "ancient," and on that account the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the goddesses were often in these words: "I am all that has been, that shall be; and none among mortals has hitherto taken off my veil." The worship of Isis was universal in Egypt, the priests were obliged to observe perpetual chastity, their head was closely shaved, and they always walked barefooted, and clothed themselves in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> garments. They never ate onions, they abstained from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> with their meat, and were forbidden to eat the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of sheep and of hogs. During the night they were employed in continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> near the statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. Cleopatra, the beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Egypt, was wont to dress herself like this goddess, and affected to be called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Isis. Isis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, a river that has its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, and flows through only a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Wiltshire. It enters this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> near its source, and begins to be navigable for boats at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRICKLADE">Cricklade</a>; but after running in a serpentine manner about four miles, it leaves Gloucestershire at a village called Castle Eaton. Isis, a genus of animals belonging to the order zoophyta, in the class vermes. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ISLAM

Pages 386-386
or Islamism; the true faith, according to the Mahometans. See Mahometanism.

ISLAND

Pages 386-386

a tract of dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> encompassed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands contradistinguished from Continent, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Terra Firma. Several naturalists are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> were formed at the deluge; others think, that there have been new islands formed by the calling up of vast heaps of clay, sand, mud, &c.; others think they have been separated from the continent by violent storms, inundations, and earthquakes. These last have observed, that the East Indies, which abound in islands more than any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world, are likewise, more annoyed with earthquakes, tempests, lightnings, volcanoes, &c. than any other part. Others again conclude, that islands are as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as the world, and that there were some at the beginning; and among other arguments, support their opinion from Gen. x. 5, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture. Varenius thinks that there have been islands produced each of these ways. St Helena, Alcetion, and other steep rocky islands, he supposes to have become so by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>'s overflowing their neighbouring campaigns; but by the heaping up huge quantities of sand, and other terrestrial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, he thinks the islands of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, &c. were formed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> and Ceylon, and most of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> islands, he thinks, were rent off from the main land; and concludes, that the islands of the Archipelago were formed in the same way, imagining it probable that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> might contribute towards it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had a notion that Delos, and a few other islands, rose from the bottom of the sea; which, how fabulous soever it may appear, agrees with later observations. Seneca takes notice, that the island Thera rose thus out of the Aegean sea in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, of which the mariners were eye witnesses. It is indeed very probable, that many islands have existed not only from the deluge, but from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the world; and we have undoubted proofs of the formation of islands in all the different ways above-mentioned. Another way, however, in which islands are frequently formed in the South sea, is by the coraline infects. On this subject there is a curious dissertation by Alexander Dalrymple, Esq. in the Philosophical Transactions for the year 1768, to which we refer the reader. See also <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Islands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">Ice</a>. See Ice Island. Floating Islands. Histories are full of accounts of floating islands; but the greatest part of them are either false or exaggerated. What we generally see of this kind is no more than the concretion of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> and more viscous matter floating on the surface of the water in cakes; and, with the roots of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, forming conglomerates of different sizes, which, not being fixed to the shore in any part, are blown about by the winds, and float on the surface. These are generally found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, where they are confined from being carried too far; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, some of them acquire a very considerable size. Seneca tells us of many of these floating islands in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and some later writers have described not a few of them in other places. But, however true these accounts might have been at the time when they were written, very few proofs of their authenticity are now to be found; the floating islands having either disappeared again, or been fixed to the sides in such a manner as to make a part of the shore. Pliny tells us of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> island which at one time swam about in the lake Cutilia in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Reatinum, which was discovered to the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by a miracle; and Pomponius tells us, that in Lydia there were several islands so loose in their foundations, that every little accident shook and removed them. Island (or Icelana) Crystal. See Crystal, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

ISLE-ADAM

Pages 386-387

a town of France, with a handsome castle, castle, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a baron; seated on the river Oise, three miles from Beaumont, and 20 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 13. N. Lat. 49. 7. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a>-de-Dieu, a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of France, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Galicyon, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Poitou, from which it is distant 14 miles. W. Long. 2. 5. N. Lat. 46. 45. Isle-de-France, is one of the 12 general governments of France under the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Picardy, on the west by Normandy, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, and on the east by that of Champagne. It is about 90 miles in length, and as much in breadth; and is watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>, Oise, and Aisne. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> fertile; and it abounds in wine, corn, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. It contains 10 small districts, and Paris is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>.

ISLEBANNS

Pages 387-387

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given to those who adopted the sentiments of a Lutheran divine of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, called John Agricola, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, a native of Isleb, whence the name; who interpreting literally some of the precepts of St Paul with regard to the Jewish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, declaimed against the law and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of good works. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTINOMIANS">Antinomians</a>.

ISLINGTON

Pages 387-387

a village of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, to which it is almost contiguous. It appears to be of Saxon origin; and in the conqueror's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was written Illedon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ifendon. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is one of the prebends of St Paul's; to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of which a certain precinct here belongs; for the probate of wills, and granting administrations. The church was a Gothic structure, erected in 1503, and stood till 1751, when the inhabitants applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for leave to rebuild it, and soon after erected the present structure, which is a very substantial brick edifice, though it does not want an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of lightness. Its houses are above 2000, including the Upper and Lower Holloways, three sides of Newington Green, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Kingland, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">Ware</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-conduit <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, so called from a white <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> conduit that stands before the entrance, has handsome gardens with good walks, and two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rooms, one above the other, for the entertainment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, &c. In the S.W. part of this village is that noble reservoir, improperly called New River Head; though they are only two basins, which receive that river from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, and from whence the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is thrown by an engine into the company's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> for the supply of London. In the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOAT">moat</a> on the north side of these basins, called Six-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a> Field, from the contents of it, which is the third field beyond the White Conduit, there appears to have been a fortress in former days, enclosed with a rampart and ditch, which is supposed to have been a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by Suetonius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a> after his retreat, which Tacitus mentions, from London, before he fell into thence, and routed the Britons under their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOADICEA">Boadicea</a>; and that which is vulgarly, but erroneously, called Jack Straw's castle, is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> place in the S.W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the field, supposed to have been the seat of the pretorium or Roman general's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>; one founded in 1613 by Dame Alice Owen, for educating 30 children. This foundation, together with that of a row of almshouses, are under the care of the brewers company. Here is an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> with its chapel, and a workhouse for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of chalybeate water, in a very pleasant garden, which for some years was honoured by the constant attendance of the princess <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMELIA">Amelia</a>, and many persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, who drank the waters. To this place, which is called New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, many people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, particularly during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the price of drinking the waters being 10s. 6d. for the season. Near this place is a house of entertainment called Saddler's Wells, where, during the summer season, people are amused with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>-masters, walking on the wire, rope-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, tumbling, and pantomime entertainments.

ISLIP

Pages 387-387

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, 56 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is noted for the birth and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> of Edward the Confessor. By means of inland <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, it has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, Darwent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c. which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles, in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, &c. It has a good market for sheep, and some remains of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, said to have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>'s. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-school. The chapel wherein Edward was baptized stood at a small distance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, is still called the king's chapel, was entirely defaced during Cromwell's usurpation, and converted to the meanest uses of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-yard; at present it has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of thatch. It is built of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, 15 yards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 7 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and retains traces of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> window at the east end. This <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> was given by Edward the Confessor to Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, to which it still belongs.

ISMAELITES

Pages 387-387

the descendants of Ishmael; dwelling from Havila to the wilderness of Sur, towards <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and thus overspreading <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, and therefore Josephus calls Ishmael the founder of the Arabs.

ISMARUS

Pages 387-387

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Cicones in Thrace, giving name to a lake. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> it is called Ifmara. Servius supposed it to be a mountain of Thrace; on which mountain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a> dwelt.

ISNARDIA

Pages 387-387

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthemae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ISNIC

Pages 387-387

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, with a Greek archbishop's see. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Nice, famous for the first general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> held here in 325. There is now nothing remaining of its ancient splendour but an aqueduct. The Jews inhabit the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it; and it is seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> fertile in corn and excellent wine. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 30. 9. N. Lat. 47. 15.

ISOCHRONAL

Pages 387-387

is applied to such vibrations of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> as are performed in the same space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; as all the vibrations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> swings of the same pendulum are, whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> it describes are shorter or longer.

ISOETES

Pages 388-388

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the cryptogamia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ISOLA

Pages 388-388

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Farther <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, with a bishop's see. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town, and is seated 15 miles south east of St Severina. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 33'. N. Lat. 39° 1'. ISOPERIMETRICAL figures, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, are such as have equal perimeters <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circumferences.

ISOPYRUM

Pages 388-388

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 26th order, Multiflora. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ISOSCELES triangle, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, one that has two equal sides.

ISPANAHAN

Pages 388-389
or, as the Persians pronounce it, Spauhawm, the capital of Persia, is situated in the province of Irac Ageni, or Persia Proper, upon the ruins, as generally supposed, of the ancient Hecatompylos, or, as others think of the Aspa of Ptolemy. Most of the eastern astronomers and geographers place it in N. Lat. 32° 25'. E. Long. 86° 40'. It stands in a very extensive plain, surrounded by mountains; and has eight districts belonging to it, that contain about 400 towns and villages. The fertility of the soil, the mildness of the seasons, and the fine temperature of the air, all conspire to render Ispahan one of the most charming and delightful cities in the world. It is unanimously agreed, that the present city is of no great antiquity; and the two parts into which it is divided, preserve the names of two contiguous towns, from the junction of which it was formed. The inhabitants of these, notwithstanding their neighbourhood, bear an inveterate antipathy to each other; which they discover on all public occasions. Spauhawm owes the glory it now possesses to the great Shah Abas; who, after the conquest of the kingdoms of Lar and Ormus, charmed with the situation of this place, made it the capital of his empire, between the years 1620 and 1628. The mountains, with which this city is surrounded, defend it alike from the sultry heats of summer and the piercing winds of the winter season; and the plain on which it stands is watered by several rivers, which contribute alike to its ornament and use. Of these rivers, the Zenderoud, after being joined by the Mahmood, passes by Spauhawm; where it has three fine bridges over it, and is as broad as the Ispahan Scine at Paris. The waters of these united streams are sweet, pleasant, and wholesome, almost beyond comparison; as indeed are all the springs found in the gardens belonging to the houses of Spauhawm. The extent of Spauhawm is very great; not less perhaps than 20 miles within the walls, which are of earth, poorly built, and so covered with houses and shaded with gardens, that in many places it is difficult to discover them. The Persians are wont to say, Spauhawm nigripetion, i.e. Spauhawm is half the world. Chardin says, that some reckon the number of inhabitants at 1,000,000; but he did not look upon it as more populous than London, or containing more than 600,000. At a distance, the city is not easily distinguished; many of the streets being adorned with plantains, and every house having its garden, the whole looks like a wood. The streets in general are neither broad nor convenient; there being three great evils which attend them: the first is, that being built on common sewers, they are frequently broke up, which is very dangerous, considering that most people are on horseback; the second is, that there are many wells or pits in them, which are not less dangerous; the third arises from the people's emptying all their ordure from the tops of their houses: this last, indeed, is in some measure qualified by the dryness of the air, and by its being quickly removed by the peasants, who carry it away to dung their grounds. Some reckon eight, and others ten gates, besides posterns; but all agree that there is no difficulty of entering at any hour of the day or night. The three principal suburbs annexed to it are, Abas-Abad, built by Shah Abas, and belonging to the people of Tauris; Julfa, inhabited by a colony of Armenians, called by some New Julfa, to distinguish it from the ancient city of that name, situated in Armenia, upon the Araxes, whence the original inhabitants of New Julfa were brought; and Ghebr-Abad, or, as the Arabs pronounce it, Kebr-Abad, the street of the magians, occupied entirely by the professors of magism, or the religion of the ancient Persians. The river Zenderoud separates the city of Ispahan and Abas-Abad from Julfa and Ghebr-Abad. This city has suffered greatly since the commencement of the dreadful revolution in 1721; the whole kingdom from that period, till a few years ago, having been almost a continued scene of blood, ravages, and confusion. A celebrated modern traveller, who was on the spot, tells us, that the inhabitants of Julfa, not many years before the above revolution happened, amounted to 30,000 souls; had 13 churches, and above 100 priests; and paid the Persian court 200 tomans yearly for the free exercise of their religion: that some of the streets were broad and handsome, and planted with trees, with canals and fountains in the middle; others narrow and crooked, and arched at top; others again, though extremely narrow, as well as turning and winding many ways, were of an incredible length, and resembled so many labyrinths: that, at a small distance from the town, there were public walks adorned with plane-trees on either hand, and ways paved with stones, fountains, and cisterns: that there were above 100 caravanserais for the use of merchants and travellers, many of which were built by the kings and prime nobility of Persia: that, as little rain fell there, the streets were frequently full of dust, which rendered the city disagreeable during a considerable considerable part of the summer; that the citizens, however, to make this inconvenience more tolerable, used to water them when the weather was warmer than usual; that there was a castle in the eastern part of the town, which the citizens looked upon as impregnable, in which the public money, and most of the military stores, were said to be kept; that notwithstanding the baths and caravanserais were almost innumerable, there was not one public hospital; that most of the public buildings were rather neat than magnificent, though the great meydan or market-place, the royal palace (which is three quarters of a league in circumference), and the alley denominated Toher bag adjoining to it, made a very grand appearance; that the former contained the royal mosque; the building denominated kayserich, where all sorts of foreign commodities were exposed to sale; and the mint, styled by the Persians ferra-bhaneh, where the current money of the kingdom was coined; that, besides the native Persians, there were then in Isfahan above 10,000 Indians all supported by trade; 20,000 Georgians, Circassians, and Tartars of Daghestan or Lefgees, with a considerable number of English, Dutch, Portuguese, and a few French; that the Capuchins, disfacedicated or barefooted Carmelites, Jesuits, Dominicans, and Austin friars, had likewise their convents here, though they were unable to make any converts; and that there were above 100 mosques and public colleges. But since the fatal period above mentioned, the suburb of Jaffa was almost totally abandoned by the Armenians. The government of Isfahan, twenty-three leagues long and as many broad, comprehending several districts, most of them formerly well peopled, appeared not many years ago little better than a desert; most of the inhabitants of that fertile and delightful tract being fled and dispersed. Multitudes of them had taken a precarious refuge in the mountains of Loristan, lying between Isfahan and Suffer, whose lands were left untilled, and their houses mouldered into ruins. In short, all the distresses of an unsuccessful war, or the invasion of a barbarous enemy, could not have plunged the people of Isfahan into greater misery than the victories of their tyrannical king Nadir Shah, who seemed more solicitous to humble his own subjects than his enemies. See Persia. ISPIDA. See Alcedo, Ornithology Index.

ISRAEL

Pages 389-389

the name which the angel gave <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, after having wrestled with him all night at Mahanaim <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Peniel (Gen. xxxii. 1, 2, and 28, 29, 30, and Hosea xii. 3.). It signifies a conqueror of God, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of God, or, according to many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who sees God. By the name of Israel is sometimes understood the person of Jacob; sometimes the whole people of Israel, or the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Jacob; and sometimes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Israel, or of the ten tribes, distinct from the kingdom of Judah.

ISRAELITES

Pages 389-389

the descendants of Israel; who were at first called Hebrews, by reason of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, who came from the other side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>; and afterwards Israelites, from Israel the father of the twelve patriarchs; and lastly Jews, particularly after their return from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, because the tribe of Judah was then much stronger and more numerous than the other tribes, and foreigners had scarcely any knowledge of this tribe.

ISSACHAR

Pages 389-389

one of the divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> by tribes; lying to the south of Zebulon, so as by a narrow slip to reach the Jordan, between Zebulon and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a> (Josh. xix.). But whether it reached to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, is a question; some holding that it did; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> not easy to be proved, as Joshua makes no mention of the sea in this tribe, nor does Josephus extend it farther than to Mount Carmel; and in Josh. xvii. 10. Ailer is said to touch Manasseh on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, which could not be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Issachar extended to the sea.

ISSOUDUN

Pages 389-389

a town of France, in Berry, which carries on a trade in wood, cattle, cloth, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, and flockings; is seated partly on a plain, and partly on an eminence. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 5. N. Lat. 46. 57.

ISSUE

Pages 389-389

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, has various applications; being sometimes taken for the children begotten between a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and his wife—sometimes for profits growing from amercements <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fines—sometimes for profits of lands and tenements—but more frequently for the point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> depending in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, whereupon the parties join, and put their cause to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. In all these occasions, issue has but one signification, which is, an effect of a cause preceding; as the children are the effect of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> between the parents; the profits growing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of any man's offence, are the effect of his transgression; the point referred to the trial of twelve men is the effect of pleading, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">Plea</a> and Issue.

ISSUES

Pages 389-389

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, are little ulcers made designedly by the surgeon in various parts of the body, and kept open by the patient, for the preservation and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>.

ISSUS

Pages 389-390

now Ajazo, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, with a harbour on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, a little to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Scanderoon. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 36. 25. N. Lat. 36. 56. Near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in a difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and the sea, Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> fought his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>. One great cause of the defeat which the Persians received here was the bad conduct of their monarch, who led his numerous forces into a narrow place, where they had not room to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Alexander was so much surprized when he first received the news that Darius was behind him, that he could scarcely believe it to be true; but when he was thoroughly satisfied of the fact, and that Darius had again passed the river Pinarus, he called a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, wherein, without asking any body's advice, he only told them, that he hoped they would remember their former actions; and that they, who were always conquerors, were about to fight people who were always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>. He further observed, that Darius seemed to be infatuated, since he had with such expedition quitted an open and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where his numbers might have acted with advantage, to fight in a place inclosed, where the Macedonian phalanx might be well drawn up, and where his numbers could only incommode him. He then made the necessary dispositions for repassing the mountains, posted guards where he found them necessary, and then commanded his troops to refresh themselves, and to take their rest till morning. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he began to repass the mountains, obliging his forces to move in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> order where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> was narrow, and to extend themselves as they had... Iffus had more room; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing keeping always close to the mountain, and the left to the sea-shore. On the right there was a battalion of heavy-armed troops, besides the targeteers under the command of Nicanor the son of Parmenio. Next these, extending to the phalanx, were the corps of Ctenus and Perdiccas; and on the left the respective bodies commanded by Amyntas, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, and Meleager. The foot appointed to support them were commanded by Craterus; but the whole left wing was committed to Parmenio, with strict orders not to decline from the sea-shore, lest the Persians should surround them. Darius ordered 20,000 foot and 30,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to retire, finding that he already wanted room to draw up the rest. His first line consisted of 30,000 Greek mercenaries, having on their right and left 60,000 heavy-armed troops, being the utmost the ground would allow. On the left, towards the mountain, he posted 20,000 men, which, from the hollow situation of the place, were brought quite behind Alexander's right wing. The rest of his troops were formed into close and useless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> behind the Greek mercenaries, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in all of 60,000 men. When this was done, he suddenly recalled the horse who had retired, sending <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> on his right against the Macedonians commanded by Parmenio; and the rest he ordered to the left towards the mountain: but, finding them unserviceable there, he sent the greatest part of them to the right; and then took upon himself, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the Persian kings, the command of the main body. As soon as Alexander perceived that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the Persian horse was disposed against his left wing, he dispatched, with as much secrecy as he could, the Thessalian cavalry thither, and supplied their places on the right by some brigades of horse from the van, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-armed troops. He also made such dispositions, that notwithstanding the mighty advantage of the hollow mountain, the Persians could not surround him. But, as these precautions had considerably weakened the centre of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, he ordered those advanced posts on the enemy's left, of which he was most apprehensive, to be attacked at the very beginning of the fight; and, when they were easily driven from them, he recalled as many troops as were necessary to strengthen his centre. When all things were in order, Alexander gave strict command, that his army should <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> very slowly. As for Darius, he kept his troops fixed in their posts, and in some places threw up ramparts; whence the Macedonians rightly observed, that he thought himself already a prisoner. Alexander at the head of the right wing engaged first, and without any difficulty broke and defeated the left wing of Darius. But, endeavouring to pass the river Pinarus after them, his troops in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> losing their order, the Greek mercenaries fell upon them in flank, and made them fight, not only for victory, but for their lives. Ptolemy the son of Seleucus, and 120 Macedonians of some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, were killed upon the spot. But the foot next to Alexander's right wing coming in feebly to its relief, fell upon the mercenaries in flank, amongst whom a dreadful carnage was made; they being in a manner surrounded by the horse and light-armed troops, which at first pursued the left wing, and the foot that now passed the river. The Persian horse on the right still fought gallantly; but, when they were thoroughly informed of the rout of their left wing and of the destruction of the Greek mercenaries, and that Darius himself was fled, they began to break, and betake themselves to flight also. The Thessalian cavalry pursued them close at the heels; and the narrow craggy <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> incommode them exceedingly, so that vast numbers of them perished. As for Darius, he fled, soon after the left wing was broken, in a chariot with a few of his favourites: as far as the country was plain and open, he escaped well enough; but, when the roads became rocky and narrow, he quitted it, and mounting a horse, rode all the night: his chariot, in which were his cloak and his bow, fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Alexander, who carried them back to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. In respect to the battle of Iffus, Diodorus informs us, that Alexander looked everywhere about for Darius; and, as soon as he discovered him, with his handful of guards attacked him and the flower of the Persian army which was about him; being as desirous of obtaining this victory by his personal valour, as of subduing the Persian empire by the courage of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. But when Oxathres, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Darius, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Alexander's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and how fiercely he fought to accomplish it, he threw himself, with the horse who were about him, between his brother's chariot and the enemy, where an obstinate fight was maintained, till the dead bodies rose like an entrenchment about the chariot of Darius. Many of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> were slain, and Alexander himself was wounded in the thigh. At last the horses in the chariot of Darius started, and became so unruly, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> himself was forced to take the reins; the enemy, however, pressed so hard upon him, that he was constrained to call for another chariot, and mounted it in great danger. This was the beginning of the rout, which soon after became general. According to this author, the Persians lost 200,000 foot, and 10,000 horse; the Macedonians 300 foot, and 150 horse. Justin informs us, that the Persian army consisted of 400,000 foot, and 100,000 horse. He says, that the battle was hard fought; that both the kings were wounded; and that the Persians still fought gallantly when their king fled, but that they were afterwards speedily and totally routed: he is very particular as to their loss, which he says amounted to 61,000 foot, 10,000 horse, and 40,000 taken prisoners; of the Macedonians he says there fell no more than 130 foot, and 150 horse. Curtius says, that of the Persians there fell 100,000 foot, and 10,000 horse: of Alexander's army 504, he says, were wounded; 32 foot and 150 horse killed. That we may not suspect any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in transcribers, his own observation confirms the fact: *Tantulo impendio ingens victoria fleuit*, "So small was the cost of so great a victory."

ISTHMIA

Pages 390-391
or **Isthmian Games**: one of the four solemn games which were celebrated every fifth year in Greece. They had the name from the isthmus of Corinth, where they were celebrated. In their first institution, according to Pausanias, they consisted only of funeral ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites and ceremonies in honour of Melicertes: but Theseus afterwards, as Plutarch informs us, in emulation of Hercules, who had appointed games at Olympia in honour of Jupiter, dedicated those to Neptune, his reputed father, who was regarded as the particular protector of the isthmus and commerce of Corinth. The same trials of skill were exhibited here as at the other three. three sacred games; and particularly those of music and poetry. These games, in which the victors were only rewarded with garlands of pine leaves, were celebrated with great magnificence and splendor as long as paganism continued to be the established religion of Greece; nor were they omitted even when Corinth was sacked and burnt by Mummius the Roman general; at which time the care of them was transferred to the Sicyonians, but was restored again to the Corinthians when their city was rebuilt.

ISTHMUS

Pages 391-391

a narrow neck, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lip of ground, which joins two continents; or joins a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> to the terra firma, and separates two seas. See PENINSULA. The most celebrated isthmuses are that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>, which joins <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> and South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; that of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, which connects <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; that of Corinth, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, in the Morea; that of Cram-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, otherwise called Taurica Cheronea; that of the peninsula Romania, and Erifio; or the isthmus of the Thracian Cheronea, twelve furlongs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, being that which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> undertook to cut through. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had several designs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the isthmus of Corinth, which is a rocky hillock, about ten miles over; but they were all in vain, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of sluices being not then known. There have been attempts too for cutting the isthmus of Suez, to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and the Mediterranean; but these also failed; and in one of them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> is said to have lost 120,000 men.

ISTRIA

Pages 391-391

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, lying in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a> on the north; and on the south, east, and west, by the sea. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is wholesome, especially near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> produces plenty of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and pastures; there are also quarries of fine marble. One part of it belongs to the Venetians, and the other to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. Cabo d'Istria is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

ITALIAN

Pages 391-391

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> spoken in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. See the article LANGUAGE. This tongue is derived principally from the Latin; and of all the languages formed from the Latin, there is none which carries with it more visible marks of its original than the Italian. It is accounted one of the most perfect among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> tongues. It is complained, indeed, that it has too many diminutives and superlatives, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather augmentatives; but without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reason: for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> those words convey nothing farther to the mind than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of things, they are no more faulty than our pleonasms and hyperboles. The language corresponds to the genius of the people, who are slow and thoughtful: accordingly their language runs heavily, though smoothly; and many of their words are lengthened out to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. They have a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for music; and to gratify their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> this way, have altered abundance of their primitive words; leaving out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>, taking in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>, softening and lengthening out their terminations, for the sake of the cadence. Hence the language is rendered extremely musical, and succeeds better than any other in operas and some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>: but it fails in strength and nervousness; and a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its words, borrowed from the Latin, become so far disguised that they are not easily Italian characterized. The multitude of sovereign states into which Italy has been divided has given rise to a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of different dialects in that language; which, however, are all good in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they are used. The Tuscan is usually preferred to the other dialects, and the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> to that of the other cities; whence the Italian proverb, Lingua Toscana in bocca Romana. The Italian is generally pretty well understood throughout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and is frequently spoken in Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. At Constantinople, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and in the ports of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, the Italian is used as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> as the language of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: indeed in those places it is not spoken so pure as in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, but is corrupted with many of the proper words and idioms of the place; whence it takes a new name, and is called Frank Italian.

ITALICA

Pages 391-391

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Baetica in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, built by Scipio Africanus, after finishing the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, for the reception of the wounded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. At first it was a municipium; afterwards a colony: which was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of wonder to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian, the privileges of a municipium being beyond those of a colony (Gellius). Famous for being the birthplace of the emperors Trajan and Adrian, and of the poet Silius Italicus. Now Sevilla Vieja, scarcely four miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>; a small village of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> on the Guadalquivir.—Corfinium in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> was thus also called.

ITALY

Pages 391-417

one of the finest countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, lying between 7 and 10 degrees of E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, and between 37 and 46 degrees of N. Lat. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, north-west, and north-east, it is bounded by France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a>, and Germany; on the east, by the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; and on the south and west, by the Mediterranean; its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to that of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOOT">boot</a>. Its length from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AOSTA">Aosta</a>, at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> in Savoy, to the utmost verge of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, is about 600 miles; but its breadth is very unequal, being in some places near 400 miles, in others not above 25 or 30. Italy was anciently known by the names of Saturnia, Oenotria, Hesperia, and Aufonia. It was called names, Saturnia from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>; who, being driven out of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> by his son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, is supposed to have taken refuge there. The names of Oenotria and Aufonia are borrowed from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants the Oenotrians and Aufones; and that of Hesperia or Western was given it by the Greeks, from its situation with respect to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. The name of Italia, or Italy, which in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prevailed all over the rest, is by some derived from Italos, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Siculi; by others, from the Greek word Italos, signifying an ox; this country abounding, by reason of its rich pastures, with oxen of an extraordinary size and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. All these names were originally peculiar to particular provinces of Italy, but afterwards applied to the whole country. This country, like most others, was in ancient times divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of petty states and kingdoms. Afterwards when the Gauls settled in the western, and many Greek colonies in the eastern parts, Italy, it was divided, with respect to its inhabitants, into three great parts, viz. Gallia Cisalpina, Italy properly so called, and Magna Graecia. The most western and northern parts of Italy were in great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> peopled by the Gauls; and hence took the name of Galia, with the epithets of Cisalpina and Citerior, because they lay on the side of the Alps next to Rome; and Togata, with relation to the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> or dress of which the inhabitants used; but this last epithet is of a much later <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> than the former. This appellation was antiquated in the reign of Augustus, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Italy into eleven provinces, introduced by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Hence it is that the name of Cisalpine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> frequently occurs in the authors who flourished before, and scarce even in those who wrote after, the reign of Augustus. This country extended from the Alps and the river Varus, parting it from Transalpine Gaul, to the river Aelius; or, as Pliny <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, in the ancient Picenum. On the north, it was divided from Rhaetia by the Alps, called Alpes Rhaeticae; and from Illyricum by the river Formio: but on this side, the borders of Italy were, in Pliny's time, extended to the river Arbia in Istria. On the south, it reached to the Ligurian sea, and the Apennines parting it from Etruria; so that under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name of Cisalpine Gaul were comprehended the countries lying at the foot of the Alps, called by Pliny and Strabo the Subalpine countries, Liguria, Gallia Cispadana and Transpadana, Italy, properly so called, extended, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Adriatic, from the city of Ancona to the river Trento, now the Fortore; and on the Mediterranean, from the Macra to the Silanus, now the Sele. Magna Graecia comprised Apulia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, and the country of the Brutii. It was called Greece, because most of the cities on the coast were Greek colonies. The inhabitants gave it the name of Great, not as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was larger than Greece, but merely out of ostentation, as Pliny informs us. All these countries were inhabited by a great number of different nations settled at different times, and from many different parts. The names of the most remarkable of them were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>, or those whose origin was utterly unknown, and consequently were thought to have none; the Sabines, Hetrurians or Tuscani, the Umbri, Samnites, Campani, Apuli, Calabri, Lucani, the Brutii, and the Latins. From a colony of the latter proceeded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who gradually subdued all these nations one after another, and held them in subjection for upwards of 700 years. All these nations were originally brave, hardy, temperate, and well skilled in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and the Romans much more so than the rest. Their subjection to Rome, however, inured them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>; their oppression by the emperors broke their spirit; and the vast wealth which was poured into the country from all parts of the world, during the time of the Roman prosperity, corrupted their manners, and made them degenerate from their former valour. Of this degeneracy the barbarous nations of the north took the advantage to invade the empire in innumerable multitudes. Though often repelled, they never failed to return; and it was found necessary to take great numbers of them into the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, in order to defend the empire against the rest of their countrymen. In the year 476, the Heruli, presuming on the services they had done the empire, demanded a third part of the lands of Italy; and being refused, chose one by the He-odoacer, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of low birth, but of great valour and ruli- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, for their king; and having totally destroyed the remains of the Roman empire, proclaimed Odoacer king of Italy. The new monarch, however, did not think proper to alter the Roman form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, but suffered the people to be governed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, consuls, &c., as before. He enjoyed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in peace till the year 488, when Zeno, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Constantinople, being hard pressed by Theodoric king of the Ostrogoths, advised him to turn his arms against Odoacer, whom he could easily overcome, and thus make himself sovereign of one of the finest countries in the world. Theodoric accepted the proposal with great joy, invaded by and set out for Italy, attended by an infinite number of people, carrying with them their wives, children, effects, on waggons. Several Romans of great distinction attended him in this war; while, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, many of his countrymen chose to remain in Thrace, where they became a separate <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and lived for a long time in amity with the Romans. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, being destitute of shipping, were obliged to go round the Adriatic. Their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> was performed in the depth of winter; and during the whole time, a violent famine and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> raged in their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. They were also opposed by the Gepidae and Sarmatians; but at last having defeated these enemies, and overcome every other obstacle, they arrived in Italy in the year 489. Theodoric advanced to the river Santius, now Zonzo, near Aquileia, where he halted for some time to refresh his troops. Here he was met by Odoacer at the head of a very numerous army, but composed of many different nations commanded by their respective chiefs, and consequently without sufficient union or zeal for the common cause. Theodoric therefore gained an easy victory, cut many of his enemies in pieces, and took their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. Odoacer retired to the plains of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, and encamped there at a small distance from the city; but Theodoric pursued him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, and soon forced him to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> engagement. The Goths obtained another victory; but it cost them dear. Odoacer's men made a much better resistance than before, and great numbers fell on both sides.
