The old league of the Italian cities no longer subsisted. It had been formed with no other view than to oppose the emperors; and since they had neglected Italy, the cities were wholly employed in aggrandizing themselves, at the expense of each other. The Florentines and the Genoese made war upon the republic of Pisa. Every city was also divided into factions within itself. In the midst of these troubles Henry VII appeared in Italy in the year 1311, and caused himself to be crowned king of Lombardy at Milan. But the Guelphs had concealed the old iron crown of the Lombard kings, as Italy if the right of reigning were attached to a small circlet of metal. Henry ordered a new crown to be made, with which the ceremony of inauguration was performed. Cremona was the first place that ventured to oppose the emperor. He reduced it by force, and laid it under heavy contributions. Parma, Vicenza, and Placentia, made peace with him on reasonable conditions. Padua paid 100,000 crowns, and received an imperial officer as governor. The Venetians presented Henry with a large sum of money, an imperial crown of gold enriched with diamonds, and a chain of very curious workmanship. Brescia made a desperate resistance, and sustained a very severe siege; in the course of which the emperor's brother was slain, and his army diminished to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that the inhabitants marched out under the command of their prefect Thibault de Druslatt, and gave him battle; but they were repulsed with great loss, after an obstinate engagement; and at last obliged to submit, and their city was dismantled. From Brescia Henry marched to Genoa, where he was received with expressions of joy, and splendidly entertained. He next proceeded to Rome; where, after much bloodshed, he received the imperial crown from the hands of the cardinals. Clement V., who had originally invited Henry into Italy, growing jealous of his success, had league with Robert king of Naples and the Urfini faction, to oppose his entrance into Rome. He entered it in spite of them by the assistance of the Colonnas. Now master of that ancient city, Henry appointed it a governor; and ordered, that all the cities and states of Italy should pay him an annual tribute. In this order he comprehended the kingdom of Naples, to which he was going to make good his claim of superiority by arms, when he died at Benevento in 1313, as is commonly supposed, of poison given him by a Dominican friar, in the consecrated wine of the sacrament. The efforts of Henry VII. were unable to restore the imperial power in Italy. From this time the authority of the emperor in that country consisted in a great measure in the conveniency which the Gibellines found in opposing their enemies under the sanction of his name. The power of the pope was much of the same nature. He was less regarded in Italy than in any other country in Christendom. There was indeed a great party who called themselves Guelphs; but they affected this distinction only to keep themselves independent of the imperialists; and the states and princes who called themselves Guelphs paid little more acknowledgment to his holiness than sheltering themselves under his name and authority. The most desperate wars were carried on by the different cities against each other; and in these wars Caltruccio Caltraccani, and Sir John Hawkwood an Englishman, are celebrated as heroes. A detail of these transactions would furnish materials for many volumes; and after all seems to be but of little importance, since nothing material was effected by the utmost efforts of valour, and the belligerent states were commonly obliged to make peace without any advantage on either side. By degrees, however, this martial spirit subsided; and in the year 1492, the Italians were so little capable of resisting an enemy, that Charles VIII. of France conquered the whole kingdom of Naples in six weeks, and might easily have subdued the whole country had it not been for his own imprudence. Another attempt on Italy was made by Louis XII. and a third by Francis I., as related under the article France. In the reigns of Louis XIII. and XIV. an obstinate war was carried on between the French and Spaniards, in which the Italian states bore a very considerable share. The war concluded in 1660, with very little advantage to the French, who have been always unsuccessful in their Italian wars. The like bad success attended them in that part of the world, in the war which commenced between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and Spain in the year 1740. But the particulars of these wars, with regard to the different states of Italy, naturally fall to be considered under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of those states into which the country is now divided; viz. Sardinia, Milan or the Milanese, Genoa, Venice, Tuscany or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, St Marino, Parma, Mantua, Modena, Rome, and Naples. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in Italy is very different, according to the different situations of the several countries contained in it. In those on the north of the Apennines it is more temperate, but on the south it is generally very warm. The air of the Campania of Rome, and of the Ferrarese, is said to be unhealthful; which is owing to the lands not being duly cultivated, nor the marshes drained. That of the other parts is generally pure, dry, and healthy. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is very great in the kingdom of Naples; and would be almost intolerable, if it was not somewhat alleviated by the sea breezes. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of Italy in general is very fertile, being watered by a great number of rivers. It produces a great variety of wines, and the best <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> in Europe; excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> in abundance; corn of all sorts, but not in such plenty as in some other countries; oranges, lemons, citrons, pomegranates, almonds, raisins, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, mulberry-trees without number, figs, peaches, nectarines, apricots, pears, apples, filberts, chestnuts, &c. Most of these fruits were at first imported by the Romans from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia Minor</a>, Greece, Africa, and Syria, and were not the natural products of the soil. The tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> are covered in winter on the north side of the Apennines, but on the south side they have no need of it. This country also yields good pasture; and abounds with cattle, sheep, goats, buffaloes, wild boars, mules, and horses. The forests are well stored with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>; and the mountains yield not only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of iron, lead, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, sulphur, marble of all sorts, alabaster, jasper, porphyry, &c. but also gold and silver; with a great variety of aromatic herbs, trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, as thyme, lavender, laurel, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, wild olive trees, tamarinds, juniper, oaks, and pines. A very extensive trade is carried on in many places in Italy, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, Genoa, Bologna, Venice, and Naples; the country having a great variety of commodities and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, especially wine, oil, perfumes, fruits, and silks. Travellers also bring large sums of money into Italy, besides what they lay out in pictures, curiosities, relics, antiquities, &c. The Italians are generally well proportioned, though their complexions are none of the best. As to dress, they follow the fashions of the countries on which they border, or to which they are subject; namely, those of France, Spain, and Germany. With respect to their genius and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, carving, and music, musick, they are thought to excel greatly, and to leave the other nations of Europe far behind them; but their music seems too soft and effeminate to deserve all the praise bestowed on it; and their houses are far inferior to those of England in respect of convenience. No country hath produced better politicians, historians, poets, painters, and sculptors; we mean since the revival of the arts and sciences, exclusive of those of ancient times. The Italians are very affable, courteous, ingenious, sober, and ready-witted; but extremely jealous, vindictive, lascivious, ceremonious, and superstitious. In respect to jealousy, indeed, it is said a very extraordinary change has taken place; and that the Italians are now less indulgent and complaisant to their wives than the most polite husbands in France itself. In their tempers, the Italians seem to be a good medium between the French and Spaniards; neither so gay and volatile as the one, nor so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and solemn as the other. Boiled snails, served up with oil and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, or fried in oil, and the hinder parts of frogs, are reckoned dainty dishes. Kites, jackdaws, hawks, and magpies, are also eaten not only by the common people but by the better sort. Wine is drank here both in summer and winter cooled by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> or snow. The women affect <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, as the Roman ladies and courtizans formerly did. They also use paint and wafles, both for their hands and faces. The day here is reckoned from sunset to sunset, as the Athenians did of old. Revolution. Amidst the convulsions which agitated Europe in consequence of the French revolution, the different states of Italy were not permitted to enjoy repose. Bonaparte, whose unprecedented and extraordinary success has hitherto even exceeded his military talents, made a rapid conquest of the whole of this country; the battles of Arcola and Lodi are memorable for the desperate valour with which they were fought, and Mantua surrendered on the 2d of February 1797, at ten o'clock at night. The immediate consequence of these successes was the conquest of the popish territories, which was not effected without the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of much blood. Different changes and modifications were made in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> after these victories, and the emperor of France was in the illus proclaimed king of Italy. A detail of military and other transactions in Italy, in so far as they stood connected with the political schemes and conquests of the French government, has already been given under the article France, to which we refer our readers. According to Boetticher, the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Italy including the islands of Sicily and Sardinia, ought not to be estimated at more than 13,000,000. The kingdom of Naples and Sicily is supposed to contain about 6,000,000; the central part about 3,000,000; and the northern part about 4,000,000.

ITCH

Pages 417-417

a cutaneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, appearing in small watery pustules on the skin; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of a mild <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, though sometimes attended with obstinate and dangerous symptoms. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Itch-Insect. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACARUS">Acarus</a>, Entomology Index. In speaking of the manner of finding these insects in the itch, Fabricius observes, that the failure of many who have sought for them has been owing to their having expected to meet with them in the larger vessels that contain a yellowish fluid like pus; in these, however, he tells us, he has never found them, but in those pustules only which are recent, and contain only a watery fluid. We must therefore, he observes, not expect to find them in the same proportionate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in patients who for many months have been afflicted with the disease, as in those in whom its appearance is recent, and where it is confined to the fingers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wrists. The cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> with respect to the pustules, he conjectures, may be owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the insect after it has deposited its eggs. A small transparent vesicle being found, a very minute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> point, distinct from the surrounding fluid, may be discovered, and very often even without the affluence of a glass; this is the insect, which may be easily taken out on the point of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> or penknife, and when placed on a green cloth may be seen much more distinctly, and observed to move. All this, we must remark, probably depends on optical deception.

ITHACA

Pages 417-417

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Epirus; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Ulysses, near Dulichium, with a town and port situated at the foot of Mount Neius. According to Pliny it is about 25 miles in compass; according to Artemidorus only 10; and is now found to be only eight miles round. It is now uninhabited, and called Isthaca.

ITINERARY

Pages 417-417

ITINERARIUM; a journal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an account of the distances of places. The most remarkable is that which goes under the names of Antoninus and Ethicus; or, as Barthius found in his copy, Antoninus Ethicus; a Christian writer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to the times of Constantine. Another, called Hierosolymitanum, from Bordeaux to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, and from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERACLEA">Heraclea</a> through Aulona and Rome to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, under Constantine.—Itinerarium denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>.

ITIUS PORTUS

Pages 417-417

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the crux geographorum, such being the difficulty of ascertaining its position. It would be endless to recite the several opinions concerning it, with the several reasons advanced in support of them. Three ports are mentioned by Caesar; two without any particular name, viz. the Higher and the Lower, with respect to the Portus Itius. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a>, St Omer, and Whitfand, have each in their turn had their several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>. Caesar gives two distinctive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> marks which seem to agree equally to Boulogne and Whitfand, namely, the shortness of the passage, and the situation between two other ports; therefore nothing can with certainty be determined about the situation of the Portus Itius.

ITYS

Pages 417-417

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a son of Tereus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thrace, by Procne <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Pandion king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He was killed by his mother when he was about six years old, and served up before his father. He was changed into a phœnix, his mother into a swallow, and his father into an owl.

ITZECUINTEPOTZOTLI

Pages 417-417
or HUNCH-BACKED DOG, a Mexican quadruped similar to a dog. It is as large as a Maltese dog, the skin of which is varied with white, tawny, and black. The characteristic mark is a great hunch which it bears from its neck to its rump. This animal abounds most in the kingdom of Michuacan.

ITZEHOA

Pages 417-418

ITZEOHA, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and handsome town of Germany, in the circle of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. It belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and is seated on the river Stoer, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 25. N. Lat. 54. 8.

IUERNUS

Pages 423-423

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town in the south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Now Dunkeram, (Camden); called Donekyne by the natives, situated on the river Maire, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>.

IVA

Pages 418-418

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monoeia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. IVAHAH is the name of a canoe of the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> islanders for short excursions to sea: it is wall-sided, flat-bottomed, and of different sizes, from 72 feet to 10: but their breadth is by no means in proportion; for those of ten feet are about a foot wide, and those of more than 70 are scarcely two. The fighting ivahah is the longest, with its head and stern considerably raised. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> ivahahs are from 40 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> to 10; those of 25 feet and upwards occasionally carry fish. The travelling ivahah is always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, and furnished with a small neat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>.

IVEACH

Pages 423-423

the name of two baronies of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">Down</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster. They are distinguished into Upper and Lower Ivecach, and the former is by much the largest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> in that county. The name of Ivecach, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Hy Veach, is said to be taken from Achaidh, in Irish called Eachach, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-father to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Coallpair, as much as to say "the territory of Eachach;" for hy, in the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> adjective, denoting not only the heads and founders of families, but also the territories possessed by them. Ivecach (including both baronies) was otherwife called Magennis's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was governed by Sir Hugh Magennis, esteemed to have been one of the most polite of all the natives in those parts. Through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this barony runs a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> considerably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, known by the name of Ivecach mountains.

IVES

Pages 423-423

St., is also the name of a town in Huntingdonshire, 64 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It has a fine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Ouse, had in the ninth century a mint, and was noted for its medicinal waters. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it was burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some years ago, but it was rebuilt. Here is a very good market on Monday for fatted cattle brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and there are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year. Here Oliver Cromwell rented a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> before he was chosen a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>.

IVICA

Pages 424-424
or **YVICA**, the name of an island in the Mediterranean. See YVICA.

IVY

Pages 19-19

IVY. See HEDERA, BOTANY Index.

IXIA

Pages 19-19

IXIA, a genus of plants belonging to the triandra class, and in the natural method ranking under the 6th order, Enateae. See Botany Index.

IXION

Pages 19-19

IXION, in fabulous history, king of the Lapiths, married Dia the daughter of Deionius, to whom he refused to give the customary nuptial presents. Deionius in revenge took from him his horses; when Ixion, dissembling his resentment, invited his father-in-law to a feast, and made him fall through a trap door into a burning furnace, in which he was immediately consumed. Ixion being afterwards stung with remorse for his cruelty, ran mad; on which Jupiter, in compassion, not only forgave him, but took him up into heaven, where he had the impiety to endeavour to corrupt Juno. Jupiter, to be the better assured of his guilt, formed a cloud in the resemblance of the goddess, upon which Ixion begat the centaurs: but boasting of his happiness, Jove hurled him down to Tartarus, where he lies fixed on a wheel encompassed with serpents, which turns without ceasing.

IXORA

Pages 19-19

IXORA, a genus of plants belonging to the tetran-dria class; and in the natural method ranking under the 47th order, Stellateae. JYNX, a genus of birds belonging to the order of picae. See Ornithology Index. K the tenth letter, and seventh consonant, of our alphabet; being formed by the voice, by a guttural expression of the breath through the mouth, together with a depression of the lower jaw and opening of the teeth. Its sound is much the same with that of the hard c, or qu: and it is used, for the most part, only before e, i, and u, in the beginning of words; as ken, kill, know, &c. It used formerly to be always joined with c at the end of words, but is at present very properly omitted, at least in words derived from the Latin: thus, for publick, musick, &c. we say, public, music, &c. However, in monosyllables, it is still retained, as jack, block, mock, &c. K is borrowed from the Greek kappa; and was but little used among the Latins: Priscian looked on it as a superfluous letter; and says, it was never to be used except in words borrowed from the Greek. Daufius, after Sallust, observes, that it was unknown to the ancient Romans.—Indeed we seldom find it in any Latin authors, excepting in the word kalender, where it sometimes stands in lieu of a c.—Carthage, however, is frequently spelt on medals with a K: SALVIS AUG. ET CAES FEL. KART. And sometimes the letter K alone stood for Carthage.—M. Berger has observed, that a capital K, on the reverse of the medals of the emperors of Constantinople, signified Konstantinus; and on the Greek medals he will have it to signify KOIAH, EYPIA, "Coelosyria." Quintilian tells us, that in his time some people had KAB Kaat's ban Kabobiquas. a mistaken notion, that wherever the letter e and a occurred at the beginning of a word, k ought to be used instead of the c. See C. Lipusius observes, that K was a stigma anciently marked on the foreheads of criminals with a red-hot iron. The letter K has various significations in old characters and diplomas; for instance, KR. flood for choue, KR. C. for cara civitas. KRM, for carmen, KR. AM. N. carus amicus nostrf, KS. chaos, KT. copite tonsus, &c. The French never use the letter k excepting in a few terms of art and proper names borrowed from other countries. Ablancourt, in his dialogue of the letters, brings in k complaining, that he has been often in a fair way to be banished out of the French alphabet, and confined to the countries of the north. K is also a numeral letter, signifying 250, according to the verse; K quoque ducentos et quinquaginta tenebit. When it had a stroke at top, K, it stood for 250,000. K on the French coinage denotes money coined at Bordeaux. KAARTA, a kingdom in Africa, through which Mr Park passed from the Gambia to the Niger. According to him, the country consists of sandy plains and rocky hills, the level part of it being the most extensive. It is inhabited by negroes, many of whom retain all their ancient superstitions, although converted to the religion of Mahomet. White men, he informs us, are strangers in the kingdom of Kaarta; and Mr Park's appearance had nearly the same effect upon them which ignorant people in our own country attribute to ghosts. Mr Park was well received by the king at Kemmoo, who at the same time informed him with ingenious frankness, that he could not protect him, being then at war with the king of Bambarra, but he gave him a guard to Jarra, the frontier town of the neighbouring kingdom of Ludamar. From our author's account of this war, it seems to be highly impolitic to liberate the negroes from slavery till civilization and Christianity be introduced into Africa. Kemmoo the metropolis of this kingdom, lies in N. Lat. 14° 15'. W. Long. 7° 20'. KAAT'S-BAAN, a town of New York, on the west bank of Hudson's river, seven miles south of Kaat's-Kill. KAAT'S-KILL, a township of New York, on the west bank of Hudson's river; five miles south of Hudson city, and 125 north of New York. It contained 1645 citizens in 1795, of whom 345 were electors, and 305 slaves. KAAT'S-KILL MOUNTAINS, a majestic ridge of mountains in the vicinity of the above township, which are the first part of the Alleghany mountains. KABA. See MEGA. KABOBIQUAS, a nation in the south of Africa, who are reported never to have seen a white man till the year 1783, when they were visited by M. Vaillant. On his approach, they felt his hair, hands, feet, and almost every part of his body. His beard astonished them, and they supposed that his whole body was covered with hair. The children were greatly alarmed, but presents of sugar candy soon reconciled them. The chief showed him every mark of respect, whom he regarded as a majestic figure, with a long mantle made of four jackal skins. The hair of the people is very short, curled, and ornamented with small copper buttons. Although they go almost naked, the females are remarkably chaste, and very reserved. Their only ornaments are glass beads. M. Vaillant assures us that he never saw a nation so disinterred, as they vied with each other in generosity. Many of them gave away gratuitously, and without receiving any thing in return, part of their herds and flocks. They are also of a courageous and martial character, making use of poisoned arrows and lances with long points. They are extremely obedient to their chief, whose will is a law. They believe in a supreme being who governs all things, and who exists far beyond the stars. They have no idea of a future existence, or of rewards and punishments, and have neither worship, sacrifices, ceremonies nor priests. Their country lies between 16° 25' and 19° 25' east of Paris, and between 23° and 25° S. Lat. KADESHE, KADESH-BARNEA, or EN-MISHPAT, in Ancient Geography, a city celebrated for several events. At Kadesh, Miriam the sister of Moses died (Num. xx. 1.). Here it was that Moses and Aaron, showing a distrust in God's power when they smote the rock at the waters of strife, were condemned to die, without the consolation of entering the promised land (Num. xxvii. 14.). The king of Kadesh was one of the princes killed by Joshua (xii. 22.). This city was given to the tribe of Judah, and was situated about eight leagues from Hebron to the south. Mr Wells is of opinion, that this Kadesh, which was situated in the wilderness of Zin, was a different place from Kadesh-barnea in the wilderness of Paran. KADMONÆI, or CADMONÆI, in Ancient Geography, a people of Palestine, said to dwell at the foot of Mount Hermon; which lies east, and is the reason of the appellation, with respect to Libanus, Phoenicia, and the north parts of Palestine. Called also Hevei (Moses). KÆMPFERIA, ZEDOARY, a genus of plants belonging to the monandra clasps; and in the natural method ranking under the 8th order, Scitamineae. See Botany Index. KAJUAGA, a kingdom of Africa, bounded on the south east and south by Bambouk; on the west by Bandon and Fouta Torra; and on the north by the river Senegal. The air and climate are more pure and healthy than at any of the settlements towards the coast; the face of the country is pleasantly diversified with hills and valleys, and the windings of the river Senegal make the scenery on its banks extremely beautiful. The inhabitants are called Serawoolies, who have a jet black complexion, in which respect they are not to be distinguished from the Jaloffs. The government is monarchical, and the regal authority, according to Mr Park, is sufficiently formidable. The people are deemed tolerably fair and just in their dealings, and indefatigable in their exertions to acquire wealth. Their language abounds with gutturals, and therefore not so harmonious as that which is spoken by the Foulaahs; but it is worth a traveller's while to obtain a knowledge of it, as it is generally understood in many kingdoms of Africa. Joag is the frontier town, entering

JABBOK

Pages 27-27

a brook on the other side of the Jordan, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> whereof is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Gilead. It falls into Jordan pretty near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Tiberias, to the south of this sea. Near this brook the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> wrestled with the angel (Gen. xxxii. 22). The Jabbok separated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a> from the Gaulanites, and the territories of Og <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Bashan.

JABESH

Pages 27-27
or JABESH-GILEAD, was the name of a city, in the half tribe of Manasseh, beyond Jordan. The scripture calls it generally Jabesh-Gilead, because it lay in Gilead, at the foot of the mountains which go by this name. Eusebius places it five miles from Pella, towards Gerafa; and consequently it must be eastward of the sea of Tiberias. JABIRU. See MYCTERIA, ORNITHOLOGY Index.

JABLONSKI

Pages 27-27

Theodore, counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and secretary of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy of sciences in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, was also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of distinguished merit. He loved the sciences, and did them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, without that ambition which is generally seen in men of learning; it was owing to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> that the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his works were published without his name. He published, in 1711, a French and German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>; a Course of Morality, in 1715; a Dictionary of Arts and Sciences, 1721; and translated Tacitus de moribus Germanorum into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Dutch, in 1724.

JABNE

Pages 27-27

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, near Joppa; called Jamnia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jamnia, by the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. In Joshua xv, it seems to be called Jabneel; but in 2 Chron. xxvi. Jabne. It was taken from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UZZIAH">Uzziah</a>, who demolished its fortifications. Its port, called Jamnitarum portus, lay between Joppa and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZOTUS">Azotus</a>. JACAMAR. See ALCEO, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JACK

Pages 27-28

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, a well-known <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for raising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> weights of any kind. The common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-jack is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> engine, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> is the power applied to overcome the friction of the parts and the weight with which the spit is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>; and a steady and uniform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is obtained by means of the fly. Jack, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> colours, displayed from a mast erected on the outer end of a ship's bowsprit. In the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> the jack is nothing more than a small union flag, composed of the interlacing of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> crosses; but in merchant-ships this union is bordered with a red field. See the article UNION. Jack is used also for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or wooden frame to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> upon; for an instrument to pull off a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of boots; for a great leathern pitcher to carry drink in; for a small bowl that serves as a mark at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a>; and for a young pike. Jack-Flag, in a ship, that is hoisted up at the sprit-sail top-mast head. Jack-Daw, the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of corvus. See CORVUS, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> is very mischievous to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> and gardener; and is of such a thievish disposition, that he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> carry away much more than he can make use of. There is a method of destroying them by a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> much used in England; and is so useful, that it ought to be made universal.—A flake of about five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> is to be driven firmly into the ground, and made so fast that it cannot move, and so sharp in the point that the bird cannot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> upon it. Within a foot of the top there must be a hole bored through it, of three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch diameter; through this hole is to be put a stick of about eight inches long; then a horse-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> or noose is to be made fast to a thin hazel-wand, and this brought up to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the short stick is placed, and carried with it through the hole, the remainder being left open under that stick. The other end of the hazel rod is to be put through a hole in the stake near the ground, and fastened there. The stake is to be planted among the jack-daw's food, and he will naturally be led to settle on it; but finding the point too sharp, he will descend to the little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> stick. This will stick with his weight, and the spring will receive his leg, and hold him fast.

JACOB

Pages 28-28

BEN NAPHTALI, a famous rabbi of the 9th century; he was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> masorets, and bred at the school of Tiberias in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> with Ben Aser, another principal masoret. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> to serve for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>, and of accents to facilitate the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are ascribed to these two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RABBIS">rabbis</a>; and said to be done in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the Jews held at Tiberias, A.D. 476.

JACOB BEN HAJIM

Pages 28-28

a rabbi famous for the collection of the Masorah in 1525; together with the text of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, the Chaldaic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a>, and Rabbinical commentaries.

JACOBINES

Pages 28-28

the name assumed by a party <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> club at the beginning of the French revolution, composed of members of the national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. This club held its meetings in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> belonging to the Jacobin friars, from which it derived its name. For an account of the views and influence of the Jacobin club in the French revolution, see France.

JACOBITES

Pages 28-28

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and Mesopotamia; so called, either from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> a Syrian who lived in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Mauritius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from one Jacob a monk who flourished in the year 550. The Jacobites are of two sects, some following the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the Latin church, and others continuing separated from the church of Rome. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> among the latter, who have two rival patriarchs. As to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, they hold but one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; with respect to purgatory and prayers for the dead, they are of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> with the Greeks and other eastern Christians: they consecrate unleavened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> at the eucharist, and are against consecration, believing that it is not of divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>.

JACOBUS

Pages 28-28

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, worth 25 shillings; so called from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. of England, in whose reign it was struck. See Coin. We usually distinguish two kinds of Jacobus, the old and the new; the former valued at 25 shillings, weighing six <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-weights ten grains; the latter, called also Carolus, valued at 23 shillings, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> five penny-weights twenty grains.

JACQUINIA

Pages 28-28

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandra clasps, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JACULATOR

Pages 28-28
or SHOOTING-FISH. See Chetodon, Ichthyology Index. JADDESESSE is the name of an inferior order of priests in Ceylon, who have the care of the chapels appropriated to the genii, who form a third order of gods among these idolaters. These priests are applied to by the people in time of disease or calamity, who offer a cock on their behalf to appease the anger of the demons.

JADE-STONE

Pages 28-28
or Lapis nephriticus, a species of Mineral. See Mineralogy Index.

JAFFATEEN ISLANDS

Pages 28-28

the name of four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, visited by Mr Bruce in his late travels. They are joined together by shoals <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sunken rocks; are crooked or bent like half a bow; and are dangerous for ships in the night <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, because there seems to be a passage between them, to which, while the pilots are paying <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, they neglect two small sunken rocks which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> almost in the middle of the entrance in deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.

JAGENDORF

Pages 28-28

a town and castle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name, seated on the river Oppa. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 47' N. Lat. 50° 4'.

JAGGERNAUT

Pages 28-29

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> pyramidal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> worshipped by the Gentoes, who pretend that it fell from heaven, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> was miraculously presented on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where there temple stands. There are many other idols of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; which, however, are all but... Jaggermaut but accounted copies from the Jaggernaut. According to the best information Mr Grofe could obtain, this stone is meant to represent the power prevailing over universal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to the genial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> acting in subordination to it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">Domestic</a> idols of the form of the Jaggernaut, and distinguished by the same name, are made by the Gentooos. These are pitched up in a kind of triumphal car, decorated with gilding and tinsel; which for some days they keep in the best apartment in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. During this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> consists in exhibiting the most obscene postures, and acting all manner of lasciviousness, in sight as it were of the idol, and as the most acceptable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of worship to that deity it represents; after which they carry it in its gilded car in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> to the Ganges, and throw in all together as an acknowledgment to that river of its congenial fertilization with that of the sun. Formerly this machine was decorated with jewels and other expensive ornaments; but the Indians are now become less extravagant, as they found that the Moors and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, watching the places where they threw in their idols, dived for them for the sake of the jewels with which they were adorned. Our author conjectures, that this pyramidal form of the Gentoo idol was originally taken from that of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, which always inclines to point upwards. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> deity he supposes the shape of the Paphian Venus to have been derived, for which Tacitus could not account. This image had nothing of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form in it, but rose orbicularly from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> basis, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> coal tapering to a narrow convex a-top; which is exactly the figure of the idol in India, consecrated to such an office as that heathen deity was supposed to preside over, and to which, on the borders of the Ganges especially, the Gentoo virgins are brought to undergo a kind of superfluous defloration before they are presented to their husbands.

JAGHIRE

Pages 29-29

an assignment made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> by an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> upon the revenue of any district, to defray civil <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> charges, pensions, gratuities, &c.

JAGO

Pages 29-29

RICHARD, an ingenious poet, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Snitterfield in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, and rector of Kimcote in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>. He was the intimate friend and correspondent of Mr Shenstone, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with him at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and, it is believed, his schoolfellow; was of University <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 9, 1739; was author of several poems in the 4th and 5th volumes of Dodley's Poems; published a sermon, in 1755, on the Causes of Impenitence considered, preached May 4, 1755, at Harbury in Warwickshire, where he was vicar, on occasion of a conversation said to have passed between one of the inhabitants and an apparition in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard there; wrote "Edge-hill," a poem, for which he obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> subscription in 1767; and was also author of "Labour and Genius," 1768, 4to; of "The Blackbirds," a beautiful elegy in the Adventurer; and of many other ingenious performances. He died May 28, 1781. [Merged from ST JAGO, p.29] a handsome and considerable town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, with a good harbour, a bishop's see, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> audience. It is seated in a large and beautiful plain, abounding with all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, at the foot of the Cordilleras, on the river Mapocho, which runs across it from east to west. Here are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> and a dyke, by means of which they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> the gardens and cool the fires.—It is very much subject to earthquakes. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 69° 35'. S. Lat. 33° 40'. St. Jago de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America, situated on the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cuba, in the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, with a good harbour, and on a river of the same name. W. Long. 76° 44'. N. Lat. 20° 0'. Jaco de los Caballeros, a town of America, and one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the island of Hispaniola. It is seated on the river Yaque, in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, but bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. W. Long. 75° 5'. N. Lat. 19° 40'. St. Jaco del <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>, a town of South America, one of the most considerable of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUCUMAN">Tucuman</a>, and the usual residence of the inquisitor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. It is seated on a large river, in a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, tygers, guanacos, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called camel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, &c. Jaco de la Vega, otherwise called Spanish-town, is the capital of the island of Jamaica, in the West Indies; and stands in 18° 1' north latitude, and 76° 45' west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. It is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, and little more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a mile in breadth, and contains between 500 and 600 houses, with about 4000 inhabitants of all colours and denominations. This town is situated in a delightful plain on the banks of the Rio Cobre, 13 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>, and 10 from Port Royal. It is the residence of the commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>: and here the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of judicature is held, four times in the year, viz. on the last Tuesdays of February, May, August, and November, and fits three weeks.—St. Jago de la Vega is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>-town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, and belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St Catherine; in which parish there are 11 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-plantations, 18 pens, and other settlements, and about 10,000 slaves.

JAGUAR

Pages 30-30
or JAQUAR, a name given to the Brazilian ounce, a species of Felis. See Felis, Mammalia Index.

JAGUEER

Pages 30-30

in East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> affairs, any pension from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Mogul; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>; generally such as are assigned for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> services.

JAGUEERDAR

Pages 30-30

the holder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> possessor of a jaguer. It comes from three Persian words, ya, "a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>;" guerifian, "to take;" and daftian, "to hold;" guafi, "a place-holder or pensioner." In the times of the Mogul empire, all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, called onrahs, were allowed jagueers, either in lands of which they collected the revenues, or assignments upon the revenues for specified sums, payable by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>: which sums were for their maintenance, and the support of such troops as they were necessitated to bring into the field when demanded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, as the condition of their jagueers, which were always revocable at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>.

JAIL-FEVER

Pages 30-30

a very dangerous distemper of the contagious kind, arising from the putrefied disposition of the blood and juices. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JAINAPATAN

Pages 28-28

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town, seated at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east end of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon in the East Indies. The Dutch took it from the Portuguese in 1618, and have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the possession of it since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They export from thence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and some elephants, which are accounted the most docile of any in the whole world. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80° 25' N. Lat. 9° 35'.

JALAP

Pages 30-30

the root of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of convolvulus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bind weed. See Convolvulus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JALEMUS

Pages 30-30

in antiquity, a kind of mournful song, used upon occasion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other affecting accident. Hence the Greek proverbs had their original, ἀλείμων ὁμοργίας, or ἀλείμων, i.e. more sad or colder than a jalemus, as τὸ ἐπικάθευσις ὑπερέχεις, worthy to be ranked among jalemuses.

JALOFFS

Pages 30-30
or YALOFFS, are a warlike people, inhabiting most of that part of Africa, lying between Senegal and the Mandingo states on the Gambia. Their lips, according to Mr Park, are not so protuberant as those of the generality of Africans; and though their skin is of the deepest black, they are esteemed by the white traders as the most frightful of the negroes in that part of the continent. They are divided into several independent states, and more resemble the Mandingoes than any other nation in their manners and government, but much exceed them in the manufacture of cotton cloth, spinning the wool to a finer thread, weaving it in a broader loom, and dyeing it of a better colour. They make excellent soap, by boiling ground nuts in water, and then adding a ley of wood ashes. They likewise manufacture very good iron, which they carry to Bandore to exchange for salt. Their language, it is said, is copious and significant, and is frequently learned by Europeans trading to Senegal. A generous disposition, according to the testimony of Mr Park, is said to distinguish them above the generality of savages; they know how to return an act of kindness thrown them by others in distress, and their conduct towards their enemies, in many instances, is said to be worthy of imitation.

JAMADAR

Pages 30-30

an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foot, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>. Also the head or superintendent of the Peons in the Seawary or train of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

JAMAICA

Pages 30-33

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the West Indies, the largest of the Antilles, lying between 17° and 19° N. Lat. and between 76° and 79° W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>.; in length near 170 miles, and about 65 in breadth. It approaches in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> to an oval. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> passage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> before it hath the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a> on the west, and Hispaniola on the east, and is about 25 leagues in breadth. This island was discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Christopher Columbus in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> voyage, who landed upon it May 5, 1494; and was so much charmed with it, as always to prefer it to the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>: in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, his son chose it for his dukedom. It was settled by Juan d'Esquivel, A.D. 1509, who built the town, which, from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, he called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, and 11 leagues farther to the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> Melilla. Orifton was on the south side of the island, seated on what is now called Blue Fields River. All these are gone to decay; but St Jago, now Spanish-town, is still the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. The Spaniards held this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> 160 years, and in their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> commodity was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CACAO">cacao</a>; they had an immense flock of horses, asses, and mules, and prodigious quantities of cattle. The English landed here under Penn and Venables, May 11, 1654, and quickly reduced the island. Cacao was also their principal commodity till the old trees decayed, and the new ones did not thrive; and then the planters from Barbados introduced <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes, which hath been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> staple ever since. The prospect of this island from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, by reason of its constant verdure, and many fair and false bays, is wonderfully pleasant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and for some miles within, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is low; but removing farther, it rises and becomes hilly. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> is divided by a ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> running east and west, some rising to a great height; and these are composed of rock and a very hard clay; through which, however, the rains that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> incessantly upon them have worn long and deep cavities, which they call gullies. These mountains, however, are far from being unpleasing, as they are crowned even to their summits with a variety of fine trees. There are also about a hundred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that issue from them on both sides: and, though none of them are navigable for any thing but canoes, are both pleasing and profitable in many other respects. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, like that of all countries between the tropics, is very warm towards the sea, and in marshy places unhealthy; but in more elevated situations, cooler; and, where people live temperately, to the full as wholesome as in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the West Indies. The rains fall heavy for about a fortnight in the months of May and October; and, as they are the cause of fertility, are styled seasons. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a> is pretty frequent, and sometimes showers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> and snow are never seen, although on the tops of the mountains, and at no very great height, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. The most eastern parts of this ridge are known under the name of the Blue Mountain. This great chain of rugged rocks defends the south side of the island from those boisterous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west winds, which might be fatal to their produce. Their streams, though small, supply the inhabitants with good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which is a great blessing, as their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> are generally brackish. The Spaniards were persuaded that these hills abounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; but we do not find that they wrought any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they did, it was only <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, of which they said the bells in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Jago were made. They have several hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, which have done great cures. The climate was certainly more temperate before the great earthquake; and the island was supposed to be out of the reach of hurricanes, which since that time it hath severely felt. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, however, is very much tempered by land and sea breezes; and it is asserted, that the hottest time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> is about eight in the morning. In the night, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the land on all sides, so that no ships can then enter their ports. In an island so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as this, which contains above five millions of acres, it may be very reasonably conceived that there are great variety of soils. Some of these are deep, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and rich, and mixed with a kind of potters <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; others shallow and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>; and some of a middle <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. There are many savannahs, or wide plains, without <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, in which the native Indians had luxuriant crops of maize, which the Spaniards turned into meadows, and kept in them prodigious herds of cattle. Some of these savannahs are to be met with even amongst the mountains. All these different soils may be justly pronounced fertile, as they would certainly be found, if tolerably cultivated, and applied to proper purposes. A sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> arise from a very cursory review of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> produce of this spacious country. It abounds in maize, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, vegetables of all kinds, meadows of fine grass, a variety of beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and as great a variety of oranges, lemons, citrons, and other rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. Useful animals there are of all sorts, horses, asses, mules, black cattle of a large size, and sheep, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of which is well tasted, though their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is hairy and bad. Here are also goats and hogs in great plenty; sea and river fish; wild, tame, and water-fowl. Amongst other commodities of great value, they have the sugar-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, cacao, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, pimento, cotton, ginger, and coffee; trees for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and other uses, such as mahogany, manchineel, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wood which no worm will touch, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, olives, and many more. Besides these, they have fustick, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wood, and various other materials for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>. To these we may add a multitude of valuable drugs, such as guaiacum, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a>, farfarailla, castia, tamarinds, vanellas, and the prickly-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a> or opuntia, which produces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>; with no inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of odoriferous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>. Near the coast they have <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-ponds, from which at one time they supplied their own consumption, and might certainly make any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> they pleased. As this island abounds with rich commodities, it is happy likewise in having a number of fine and safe ports. Point Morant, the eastern extremity of the island, hath a fair and commodious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>. Passing on to the south, there is Port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>: on a neck of land which forms one side of it, there stood once the fairest town in the island; and the harbour is as fine a one as can be wished, capable of holding a thousand large vessels, and still the station of our squadron. Old Harbour is also a convenient port, so is Maccary Bay; and there are at least twelve more between this and the western extremity, which is Point Negrillo, where our ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> when there is a war with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. On the north side there is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> bay, Cold harbour, Rio Novo, Montego bay, Port Antonio, one of the finest in the island, and several others. The north-west winds, which sometimes blow furiously on this coast, render the country on that side less fit for canes, but pimento thrives wonderfully; and certainly many other staples might be raised in small plantations, which are frequent in Barbadoes, and might be very advantageous here in many respects. The town of Port Royal stood on a point of land running far out into the sea, narrow, sandy, and incapable of producing anything. Yet the excellence of the port, the convenience of having ships of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hundred tons coming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> up to their wharfs, and other advantages, gradually attracted inhabitants in such a manner, that though many of their habitations were built on piles, there were near two thousand houses in the town in its most flourishing state, and which let at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rents. The earthquake by which it was overthrown happened on the 7th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1692, and numbers of people perished in it. This earthquake was followed by an epidemic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, of which upwards of three thousand died: yet the place was rebuilt; but the greatest part was reduced to ashes by a fire that happened on the 9th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1703, and then the inhabitants removed mostly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>. It was, however, rebuilt for the third time; and was rising towards its former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, when it was overwhelmed by the sea, August 28, 1742. There is, notwithstanding, a small town there at this day. Hurricanes since that time have often happened, and occasioned terrible devastations. The island is divided into three counties, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, Surry, and Cornwall; containing 20 parishes, over each of which presides a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> styled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>; but there these parishes in point of size are a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>. The whole contain 36 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, 18 churches and chapels, and about 23,000 white inhabitants. The administration of public affairs is by a governor and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of royal appointment, and the representatives of the people in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. They meet at Spanish-town, and things are conducted with great order and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor and commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> has 500l. currency, or 3571l. 8s. 6½d. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> besides which, he has a houle in Spanish-town, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> or a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> adjoining, and a polin or mountain for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>: a secretary, an under-secretary, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> the council consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> and 10 members; with a clerk, at 270l. a chaplain 100l., usher of the black rod and messenger 250l. The honourable the assembly consists of 43 members, one of whom is chosen speaker. To this assembly belong a clerk, with 100l. salary; a chaplain, 150l.; messenger, 700l.; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, 100l.; and printer, 200l. The number of members returned by each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> are, for Middlesex 17, viz. St Catharine 3, St Dorothy 2, St John 2, St Thomas in the Vale 2, Clarendon 2, Vere 2, St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> 2, St Ann 2: For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a> 16, viz. Kingston 3, Port Royal 3, St Andrew 2, St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> 2, St Thomas in the Elst 2, Portland 2, St George 2: For Cornwall 10, viz. St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> 2, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a> 2, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> 2, St James 2, Trelawney 2. The high <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> consists of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> (governor for the time being), 25 masters in ordinary, and 20 masters extraordinary; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, and clerk of the patents; serjeant at arms, and mace-bearer. The court of vice <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> has a sole judge, judge surrogate, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s advocate, principal registrar, marshal, and a deputy-marshal. The court of ordinary, consists of the ordinary (governor for the time being), and a clerk. The supreme court of judicature has a chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, 120l. and 16 assistant judges; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>, 400l.; clerk of the court, 100l.; clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, 350l.; solicitor for the crown: 33 commissioners for taking affidavits; a provost-marshal-general, and eight deputies; 18 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRISTERS">barristers</a>, besides the attorney-general and advocate-general; and upward of 120 practising attorneys at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Jamaica is very considerable, not only with all parts of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, but with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, North and South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the West Indies, and the Spanish main. The ships annually employed are upwards of 500 sail. The following account of the exports of this island in 1770, as given by Abbé Raynal, but which in several particulars appears to be under-rated, will contribute more than all that hath been said, to show the importance of Jamaica. They consisted in 2249 bales of cotton, which at 10 pounds per <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">bale</a>, the price in the island, amounts to 22,490l.; 1873 hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of coffee, at three pounds five shillings per hundred, 6088l.; 2753 bags of ginger, at two pounds five shillings per bag, 6194l.; 2211 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, at seven shillings per hide, 773l.; 16,475 puncheons of rum, at 10l. per puncheon, 164,750l. Mahogany, 15,282 pieces and 8500 feet, 50,000l. Of pimento, 2,089,734 pounds weight, 52,243l. Sugar, 57,675 hogheads, 6425 tierces, 52 barrels, at seventeen pounds ten shillings per hoghead, twelve pounds per tierce, and four pounds per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, amounting in the whole to 1,086,620l. Saraparilla, 205 bags, at ten pounds per bag, 2250l. Exports to Great Britain and Ireland, 1,301,210l. To North America, 1,463,24l. To the other islands, 595l. Total of the exports, 1,538,730l.
