The following is a general view of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and chief produce of the whole island in 1786, as prefixed by Mr Beckford to his descriptive account of Jamaica. | Counties | Sugar Estates | Other Settlements | Slaves | Produce Hhds. of Sugar | Cattle | |----------|---------------|-------------------|--------|-----------------------|--------| | Middlesex| 323 | 917 | 87100 | 31500 | 75000 | | Surrey | 350 | 540 | 75600 | 34900 | 80000 | | Cornwall | 388 | 561 | 90000 | 39000 | 69500 | | Total | 1061 | 2018 | 255700 | 105400 | 224500 | It should be here observed, that where two hogheads of sugar are made, there is at least one puncheon of rum; but the proportion has been of late years more considerable: the quantity of the latter will therefore be 52,700 puncheons. A comparative view between the years 1768 and 1786. | | Middlesex in 1768 | Middlesex in 1786 | Surrey in 1768 | Surrey in 1786 | Cornwall in 1768 | Cornwall in 1786 | Total in 1768 | Total in 1786 | Amount of Increase | |------------------|-------------------|-------------------|----------------|----------------|-----------------|-----------------|--------------|--------------|------------------| | Sugar Estates | 239 | 323 | 146 | 350 | 266 | 388 | 651 | 1061 | 410 | | Sugar Hhds. | 24050 | 31500 | 15010 | 34900 | 29100 | 39000 | 68160 | 105400 | 37240 | | <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a> | 66744 | 87100 | 39542 | 75600 | 60614 | 93000 | 166900 | 255700 | 88800 | | Cattle | 59510 | 73000 | 21465 | 80000 | 54775 | 69500 | 133750 | 224500 | 88750 | From the above scheme it appears, how considerable has been the increase of sugar-estates, and consequently of produce of negroes and cattle in eighteen years; and in the same portion of time (it is said), if proper encouragement were given, they might be augmented in a threefold proportion. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> valuation of an estate in Jamaica is as follows: | Item | Sterling | |-----------------------------|----------| | Cane land (the canes upon it valued separately) at | £22 per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a> | 22 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a> | | Cane land, in ratoons and young plants, | 15 ditto | | Pasture land | 8 ditto | | Wood land | 4 ditto | | Provisions | 14 ditto | | Negroes | 57 ditto | | Mules | 22 ditto | | Steers | 10 ditto | | Breeding cattle, &c. | 5 ditto | | Works, water, carts, &c. | from 7 to 10,000 | If a planter would wish to leave his estate for a number of years, his income would be large if he could get only 10d. sterling a day for his negroes (the loss made good), without requiring anything for his land or works.

JAMBI

Pages 33-33
or JAMBIS, a sea-port town and small kingdom of Asia, on the eastern coast of the island of Sumatra. It is a trading place. The Dutch have a fort here; and export pepper from thence, with the best sort of canes. E. Long. 105° 55'. S. Lat. 0° 30'. JAMBIA VICUS. See YAMBO.

JAMBICUS

Pages 33-33

the name of two celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosophers, one of whom was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>, and the other of Apamea in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. The first, whom Julian equals to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Anatolius and Porphyry, and died under the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> also enjoyed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. Julian wrote several letters to him, and it is said he was poisoned under the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a>.—It is not known to which of the two we ought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the works we have in Greek under the name of Jamblicus, viz. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, and the feet of the Pythagoreans. 2. An exhortation to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. 3. A piece against Porphyry's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Egyptians.

JAMBOLIFERA

Pages 33-33

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the oculandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JAMES

Pages 33-37

St., called the Less, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Jude, and the son of Cleophas and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, the sister of the mother of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, is called in Scripture the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a>, and the brother of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, who appeared to him in particular after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>. He was the first bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, when Annianus II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the Jews, caused him to be condemned, and delivered him into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the people and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>, who threw him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the steps of the temple, when a fuller dashed out his brains with a club, about the year 62. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was so holy, that Josephus con- James fiders the sin of Jerusalem as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted on that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was the author of the epistle which bears his name. St James of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">Sword</a>, (San Jago del Espada), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, instituted in 1170, under the reign of Ferdinand II, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Leon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>. Its end was to put a stop to the incursions of the Moors; three knights obliging themselves by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> to secure the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>. An union was proposed and agreed to in 1170 between these and the canons of St Eloy; and the order was confirmed by the pope in 1175. The highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in that order is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, which has been united to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Spain. The knights are obliged to make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from families that have been noble for four generations on both sides; they must also make it appear, that their said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> have neither been Jews, Saracens, nor heretics; nor even to have been called in question by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>. The novices are obliged to serve six months in the galleys, and to live a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. Heretofore they were truly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, and took a vow of celibacy; but Alexander III. gave them a permission to marry. They now make no vows but of poverty, obedience, and conjugal fidelity; to which, since the year 1624, they have added that of defending the immaculate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the holy Virgin. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cloak, with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. This is esteemed the most considerable of all the military orders in Spain; the king carefully preserves the office of grand master in his own family, on account of the rich revenues and offices, whereof it gives him the disposal. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of knights is much greater now than formerly, all the grandees choosing rather to be received into this than into the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>; insomuch as this puts them in a fair way of attaining to commands, and gives them many considerable privileges in all the provinces of Spain, but especially in Catalonia. James, the name of several kings of Scotland and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. See (Histories of) Scotland and Britain. James I, king of Scotland in 1423, the first of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Stuart, was not only the most learned king, but the most learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he flourished. This ingenious and amiable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> fell into the hands of the enemies of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in his tender youth, when he was <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> from the snares of his unnatural ambitious uncle, who governed his dominions, and was suspected of designs against his life. Having secretly embarked for France, the ship was taken by an English privateer off Flamborough-head; and the prince and his attendants (among whom was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Orkney) were confined in a neighbouring castle until they were sent to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. See (<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) Scotland. The king of England knew the value of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> he had obtained, and kept it with the most anxious care. The prince was conducted to the Tower of London immediately after he was seized, April 12. A.D. 1405, in the 13th year of his age; and there kept a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> prisoner till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 10. A.D. 1407, when he was removed to the castle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, from whence he was brought back to the Tower, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1. A.D. 1414, and there confined till August 3. in the same year, when he was conveyed to the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, where he was detained till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of A.D. 1417; when Henry V. for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> reasons, carried him with him into France in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> expedition. In all these fortresses, his confinement, from his own account of it, was so severe and strict, that he was not so much as permitted to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. In this melancholy situation, so unsuitable to his age and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, books were his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> companions, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> his greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He rose early in the morning, immediately applied to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, to divert him from painful reflections on his misfortunes, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his studies, with little interruption, till late at night. James being naturally sensible, ingenious, and fond of knowledge, and having received a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in his early youth, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Walter Wardlaw bishop of St Andrews's, by this close application to study, became an universal scholar, an excellent poet, and exquisite musician. That he wrote as well as read much, we have his own testimony, and that of all our historians who lived near his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Bowmanker, the continuator of Fordun, who was his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a>, and personally acquainted with him, spends ten chapters in his praises, and in lamentations on his death; and, amongst other things, says, that his knowledge of the scriptures, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, was incredible. Hector Boece tells us, that Henry IV. and V. furnished their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> prisoner with the best teachers in all the arts and sciences; and that, by their affluence, he made great proficiency in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of learning and the fine arts; that he became a perfect master in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, music, and all the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, and was inferior to none in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and law. He observes further, that the poems he composed in his native tongue were so beautiful, that you might easily perceive he was born a poet; but that his Latin poems were not so faultless; for though they abounded in the most sublime sentiments, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> was not so pure, owing to the rudeness of the times in which he lived. This prince's skill in music was remarkable. Walter Bower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Inchcolm, who was intimately acquainted with that prince, assures us, that he excelled all mankind in that art both vocal and instrumental; and that he played on eight different instruments (which he names), and especially on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, with such exquisite skill, that he seemed to be inspired. King James was not only an excellent performer, but also a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> composer, both of sacred and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> music; and his fame on that account was extensive, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Above a century after his death, he was celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> as the inventor of a new and pleasing kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, which had been admired and imitated in that country. This appears from the following testimony of Alessandro Tafioni, a writer who was well informed, and of undoubted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. "We may reckon among us moderns, James king of Scotland, who not only composed many sacred pieces of vocal music, but also of himself invented a new kind of music, plaintive and melancholy, different from all others; in which he hath been imitated by Carlo Gesualdo prince of Venosa, who, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALESSANDRIA">Alessandria</a>, our age, hath improved music with new and admirable inventions." As the prince of Venosa imitated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, King James, the other musicians of Italy imitated the John Hawkins, prince of Venosa. "The most noble Carlo Gesualdo, kins, vol. iv., do p. 51, 61. James do, the prince of musicians of our age, introduced such a style of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>, that other musicians yielded the preference to him; and all singers and players on stringed instruments, laying aside that of others, everywhere embraced his. All the lovers, therefore, of Italian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Scotch music, are much indebted to the admirable genius of King James I., who, in the gloom and solitude of a prison, invented a new kind of music, plaintive indeed, and suited to his situation, but at the same time so sweet and soothing, that it hath given pleasure to millions in every succeeding age. As James I. of Scotland was one of the most accomplished princes that ever filled a throne, he was also one of the most unfortunate. After spending almost 20 years in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, and encountering many difficulties on his return into his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, he was murdered by barbarous assassins in the prime of life. In the monuments of his genius, he hath been almost equally unfortunate. No vestiges are now remaining of his skill in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>; though we are assured by one who was well acquainted with him, that he excelled in all these arts*. Many of the productions of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> have also perished; for he tells us himself that he wrote much†; and we know of only three of his poems that are now extant, viz. Chrift's Kirk on the Green—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEEBLES">Peebles</a> at the Play—and the King's Quair, which was lately discovered by Mr Warton, and hath been published by another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>‡. But slender as these remains are, they afford sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, that the genius of this royal poet was not inferior to that of any of his contemporaries; and that it was equally fitted for the gayest or the gravest strains. James II. king of Scotland, 1437, succeeded his father, being then not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of age; and was killed at the siege of Roxburgh in 1460, aged 29. James III. king of Scotland, succeeded his father, in 1460, in the 7th year of his age. The most striking feature in the character of this prince, unjustly represented as tyrannical by several historians, was his fondness for the fine arts, and for those who excelled in them, on whom he bestowed more of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, confidence, and favour, than became a king in his circumstances. This excited in his fierce and haughty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> dislike and contempt of their sovereign, and indignation against the objects of his favour; which produced the most pernicious consequences, and ended in a rebellion that proved fatal to James, who was slain in 1488, aged 36. James IV. king of Scotland, succeeded his father in 1488. He was a pious and valiant prince; subdued his rebellious subjects; and afterwards, taking part with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. against Henry VIII. of England, he was slain in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Flodden-field in 1513, aged 41.—This king is acknowledged to have had great accomplishments both of mind and body. His Latin epistles are classical, compared with the barbarous style of the foreign princes with whom he corresponded. Like his father, he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the fine arts, particularly that of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> he paid to the civilization of his people, and his distribution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, merit the highest praise. After all, the virtues of James appear to have been more shining than <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>; and his character was that of a fine gentleman and a brave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, rather than a wife or a great monarch. At the time of his death, he was only in his forty first year. Like all the princes of his family (to his great grandson James VI.) his person was handsome, vigorous, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. From their coins, it does not appear that either he, or any of his predecessors of the Stuart <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, wore their beards, as did all his successors, to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. James V. king of Scotland, in 1513, was but 18 months old when his father lost his life. When of age, he assisted Francis I. king of France against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Charles V.; for which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> Francis gave him his eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, in 1535. This princess died in two years; and James married Mary of Lorraine, daughter of Claud duke of Guise, and widow of Louis d'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, by whom he had only one child, the unfortunate Mary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Scots, born only eight days before his death, which happened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 13, 1542, in the 35th year of his age. This was the first prince of his family who died a natural death since its elevation to the throne. He died, however, of a broken heart, occasioned by differences with his barons. He was formed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to be the ornament of a throne and a blessing to his people; but his excellent endowments were rendered in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> ineffectual by an improper education. Like most of his predecessors, he was born with a vigorous, graceful person, which, in the early part of his reign, was improved by all the manly exercises then in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. This prince was the author of a humorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in poetry, which goes by the name of the Gaberlunzie Man. James VI. king of Scotland in 1567, and of England in 1603, was son of Mary queen of Scots; whom he succeeded in Scotland, as he did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> in England. Strongly attached to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he dignified himself in its support; which gave rise to the horrid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of the Papists to destroy him and all the English <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">Gunpowder</a> Plot, discovered November 5, 1605. The following year, a political test of loyalty was required, which secured the king's person, by clearing the kingdom of those disaffected Roman Catholic subjects who would not submit to it. The chief <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of this king's reign consisted in the establishment of new colonies, and the introduction of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> enjoyed peace, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> flourished during his reign. Yet his administration was despaired both at home and abroad: for, being the head of the Protestant cause in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, he did not support it in that great crisis, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>; abandoning his son-in-law the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine; negotiating when he should have fought, deceived at the same time by the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>; continually sending illustrious ambassadors to foreign powers, but never making a single ally. He valued himself much upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a> writings; and so fond was he of theological disputations, that to keep them alive, he founded, for this express purpose, Chelsea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; which was converted to a much better use by Charles II. His Basilicon Doron, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>, writings against Bellarmine, and his Demonologia, or doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a>, are sufficiently known. There is a collection of his writings and speeches in one folio volume. Several other pieces of his are extant; some of them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABALA">Cabala</a>, others in manuscript in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, James, and others in Howard's collection. He died in 1625, in the 59th year of his age, and 23rd of his reign. James II, king of England, Scotland, &c., 1685, grandson of James I. succeeded his brother Charles II. It is remarkable, that this prince wanted neither courage nor political abilities whilst he was duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; on the contrary, he was eminent for both: but when he ascended the throne, he was no longer the same man. A bigot from his infancy to the Romish religion and to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>, he sacrificed everything to establish them, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> he had acquired, during the long reign of his brother, of the genius and character of the people he was to govern. Guided by the Jesuit Peters his confessor, and the infamous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Jeffries, he violated every law enacted for the security of the Protestant religion; and then, unable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> the resentment of his injured subjects, he fled like a coward, instead of disarming their rage by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of his Popish ministers and priests. He rather chose to live and die a bigot, or, as he believed, a saint, than to support the dignity of his ancestors, or perish beneath the ruins of his throne. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was the revolution in 1689. James II. died in France in 1710, aged 68. He wrote <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of his own life and campaigns to the restoration; the original of which is preserved in the Scotch college at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. This piece is printed at the end of Ramsay's life of Marshal Turenne. 2. Memoirs of the English affairs, chiefly naval, from the year 1660 to 1673. 3. The royal sufferer, King James II. consisting of meditations, folliques, vows, &c. said to be composed by his majesty at St Germain. 4. Three letters; which were published by William Fuller, gent. in 1702, with other papers relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of St Germain, and are said in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> page to be printed by command. James, Thomas, a learned English critic and divine, born about the year 1571. He recommended himself to the office of keeper of the public library at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, by the arduous undertaking of publishing a catalogue of the MSS in each college library at both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. He was elected to this office in 1602, and held it 18 years, when he resigned it to prosecute his studies with more freedom. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> held with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> at Oxford in 1625, of which he was a member, he moved to have proper commissioners appointed to collate the MSS of the fathers in all the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in England, with the Popish editions, in order to detect the forgeries in the latter; but this proposal not meeting with the desired encouragement, he engaged in the laborious task himself, which he continued until his death in 1629. He left behind him a great number of learned works. James, Richard, nephew of the former, entered into orders in 1615; but, being a man of humour, of three sermons preached before the university, one concerning the observation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> was without a text, according to the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manner; another against the text; and the third beside it. About the year 1619, he travelled through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, Scotland, Shetland, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> and Russia, of which he wrote observations. He assisted Selden in composing his Marmora Arundeliana; and was very serviceable to Sir Robert Cotton, and his son Sir Thomas, in defining and settling their noble library. He died in 1683; and has an extraordinary character given him by Wood for learning and abilities. James, Dr Robert, an English physician of great eminence, and particularly distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of a most excellent fever-powder, was born at Kinverton in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, A.D. 1723; his father a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, his mother a sister of Sir Robert Clarke. He was of St John's college in Oxford, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of A.B. and afterwards practised physic at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>, Lichfield, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> successively. Then he removed to London, and became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICENTIATE">licentiate</a> in the college of physicians; but in what years is not known. At London he applied himself to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> as well as practising physic; and in 1743, published a Medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, in 3 vols folio. Soon after he published an English translation, with a supplement by himself, of Ramazzini de morbis aris- cum; to which he also prefixed a piece of Frederic Hoffman upon Endemical Distempers, 8vo. In 1746, The Practice of Physic, 2 vols 8vo; in 1760, On Canine Madness, 8vo; in 1764, A Diffenatory, 8vo. June 25, 1755, when the king was at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, James was admitted by mandamus to the doctorship of physic. In 1788, were published, A Dissertation upon Fevers, and A Vindication of the Fever-powder, 8vo; with A Short Treatise on the Disorders of Children, and a very good print of Dr James. This was the 8th edition of the Dissertation, of which the first was printed in 1751; and the purpose of it was, to set forth the success of this powder, as well as to describe more particularly the manner of administering it. The Vindication was posthumous and unfinished; for he died March 23, 1776, while he was employed upon it.—Dr James was married, and left several sons and daughters. James's Powder, a medicine prepared by Robert James, which is known also by the name of James's fever powder. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. James's Town, a borough and market town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEITRIM">Leitrim</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Connaught; situated five miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRICK">Carrick</a>, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a>, and 73 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, in N. Lat. 53° 44'. W. Long. 8° 15'. It has a barrack for a company of foot, and returns two members to parliament; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> in the family of King.—It has three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. St James's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, a festival of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, observed on the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of St James the greater, son of Zebedee. Epistle of St James, a canonical book of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, being the fifth of the catholic or general epistles; which are so called, as not being written to one but to several Christian churches. This general epistle is addressed partly to the believing and partly to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a> Jews; and is designed to correct the errors, soften the ungoverned zeal, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the indecent behaviour of the latter; and to comfort the former under the great hardships they then did, or shortly were to suffer, for the sake of Christianity. Jamesone, George, an excellent painter, justly termed the Van Dyck of Scotland, was the son of Andrew Jameone, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>; and was born at Aberdeen, in 1586. He studied under Rubens, at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>; and, after his return, applied with indefatigable industry to portraits in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, though he sometimes practised practised in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>, and also in history and landscapes. His largest portraits were somewhat less than life. His earliest works were chiefly on board, afterwards on fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth smoothly primed with a proper tone to help the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of his shadows. His excellence is said to consist in delicacy and softness, with a clear and beautiful colouring; his shades not <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>, but helped by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>, with little appearance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>. When King Charles I visited Scotland in 1633, the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, knowing his majesty's taste, employed this art to make drawings of the Scottish monarchs; with which the king was so pleased, that, encouraging the painter, he sat to him, and rewarded him with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> from his own finger. It is observable, that Jamyn always drew himself with his hat on, either in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of his master Rubens, or on having been indulged in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> by the king when he sat to him. Many of Jamyn's works are in both the colleges of Aberdeen; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIBYLS">Sibyls</a> there he is said to have drawn from living beauties in that city. His best works are from the year 1630 to his death, which happened at Edinburgh in 1644.

JAMYN

Pages 37-37

AMADIS, a celebrated French poet in the 16th century. He is esteemed the rival of Ronsard, who was his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> and friend. He was secretary and chamber-reader in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX. and died about 1585. He wrote, 1. Poetical works, two vols. 2. Philosophical discourses to Paficarhis and Rodanthe, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> academical discourses. 3. A translation of the Iliad of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, begun by Hugh Sabel, and finished by Jamyn; with a translation into French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of the three first books of the Odyssey. JANE of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, a remarkable lady, who seems to have possessed in her own person all the excellent qualities of both sexes, was the wife of John de Mountfort, a competitor for the dukedom of Brittany upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of John III. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, dying without issue, left his dominions to his niece Jane, married to Charles de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a> nephew to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France; but John de Mountfort, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the late duke though by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, claimed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, and was received as successor by the people of Nantes. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> swore fealty to Charles de Blois, thinking him best supported. This dispute occasioned a civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; in the course of which John was taken prisoner, and sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. This misfortune would have entirely ruined his party, had not his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> been supported by the extraordinary abilities of his wife, Jane of Flanders. Bold, daring, and intrepid, she fought like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> in the field; shrewd, sensible, and sagacious, she spoke like a politician in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; and endowed with the most amiable manners and winning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, she was able to move the minds of her subjects by the force of her eloquence, and mould them exactly according to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. She happened to be at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RENNES">Rennes</a> when she received the news of her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>; but that disaster, instead of depressing her spirits, served only to raise her native courage and fortitude. She forthwith assembled the citizens; and, holding in her arms her infant son, recommended him to their care and protection in the most pathetic terms, as the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> heir of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dukes, who had always governed them with lenity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, and to whom they had ever professed the most zealous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>. She declared herself willing to run all hazards with them in Jane's cause; pointed out the resources that still remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> of England; earnestly beseeching them to make one vigorous effort against an usurper, who being forced upon them by the intrigues of France, would, as a mark of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, sacrifice the liberties of Brittany to his protector. The people moved by the affecting appearance, and animated by the noble conduct of the princess, vowed to live and die with her in defending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of her family; and their example was followed by almost all the Bretons. The countess went from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, encouraging the garrisons of the several fortresses, and providing them with every thing necessary for their subsistence; after which she shut herself up with her son in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HENNEBON">Hennebon</a>, where she resolved to wait for the succours which the king of England (Edward III.) had promised to send to her assistance. Charles de Blois, accompanied by the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>, and many other noblemen, took the field with a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and having reduced Rennes, laid siege to Hennebon, which was defended by the countess in person. This heroine repulsed the assailants in all their attacks with the most undaunted courage; and observing one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> that their whole army had left the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> to join in a general storm, she rushed forth at a postern-gate, with three hundred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, set fire to their tents and baggage, killed their tutors and servants, and raised such a terror and consternation through all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, that the enemy gave over their assault, and getting betwixt her and the walls, endeavoured to cut off her retreat to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Thus intercepted, she put the spurs to her horse, and without halting, galloped directly to Brest, which lay at the distance of two-and-twenty miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. There being supplied with a body of five hundred horse, she immediately returned, and fighting her way through one part of the French camp, was received into Hennebon, amidst the acclamations of the people. Soon after this the English succours appeared, and obliged the enemy to raise the siege.

JANEIRO

Pages 37-37
or RIO-JANEIRO, a river and province of Brazil in South America, seated between the tropic of Capricorn and 22° of S. Lat. See RIO-JANEIRO.

JANICULUM

Pages 37-37
or JANICULARIS, a hill of ancient Rome, added by Ancus Martius; the burial place of Numa, and of Statius Cecilius the poet; to the east and south, having the Tiber; to the west, the fields; to the north, a part of the Vatican. So called, either from an ancient city, (Virgil;) or because it was a jama, or gate, from which to issue out and make incursions on the Tuscani, (Verrius Flaccus.) Now called Mons Aureus, corruptly Montesaurus, from its sparkling sands. From this hill, on account of its height, is the most extensive prospect of Rome: but it is least inhabited, because of its gloomy air; neither is it reckoned among the seven hills. Hither the people retired, and were hence afterwards recalled by Q. Hortensius the dictator, (Pliny.)

JANIZARIES

Pages 37-39

an order of infantry in the Turkish armies; reputed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> seignior's foot-guards. Vossius derives the word from genosvera, which in the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies new homines <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> militae. D'Herbelot tell us, that janizarii signifies a new band, or troop; and that the name was first given by Amurath. Janizaries, rath I. called the Conqueror, who choosing out one-fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Christian prisoners whom he had taken from the Greeks, and instructing them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and the doctrines of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, sent them to Hagi Bekta sche (a person whose pretended piety rendered him extremely revered among the Turks), to the end that he might confer his blessing on them, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> give them some mark to distinguish them from the rest of the troops.—Bekta sche, after blessing them in his manner, cut off one of the sleeves of the fur-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> which he had on, and put it on the head of the leader of this new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>; from which time, viz. the year of Christ 1361, they have still retained the name jenicheri, and the fur-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. As, in the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the European troops are distinguished from those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; the janizaries are also distinguished into janizaries of Constantinople, and of Damascus. Their pay is from two aspers to twelve per diem; for when they have a child, or do any signal piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, their pay is augmented.—Their dress consists of a dolman, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> gown, with short sleeves, which is given them annually by the grand seignior on the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of Ramazan. They wear no turbeau; but, in lieu of that, a kind of cap, which they call zarcola, and a long hood of the same stuff hanging on their shoulders. On solemn days they are adorned with feathers, which are stuck in a little cage on the fore part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a>.—Their arms, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in time of war, are a sabre, a carbine or musket, and a cartouch-box hanging on the left side. At Constantinople, in time of peace, they wear only a long <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. In Asia, where powder and firearms are more uncommon, they wear a bow and arrows, with a poignard, which they call lianiere.—Though the janizaries are not prohibited <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, yet they rarely marry, nor then but with the consent of their officers; as imagining a married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to make a worse soldier than a bachelor.—It was Ofman, or Ottoman, or, as others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, Amurath, who first instituted the order of janizaries. They were at first called jaja, that is, footmen, to distinguish them from the other Turks, the troops whereof consisted mostly of cavalry. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of janizaries is generally above 40,000; divided into 162 companies or chambers called odas, in which they live together at Constantinople as in a convent. They are of a superior <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> to all other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and are also more arrogant and factious, and it is by them that the public tranquillity is mostly disturbed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> may therefore be said to be in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the janizaries. They have, however, some good qualities: they are employed to escort travellers, and especially ambassadors and persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rank, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, they behave with the utmost zeal and fidelity. Janizaries, at Rome, are officers or pensioners of the pope, called also participantes, on account of certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> or duties which they enjoy in the annates, bulls, or expeditions, and the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>.—Most authors are mistaken in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their office: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, they are officers of the third <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the Roman chancery. The first bench consists of writers, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of abbreviators, and the third of janizaries; who are a kind of correctors and revisors of the pope's bulls. Jansen, Cornelius, bishop of Ypres, one of the most learned divines of the 17th century, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> called from his name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JANSENISTS">Jansenists</a>. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> of Catholic parents, and studied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>. Being sent to foment some bufaloes of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> relating to the university, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, viewing with a jealous eye the intriguing policy of France, engaged him to write a book to expose the French to the pope as no good Catholics, since they made no scruple of forming alliances with Protestant states. Jansen performed this task in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> Gallicus; and was rewarded with a mitre, being promoted to the see of Ypres in 1635. He had, among other writings, before this, maintained a controversy against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a>; but his Augustinus was the principal labour of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, on which he spent above 20 years. See the next article. Jansenists, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a sect of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> in France, who followed the opinions of Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Louvain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>, in relation to grace and predestination. In the year 1640, the two universities <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, and particularly Father Molina and Father Leonard Cellius, thought fit to condemn the opinions of the Jesuits on grace and free-will. This having set the controversy on foot, Jansenius opposed to the doctrine of the Jesuits the sentiments of St Augustine; and wrote a treatise on grace, which he entitled Augustinus. This treatise was attacked by the Jesuits, who accused Jansenius of maintaining dangerous and heretical opinions; and afterwards, in 1642, obtained of Pope Urban VIII. a formal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of the treatise written by Jansenius: when the partizans of Jansenius gave out that this bull was spurious, and composed by a person entirely devoted to the Jesuits. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Urban VIII., the affair of Jansenius began to be more warmly controverted, and gave birth to an infinite number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a> writings concerning grace. And what occasioned some mirth, was the titles which each party gave to their writings; one writer published The torch of St Augustine, another found Snuffers for St Augustine's torch, and Father Veron formed Agag for the Jansenists, &c. In the year 1650, 68 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of France subscribed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Pope Innocent X. to obtain an inquiry into and condemnation of the five following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, extracted from Jansenius's Augustinus: 1. Some of God's commandments are impossible to be observed by the righteous, even though they endeavour with all their power to accomplish them. 2. In the state of corrupted nature, we are incapable of resisting inward grace. 3. Merit and demerit, in a state of corrupted nature, does not depend on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> which excludes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, but on a liberty which excludes constraint. 4. The Semipelagians admitted the necessity of an inward preventing grace for the performance of each particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, even for the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>: but they were heretics in maintaining that this grace was of such a nature, that the will of man was able either to resist or obey it. It is Semipelagianism to say, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ died, or shed his blood, for all mankind in general. In the year 1652, the pope appointed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> for examining into the dispute in relation to grace. In this congregation Jansenius was condemned; and the Janssens, the bull of condemnation, published in May 1653, filled all the pulpits in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> with violent outcries and alarms against the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> of the Jansenists. In the year 1656, Pope Alexander VII issued another bull, in which he condemned the five propositions of Janfe- nus. However, the Jansenists affirm, that these propo- sitions are not to be found in this book; but that some of his enemies having caused them to be printed on a sheet, inserted them in the book, and thereby de- ceived the pope. At last Clement XI put an end to the di- pute by his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 17, 1705, in which, after having recited the constitutions of his predeces- sors in relation to this affair, he declares, "That in order to pay a proper obedience to the papal constitu- tions concerning the present question, it is necessary to receive them with a respectful silence." The clergy of Paris, the same year, approved and accepted this bull, and none dared to oppose it. This is the famous bull Unigenitus, so called from its beginning with the words Unigenitus Dei Filius, &c., which has occasioned so much confusion in France.

JANSSEN

Pages 39-40

Cornelius, called Johnson, an eminent paint- er of portraits, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> (though in the Chronological tables, and in Sandrart, it is im- properly asserted that he was born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>), and he resided in England for several years; where he was engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. and painted several excellent portraits of that monarch, as also of his children and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. He had not the freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, nor the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of Vandyck; but in other respects he was accounted his equal, and in the finishing his pictures superior. His paintings are easily distinguished by their smooth, clear, and delicate tints, and by that character of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with which they are strongly marked. He generally painted on board; and, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, his draperies are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; probably because the opposition of that tint made his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> colours appear more beauti- fully bright, especially in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> figures. It is said that he used a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ULTRAMARINE">ultramarine</a> in the black colours, as well as in his carnations; which may be one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cause of their preserving their original lustre even to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Frequently he painted in a small size in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and often copied his own works in that manner. His fame began to be somewhat obscured, on the ar- rival of Vandyck in England; and the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>- ing out some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, induced him to return to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where his paintings were in the highest esteem. He died in 1685. Sr JANUARIUS, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> saint of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, where his head is occasionally carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, in order to stay the eruption of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>. The lique- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> of his blood is a famous miracle at Naples. The saint suffered martyrdom about the end of the third century. When he was beheaded, a pious lady of Naples caught about an ounce of his blood, which has been carefully preserved in a bottle ever since, without having lost a single grain of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. This of itself, were it equally demonstrable, might be con- sidered as a greater miracle than the circumstance on which the Neapolitans lay the whole stress, viz., that the blood which has congealed, and acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> form. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> and February were introduced into the year by Numa Pompilius; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>'s year beginning in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> first day of this month, was under the protection of Juno, and in a peculiar manner consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> by an offering of a cake made of new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> and new <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, with new frankincense and new wine. On the first day of January a beginning was made of every intended <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the consuls elect took possession of their office, who, with the flamens, offered sacrifices and prayers for the prosperity of the empire. On this day all animosities were suspended, and friends gave and received new year's gifts, called Strene. On this day too the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> above all things took care to be merry and divert themselves, and oftentimes such a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a> was exhibited, that they might with propriety enough have distinguished it with the name of All-fools day. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> heretofore faltered on the first day of January, by way of opposition to the superstitions and debaucheries of the heathens.

JANSSENS

Pages 39-39

Victor Honorius, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> in 1664, and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of one Volders, under whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years; in which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he gave many proofs of a genius far superior to those who were instructed in the same school. He afterwards went to Rome, where he attended par- ticularly the works of Raphael; he designed after the antiques, and sketched the beautiful scenes around that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and in a short time his paintings rose in esteem, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of Rome were desirous to employ him. He associated with Tempesta, the cele- brated landscape-painter, for several years, and painted the figures in the works of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as they resided together. Janssens composed historical subjects, both in a small and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> size; but he found the demand for his small pictures so considerable, that he was induced to paint most frequently in that size. During 11 years he continued at Rome, which barely sufficed for his finishing those pictures for which he was engaged; nor could he have even then been at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, had he not limited himself to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and determined not to un- dertake more.—Returning to Brussels, his performances were as much admired there as they had before been in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; but having married, and gradually become the father of 11 children, he was compelled to change his manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in small, and to undertake only those of the large kind, as being more lucrative, more expeditious, and also more agreeable to his gen- ius and inclination. He adorned most of the churches and palaces of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with his compositions. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> was fruitful; he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>- ed correctly, his colouring is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and pleasing, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> free, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of his heads have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and elegance. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between his large and small paintings, it is observed, that in correctness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> they had an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of merit; but the co- louring of the former appears more raw and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> than the colouring of the latter; and it is agreed, that for small historical pictures, he was preferable to all the painters of his time.

JANUS

Pages 40-40

in the heathen worship, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, who, it is said, received <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> into his dominions, after his being driven from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. He tempered the manners of his subjects, and taught them civility; and from him they learned to improve the vine, to sow corn, and to make <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he was adored as a god. This deity was thought to preside over all new undertakings. Hence, in all sacrifices, the first libations of wine and wheat were offered to Janus, all prayers prefaced with a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to him; and the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the year was dedicated to and named from him. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">JANUARY</a>. Janus was represented with two faces, either to denote his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that he views at once the past and approaching years; he had a sceptre in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> in his left, to signify his extensive authority, and his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of locks. Though this is properly a Roman deity, the abbé la Pluche represents it as derived from the Egyptians, who made known the rising of the dog-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>, which opened their solar year, with an image with a key in its hand, and two faces, one old and the other young, to typify the old and new year. Temple of Janus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> at Rome (as some say) of entire <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, erected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, and so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as to contain a statue of Janus five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, with brazen gates on each side, which were always kept open in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and shut in time of peace. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were so much engaged in war, that this temple was shut only twice from the foundation of Rome till the reign of Augustus, and six times afterwards. It was first shut during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> reign of Numa, who instituted this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. 2. In the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> 519, after the end of the first Punic war. 3. By Augustus after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>, in the year of Rome 725. 4. On Augustus's return from the war which he had against the Cantabrians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the year of Rome 729. 5. Under the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, in 744, about five years before the birth of Christ, when there was a general peace throughout the whole Roman empire, which lasted 12 years. 6. Under Nero, 811. 7. Under Vespasian, 824. 8. Under Constantius, when, upon Magnentius's death, he was left sole possessor of the empire, 1105. Some dispute the authority...

JAPAN

Pages 40-48

a general name for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> lying between the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and the western coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and which all together form a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and powerful empire. They extend from the 30th to the 41st <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and from the 130th to the 147th of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. Were South and North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> divided by an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, Japan might be most aptly compared to England, Scotland, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, with their respective smaller islands, peninsulas, bays, channels, &c., all under the same monarch. The Europeans call the empire Japan; but the inhabitants Nippon, from the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> belonging to it; and the Chinese Cipbon, probably on account of its eastern situation; these names signifying, in both languages, the Basis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Foundation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>. It was first discovered by the Portuguese about the year of Christ 1542. Most of the islands which compose it are surrounded with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> craggy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and such shallow and boisterous seas, that failing about them is extremely dangerous; and the creeks and bays are choked up with such rocks, shelves, and sands, that it looks as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> had designed it to be a kind of little world by itself. These seas have likewise many dangerous whirlpools, which are very difficult to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> suck in and swallow up the largest vessels, and all that comes within the reach of their vortex, dashing them against the rocks at the bottom; inasmuch that some of them are never seen again, and others thrown upon the surface at some miles distance. Some of these whirlpools also make a noise terrible to hear. The Chinese pretend that the Japan islands were first peopled by themselves; but it is more probable that the original inhabitants were a mixture of different nations, driven thither by those tempestuous seas, at different times. As these islands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the fifth and sixth climates, they would be much hotter in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> than England, were not the heats refreshed by the winds which continually blow from the sea around them, and to which they are much exposed by the height of their situation: this circumstance, however, not only renders their winters excessively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but the seasons more inclement. They have great falls of snow in winter, which are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> followed by hard frosts. The rains in summer are very violent, especially in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, which on that account are called satuki, or water-months. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is also much subject to dreadful thunders and lightnings, as well as storms and hurricanes, which frequently do a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of damage. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, though naturally barren and mountainous, by the industry of the inhabitants, not only supplies them with every necessary of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, but also furnishes other countries with them; producing, besides corn, the finest and whitest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and other grains, with a great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and vast numbers of cattle of all sorts. Besides rice, and a sort of wheat and barley, with two sorts of beans, they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> wheat, millet, and several other kinds in great abundance. Their seas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, abound with fish; and their mountains, woods, and forests, are well stocked with horses, elephants, deer, oxen, buffaloes, sheep, hogs, and other useful animals. Some of their mountains also are enriched with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, exquisitely fine, besides tin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and various other minerals and fossils; whilst others abound with several sorts of marble and precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Of these mountains, some may be justly ranked among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rarities of this country; one, in particular, in the great island of Nippon, is of such prodigious height as to be easily seen forty leagues off at sea, though its distance from the shore is about eighteen. Some authors think it exceeds the famous Peak of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>; but it may rather be called a clutter or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of mountains, among which are no less than eight dreadful volcanoes, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> with incredible fury, and often laying waste the country round about them; but, to make some amends, they afford great variety of medicinal waters, of different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; one of these, mentioned by Varenius, is said to be as hot as burning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and to torch and consume everything thrown into it. The many brooks and rivers that have their sources among the mountains, form a great number of delightful cascades, as well as some dreadful cataracts. Among the great variety of trees in the forests here, the cedars exceed all of that kind through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, for straightness, height, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. They abound in most of the islands, especially the largest. Their seas, besides fish, furnish them with great quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> coral, and some pearls of great value, besides a variety of sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and shells; which last are not inferior to those that are brought from Ambon, the Molucca and other eastern islands.
