The vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sulphur with which most of the Japan islands abounds, makes them subject to frequent and dreadful earthquakes. The inhabitants are so accustomed to them, that they are scarcely alarmed at any, unless they chance to be very terrible indeed, and lay whole <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in ruins, which very often proves the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. On these occasions, they have recourse to extraordinary sacrifices, and acts of worship, to their deities or demons, according to the different notions of each fact, and sometimes even proceed to offer <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> victims; but in this case they only take some of the vilest and most abandoned fellows they can meet with, because they are only sacrificed to the malevolent deities. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> throughout Japan, it is well known, is Pagan, split into several sects, who live together in the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> has its own temple and priests. The spiritual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, the Dairi, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of their religion. They acknowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> a Supreme Being. The author of this relation (Dr Thunberg) <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of the God of gods of a majestic height. The idol that represented this god was of gilded wood, and of so prodigious a size, that upon his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> six persons might fit in the Japanese fashion; his shoulders were five toises <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. In the other temple, the infinite power of this god was represented by little gods to the number of 33,333; all standing round the great idol that represented God. The priests, who are numerous in every temple, have nothing to do but to clean the pavement, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> the lamps, and dress the idol with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. The temples are open to everybody, even to the Hollanders; and in case they are in want of a lodging in the suburbs, when they go to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Jeddo, they are entertained with hospitality in these temples. The Roman Catholic religion had once made a considerable progress in this country, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a mission conducted by the Portuguese and Spanish Jesuits; among whom the famous Saint Francis Xavier was employed, but soon relinquished the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. There were also some Franciscan friars of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> engaged at last. The Jesuits and friars were supplied from Goa, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACAO">Macao</a>, and the Manilhas. At first the undertaking proceeded with the most rapid success, but ended at last in the most tragic manner, all owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and haughtiness, the misconduct, rapacity, and tenacity of extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of the fathers against the state. This folly and madness produced a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of 40 years <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, terminated by a most horrible and bloody massacre, not to be paralleled in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. After this the Portuguese, as likewise the Christian religion, were totally expelled the country, and the most effectual means taken for preventing their return. The natives are for this purpose prohibited from going out of the country; and all foreigners are excluded from an open and free trade; for as to the Dutch and Chinese, under which last name some other eastern nations go thither, they are shut up whilst they remain there, and a most strict watch is kept upon them, inasmuch that they are no better than prisoners; and the Dutch, it is said, to obtain a privilege even so far, declared themselves to be no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, but Dutchmen. This calumny, however, Dr Kempfer has endeavoured to wipe off, but not altogether to satisfaction. It was about the year of Christ 1549, or six years after the first discovery, that the fathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> arrived there, being induced by the favourable representations of a young Japanese who had fled to Goa. Till the year 1625, or near 1630, the Christian religion spread through most of the provinces of the empire, many of the princes and lords openly embracing it; and "there was very good reason to hope, that within a short compass of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the whole empire would have been converted to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of our Saviour, had not the ambitious views, and the impatient endeavours of the fathers to reap the temporal as well as the spiritual fruits of their care and labour, so provoked the supreme majesty of the empire as to raise against themselves and their converts a persecution which hath not its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> in history, whereby the religion they preached, and all those that professed it, were in a few years time entirely exterminated."—The fathers had made a progress so great, that the princes of Bungu, Arima, and Omura who had been baptized, "sent, in the year 1582, some of their nearest relations, with letters and presents to pay homage to the then pope, Gregory XIII, and to assure his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> submission to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; an account of which most celebrated embassy hath been given in the works of that incomparable historian Thuanus, and by many other Roman catholic writers." But notwithstanding this pleasing prospect, the emperor, anno 1586, issued proclamations for the suppression of the religion, and the persecution began. This, however, at first had not that effect which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> expected; for though, according to the letters of the Jesuits, 20,570 persons suffered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for the faith of Christ in the year 1590 only, yet in 1591 and 1592, when all the churches were actually shut up, they made 12,000 new converts. The business was finally concluded by the massacre at Simabara, about the year 1640. The reasons of the emperor's proclamations, making it death to embrace the religion, were as follow: 1. The new religion occasioned considerable alterations in the Japanese church, and was prejudicial in the highest degree to the heathen clergy. 2. It was feared the innovation in religion might be attended with fatal consequences even in regard to the sick; but what more immediately gave rise to them was, as the Japanese of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> confessed to Dr Kempfer, pride and covetousness; pride among the great ones, and covetousness in people of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>; the spiritual fathers aiming not only at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of their souls, but having an eye also to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and lands, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> disposing of their goods in the most furious and unreasonable manner. To confine ourselves to the clergy here: they "thought it beneath their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to walk on foot any longer; nothing would serve them but they must be carried about in stately chairs, mimicking the pomp of the pope and his cardinals at Rome. They not only put themselves on an equal footing with the greatest men of the empire, but, swelled with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> pride, fancied that even a superior <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> was nothing but their due. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> happened, that a Portuguese bishop met upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> one of the counsellors of state on his way to court. The haughty prelate would not order his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> to be stopped, in order to alight and to pay his respects to the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, as is usual in that country; but without taking any notice of him, nay, indeed without showing him so much as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> marks of civility, he very contemptuously bid his men carry him by. The great man, exasperated to so signal an affront, thenceforward bore a mortal hatred to the Portuguese, and, in the height of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> resentment, made his complaint to the emperor himself, with such an odious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the insolence, pride, and vanity of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, as he expected could not but raise the emperor's utmost indignation." This happened in 1566. The next year the persecution began anew, and 26 persons, of the number whereof were two foreign Jesuits, and several other fathers of the Franciscan order, were executed on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. The emperor Jijoas had usurped the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his pupil Tidajori, who, as likewise the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his court and party, had been either Christians themselves, elves, or at least very favourably inclined to that religion; so that reasons of state mightily co-operated to forward the persecution. Some Franciscan friars, whom the governor of the Manilhas had sent as his ambassadors to the emperor of Japan were guilty at this time of a most imprudent step: they, during the whole time of their abode in the country, preached openly in the streets of Macao where they resided; and of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> built a church, contrary to the imperial commands, and contrary to the advice and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> solicitations of the Jesuits. Some time after, a discovery of a dangerous conspiracy, which the fathers, and the yet remaining adepts of their religion, entered into against the person of the emperor as a heathen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, put a finishing stroke to the affair, and hastened the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> which was pronounced soon after, that the Portuguese should for ever be banished the emperor's dominions; for till then the state seemed disposed to spare the merchants and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> persons, for the purpose of continuing trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with them, which was looked upon as an affair independent of religion. The affair of the conspiracy was as follows: the Dutch had had an eye to the trade of Japan before 1602, and in 1611 had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of a free commerce granted them by the imperial letters patent, and had actually a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> at Firando. The Dutch were then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Spain, which was then sovereign of the Portuguese dominions; so that it was natural for them to be trying to supplant them. The Portuguese, on their parts, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all malicious inventions to blacken their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, calling them rebels and pirates, whence it was natural for the Dutch to endeavour to clear, and even to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, themselves. Now they "took an homeward-bound Portuguese ship near the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, on board of which they found some traitorous letters to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, written by one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Moro, who was chief of the Portuguese in Japan, himself a Japanese by birth, and a great zealot for the Christian religion. The Dutch took special care to deliver the said letters to their protector the prince of Firando, who communicated them without loss of time to the governor of Nagasaki, a great friend to the Portuguese. Captain Moro having been taken up, boldly, and with great assurance, denied the fact, and so did all the Portuguese then at Nagasaki. However, neither the governor's favour, nor their constant denial, were able to clear them, and to keep off the cloud which was ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> over their heads. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">Hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> convinced them; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was sent up to court, and Captain Moro sentenced to be burnt alive on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, which was executed accordingly. This letter laid open the whole plot which the Japanese Christians, in conjunction with the Portuguese, had laid against the emperor's life and throne; the want they stood in of ships and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, which were promised them from Portugal; the names of the Japanese princes concerned in the conspiracy; and lastly, to crown all, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the papal blessing. This discovery made by the Dutch was afterwards confirmed by another letter written by the said Captain Moro to the Portuguese government at Macao, which was intercepted and brought to Japan by a Japanese ship." Considering this, and the suspicions which the court had then already conceived against the Portuguese, it was no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> thoroughly to ruin the little credit and favour they had as yet been able to preserve; and the rather, since the strict imperial orders notwithstanding, they did not leave off privately to bring over more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>. Accordingly, in the year 1637, an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was sent to the governors of Nagasaki, with orders to see it put in execution. It was then that the empire of Japan was shut for ever both to foreigners and natives. Now, although the governors of Nagasaki, on receipt of these commands, took care they should be obeyed, yet the directors of the Portuguese trade maintained themselves in Japan two years longer, hoping to obtain leave to stay in the island of Delima, and there to continue their trade. But they found themselves at last wholly disappointed; for the emperor was resolved to get rid of them; and on assurance given him by the Dutch East India <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> that they would supply for the future what commodities had been imported by the Portuguese, he declared the Portuguese and the Castilians, and whoever belonged to them, enemies of the empire, forbidding the importation of even the goods of their country, Spanish wines only excepted, for the use of the court. And thus the Portuguese lost their profitable trade and commerce with Japan, and were totally expelled the country before the latter end of the year 1639 or 1640; and thus ended the fruitless popish mission in this empire, for the Portuguese have never been able to restore themselves; and the Dutch have it not in their power to do any one thing in favour of religion, were they so inclined; but, as it appears, they are very indifferent as to that, and are in but little credit with the Japanese. According to Dr Thunberg's researches, the Japanese have never been subdued by any foreign power, not even in the most remote periods; their chronicles contain such accounts of their valour, as one would rather incline to consider as fabulous inventions than actual occurrences, if later ages had not furnished equally striking proofs of it. When the Tartars, for the first time in 792, had overrun part of Japan, and when, after a considerable time had elapsed, their fleet was destroyed by a violent storm in the course of a single night, the Japanese general attacked, and so totally defeated his numerous and brave enemies, that not a single person survived to return and carry the tidings of such an unparalleled defeat. In like manner, when the Japanese were again, in 1281, invaded by the warlike Tartars, to the number of 240,000 fighting men, they gained a victory equally complete. The extirpation of the Portuguese, and with them of the Christian religion, towards the beginning of the 17th century, as already mentioned, was so complete, that scarce a vestige can now be discerned of its ever having existed there. With respect to the government of these islands, it is and has been for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time monarchical; though formerly it seems to have been split into a great number of petty kingdoms, which were at length all swallowed by one. The imperial dignity had been enjoyed for a considerable time before the year 1500, by a regular succession of princes, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of daimios, a name supposed to have been derived from Dairo the head of that family. Soon after that epoch, such a dreadful civil war broke out, and lasted so many years, that the empire was quite ruined. During these distractions and confusions, a common fol- Japan, died, by name Tayckoy, a person of obscure birth, but of an enterprising genius, found means to raise himself to the imperial dignity; having, in little more than three years time, by an uncommon share of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, subdued all his competitors and opponents and reduced all their cities and castles. The dairo not being in a condition to obstruct or put a stop to his progress, was forced to submit to his terms; and might perhaps have been condemned to much harder, had not Tayckoy been apprehensive lest his soldiers, who still revered their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> natural monarch, should have revolted in his favour. To prevent this, he granted him the supreme power in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> matters, with great privileges, honours, and revenues annexed to it; whilst himself remained invested with the whole civil and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> power, and was acknowledged and proclaimed king of Japan. This great revolution happened in 1517, and Tayckoy reigned several years with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and tranquillity; during which he made many wholesome laws and regulations, which still subsist, and are much admired to this day. At his death, he left the crown to his son Tayckofama, then a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>; but the treacherous prince under whose guardianship he was left deprived him of his life before he came of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. By this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, the crown passed to the family of Jejafama, in which it still continues. Tayckoy and his successors have contented themselves with the title of cubo, which, under the dairos, was that of prime minister, whose office is now supprested; so that the cubo, in all secular concerns, is quite as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and despotic, and has as extensive a power over the lives and fortunes of all his subjects, from the petty kings <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the lowest persons, as ever the dairos had. The dairo resides constantly at Meaco, and the cubo at Jeddo. The inhabitants of Japan are well-grown, agile, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and at the same time stout-limbed, though they do not equal in strength the northern inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> is commonly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; which sometimes varies to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and sometimes to white. The inferior fort, who during their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in summer have often the upper parts of the body naked, are sun-burnt and brown; women of distinction, who never go uncovered into the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, are perfectly white. The national character, consists in intelligence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, frankness, obedience, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, good-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and civility, curiosity, industry, and dexterity, economy and sobriety, hardiness, cleanliness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and uprightness, honesty and fidelity; in being also mistrustful, superstitious, haughty, resentful, brave and invincible. In all its transactions, the nation shows great intelligence, and can by no means be numbered among the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> and uncivilized, but rather is to be placed among the polished. The present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of government, admirable skill in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, sparing mode of life, way of trading with foreigners, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, &c., afford convincing proofs of their cunning, firmness, and intrepid courage. Here there are no appearances of that vanity so common among the Asiatics and Africans, of adorning themselves with shells, glass-beads, and polished metal plates: neither are they fond of the useless European ornaments of gold and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, jewels, &c., but are careful to provide themselves, from the productions of their own country, with neat clothes, well-tasted food, and good weapons. Their curiosity is excessive; nothing imported by the Europeans escapes it. They ask for information concerning every article, and their questions continue till they become wearisome. It is the physician, among the traders, that is alone regarded as learned, and particularly during the journey to court and the residence at Jeddo, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the empire, that he is regarded as the oracle, which they trust can give responses in all things, whether in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, physics, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, medicine, &c. Economy has its peculiar abode in Japan. It is a virtue admired as well in the emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> as in the meanest cottage. It makes those of small pretensions content with their little, and it prevents the abundance of the rich from overflowing in excess and voluptuousness. Hence it happens, that what in other countries is called scarcity and famine, is unknown here; and that, in so very populous a state, scarce a person in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, or a beggar, should be found. The names of families, and of single persons, are under very different regulations from ours. The family name is never changed, but is never used in ordinary conversation, and only when they sign some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; to which they also for the most part affix their seal. There is also this peculiarity, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> is always placed first; just as in botanical books the generic name is always placed before the specific name. The praenomen is always used in addressing a person; and it is changed several times in the course of life. A child receives at birth from its parents a name, which is retained till it has itself a son arrived at maturity. A person again changes his name when he is invested with any office; as also when he is advanced to a higher trust; some, as emperors and princes, acquire a new name after death. The names of women are less variable; they are in general borrowed from the most beautiful flowers. After <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the wife is confined to her own apartment, from whence she hardly ever flirts, except once a-year to the funeral-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of her family; nor is she permitted to see any man, except perhaps some very near relation, and that as seldom as can be. The wives, as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and other parts of the east, bring no portion with them, but are rather bought by the husband of their parents and relations. The bridegroom most commonly sees his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> for the first time upon her being brought to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the nuptial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>: for in the temple where it is performed she is covered over with a veil, which reaches from the head to the feet. A husband can put his wives to a more or less severe death, if they give him the least cause of jealousy, by being seen barely to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with another man, or suffering one to come into their apartment. The dress of the Japanese deserves, more than that of any other people, the name of national; since they are not only different from that of all other men, but are also of the same form in all ranks, from the monarch to his meanest subject, as well as in both sexes; and what exceeds all credibility, they have not been altered for at least 2444 years. They universally consist of night-gowns, made long and wide, of which several veral are worn at once by all ranks and all ages. The more distinguished and the rich have them of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; the poorer sort of cotton. Those of the women reach down to the ground, and sometimes have a train; in the men, they reach down to the heels; travellers, soldiers, and labourers, either tuck them up, or wear them only down to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the men is generally of one colour; the women have theirs variegated and frequently with flowers of gold interwoven. In summer, they are either without lining, or have but a thin one; in winter they are stuffed to a great thickness with cotton or silk. The men seldom wear a great number; but the women thirty, fifty, or more, all so thin, that they scarce together amount to five pounds. The undermost serves for a shirt, and is therefore either white or blue, and for the most part thin and transparent. All these gowns are fastened round the waist with a belt, which in the men are about a hand's-breadth, in the women about a foot; of such a length that they go twice round the waist, and afterwards are tied in a knot with many ends and bows. The knot, particularly among the fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, is very conspicuous, and immediately informs the spectator whether they are married or not. The unmarried have it behind, on their back; the married before. In this belt the men fix their sabres, fans, pipe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and medicine boxes. In the neck the gowns are always cut round, without a collar; they therefore leave the neck bare; nor is it covered with cravat, cloth, or any thing else. The sleeves are always ill made, and out of all proportion wide; at the opening before, they are half sewed up, so that they form a sack, in which the hands can be put in cold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; they also serve for a pocket. Girls in particular have their sleeves so long that they reach down to the ground. Such is the simplicity of their habit, that they are soon dressed; and to undress, they need only open their girdle and draw in their arms. As the gowns, from their length, keep the thighs and legs warm, there is no occasion for stockings; nor do they use them in all the empire. Among poorer persons on a journey, and among soldiers, who have not such long gowns, one sees bulkins of cotton. Shoes, or, more properly speaking, flippers, are of all that is worn by the Japanese, the simplest, the meanest, and the most miserable, though in general used among high and low, rich and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. They are made of interwoven rice-straw; and sometimes, for persons of distinction, of reeds split very thin. They consist only of a sole, without upper leathers or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. Before, there palls over, transversely, a bow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, of a finger's breadth; from the point of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> to this bow goes a thin round band, which running within the great toe, serves to keep the shoe fixed to the foot. The shoe being without quarters, slides, during walking, like a flipper. Travellers have three bands of twisted straw, by which they fasten the shoe to the foot and leg, to prevent its falling off. The Japanese never enter their houses with shoes, but put them off in the entrance. This precaution is taken for the sake of their neat carpets. During the time the Dutch reside in Japan, as they have sometimes occasion to pay the natives visits in their houses, and as they have their own apartment at the factory covered with the same sort of carpets, they do not wear European shoes, but have in their stead red, green, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> slippers, which can easily be put off at entering in. They, however, wear stockings, with toes of cotton, fastened by buckles. These shoes are made in Japan, and may be washed whenever they become dirty. The way of dressing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is not less peculiar to this people, and less universally prevalent among them, than the use of their long gowns. The men shave the head from the forehead to the neck; and the hair remaining on the temples, and in the nape, is well befineared with oil, turned upwards, and then tied with a white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> thread, which is wrapped round several times. The ends of the hair beyond the head, are cut crofs-ways, about a finger's length being left. This part, after being patted together with oil, is bent in such a manner that the point is brought to the crown of the head; in which situation it is fixed by patting the same thread round it once. Women, except such as happen to be separated from their husbands, have no part of their head. The head is never covered with hat or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> in winter or in summer, except when they are on a journey; and then they use a conical hat, made of a sort of grass, and fixed with a ribband. Some travelling women, who are met with on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, have a bonnet like a shaving basin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> on the head, which is made of cloth, in which gold is interwoven. On other occasions, their naked heads are preferred, both from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and the sun, by umbrellas. Travellers, moreover, have a sort of riding-coat, made of thick paper oiled. They are worn by the upper servants of princes, and the suite of other travellers. Dr Thunberg and his fellow-travellers, during their journey to court, were obliged to provide such for their attendants when they passed through the place where they are made. A Japanese always has his arms painted on one or more of his garments, especially on the long and short gowns, on the sleeves, or between the shoulders; so that nobody can steal them; which otherwise might easily happen in a country where the clothes are so much alike in stuff, shape, and size. The weapons of the Japanese consist of a bow and arrows, sabre, halbert, and mukket. The bows are very large, and the arrows long, as in China. When the bows are to be bent and discharged, the troop always rests on one knee, which hinders them making a speedy discharge. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> the troops assemble to practice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> at a mark. Mukkets are not general; Dr Thunberg only saw them in the hands of persons of distinction, in a separated and elevated part of the audience room. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> is of the common length; but the stock is very short, and there is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> in the lock. The sabre is their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and best weapon, which is universally worn, except by the peasants. They are commonly a yard long, a little crooked, and thick in the back. The blades are of an incomparable goodness, and the old ones are in very high esteem. They are far superior to the Spanish blades so celebrated in Europe. A tolerably thick nail is easily cut in two without any damage to the edge; and a man, according to the account of the Japanese, may be clefled asunder. A separate faith is never used, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> is stuck in the belt, on the left side, with the edge upwards, which to a European appears ridiculous. All persons in office wear two such sabres, one of their own, and and the other the sword of office, as it is called; the latter is always the longer. Both are worn in the belt on the same side, and so disposed as to cross each other. When they are fitting, they have their sword of office laid on one side or before them. The sciences are very far from having arrived at the same height in Japan as in Europe. The history of the country is, notwithstanding, more authentic, perhaps, than that of any other country; and it is studied, without distinction, by all. Agriculture, which is considered as the art most necessary, and most conducive to the support and prosperity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, is nowhere in the world brought to such perfection as here; where neither civil nor foreign war, nor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a>, diminishes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>; and where a thought is never entertained, either of getting possession of other countries, or to import the useless and often hurtful productions of foreign lands; but where the utmost care is taken that no turf lies uncultivated, and no produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> unemployed. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> is pursued and respected; but the natives are unable, without the aid of Chinese, and sometimes of Dutch almanacks, to form a true <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, or calculate an eclipse of the sun or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> within minutes and seconds. Medicine has neither arrived, nor is it likely to arrive, at any degree of perfection. Anatomy is totally unknown; the knowledge of diseases imperfect, intricate, and often fabulous. Botany, and the knowledge of medicines, constitute the whole of their skill. They use only simples; and these generally in diuretic and diaphoretic decoctions. They are unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> medicines. Their physicians always indeed feel the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>; but they are very tedious, not quitting it for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; besides, they examine first one, and then the other arm, as if the blood was not driven by the same heart to both pulses. Besides those diseases which they have in common with other countries, or peculiar to themselves, the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> is very frequent, which they only understand how to alleviate by decoctions, thought to purify the blood. Salivation, which their physicians have heard mentioned by the Dutch surgeons, appears to them extremely formidable, both to conduct and to undergo; but they have lately learned the art of employing the sublime with much success.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">Jurisprudence</a> is not an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in Japan. No country has thinner <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, or fewer judges. Explanations of the law, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>, are things altogether unknown; but nowhere, perhaps, are the laws more certainly put in force, without respect to persons, without partiality or violence. They are very strict, and lawsuits very short. The Japanese know little more of physics or chemistry than what they have learned of late years of the Europeans. Their computation of time takes its rise from Min-o, or 660 years before Christ. The year is divided according to the changes of the moon; so that some years consist of twelve, and others of thirteen, months; and the beginning of the year falls out in February or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. They have no weeks consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days, or of six working days, and a holiday; but the first and fifteenth days of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> serve for holidays. On these days no work is done. On new-year's day they go round to wish one another a new year, with their whole families, clad in white and blue chequered, their holiday-dresses; and they rest almost the whole of the first month. The day is divided only into twelve hours; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> they are directed the whole year by the rising and setting of the sun. They reckon six o'clock at the rising, and five likewise at the setting of the sun. Mid-day and mid-night are always at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. Time is not measured by clocks or hour-glasses, but with burning matches, which are twisted together like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, and divided by knots. When the match is burnt to a knot, which indicates a certain portion of time elapsed, notice is given during the day, by striking the bells of the temples; and in the night, by the watchmen striking two boards against one another. A child is always reckoned a year old at the end of the year of his birth, whether this happen at the beginning or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. A few days after the beginning of the year, is performed the horrid ceremony of trampling on images representing the cross and the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> with her child. The images are of melted copper, and are said to be scarce a foot in height. This ceremony is intended to impress every individual with hatred of the Christian doctrine, and the Portuguese, who attempted to introduce it there; and also to discover whether there is any remnant of it left among the Japanese. It is performed in the places where the Christians chiefly resided. In Nagasaki it lasts four days; then the images are conveyed to the circumjacent places, and afterwards are laid aside against the next year. Every person, except the Japanese governor and his attendants, even the smallest child, must be present; but it is not true, as some have pretended, that the Dutch are also obliged to trample on the image. Overseers are appointed in every place, who assemble the people in companies in certain houses, call over the name of everyone in his turn, and take care that everything goes on properly. The children, not yet able to walk, have their feet placed upon it; older persons pass over it from one side of the room to the other. The Japanese are much addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, music, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>: the first is said to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> as to the style and imagery, loveliness, and cadence; but, like that of the Chinese, is not easily understood or relished by the Europeans. The same may be said of their music, both vocal and instrumental; the best of which, of either kind, would hardly be tolerable to a nice European <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. They pretend, like the Chinese, to have been the inventors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> from time immemorial, and their method is the same with theirs on wooden blocks; but they excel them in the neatness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them, as well as in the goodness of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> and paper. They likewise lay claim to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>; and are vastly superior to the Chinese in the use of all sorts of fire-arms, especially of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, as well as the curiosities of their fire-works. Their manner of writing is much the same as that of the Chinese, viz. in columns from top to bottom, and the columns beginning at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and ending at the left hand. Their characters were also originally the same, but now differ considerably. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> hath some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with the Chinese, though it appears from its various dialects to have been a kind of compound of that and other languages, derived from the various nations that first peopled those islands. It is not only very regular, polite, elegant, and copious, but abounds with a great variety of synonyms, nonyma, adapted to the nature of the subject they are upon, whether sublime, familiar, or low; and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, age, and sex, both of the speaker and person spoken. The Japanese are commonly very ingenious in most handicraft trades; and excel even the Chinese in several manufactures, particularly in the beauty, goodness, and variety of their silks, cottons, and other stuffs, and in their Japan and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> wares. No eastern nation comes up to them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERING">tempering</a> and fabricating of scimitars, swords, muskets, and other such weapons. The Japanese <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is much in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and style as that of the Chinese, especially as to their temples, palaces, and other public buildings; but in private ones they affect more plainness and neatness than show. These last are of wood and cement, consisting of two stories: they dwell only in the lower; the upper chamber serving for wardrobes. The roofs are covered with rush-mats three or four inches thick. In every house there is a small court, ornamented with trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and flower-pots; as likewise with a place for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">Chimneys</a> are unknown in this country, although fire is needed from the cold month of October till the end of March. They heat their rooms with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> contained in a copper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, which they sit round. Their cities are generally spacious, having each a prince or governor residing in them. The capital of Jeddo is 21 French leagues in circumference. Its streets are straight and large. There are gates at little distances, with an extremely high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a>, which they ascend to discover fires. Villages differ from cities in having but one street; which often extends several leagues. Some of them are situated so near each other, that they are only separated by a river or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. The principal furniture of the Japanese consists in straw-mats, which serve them for seats and beds; a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> for every one who chooses to eat is the only movable. The Japanese sit always upon their haunches. Before dinner begins, they make a profound bow and drink to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the guests. The women eat by themselves. During the courses, they drink a glass of sakki, which is a kind of beer made of rice kept constantly warm; and they drink at each new morsel. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">Tea</a> and sakki are the most favourite drink of this people; wine and spirits are never used, nor even accepted when offered by the Dutch. Sakki, or rice beer, is clear as wine, and of an agreeable taste; taken in quantity, it intoxicates for a few moments, and causes headache. Both men and women are fond of tobacco, which is in universal vogue and smoked continually. The gardens about their houses are adorned with a variety of flowers, trees, verdure, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, terraces, and other embellishments. The furniture and decorations of the houses of persons of distinction consist in Japan-work of various colours, curious paintings, beds, couches, screens, cabinets, tables, a variety of porcelain jars, vases, tea-equipment, and other vessels and figures, together with swords, guns, scimitars, and other arms. Their retinues are more or less numerous and splendid according to their rank; but there are few of the lords who have less than 50 or 60 men richly clad and armed, some on foot, but most on horseback. As for their petty kings and princes, they are seldom seen without 300 or 200 at least, when they either wait on the emperor, which is Japan one-half of the year, or attend him abroad. When a prince or great man dies, there are commonly about 10, 20, or more youths of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and such as were his greatest favourites, who put themselves to a voluntary death, at the place where the body is buried or burned: as soon as the funeral pile, consisting of odoriferous woods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, spices, oils, and other ingredients, is set on fire, the relations and friends of the deceased throw their presents into it, such as clothes, arms, victuals, money, sweet herbs, flowers, and other things which they imagine will be of use to him in the other world. Those of the middle or lower rank commonly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead, without any other burning than that of some odoriferous woods, gums, &c. The sepulchres in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and ashes of persons of rank are deposited, are generally very magnificent, and situated at some distance from the towns. The Dutch and Chinese are the only nations allowed to traffic in Japan. The Dutch at present send but two ships annually, which are fitted out at Batavia, and sail in June, and return at the end of the year. The chief merchandise is Japanese copper and raw camphor. The wares which the Dutch company import are, coarse <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, a great quantity of tin and lead, a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> iron, various kinds of fine chintzes, Dutch cloth of different colours and fineness, ferge wood for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORTOISE_SHELL">tortoise-shell</a>, and coqus Arabicus. The little merchandise brought by the officers on their own account, consists of saffron, theriac, sealing-wax, glass-beads, watches, &c., &c. About the time when the Dutch ships are expected, several outposts are stationed on the highest hills by the government; they are provided with telephones, and long before their arrival give the governor of Nagasaki notice. As soon as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in the harbour, the upper and under officers of the Japanese immediately betake themselves on board, together with interpreters; to whom is delivered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, in which all the sailors' books, the muster-roll of the whole crew, six small barrels of powder, six barrels of balls, six muskets, six bayonets, six pistols, and six swords are deposited; this is supposed to be the whole remaining ammunition after the imperial garrison has been saluted. These things are conveyed on shore, and preserved in a separate warehouse, nor are they returned before the day the ship quits the harbour. Duties are quite unknown as well in the inland part as on the coast; nor are there any customs required either for exported or imported goods; an advantage enjoyed by few nations. But, to prevent the importation of any forbidden wares, the utmost vigilance is observed; then the men and things are examined with the eyes of Argus. When any European goes on shore, he is examined before he leaves the ship, and afterwards on his landing. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> search is exceedingly strict; so that not only the pockets and clothes are broached with the hands, but the pudenda of the meaner sort are pressed, and the hair of the flaves. All the Japanese who come on board are searched in like manner, except only their superior officers: so also are the wares either exported or imported, first on board, and then at the factory, except the great chests, which are opened at the factory, and so carefully examined that they strike the very sides lest they should be hollow. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-clothes are often opened, and the feathers examined; rods of iron are run into the pots of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> and confections: a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole is made in the cheese, and a long pointed iron is thrust into it in all directions. Their suspicion is carried so far, that they take out and break one or two of the eggs brought from Batavia. The interpreters are all natives; they speak Dutch in different degrees of purity. The government permits no foreigner to learn their language, lest they should by means of this acquire the knowledge of the manufactures of the country; but 40 or 50 interpreters are provided to serve the Dutch in their trade, or on any other occasion. The interpreters are very inquisitive after European books, and generally provide themselves with some from the Dutch merchants. They peruse them with care, and remember what they learn. They besides endeavour to get information from the Europeans; for which purpose they ask numberless questions, particularly respecting medicine, physics, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural history</a>. Most of them apply to medicine, and are the only physicians of their nation who practise in the European manner, and with European medicines, which they procure from the Dutch physicians. Hence they are able to acquire money, and to make themselves respected. Among the vegetable productions peculiar to Japan, we may take notice of the aletris japonica, camellia japonica, and the volkameria japonica. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>-flower, or bignonia catalpa of Linnaeus, is very common, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a resemblance to the epidendrum vanilla, the berries of which are said to constitute an article of commerce. Here also we find the mimosa arborea, and tallow tree, together with the plantain, cocoa-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> tree, the chamereps excelsa, and the cycas circinalis, adorning the woods near the sea shore. It is a singular circumstance, that in the whole empire of Japan, neither sheep nor goats are to be met with, the goats being deemed pernicious to cultivation; and the vast quantities of silk and cotton with which it abounds, are considered as an excellent substitute for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. There are few <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> of any kind, either swine, horses, or cattle, as the Japanese live upon fish, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, and vegetables. Some wolves are seen in the northern provinces; and foxes are considered as demons incarnate. Gold and silver abound in Japan, and copper richly impregnated with gold, which constitutes the chief wealth of many provinces. Iron is said to be scarcer than any other metal, which of consequence they are not fond of exporting. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">Amber</a>, sulphur, pit-coal, red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, asbestos, porcelain, clay, pumice and white marble, are also found in considerable quantities; but, according to Kempfer, neither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. As Europeans have seldom visited the interior parts of the country, the natural curiosities of Japan are but very little known. Japan Earth. See Mimosa and Terra Japonica, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JAPANNING

Pages 48-50

the art of varnishing and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> figures on wood, in the same manner as is done by the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> in the East Indies. The substances which admit of being japanned are almost every kind that are dry and rigid, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not too <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>; as wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> prepared. Wood and metals do not require any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, but to have their surface perfectly even and clean; but leather should be securely strained either on frames or on boards; as its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> or forming folds would otherwise crack and force off the coats of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>; and paper should be treated in the same manner, and have a previous strong coat of some kind of size; but it is rarely made the subject of japanning till it is converted into papier mâché, or wrought by other means into such form, that its original state, particularly with respect to flexibility, is lost. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from the method formerly used in japanning is, the using or omitting any priming or undercoat on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to be japanned. In the older practice, such priming was always used; and is at present retained in the French manner of japanning coaches and snuff-boxes of the papier mâché; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> manufacture here, it has been always rejected. The advantage of using such priming or undercoat is, that it makes a saving in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of varnish used; because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of which the priming is composed fills up the inequalities of the body to be varnished; and makes it easy, by means of rubbing and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-polishing, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> an even surface for the varnish; and this was therefore such a convenience in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of wood, as the giving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and firmness to the ground was also in the case of leather, that it became an established method; and is therefore retained even in the instance of the papier mâché by the French, who applied the received method of japanning to that kind of work on its introduction. There is nevertheless this inconvenience always attending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of an undercoat of size, that the japan coats of varnish and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be constantly liable to be cracked and peeled off by any violence, and will not endure near so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the bodies japanned in the same manner, but without any such priming; as may be easily observed in comparing the wear of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and Birmingham snuff-boxes; which latter, when good of their kind, never peel or crack, or suffer any damage, unless by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> violence, and such a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> rubbing as wastes away the substance of the varnish; while the japan coats of the Parisians crack and fly off in flakes, whenever any knock or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, particularly near the edges, expose them to be injured. But the Birmingham manufacturers, who originally practised the japanning only on metals, to which the reason above given for the use of priming did not extend, and who took up this art of themselves as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, of course omitted at first the use of any such undercoat; and not finding it more necessary in the instance of papier mâché than on metals, continue still to reject it. On which account, the boxes of their manufacture are, with regard to the wear, greatly better than the French. The laying on the colours in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water, instead of varnish, is also another variation from the method of japanning formerly practised; but the much greater strength of the work, where they are laid on in varnish or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, has occasioned this way to be exploded with the greatest reason in all regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>: however, they who may practise japanning on cabinets, or other such pieces as are not exposed to much wear and violence, Japanning violence, for their amusement only, and consequently may not find it worth their while to encumber themselves with the preparations necessary for the other methods, may paint with water-colours on an undercoat laid on the wood or other substance of which the piece to be japanned is formed; and then finished with the proper coats of varnish, according to the methods below taught: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the colours are tempered with the strongest ifinglafs size and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, instead of gum-water, and laid on very flat and even, the work will not be much inferior in appearance to that done by the other method, and will last as long as the old Japan. Of Japan Grounds.—The proper grounds are either such as are formed by the varnish and colour, where the whole is to remain of one simple colour; or by the varnish either coloured or without colour, on which some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> or other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> is afterwards to be laid. It is necessary, however, before we proceed to speak of the particular grounds, to show the manner of laying on the priming or undercoat, where any such is used. This priming is of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with that called clear coating, or vulgarly clear-coating, practised erroneously by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-painters; and consists only in laying on and drying in the moist even manner a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of size and whiting, or sometimes lime instead of the latter. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> size has been generally used for this purpose; but where the work is of a nicer kind, it is better to employ the glovers or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> size; and if a third of ifinglafs be added, it will be still better, and, if not laid on too thick, much less liable to peel and crack. The work should be prepared by this priming, by being well smoothed with the fifth-flake or glass-blaver; and, being made thoroughly clean, should be brushed over once or twice with hot size, diluted with two-thirds of water, if it be of the common strength. The priming should then be laid on with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> as even as possible; and should be formed of a size whose consistence is between the common kind and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>, mixed with as much whiting as will give it a sufficient body of colour to hide the surface of whatever it is laid upon, but not more. If the surface be very clean on which the priming is used, two coats of it laid on in this manner will be sufficient; but if, on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> with a fine wet rag, it will not receive a proper water polish on account of any inequalities not sufficiently filled up and covered, two or more coats must be given it; and whether a greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> be used, the work should be smoothed, after the last coat but one is dry, by rubbing it with the Dutch rushes. When the last coat is dry, the water polish should be given, by passing over every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it with a fine rag gently moistened, till the whole appear perfectly plain and even. The priming will then be completed, and the work ready to receive the painting or coloured varnish; the rest of the proceedings being the same in this case as where no priming is used. When wood or leather is to be japanned, and no priming is used, the best preparation is to lay two or three coats of coarse varnish composed in the following manner: "Take of rectified spirit of wine one pint, and of coarse feed-lac and resin each two ounces. Dissolve the japanning-feed-lac and resin in the spirit; and then strain off the varnish." This varnish, as well as all others formed of spirit of wine, must be laid on in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and, if it can be conveniently managed, the piece of work to be varnished should be made warm likewise; and for the same reason all dampness should be avoided; for either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> or moisture chills this kind of varnish, and prevents it taking proper hold of the substance, on which it is laid. When the work is so prepared, or by the priming with the composition of size and whiting above described, the proper japan ground must be laid on, which is much the best formed of shell-lac varnish, and the colour desired, if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> be not in question, which demands a peculiar treatment, or great brightness be not required, when also other means must be pursued. The colours used with the shell-lac varnish may be any pigments whatever which give the tint of the ground desired; and they may be mixed together to form browns or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> colours. As metals never require to be undercoated with whiting, they may be treated in the same manner as wood or leather, where the undercoat is omitted, except in the instances particularly spoken of below. White Japan Grounds.—The forming a ground perfectly white, and of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of hardness, remains hitherto a desideratum, or matter sought for, in the art of japanning, as there are no substances which form a very hard varnish but what have too much colour not to deprive the whiteness, when laid on of a due thickness over the work. The nearest approach, however, to a perfect white varnish, already known, is made by the following composition: "Take flake white, or white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, washed over and ground up with a sixth of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, and then dried; and temper it properly for spreading with the mastick varnish prepared as under the article VARNISH. "Lay these on the body to be japanned, prepared either with or without the undercoat of whiting, in the manner as above ordered; and then varnish it over with five or six coats of the following varnish: "Provide any quantity of the best feed-lac; and pick out of it all the clearest and whitest grains, reserving the more coloured and fouler parts for the coarse varnishes, such as that used for priming or preparing wood or leather. Take of this picked feed-lac two ounces, and of gum-animal three ounces; and dissolve them, being previously reduced to a grofs powder, in about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of spirit of wine; and strain off the clear varnish." The feed-lac will yet give a slight tinge to this composition; but cannot be omitted where the varnish is wanted to be hard; though, when a softer will answer the end, the proportion may be diminished, and a little crude turpentine added to the gum animal to take off the brittleness. A very good varnish, free entirely from all brittleness, may be formed by dissolving as much gum animal as the oil will take, in old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> or poppy oil; which must be made to boil gently when the gum is put into it. The Japaning ground of white colour itself may be laid on in this varnish, and then a coat or two of it may be put over the ground; but it must be well diluted with oil of turpentine when it is used. This, though free from brittleness, is nevertheless liable to suffer by being indented or bruised by any slight strokes; and it will not well bear any polish, but may be brought to a very smooth surface without, if it be judiciously managed in the laying it on. It is likewise somewhat tedious in drying, and will require some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> where several coats are laid on; as the lac ought not to contain much oil of turpentine. Blue Japan Grounds.—Blue japan grounds may be formed of bright Prussian blue, or of verditer glazed over by Prussian blue, or of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMALT">smalt</a>. The colour may be best mixed with shell-lac varnish, and brought to a polishing state by five or six coats of varnish of seed-lac: but the varnish, nevertheless, will somewhat injure the colour by giving to a true blue a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of green, and fouling in some degree a warm blue by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> it contains: where, therefore, a bright blue is required, and a less degree of hardness can be dispensed with, the method before directed in the case of white grounds must be pursued. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Japan Grounds.—For a scarlet japan ground, vermillion may be used: but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> has a glaring effect, that renders it much less beautiful than the crimson produced by glazing it over with carmine or fine lake: or even with rose-pink, which has a very good effect used for this purpose. For a very bright crimson, nevertheless, instead of glazing with carmine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> lake should be used, dissolved in the spirit of which the varnish is compounded, which it readily admits of when good: and, in this case, instead of glazing with the shell-lac varnish, the upper or polishing coats need only be used; as they will equally receive and convey the tinge of the Indian lake, which may be actually dissolved by spirit of wine: and this will be found a much cheaper method than the using carmine. If, nevertheless, the highest degree of brightness be required, the white varnishes must be used. Yellow Japan Grounds.—For bright yellow grounds, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s yellow, or the turpeth mineral, should be employed, either alone or mixed with fine Dutch pink: and the effect may be still more heightened by dissolving powdered turmeric root in the spirit of wine of which the upper or polishing coat is made; which spirit of wine must be strained from off the dregs before the seed-lac be added to it to form the varnish. The shell-lac varnish is not equally injurious here, and with greens, as in the case of other colours; because, being only tinged with a reddish yellow, it is little more than an addition to the force of the colours. Yellow grounds may be likewise formed of the Dutch pink only; which, when good, will not be wanting in brightness, though extremely cheap. Green Japan Grounds.—Green grounds may be produced by mixing the king's yellow and bright Prussian blue, or rather the turpeth mineral and Prussian blue; and a cheap, but fouler kind, by verdigris with a little of the above-mentioned yellows, or Dutch pink. But, where a very bright green is wanted, the crystals of verdigris, called distilled verdigris, should be employed; and to heighten the effect, they should be laid on a ground of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which renders the colour extremely brilliant and pleasing. They may any of them be used successfully with good seed-lac varnish, for the reason before given; but will be still brighter with white varnish. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>-coloured Japan Grounds.—Orange-coloured japan grounds may be formed by mixing vermillion or red-lead with king's yellow, or Dutch pink; or the orange-lac, which will make a brighter orange ground than can be produced by any mixture. Purple Japan Grounds.—Purple japan grounds may be produced by the mixture of lake and Prussian blue; or a fouler kind, by vermillion and Prussian blue. They may be treated as the rest with respect to the varnish. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Japan Grounds to be produced with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">Heat</a>.—Black grounds may be formed by either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>-black or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> black: but the former is preferable where it is perfectly good. These may be always laid on with shell-lac varnish; and have their upper or polishing coats of common seed-lac varnish, as the tinge or fulness of the varnish can be here no injury. Common Black Japan Grounds on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a>, produced by means of Heat.—For forming the common black japan grounds by means of heat, the piece of work to be japanned must be painted over with drying oil; and, when it is of a moderate dryness, must be put into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a> of such degree of heat as will change the oil to black, without <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> it so as to destroy or weaken its tenacity. The stove should not be too hot when the work is put into it, nor the heat increased too fast; either of which errors would make it blister: but the slower the heat is augmented, and the longer it is continued, provided it be restrained within the due degree, the harder will be the coat of japan. This kind of varnish requires no polish, having received, when properly managed, a sufficient one from the heat.

JAPHETH

Pages 52-52

the son of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>. His descendants possessed all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and the isles in the Mediterranean, as well those which belong to Europe, as others which depend on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. They had all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, and the northern parts of Asia above the sources of the Tigris and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. Noah, when he blessed Japheth, said to him, "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a> shall be his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>." This blessing of Noah was accomplished, when the Greeks, and after them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, carried their conquests into Asia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, where were the dwellings and dominions of Shem and Canaan. The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Methhech, and Tiras. The scripture says, "that they peopled the isles of the Gentiles, and settled in different countries, each according to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, family, and people." It is supposed, that Gomer was the father of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cimmerians; Magog of the Scythians; Madai of the Macedonians or Medes; Javan of the Ionians and Greeks; Tubal of the Tibareniens; Methhech of the Mucovents or Ruthenians; and Tiras of the Thracians. By the isles of the Gentiles, the Hebrews understand the isles of the Mediterranean, and all the countries separated by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; whether also the Hebrews could go by sea only, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, Asia Minor. Japheth was known by profane authors under the name of Japetus. The poets make him the father of heaven and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The Greeks believe that he was the father of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, and acknowledged nothing more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> than him. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sons of Japheth above mentioned, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, Eusebius, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, and St Austin, give him an eighth called Eliza, who is not mentioned either in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> or Chaldee, and the eastern people affirm that Japheth had eleven children.

JAPYDIA

Pages 52-52

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a western district of Illyricum, anciently threefold; the first Japydia extending from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Timavus to Istri; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, from the river Arisa to the river Tadinius; and the third, called Inalpina, situated in Mount Albius and the other <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, which run out above Istri. Japodes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Japules, the people. Now constituting the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>, and the west of Austrian Croatia.

JAPYGLA

Pages 52-52
