CALABRIA anciently so called by the Greeks. Japuges, the people.

JAPYGUM

Pages 52-52

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>; called also Salentinum. Now Capo di S. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> di <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEUCA">Leuca</a>.

JAQUELOT

Pages 52-52
ISAAC, a celebrated French Protestant divine, born in 1647, at Vassy in Champagne, where his father was minister. The revocation of the edict of Nantes obliging him to quit France, he took refuge first at Heidelberg, and then at the Hague, where he procured an appointment in the Walloon church. Here he continued till that capital was taken by the king of Prussia, who, hearing him preach, made him his French minister in ordinary at Berlin; to which city he removed in 1702. While he lived at Berlin, he entered into a warm controversy with M. Bayle on the doctrine advanced in his dictionary favouring manicheism, which continued until death imposed silence on both parties: and it was in this dispute that M. Jaquelot openly declared in favour of the Remontrants. He wrote, among other works, 1. Dissertations sur l'existence de Dieu. 2. Dissertations sur le Meffe. 3. Lettres à Messieurs les Prelats de l'Eglise Gallicane. He was employed in finishing an important work upon the divine authority of the holy scriptures, when he died suddenly in 1708, aged 61.

JARCHI

Pages 52-52
SOLOMON, otherwife Raschi and Isaaki Solomon, a famous rabbi, born at Troyes in Champagne, who flourished in the 12th century. He was a perfect master of the talmud and gemara; and he filled the potsils of the bible with so many talmudical reveries, as totally extinguished both the literal and moral ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense of it. A great part of his commentaries are printed in Hebrew, and some have been translated into...

JARDYN

Pages 52-53
or JARDIN, KAREL DU, painter of conversations, landscapes, &c., was born at Amsterdam in 1649, and became a disciple of Nicholas Berchem. He travelled to Italy whilst he was yet a young man; and arriving at Rome, he gave himself alternately up to study and dilillation. Yet, amidst this irregularity of conduct, his proficiency in the art was surprising; and his paintings rose into such high repute, that they were exceedingly coveted in Rome, and bought up at great prices. With an intention to visit his native city he at last left Rome; but passing through Lyons, and meeting some agreeable companions, they prevailed on him to stay there for some time, and he found as much employment in that city as he could possibly undertake or execute. But the profits which arose from his paintings were not proportionate to his profession; and in order to extricate himself from the encumbrances in which his extravagant life had involved him, he was induced to marry his hostess, who was old and disagreeable, but very rich. Mortified and ashamed at that adventure, he returned as expeditiously as possible to Amsterdam, accompanied by his wife, and there for some time followed his profession with full as much success as he had met with in Italy or Lyons. He returned to Rome the second time; and after a year or two spent there in his usual extravagant manner, he settled at Venice. In that city his merit was well known before his arrival, which procured him a very honourable reception. He lived there highly cared for, and continually employed; but died at the age of 38. He was sumptuously interred, out of respect to his talents; and although a Protestant, permitted to be laid in consecrated ground. This painter, in his colouring and touch, resembled his master Berchem; but he added to that manner a force which distinguishes the great masters of Italy; and it is observed, that most of his pictures seem to express the warmth of the sun, and the light of mid-day. His pictures are not much encumbered; a few figures, some animals, and a little landscape for the back-grounds, generally comprise the whole of his composition. However, some of his subjects are often more extensive, containing more objects, and a larger design. His works are as much sought after, as they are difficult to be met with.

JARGON

Pages 53-53
or Zircon, a kind of precious stone found in Ceylon. This mineral contains a peculiar earth, called jargonia, or zirconia; for an account of the properties of which, see Chemistry, page 611; see also Mineralogy Index.

JARGONIA

Pages 53-53
or Zirconia, in Chemistry, a peculiar earth obtained from the preceding mineral. See Chemistry, p. 611.

JARMUTH

Pages 53-53

Jarmuth, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jerimoth, Josh. xv. a town reckoned to the tribe of Judah, four miles from Eleutheropolis, westward, (Jerome.) Thought to be the same with Ramoth and Remeth, Joshua xix. and Nehem x. 2. (Reland.)

JARNAC

Pages 53-53

a town of France, in Orleanois, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a>, remarkable for a victory gained by Henry III. over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a> in 1569. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 13. N. Lat. 45° 40'.

JAROSLOW

Pages 53-53

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of Ruslia, with a strong citadel. It is remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fair, its handsome buildings, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> gained by the Swedes in 1656, after which they took the town. It is seated on the river Saine, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. 23. N. Lat. 49° 58'.

JASHER

Pages 53-53

The Book of. This is a book which Joshua mentions, and refers to in the following passage: "And the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> stood still, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies: is not this written in the book of Jasher?" It is difficult to determine what this book of Jasher; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "the upright," is. St Jerome and the Jews believed it to be <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, or some other book of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, wherein God foretold he would do wonderful things in favour of his people. Huettius supposes it was a book of morality, in which it was said that God would subvert the course of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in favour of those who put their trust in him. Others pretend, it was public annals, or records, which were styled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> or upright, because they contained a faithful account of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Israelites. Grotius believes, that this book was nothing else but a song, made to celebrate this miracle and this victory. This seems the more probable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, because the words cited by Joshua as taken from this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibbon, and thou moon in the valley of Ajalon," are such poetical expressions as do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with historical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>; besides that in the 2d book of Samuel (i. 18.) mention is made of a book under the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, on account of a song made on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a>.

JASIONE

Pages 53-53

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the genygeneta class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 29th order, Campanaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. JASMINE. See Jasminum. Arabian Jasmine. See Nyctanthes; Botany Index.

JASMINUM

Pages 53-53

Jasmine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jessamine tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 44th order, Sepiariae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JASON

Pages 53-53

the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> who undertook the Argonautic expedition, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of which is obscured by fabulous traditions, flourished about 937 B.C. See Argonauts. JASPACHATES. See Jade-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JASPER

Pages 53-53

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of a mineral belonging to the argillaceous genus of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and of which there are many varieties, some of which being extremely beautiful, are much sought after, and employed as trinkets and ornaments. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JASPONYX

Pages 53-53

an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a>, importing, as appears from the name, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of jasper and onyx.

JATROPHA

Pages 53-53

the Cassada plant, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocotyledonous class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricocca. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JAVA

Pages 53-59

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the East Indies, lying between 105° and 116° E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. and from 6° to 8° S. Lat. extending in length 700 miles, and in breadth about 100. It is situated to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORNEO">Borneo</a>, and fourth-cut. Java, south-east from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> lying before it, from which it is separated by a narrow passage, now so famous in the world by the name of the Straits of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUNDA">Sunda</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is mountainous and woody in the middle; but a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, full of bogs and marshes, renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> unhealthy. It produces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, coffee, cocoa-nuts, plantains, cardamoms, and other tropical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> also, but in no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities, hath been found in it. It is diversified by many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, woods, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; in all which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has very bountifully bestowed her treasures. Many of the mountains are so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to be seen at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of leagues. That which is called the Blue Mountain is by far the highest of them all, and seen the farthest off at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. They have frequent and very terrible earthquakes in this island, which shake the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Batavia and places adjacent, to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the houses is expected every moment. The waters in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> are excessively agitated, inasmuch that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> resembles that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> pot; and in some places the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> opens, which affords a strange and terrible spectacle. The inhabitants are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that these earthquakes proceed from the mountain Parang, which is full of sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and bitumen. The fruits and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of this island are in their several kinds excellent, and almost out of number. There are abundance of forests scattered over it, in which are all kinds of wild beasts, such as buffaloes, tygers, rhinoceroses, and wild horses, with an infinite variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, some of them of an enormous size. Crocodiles are prodigiously large in Java, and are found chiefly about the mouths of rivers; for, being amphibious animals, they delight mostly in marshes and savannahs. This creature, like the tortoise, lays its eggs in the hot sands, without taking any further care of them; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a> them at the proper season, when the young run instantly into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. There is, in short, no kind of animal wanting here: fowls they have of all sorts, and exquisitely good, especially peacocks, partridges, pheasants, wood-pigeons; and, for curiosity, they have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> bat, which differs little in form from ours; but its wings, when extended, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a full yard, and the body of it is of the size of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RAT">rat</a>. They have fish in great plenty, and very good; so that for the value of three-pence there may be enough bought to dine six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> men. They have likewise a multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TORTOISES">tortoises</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of which is very little inferior to veal, and there are many who think it better. It is said, that there are in the island upwards of 40 great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, which, from the number of their inhabitants, would, in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world, merit the name of cities; and more than 4500 villages, besides hamlets, and straggling houses, lying very near each other, upon the sea coast, and in the neighbourhood of great towns: hence, upon a fair and moderate computation, there are within the bounds of the whole island, taking persons of both sexes, and of all ranks and ages, more than thirty millions of souls; so that it is thrice as populous as France, which, though twice as big, is not computed to have more than twenty millions of inhabitants. There are a great many princes in the island, of which the most considerable are, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACASSAR">Macassar</a>, who resides at Katalura, and the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANTAM">Bantam</a> and Japara. Upon the first of these many of the petty princes are dependent; but the Dutch are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> masters of the greatest part of the island, particularly of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> coast, though there are some of the princes beyond the mountains, on the south coast, who still maintain their independency. The natives of the country, who are established in the neighbourhood of Batavia, and for a tract of about 40 leagues along the mountains of the country of Bantam, are immediately subject to the governor-general. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> send droffards, or commissaries, among them, who administer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and take care of the public revenues. The city of Batavia is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> not only of this island but of all the Dutch dominions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. It is an exceeding fine city, situated in the latitude of 6° south, at the mouth of the river Jucatra, and in the bosom of a large commodious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, which may be considered not only as one of the safest harbours in India, but in the world. The city is surrounded by a rampart 21 feet thick, covered on the outside with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and fortified with 22 bastions. This rampart is environed by a ditch 45 yards over, and full of water, especially when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> are high, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. The avenues to the town are defended by several forts, each of which is well furnished with excellent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> cannon: no person is suffered to go beyond these forts without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSPORT">passport</a>. The river Jucatra passes through the midst of the town, and forms 15 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> of running water, all faced with free-stone, and adorned with trees that are ever green; over these canals are 56 bridges, besides those which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> without the town. The streets are all perfectly straight, and each, generally speaking, 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The houses are built of stone, after the manner of those in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The city is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> and a half in circumference, and has five gates; but there are ten times the number of houses without that there are within it. There is a very fine town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, four Calvinist churches, besides other places of worship for all sorts of religions, a spin-huys or house of correction, an orphan house, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of sea stores, several for spices, with wharfs and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> manufactories, and many other public buildings. The garrison consists <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of between 2000 and 3000 men. Besides the forts mentioned above, there is the citadel of Batavia, a very fine regular fortification, situated at the mouth of the river, and flanked with four battions; two of which command the sea, and the other two the town. It is in the citadel that the governor-general of the Indies has his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; over against which is that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>-general, who is the next person to the governor. The counsellors, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers of the company, have also their apartments there; as have likewise the physician, the surgeon, and the apothecary. There are in it, besides, arsenals and magazines furnished with ammunition for many years. The city of Batavia is not only inhabited by Dutch, French, Portuguese, and other Europeans, established here on account of trade; but also by a vast number of Indians of different nations, Javanese, Chinese, Malaysians, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a>, Ambonese, Armenians, natives of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Bali, Mardykers or Topasses, Macaffers, Timors, Bougis, &c. Of the Chinese, there are, it is said, said, about 100,000 in the island; of which near 30,000 resided in the city till the year 1740, when the Dutch, pretending that they were in a plot against them, sent a body of troops into their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, and demanded their arms, which the Chinese readily delivered up; and the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> the governor sent another body, with orders to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> and massacre every one of the Chinese, men, women, and children. Some relate there were 20,000, others 30,000, that were put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, without any manner of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>; and yet the barbarous governor, who was the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of this cruel proceeding, had the assurance to embark for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, imagining he had amassed wealth enough to secure him against any prosecution in Holland: but the Dutch, finding themselves detested and abhorred by all mankind for this piece of tyranny, endeavoured to throw the odium of it upon the governor, though he had the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of all the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Batavia, except one, to the order for the massacre. The states, therefore, dispatched a packet to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, containing orders to apprehend the governor, and send him back to Batavia to be tried. He was accordingly apprehended at the Cape; but was never heard of afterwards. It supposed he was thrown over-board in his passage to Batavia, that there might be no farther inquiries into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and it is said, all the wealth this merciful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> had amassed, and sent over before him in four ships, was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away in the passage. Besides the garrison here, the Dutch had formerly about 15,000 men in the island, either Dutch, or formed out of the several nations they had enslaved; and they had a fleet of between 20 and 30 men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, with which they gave <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to every power on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and to all the European powers that visit the Indian ocean, unless we should except the British: it was, however, but a little before the revolution that they expelled us from our settlement at Bantam. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAVELIN">Javelin</a>, in antiquity, a sort of spear five feet and an half long; the shaft of which was of wood, with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> point.—Every soldier in the Roman armies had seven of these, which were very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and slender. Jawer, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, capital of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name, with a citadel, and a large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, surrounded with piazzas. It is 12 miles south-east of Lignitz, 30 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, and 87 east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>. E. Long. 15. 29. N. Lat. 50. 56. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">Jaundice</a> (derived from the French jaunisse "yellowness," of jaune "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>"); a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> consisting in a suffusion of the bile, and a rejection thereof to the surface of the body, whereby the whole exterior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is discoloured. Dr Maculog is of opinion, that the bile returns into the circulation in this disorder by the course of the lymphatics. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Jaws. See Maxilla. Locked jaw, is a spasmodic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the lower jaw, commonly produced by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> injury affecting the tendons or ligaments. See Medicine Index. Jay, see Corvus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index. Jay, Guy Michael le, a French gentleman, who distinguished himself by causing a polyglot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> to be printed at his own expense in 10 vols folio: but he ruined himself by that imprudence, first because he would not suffer it to appear under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Richelieu, who, after the example of Cardinal Ximenes, was ambitious of eternalizing his name by this means; and next, because he made it too dear for the English market; on which Dr Walton undertook his polyglot bible, which, being more commodious, reduced the price of M. le Jay's. After the death of his wife, M. le Jay took orders, was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Veze-lay in the Nièvre, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of counsellor of state. Jazer, or Jaser, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a Levi-tical city in the territory of the Amorites beyond Jordan, 10 miles to the west, or rather south-west, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, and 15 miles from Elebon, and therefore situated between Philadelphia and Hethbon, on the east border of the tribe of Gad, supposed to be the Jazerem of Josephus. In Jeremiah xlviii. mention is made of the sea of Jazer, that is, a lake; taken either for an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> or overflowing of the Arnon, a lake through which it passes, or from which it takes its rise. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IBERIA">Iberia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> so called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, from the river Iberus. Iberes the people, from the native Iber. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HISPANIA">Hispania</a>. Iberia was also the name of an inland country of Asia, having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> to the west, with a part of Pontus; to the north Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>; on the east <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>; and on the south <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> Magna: Now the western part of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> (See Georgia). Iberia, according to Josephus, was first peopled by Tubal, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Gomer and Magog. His opinion is confirmed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>; for Melhech and Tubal are by these interpreters rendered Mochei and Iberians. We know little of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the country till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, when their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, named Artaces, siding with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> against Lucullus, and afterwards against Pompey, was defeated by the latter with great slaughter; but afterwards obtained a peace, upon delivering up his sons as hostages. Little notice is taken of the succeeding kings by the ancient historians. They were probably tributary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> till that empire was overturned, when this, with the other countries in Asia bordering on it, fell successively under the power of the Saracens and Turks. Iberis, sciatica cresses, or Candytuft, a genus of plants belonging to the tetradyneia clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 39th order, Sili-quoideae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Ibex, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of goat. See Capra, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. Ibis. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANTALUS">Tantalus</a>, Ornithology Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IBYCUS">Ibycus</a>, a Greek lyric poet, of whose works there are only a few fragments remaining, flourished 550 B.C. It is said, that he was assassinated by robbers; and that, when dying, he called upon some cranes he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> to bear witness. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> seeing some cranes, said to his companions, "There are the witnesses of Ibycus's death;" which being reported to the magistrates, the assassins were put to the torture, and having confessed the fact, were hanged. Thence arose the proverb Ibyci Grues. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">Ice</a>, in Physiology, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, transparent, and brittle body. ICE The younger Lemery observes, that ice is only a re-establishment of the parts of water in their natural state; that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> absence of fire is sufficient to account for this re-establishment; and that the fluidity of water is a real fusion, like that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> exposed to the fire; differing only in this, that a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fire is necessary to the one than the other. Galileo was the first that observed ice to be <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the water which composed it; and hence it happens, that ice floats upon water, its specific gravity being to that of water as eight to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. This rarefaction of ice seems to be owing to the air-bubbles produced in water by freezing; and which, being considerably large in proportion to the water frozen, render the body so much specifically lighter: these air-bubbles, during their production, acquire a great expansive power, so as to burst the containing vessels, though ever so strong. M. Mairan, in a dissertation on ice, attributes the increase of its bulk chiefly to a different arrangement of the parts of the water from which it is formed; the icy skin on the water being composed of filaments, which, according to him, are found to be constantly and regularly joined at an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of 60°; and which, by this angular disposition, occupy a greater volume than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>. He found the augmentation of the volume of water by freezing, in different trials, a 14th, an 18th, a 19th; and when the water was previously purged of air, only a 22d part: that ice, even after its formation, continues to expand by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; for, after water had been frozen to some thickness, the fluid part being let out by a hole in the bottom of the vessel, a continuance of the cold made the ice convex; and a piece of ice, which was at first only a 14th part specifically lighter than water, on being exposed some days to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, became a 12th part lighter. To this cause he attributes the bursting of ice on ponds. Wax, resins, and animal fats, made fluid by fire, instead of expanding like watery liquors, shrink in their return to solidity: for solid pieces of the same bodies sink to the bottom of the respective <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that these bodies are more dense in their solid than in their fluid state. The oils which congeal by cold, as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> olive, and the essential oil of aniseeds, appear also to shrink in their congelation. Hence, the different dispositions of different kinds of trees to be burnt by, or to resist, strong frosts, are by some attributed to the juices with which the tree abounds; being in the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> watery, and in the other resinous or oily. Though it has been generally supposed that the natural crystals of ice are stars of five rays, forming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of 60° with each other, yet this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a> of water, as it may properly be called, seems to be as much affected by circumstances as that of salts. Hence we find a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the accounts of those who have undertaken to describe these crystals. M. Mairan informs us, that they are stars with five radii; and his opinion is confirmed by observing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of frost on glass. M. Rome de L'Isle determines the form of the solid crystal to be an equilateral octahedron. M. Hassenfratz found it to be a prismatic hexaedron; but M. d'Antic found a method of reconciling these seemingly opposite opinions. In a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>-storm, where the hailstones were very large, he found they had sharp wedge-like angles of more than half an inch; and in these he supposed it impossible to see two pyramidal tetraedra joined laterally, and not to conclude that each grain was composed of octaedrons converging to a centre. Some had a cavity in the middle; and he saw the opposite extremities of two opposite pyramids, which constitute the octahedron; he likewise saw the octahedron entire united in the middle: all of them were therefore similar to the crystals formed on a thread immersed in a saline solution. On these principles M. d'Antic constructed an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> octahedron resembling one of the largest hailstones; and found that the angle at the summit of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> was 45°, but that of the junction of the two pyramids 145°. It is not, however, easy to procure regular crystals in hailstones where the operation is conducted with such rapidity: in snow and hoar-frost, where the crystallization goes on more slowly, our author is of opinion that he sees the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of octaedra. Ice forms generally on the surface of the water: but this too, like the crystallization, may be varied by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the circumstances. In Germany, particularly the northern parts of that country, it has been observed that there are three kinds of ice. 1. That which forms on the surface. 2. Another kind formed in the middle of the water, resembling nuclei or small hail. 3. The ground ice which is produced at the bottom, especially where there is any <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> substance to which it may adhere. This is full of cells like a wasp's nest, but less regular; and performs many strange effects in bringing up very heavy bodies from the bottom, by means of its inferiority in specific gravity to the water in which it is formed. The ice which forms in the middle of the water rises to the top, and there unites into large masses; but the formation both of this and the ground ice takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> only in violent and sudden colds, where the water is shallow, and the surface disturbed in such a manner that the congelation cannot take place. The ground ice is very destructive to dykes and other aquatic works. In the more temperate European climates these kinds of ice are not met with. In many countries the warmth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> renders ice not only a desirable, but even a necessary article; so that it becomes an object of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to fall upon a ready and cheap method of procuring it. We shall here take notice of some attempts made by Mr Cavallo to discover a method of producing a sufficient degree of cold for this purpose by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of volatile liquors. He found, however, in the course of these experiments, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> was incomparably superior to any other fluid in the degree of cold it produced. The price of the liquor naturally induced him to fall upon a method of using it with as little waste as possible. The thermometer he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of had the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> quite detached from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> piece on which the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> was engraved. The various fluids were then thrown upon the ball through the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> aperture of a small glass vessel shaped like a funnel; and care was taken to throw them upon it so slowly, that a drop might now and then fall from the under part, excepting when these fluids were used, which which evaporate very slowly; in which case it was sufficient barely to keep the ball moist, without any drop falling from it. During the experiment, the thermometer was kept very gently <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round its axis, that the fluid made use of might fall upon every part of its ball. He found this method preferable to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the ball of the thermometer into the fluid and taking it out again immediately, or even of anointing it constantly with a feather. The evaporation, and consequently the cold, produced by it, may be increased by blowing on the thermometer with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of bellows; though this was not used in the experiments now to be related, on account of the difficulty of its being performed by one person, and likewise because it occasions much uncertainty in the results. The room in which the experiments were made was heated to 64° of Fahrenheit; and with water it was reduced to 56°, viz. 8° below that of the room or of the water employed. The effect took place in about two minutes; but though the operation was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for a longer time, it did not sink lower. With spirit of wine it sunk to 48°. The cold was greater with highly rectified spirit than with the weaker fort; but the difference is less than would be expected by one who had never seen the experiment made. The pure spirit produces its effect much more quickly. On using various other fluids which were either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of water and spirituous liquors, or pure essences, he found that the cold produced by their evaporation was generally some intermediate degree between that produced by water and the spirit of wine. Oil of turpentine sunk the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> three degrees; but olive oil and others, which evaporate very slowly, or not at all, did not sensibly affect the thermometer. To observe how much the evaporation of spirit of wine, and consequently the cold produced by it, would be increased by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, he put the tube containing it into an insulating handle, and connected it with the conductor of an electrical machine, which was kept in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> during the time of making the experiment; by which means one degree of cold seemed to be gained, as the mercury now sunk to 47° instead of 48°, at which it had stood formerly. On trying the three mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, he found that they heated the thermometer instead of cooling it; which effect he attributes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> they themselves acquired by uniting with the moisture of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. The vitriolic acid, which was very strong and transparent, raised the mercury to 102°, the smoking nitrous acid to 72°, and the marine to 66°. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> for using the least possible quantity of ether for freezing water consists in a glass tube (fig. 1.) terminating in a capillary aperture, which is to be fixed upon the bottle containing the ether. Round the lower part of the neck at A some thread is wound, in order to let it fit the neck of the bottle. When the experiment is to be made, the stopper of the bottle containing the ether is to be removed, and the tube <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned put in its room. The thread round the tube ought also to be previously moistened with water or spit before it is put into the neck of the bottle, in order the more effectually to prevent the escape of the ether betwixt the neck of the phial and tube. Hold then the bottle by its bottom FG (fig. 2.) Vol. XI. Part I. and keeping it inclined as in the figure, the small stream of ether issuing out of the aperture D of the tube DE, is directed upon the ball of the thermometer, or upon a tube containing water or other liquor that is required to be congealed. As ether is very volatile, and has the remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of increasing the bulk of air, there is no aperture requisite to allow the air to enter the bottle while the liquid flows out. The heat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is more than sufficient to force out the ether in a continued stream at the aperture D. In this manner, throwing the stream of ether upon the ball of a thermometer in such a quantity that a drop might now and then, every ten seconds for instance, fall from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> of the thermometer, Mr Cavallo brought the mercury <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to 3°, or 29° below the freezing point, when the atmosphere was somewhat hotter than temperate. When the ether is very good, i.e. capable of dissolving <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, and has a small bulb, not above 20 drops of it are required to produce this effect, and about two minutes of time; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fort must be used in greater quantity, and for a longer time; though at last the thermometer is brought down by this very nearly as low as by the best fort. To freeze water by the evaporation of ether, Mr Cavallo takes a thin glass tube about four inches long, and one-fifth of an inch diameter, hermetically sealed at one end, with a little water in it, so as to take up about half an inch of the cavity, as is shewn at CB in fig. 3. Into this tube a slender wire H is also introduced, the lower extremity of which is twisted into a spiral, and serves to draw up the bit of ice when formed. He then holds the glass tube by its upper part A with the fingers of the left hand, and keeps it continually and gently turning round its axis, first one way and then the other: whilst with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand he holds the phial containing the ether in such a manner as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the stream on the outside of the tube, and a little above the surface of the water contained in it. The capillary aperture D should be kept almost in contact with the surface of the tube containing the water; and by continuing the operation for two or three minutes, the water <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be frozen as it were in an instant; and the opacity will ascend to C in less than half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of time, which makes a beautiful appearance. This congelation, however, is only superficial: and in order to congeal the whole quantity of water, the operation must be continued a minute or two longer; after which the wire H will be found kept very tight by the ice. The hand must then be applied to the outside of the tube, in order to soften the surface of the ice; which would otherwise adhere very firmly to the glass; but when this is done, the wire H easily brings it out. Sometimes our author was accustomed to put into the tube a small thermometer instead of the wire H; and thus he had an opportunity of observing a very curious phenomenon unnoticed by others, viz. that in the winter time water requires a smaller degree of cold to congeal it than in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. In the winter, for instance, the water in the tube <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> will freeze when the thermometer stands about 30°; but in the summer, or even when the thermometer stands at 60°, the quicksilver must be brought down to 10, 15, or even more degrees. grces below the freezing point before any congelation can take place. In the summer time therefore a greater quantity of ether, and more time, will be required to congeal any given quantity of water than in winter. When the temperature of the atmosphere has been about 40°, our author has been able to congeal a quantity of water with an equal quantity of good ether; but in summer, two or three times the quantity are required to perform the effect. "There seems (says he) to be something in the air, which, besides heat, interferes with the freezing of water, and perhaps of all fluids; though I cannot say from my own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> whether the above-mentioned difference between the freezing in winter and summer takes place with other fluids, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, oils, wines," &c. The proportion of ether requisite to congeal water seems to vary with the quantity of the latter; that is, a large quantity of water seems to require a proportionably less quantity of ether to freeze it than a smaller one. "In the beginning of the spring (says Mr Cavalli), I froze a quarter of an ounce of water with about half an ounce of ether: the apparatus being larger, though similar to that described above. Now as the price of ether, sufficiently good for the purpose, is generally about 18d. or 2s. per ounce, it is plain, that with an expense under two shillings, a quarter of an ounce of ice, or ice-cream, may be made in every climate, and at any time, which may afford great satisfaction to those persons, who, living in those places where no natural ice is to be had, never saw or tasted any such delicious refreshment. When a small piece of ice, for instance, of about ten grains <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, is required, the necessary apparatus is very small, and the expense not worth mentioning. I have a small box four inches and a half long, two inches broad, and one and a half deep, containing all the apparatus necessary for this purpose; viz. a bottle capable of containing about one ounce of ether; two pointed tubes, in case one should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>; a tube in which the water is to be frozen, and a wire. With the quantity of ether contained in this small and very portable apparatus, the experiment may be repeated about ten times. A person who wishes to perform such experiments in hot climates, and in places where ice is not easily procured, requires only a larger bottle of ether besides the whole apparatus described above." Electricity increases the cold produced by means of evaporating ether but very little, though the effect is perceptible. Having thrown the electrified and also the unelectrified stream of ether upon the bulb of a thermometer, the mercury was brought down two degrees lower in the former than in the latter case. Our author observes, for the sake of those who may be inclined to repeat this experiment, that a cork confined this volatile fluid much better than a glass stopple, which is almost impossible to grind with such exactness as to prevent entirely the evaporation of the ether. When a stopple, made very nicely out of an uniform and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> piece of cork, which goes rather tight, is put upon a bottle of ether, the smell of that fluid cannot be perceived through it; but he never saw a glass stopple which could produce that effect. In this manner, ether, spirit of wine, or any other volatile fluid, may be preserved, which does not corrode cork by its fumes. When the stopple, however, is very often taken out, it becomes loose, as it will also be by long keeping: in either of which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it must be changed. Blink of the Ice, is a name given by the pilots to a bright appearance near the horizon, occasioned by the ice, and observed before the ice itself is seen. Ice-Boats, boats so constructed as to sail upon ice, and which are very common in Holland, particularly upon the river Maese and the lake Y. See Plate CCLXXVIII. They go with incredible swiftness, sometimes so quick as to affect the breath, and are found very useful in conveying goods and passengers over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and great rivers in that country. Boats of different sizes are placed in a transverse form upon a 2½ or 3 inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> board; at the extremity of each end are fixed irons, which turn up in the form of skids; upon this plank the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> rests, and the two ends serve as out-riggers to prevent upsetting; whence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> are fastened that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the head of the mast in the nature of throats, and others passed through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> across the bowprit; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a> is made somewhat like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a> with the head placed downward, which being pressed down, cuts the ice, and serves all the purposes of a rudder in the water, by enabling the helmsman to steer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACK">tack</a>, &c. Method of making Ice-Cream. Take a sufficient quantity of cream, and, when it is to be mixed with raspberry, or currant, or pine, a quarter part as much of the juice or jam, as of the cream: after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> and straining the mixture through a cloth, put it with a little juice of lemon into the mould, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a> vessel, and varying in size and shape at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; cover the mould, and place it in a pail about two-thirds full of ice, into which two handfuls of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> have been thrown; turn the mould by the hand-hold with a quick motion to and fro, in the manner used for milling chocolate, for eight or ten minutes; then let it rest as long, and turn it again for the same time; and having left it to stand half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, it is fit to be turned out of the mould and to be sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Lemon juice and sugar, and the juices of various kinds of fruits, are frozen without cream; and when cream is used, it should be well mixed. Ice-Hills, a sort of structure or contrivance common upon the river Neva at Petersburg, and which afford a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of amusement to the populace. They are constructed in the following manner. A scaffolding is raised upon the river about 30 feet in height, with a landing place on the top, the ascent to which is by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a>. From this summit a sloping <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of boards, about four yards broad and 30 long, descends to the superficies of the river; it is supported by strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> gradually decreasing in height, and its sides are defended by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> of planks. Upon these boards are laid square masses of ice about four inches thick, which being first smoothed with the axe and laid close to each other, are then sprinkled with water; by these means they coalesce, and, adhering to the boards, immediately form an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined plane</a> of pure ice. From the bottom of this plane the snow is cleared away for the length of 200 yards, and the breadth of four, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the river; and the sides of this course, as well as the sides and top of the scaffolding, are ornamented with firs and pines. Each person, being provided with ICE a fledge, mounts the ladder; and having attained the summit, he feats himself upon his fledge at the upper extremity of the inclined plane, down which he suffers it to glide with considerable rapidity, poising it as he goes down; when the velocity acquired by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> carries it above 100 yards upon the level ice of the river. At the end of this course, there is usually a similar ice-hill, nearly parallel to the former, which begins where the other ends; so that the person immediately mounts again, and in the same manner glides down the other inclined plane of ice. This diversion he repeats as often as he pleases. The boys also are continually employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SKATING">skating</a> down these hills; they glide chiefly upon one skait, as they are able to poise themselves better upon one leg than upon two. These ice-hills exhibit a pleasing appearance upon the river, as well from the trees with which they are ornamented, as from the moving objects which at particular times of the day are defending without intermission.

JEALOUSY

Pages 139-139

in Ethics, is that peculiar uneasiness which arises from the fear that some rival may rob us of the affection of one whom we greatly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suspicion that he has already done it. The first sort of jealousy is inseparable from love, before it is in possession of its object; the latter is often unjust, generally mischievous, always troublesome. Waters of Jealousy. See Waters.

JEDBURGH

Pages 139-139

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> town of Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Tiviotdale <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROXBURGHSHIRE">Roxburghshire</a>, is situated nearly in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, on the banks of the river Jed, whence it derives its name. It is well built and populous, and has a good market for corn and cattle. On the west side of the river, near its junction with the Teviot, stand the beautiful ruins of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> founded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I., a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> pile still serves for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>.—Jedburgh is the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> and of a presbytery. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of this town in 1793 was estimated at 2000.

JEDDO

Pages 139-140

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> resides. It is open on all sides, having neither walls nor ramparts; and the houses, Jeffersonia houses are built with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and boarded on the outside to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> from destroying the walls. In every street there is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> gate, which is shut up in the night; and a kind of customhouse or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, to put merchandise in. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, being <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles in length and six in breadth, and contains 1,000,000 of inhabitants. A fire happened in 1658, which, in the space of 48 hours, burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> 100,000 houses, and in which a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants perished. The emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and all the rest were reduced to ashes; but they are all rebuilt again. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> palace is in the middle of the town; and is defended with walls, ditches, towers, and bastions. Where the emperor resides, there are three towers nine stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, each covered with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of audience is said to be supported by pillars of maffy gold. Near the palace are several others, where the relations of the emperor live. The empress has a palace of her own, and there are 20 small ones for the concubines. Besides, all the vassal kings have each a palace in the city, with a handsome garden, and stables for 2000 horses. The houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort are nothing but a ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, and the rooms are parted by folding screens; so that they can make the rooms larger or smaller at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. It is seated in an agreeable plain, at the bottom of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>; and the river which crosses it, is divided into several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 140. N. Lat. 35. 32.

JEFFERSONIA

Pages 140-140

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas pendantia, and order monogynia. The calyx is composed of five short oval imbricated leaves; the corolla is monophyllous and funnel-shaped; the margin hypocrateriform; the stigma is quadrifid. One <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> only has been discovered, simpervirens, which is a shrub with round, polished, shining stems, which climb on bushes and small trees. This shrub is very abundant in the woods of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where it was discovered by Dr Brickel, and it is covered with blossoms for many months of the year. JEFFERY. See GEOFFREY.

JEFFREYS

Pages 140-140

Sir GEORGE, Baron Wem, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Judge Jeffreys, was the sixth son of John Jeffreys, Esq. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTON">Acton</a> in Denbighshire; and was educated at Westminster school, whence he removed to the Inner Temple, where he applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">Alderman</a> Jeffreys, who was probably related to him, introduced him among the citizens of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and he being a merry bottle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, soon came into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> business, and was chosen their recorder. He was afterwards chosen solicitor to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and in 1680 was knighted, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. At length, resigning the recordership, he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of chief-justice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, and, soon after the accession of James II., the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. During the reign of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., he showed himself a bitter enemy to those dissenting ministers who, in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, were tried by him: he was one of the greatest advisers and promoters of all the oppressions and arbitrary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> carried on in the reign of James II.; and his sanguinary and inhuman proceedings against Monmouth's unhappy adherents in the well <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ever render his name infamous. Whenever the prisoner was of a different party, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> he could please the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> by condemning him, instead of appearing, according to the duty of his office, Jeffreys, as his counsel, he would scarce allow him to speak for himself; but would load him with the grossest and most vulgar abuses, browbeat, insult, and turn to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> the witnesse that spoke in his behalf; and even threaten the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> with fines and imprisonment, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they made the least hesitation about bringing in the prisoner guilty. Yet it is said, that when he was in temper, and matters perfectly indifferent came before him, no one became a seat of justice better. Nay, it even appears, that, when he was under no state influence, he was sometimes inclined to protect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of mankind, of which the following instance has been given:—The mayor and aldermen of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> had been used to transport convicted criminals to the American plantations, and fell them by way of trade. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to good account when any pilferers or petty rogues were brought before them, they threatened them with hanging; and then some officers who attended, earnestly persuaded the ignorant intimidated creatures to beg for transportation, as the only way to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> them; and in general their advice was followed. Then, without more form, each alderman in course took one, and sold him for his own benefit; and sometimes warm disputes arose between them about the next turn. This infamous trade which had been carried on many years, coming to the knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chief justice, he made the mayor descend from the bench and stand at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, in his scarlet and fur, with his guilty brethren the aldermen, and plead as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> criminals. He then obliged them to give securities to answer informations; but the proceedings were stopped by the Revolution.—However, the brutality Jeffreys commonly showed on the bench, where his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and visage were equally terrible, at length exposed him to a severe mortification. A scrivener of Wapping having a cause before him, one of the opponent's counsel said he was a strange fellow, and sometimes went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and sometimes to conventicles; and it was thought he was a trimmer. At this the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> fired: "A trimmer?" (said he); I have heard much of that monster, but never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> one. Come forth Mr Trimmer, and let me see your shape." He then treated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> fellow so roughly, that, on his leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, he declared he would not undergo the terrors of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> again to save his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and he should certainly retain the frightful impressions of it as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived. Soon after, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> coming, the lord chancellor, dreading the public resentment, disguised himself in a seaman's dress, in order to leave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and was drinking in a cellar, when this scrivener coming into the cellar, and seeing again the face which had filled him with such horror, started; on which Jeffreys, fearing he was known, feigned a cough, and turned to the wall with his pot of beer in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. But Mr Trimmer going out, gave notice that he was there; and the mob rushing in seized him, and carried him before the lord mayor, who sent him with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> to the lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, by whom he was committed to the Tower, where he died in 1689.—It is remarkable, that the late countess of Pomfret met with very rude insults from the populace on the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, only because she was granddaughter to the inhuman Jeffreys.

JEFOFAILE

Pages 142-142

(compounded of three French words, "J'<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AY">ay</a> failli," "I have failed"), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, used for an oversight in pleading <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other proceeding at law. The shewing of these defects or oversights was formerly often practised by the counsel; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> came into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in order to try the issue, they said, This inquest you ought not to take; and after verdict they would say to the court, To judgment you ought not to go. But several statutes have been made to avoid the delays occasioned by such suggestions; and a judgment is not to be stayed after verdict for mistaking the Christian or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of either of the parties, or in a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, year, &c. where the same are rightly named in any preceding record.

JEHOVAH

Pages 140-141

Jehovah JEHOVAH, one of the Scripture names of God, signifying the Being who is self-existent and gives existence to others. So <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a veneration had the Jews for this name, that they left off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of pronouncing it, whereby its true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> was forgotten. They call it tetragrammaton, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "the name with four letters;" and believe, that whoever knows the true pronunciation of it cannot fail to be heard by God. JEJUNE STYLE. See STYLE.

JEJUNUM

Pages 141-141

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of the small guts; thus called from the Latin jejuns, "hungry," because always found empty. See ANATOMY, N° 93. JELLALÆAN, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> GELALÆAN <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">Calendar</a>, EPOCHA, and Year. See CALENDAR, EPOCHA, and YEAR.

JELLY

Pages 141-141

a form of food, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> medicine, prepared from the juices of ripe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, boiled to a proper consistence with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; or the strong decoctions of the horns, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, or extremities of animals, boiled to such a height as to be stiff and firm when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, without the addition of any sugar.—The jellies of fruits are cooling, saponaceous, and acelcent, and therefore are good as medicines in all disorders of the prime vice, arising from alkalecent juices, especially when not given alone, but diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. On the contrary, the jellies made from animal substances are all alkalecent, and are therefore good in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which an acidity of the humours prevails: the alkalecent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of these is, however, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> taken off, by adding lemon juice and sugar to them. There were formerly a sort of jellies much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> jellies; these had the restorative medicinal drugs added to them, but they are now scarce ever heard of.

JELLY-OAT

Pages 141-141

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> oats, recommended by many of the German physicians in all hectic disorders, to be taken with broth of snails <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cray fish.—It is made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of oats, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HULK">hulk</a> taken off, with some hartshorn shavings, and currants, together with a leg of veal cut to pieces, and with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> all broken; these are to be set over the fire with a large quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, till the whole is reduced to a sort of jelly; which when strained and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be very firm and hard. A few spoonfuls of this are to be taken every morning, diluted with a balon of either of the above mentioned broths, or any other warm liquor.

JEMPTERLAND

Pages 141-141

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Angermania, on the east by Medalpadia, on the south by Helsingia, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>. It is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Refundt, Lich, and Docra.

JENCAPORE

Pages 141-141

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in Indostan, and in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name. It is seated on the river Chaul, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76. 25. N. Lat. 30. 30.

JENCOPING

Pages 141-141

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Smaland, seated on the south side of the lake Werter, with a strong citadel. The houses are all built with wood. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 20. N. Lat. 57. 22.

JENISA

Pages 141-141

a river of the Ruffian empire that runs from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, and falls into the Frozen ocean.

JENISKOI

Pages 141-141

a town of the Ruffian empire, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, seated on the river Jenila. It is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and pretty strong; and there are villages for several miles round it. It is subject to the Tungufans, who are Pagans, and live chiefly on the above river. They pay a tribute to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> for every bow, reckoning a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and a woman for one. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; and no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> grow there but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> currants, strawberries, and gooseberries. Corn, butchers meat, and wild fowls, are very cheap. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 92. 35. N. Lat. 57. 46.

JENKINS

Pages 141-141

HENRY. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGEVITY">LONGEVITY</a>. Jenkins, Sir Leoline, a learned civilian and able statesman of the 17th century, born in Glamorganshire about the year 1623. Being rendered obnoxious to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> during the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> by adhering to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s cause, he consulted his safety by flight; but returning on the Restoration, he was admitted an advocate in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, and succeeded Dr Exton as judge.
