or Jezreel, a town in the north of Samaria, towards Mount Carmel, where stood a palace of the kings of Israel, (1 Kings xxi. 18.) On the borders of Galilee (Joshua xix.) said to be one of the towns of Issachar.—The valley of Jezreel (Judges vi. 17.) was situated to the north of the town, running from west to east for ten miles, between two mountains; the one to the north, commonly called Hermon, near Mount Tabor; the other Gilboa: in breadth two miles.

JIB

Pages 177-178

the foremost sail of a ship, being a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> staysail extended from the outer end of the bowsprit prolonged by the jib-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, towards the fore-top mast head. See Sail. The jib is a sail of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> command with any side-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, but especially when the ship is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> hauled, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> has the wind upon her beam; and its effort in raising the ship, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> her head to leeward, is very powerful, and of great utility, particularly when the ship is working through a narrow channel. JIB-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOM">Boom</a>, a boom run out from the extremity of the bowsprit, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to its length, and serving to extend the bottom of the jib, and the stay of the fore-top-gallant mast. This boom, which is nothing more than a continuation of the bowsprit forward, to which it may be considered as a top-mast, is usually attached to the bowsprit by means of two large boom-irons, or by one boom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> on the outer end of the bowsprit; or, finally, by the cap without and a strong lashing within, instead of a boom iron, which is generally the method of securing it in small merchant-ships. It may therefore be drawn in upon the bowsprit as occasion requires; which is usually practised when the ship enters a harbour, where it might very soon be broken or carried away, by the vessels which are moored therein, or passing by under sail. JIBBEL or Gebbel Aurey, the Mons Auratus of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, an assemblage of many very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Algiers. Here Mr Bruce met with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people much fairer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> than any of the nations to the southward of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>: their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, and their eyes blue: they maintain their independence, and are of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> disposition, so that our traveller found it difficult to approach them with safety. They are called Neardia; and each of them has a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> in the middle between the eyes, marked with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>. They are divided into tribes, but, unlike the other Arabs, have huts in the mountains built of mud and straw; and are, by our author, supposed to be a remnant of the Vandals. He even thinks that they may be descended from the remainder of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Vandals mentioned by Procopius, which was defeated among these mountains. They live in perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Moors, and boast that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. They pay no taxes.

JIDDA

Pages 178-178

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, situated, according to Mr Bruce, in N. Lat. 28° 1' E., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 39° 16' 55", while others make it 21° 28', and E. Long. 39° 22'. It is situated in a very unwholesome, barren, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Immediately without the gate to the eastward is a desert plain filled with the huts of the Bedouins <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> country Arabs, built of long bundles of spartum or bent-grass put together like fascines. These people supply the town with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. "There is no stirring out of the town (says Mr Bruce) even for a walk, unless for about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> on the south side by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, where there is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stinking pools of stagnant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which contributes to make the town very unwholesome." From the disagreeable and inconvenient situation of this port, it is probable, that it would have been long ago abandoned, had it not been for its vicinity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, and the vast annual influx of wealth occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> trade; which, however, does not continue, but passes on to Mecca, whence it is dispersed all over the east. The town of Jidda itself receives but little advantage, for all the customs are immediately sent to the needy and rapacious sherif of Mecca and his dependents. "The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> (says Mr Bruce) is returned in bags and boxes, and passes on as rapidly to the ships as the goods do to the market, and leaves as little profit behind. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> rise to a prodigious price, and this falls upon the townsmen, while all the profit of the traffic is in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of strangers; most of whom, after the market is over (which does not last six weeks), retire to Yemen and other neighbouring countries, which abound in every sort of provision. From this scarcity, Mr Bruce supposes it is that polygamy is less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> here than in any other part of Arabia. "Few of the inhabitants of Jidda (says our author) can avail themselves of the privilege granted by Mahomet. He cannot marry more than one wife, because he cannot maintain more; and from this cause arises the want of people and the number of unmarried women." The trade at Jidda is carried on in a manner which appeared very strange to our traveller. "<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> ships (says he) were there from India; some of them worth, I suppose 200,000l. One merchant, a Turk, living at Mecca, 30 hours journey off, where no Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> go, whilst the continent is open to the Turk for escape, offers to purchase the cargoes of four out of these nine ships himself; another of the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> comes and says he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> buy none unless he has them all. The samples are shown, and the cargoes of the whole nine ships are carried into the wildest parts of Arabia by men with whom one would not wish to trust himself alone in the field. This is not all; two India brokers come into the room to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the price; one on the part of the India <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, the other on that of the buyer the Turk. They are neither Mahomets nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, but have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> with both. They sit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the carpet, and take an India shawl which they carry on their shoulder like a napkin, and spread it over their hands. They talk in the mean time indifferent conversation, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were employed in no serious business whatever. After about 20 minutes spent in handling each other's fingers below the shawl, the bargain is concluded, say for nine ships, without one word ever having been spoken on the subject, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> used in any shape whatever. There never was one instance of a dispute happening in these sales. But this is not all; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is yet to be paid. A private Moor, who has nothing to support him but his character, becomes responsible for the payment of these cargoes. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> delivers a number of coarse hessian bags full of what is supposed to be money. He marks the contents upon the bag, and puts his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> upon the string that ties the mouth of it. This is received for what is marked upon it without any one ever having opened one of the bags; and in India it is current for the value marked upon it as long as the bag lasts. The port of Jidda is very extensive, and contains numberless shoals, small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and sunk rocks, with deep channels, however, between them; but in the harbour itself ships may ride secure, whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows. The only danger is in the coming in or going out; but as the pilots are very skilful, accidents are never known to happen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> of this harbour, as Mr Bruce informs us, are exceedingly erroneous. While he laid here, he was desired by Captain Thornhill to make a new chart of the harbour; but finding that it had been undertaken by another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, Captain Newland, he dropped it. He argues in the strongest terms against the old maps, which he says can be of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, but the contrary; and he gives it as a characteristic of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Sea, "scarce to have foundings in any part of the channel, and often on both sides; whilst ashore, foundings are hardly found a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> length from the main. To this, says he, I will add, that there is scarce one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on which I ever was, where the bowspirit was not over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, while there were no foundings by a line heaved over the stern. Of all the vessels in Jidda, only two had their log-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> properly divided, and yet all were so fond of their supposed accuracy, as to aver they had kept their course within five leagues between India and Babelmandel. Yet they had made no estimation of the currents without the straits, nor the different very strong ones soon after passing Socotra; their half-minute glasses, upon a medium, ran 57 seconds; they had made no observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> or currents in the Red Sea, either in the channel or in the inward passage; yet there is delineated in this map a chart of Captain Newland's, which he kept in the middle of the channel, full of sharp <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> and short stretches; you would think every yard was measured and founded!" JIG. See Music, No. 252.

JILLIFREE

Pages 178-179

JILLIFREE, a town on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>, opposite to James's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, where the English had formerly a small port. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Barra, in which it is situated, produces abundance of the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trade of the inhabitants is in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which they carry up the river in canoes; and, in return, bring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, cotton-cloths, elephants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, small quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> dust, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of canoes and people continually employed in this trade, make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Barra, according to Mr. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, more formidable to Europeans, than any other chieftain on the river, and have encouraged him to establish those extravagant duties, which traders of all nations are obliged to pay at entry, amounting almost to £20l. on each vessel, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and small. These duties are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> collected in person by the governor of Jillifree, who is attended by a troublesome train of dependants, who have some knowledge of the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their intercourse with them, and beg with such importunity, that traders are often under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of complying with their demands, in order to get rid of them. N. Lat. 13° 16'. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 10' from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. JIN. See Genii.

JOAB

Pages 327-327

general of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, defeated the Syrians and the other enemies of David, and took the fort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZION">Zion</a> from the Jebuflites, who, thinking it impregnable, committed it to the care of the lame and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, whom they placed on the walls. He finalized himself in all David's wars, but was guilty of basely murdering Abner and Amasa. He procured Joachimites a reconciliation between Absalom and David; and afterwards flew Absalom, contrary to the express orders of the king. He at length joined Adonijah's party; and was put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the order of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, 1014 B.C.

JOACHIMITES

Pages 327-327

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the disciples of Joachim a Cistercian monk, who was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Flora in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pretender to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. The Joachimites were particularly fond of certain tenets: The Father, they said, operated from the beginning till the coming of the Son; the Son, from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to theirs, which was the year 1265; and from that time the Holy Spirit was to operate in his turn. They also divided everything relating to men, to doctrine, and the manner of living, into three classes, according to the three persons in the Trinity: The first ternary was that of men; of whom the first class was that of married men, which had lasted during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the Father; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was clerks, which had lasted during the time of the Son; and the last was that of the monks, in which there was to be an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> by the Holy Spirit: The second ternary was that of doctrine, viz., the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, the New, and the everlasting Gospel; the first they ascribed to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Holy Spirit: A third ternary consisted in the manner of living, viz., under the Father, men lived according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; under the Son, they lived according to the flesh and the spirit; and under the Holy Ghost, they were to live according to the spirit only.

JOAN

Pages 327-328

Pope, called by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">Platina</a> John VIII., is said to have held the holy see between Leo IV., who died in 855, and Benedict III., who died in 858. Marianus Scotus says, he sat two years five months and four days. Numbersless have been the controversies, fables, and conjectures, relating to this pope. It is said that a German girl, pretending to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, where she made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in the sciences; and afterward came to Rome in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. As she had a quick genius, and spoke with a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> in the public disputations and lectures, her great learning was admired, and every one loved her extremely; so that after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Leo, she was chosen pope, and performed all offices as such. Whilst she was in possession of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, she was got with child; and as she was going in a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> to the Lateran <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, she was delivered of that child, between the Coliseum and St Clement's church, in a most public street, before a crowd of people, and died on the spot, in 857. By way of embellishing this story, may be added the precaution reported to have been afterward taken to avoid such another accident. After the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a pope, he was placed on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> with an open seat, called the "groping chair," when a deacon came most devoutly behind and satisfied himself of the pontiff's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> by feeling. This precaution, however, has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> deemed unnecessary, because the cardinals, it is alleged, take care to become fathers before they arrive at the pontificate. Joan d'Arc, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Maid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, whose heroic behaviour in reanimating the expiring valour of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, though by the most superstitious means, (pretending JOE Joanna (pretending to be inspired), deserved a better fate. She was burnt by the English as a sorceress in 1421, aged 24. See FRANCE, No. 101.

JOANNA

Pages 328-328

St., <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HINZUAN">HINZUAN</a>, one of the Comora <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 44. 15. S. Lat. 12. 30. See HINZUAN.

JOB

Pages 328-328
or Book of Job, a canonical book of the Old Testament, containing a narrative of a series of misfortunes which happened to a man whose name was Job, as a trial of his virtue and patience; together with the conferences he had with his cruel friends on the subject of his misfortunes, and the manner in which he was restored to ease and happiness. This book is filled with those noble, bold, and figurative expressions, which constitute the very soul of poetry. Many of the Jewish rabbins pretend that this relation is altogether a fiction; others think it a simple narrative of a matter of fact just as it happened: while a third sort of critics acknowledge, that the groundwork of the story is true, but that it is written in a poetical strain, and decorated with peculiar circumstances, to render the narration more profitable and entertaining. The time is not set down in which Job lived. Some have thought that he was much ancienier than Moses, because the law is never cited by Job or his friends, and because it is related that Job himself offered sacrifices. Some imagine that this book was written by himself; others say, that Job wrote it originally in Syrian or Arabic, and that Moses translated it into Hebrew: but the rabbins generally pronounce Moses to be the author of it; and many Christian writers are of the same opinion.

JOBBER

Pages 328-328

a person who undertakes jobs, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> small pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. In some statutes, jobber is used for a person who buys and sells for others. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROKER">BROKER</a>.

JOBBERING

Pages 328-328

the business of a jobber. Stock-Jobbing, denotes the practice of trafficking in the public funds, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of buying and selling stock with a view to its rise or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> applied to the illegal practice of buying and selling stock for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, or of accounting for the differences in the rise or fall of any particular stock for a stipulated time, whether the buyer or seller be possessed of any such real stock or not. See Stock-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROKER">Broker</a>.

JOCASTA

Pages 328-328

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Menoeceus, who married Laius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes, by whom she had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OEDIPUS">Oedipus</a>. She afterwards married her son Oedipus, without knowing who he was, and had by him Eteocles, Polynices, &c. When she discovered that she had married her own son and been guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INCEST">incest</a>, she hanged herself in despair. She is called Epigone by some mythologists.

JOCKEY

Pages 328-328

in the management of horses; the person who trims up, and rides about horses for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>.

JOEL

Pages 328-328
or the Prophecy of Joel, a canonical book of the Old Testament. Joel was the son of Pethuel, and the second of the twelve lesser prophets. The style of this prophet is figurative, strong, and expressive. He upbraids the Israelites for their idolatry, and foretells the calamities they should suffer as the punishment of that sin: but he endeavours to support them with the comfort that their miseries should have an end upon their reformation and repentance. Some writers, inferring the order of time in which the minor prophets lived from the order in which they are placed in the Hebrew copies, conclude that Joel prophesied before Amos, who was contemporary with Uzziah, king of Judah. Archbishop Usher makes this inference from Joel's foretelling that drought, chap. iv. 7, 8, 9. If we consider the main design of Joel's prophecy, we shall be apt to conclude, that it was uttered after the captivity of the ten tribes; for he directs his discourse only to Judah, and speaks distinctly of the sacrifices and oblations that were daily made in the temple.

JOGHIS

Pages 328-328

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heathen <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> in the East Indies, who never marry, nor hold any thing in private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>; but live on alms, and practise strange levities on themselves. They are subject to a general, who sends them from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to another to preach. They are, properly, a kind of penitent pilgrims; and are supposed to be a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Gymnosophists. They frequent, principally, such places as are consecrated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of the people, and pretend to live several days together without eating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> drinking. After having gone through a course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they look on themselves as impeccable, and privileged to do any thing; upon which they give a loofe to their passions, and run into all manner of debauchery.

JOGUES

Pages 328-329
or Yoogs, certain ages, eras, or periods, of extraordinary length, in the chronology of the Hindoos. They are four in number; of which the following is an account, extracted from Halhed's Preface to the Code of Gentoo Laws, p. xxxvi. 1. The Suttee Jogue (or age of purity) is said to have lasted three million two hundred thousand years; and they hold that the life of man was extended in that age to one hundred thousand years, and that his stature was 21 cubits. 2. The Tirtah Jogue (in which one-third of mankind was corrupted) they suppose to have continued of two million four hundred thousand years, and men lived to the age of ten thousand years. 3. The Dwapaar Jogue (in which half of the human race became depraved) endured one million six hundred thousand years, and the life of man was then reduced to a thousand years. 4. The Collee Jogue (in which all mankind are corrupted, or rather lessened, for that is the true meaning of Collee) is the present era, which they suppose ordained to fulfill four hundred thousand years, of which near five thousand are already past; and the life of man in that period is limited to one hundred years. Concerning the Indian chronology, we have already had occasion to be pretty copious; see HINDOOS, No. 19, 22. We shall here, however, subjoin Dr Robertson's observations on the above periods, from the Notes to his Historical Disquisition concerning India. "If (says he *) we suppose the computation of time * p. 360, in the Indian chronology to be made by solar or even by lunar years, nothing can be more extravagant in itself, or more repugnant to our mode of calculating the duration of the world, founded on sacred and infallible authority. From one circumstance, however, which merits attention, we may conclude, that the informa- tion which we have hitherto received concerning the chronology of the Hindoos is very incorrect. We have, as far as I know, only five original accounts of the different Jogue or eras of the Hindoos. The first is given by M. Rogers who received it from the Brahmins on the Coromandel coast. According to it, the Suttee Jogue is a period of one million seven hundred and twenty-eight thousand years; the Tirtah Jogue is one million two hundred and ninety-six thousand years; the Dwapaa Jogue is eight hundred and sixty-four thousand. The duration of the Collee Jogue he does not specify; (Porte Ouverte, p. 179.). The next is that of M. Bernier, who received it from the Brahmins of Benares. According to him, the duration of the Suttee Jogue was two million five hundred thousand years; that of the Tirtah Jogue, one million two hundred thousand years; that of the Dwapaa Jogue is eight hundred and sixty-four thousand years. Concerning the period of the Collee Jogue, he likewise is silent; (Voyager, tom. ii. p. 163.). The third is that of Colonel Dow; according to which the Suttee Jogue is a period of fourteen million of years, the Tirtah Jogue one million eighty thousand, the Dwapaa Jogue seventy-two thousand, and the Collee Jogue thirty-five thousand years; (Hist. of Hindost., vol. i. p. 2.). The fourth account is that of M. le Gentil, who received it from the Brahmins of the Coromandel coast; and as his information was acquired in the same part of India, and derived from the same source with that of M. Roger, it agrees with his in every particular; (Mem. de l'Academ. des Sciences pour 1772, tom. ii. part i. p. 176.). The fifth is the account of Mr Halhed, which has been already given. From this discrepancy, not only of the total numbers, but of many of the articles in the different accounts, it is manifest that our information concerning Indian chronology is hitherto as uncertain as the whole system of it is wild and fabulous. To me it appears highly probable, that when we understand more thoroughly the principles upon which the fictitious eras or jogues of the Hindoos have been formed, that we may be more able to reconcile their chronology to the true mode of computing time, founded on the authority of the Old Testament; and may likewise find reason to conclude, that the account given by their astronomers of the situation of the heavenly bodies at the beginning of the Collee Jogue, is not established by actual observation, but the result of a retrospective calculation.

JOHN

Pages 329-331

St, the Baptist, the forerunner of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, was the son of Zacharias and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. He retired into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, where he lived on locusts and wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; and about the year 29 began to preach <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, and to declare the coming of the Messiah. He baptized his disciples, and the following year Christ himself was baptized by him in the river Jordan. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, having reproved Herod Antipas, who had a criminal correspondence with Herodias his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>'s wife, he was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into prison, where he was beheaded. His head was brought to Herodias; who, according to St Jerome, pierced his tongue with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BODKIN">bodkin</a> she used to fasten up her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> herself after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for the freedom of his reproaches. John, St, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the evangelist, was the brother of St James the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and the son of Zebedee. He quitted the business of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> to follow Jesus, and was his beloved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>. He was witness to the actions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>; was present at his transfiguration on Mount Tabor; and was with him in the garden of Olives. He was the only apostle who followed him to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>; and to him Jesus left the care of his mother. He was also the first apostle who knew him again after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>. He preached the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; and principally resided at Ephesus, where he maintained the mother of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. He is said to have founded the churches of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, Pergamos, Thyatira, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, and Laodicea. He is also said to have preached the gospel amongst the Parthians, and to have addressed his first epistle to that people. It is related, that, when at Rome, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Domitian caused him to be thrown into a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALDRON">caldron</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, when he came out unhurt; on which he was banished to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATMOS">Patmos</a>, where he wrote his Apocalypse. After the death of Domitian, he returned to Ephesus, where he composed his Gospel, about the year 95; and died there, in the reign of Trajan, about the year 100, aged 94. Gospel of St John, a canonical book of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, containing a recital of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, actions, doctrine, and death, of our Saviour Jesus Christ, written by St John the apostle and evangelist. St John wrote his Gospel at Ephesus, after his return from the isle of Patmos, at the desire of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of Asia. St Jerome says, he would not undertake it, but on condition that they should appoint a public fast to implore the affluence of God; and that, the fast being ended, St John, filled with the Holy Ghost, broke out into these words: "In the beginning was the Word," &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> assign two reasons for this undertaking: the first is, because, in the other three Gospels, there was wanting the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the beginning of Jesus Christ's preaching, till the imprisonment of John the Baptist, which therefore he applied himself particularly to relate. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> reason was, in order to remove the errors of the Cerinthians, Ebionites, and other sects. But Mr Lampe and Dr Lardner have urged several reasons to show that St John did not write against Cerinthus or any other heretics in his Gospel. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> of St John. See Apocalypse. John of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, bishop of Chartres in France, was born at Salisbury in Wiltshire, in the beginning of the 12th century. Where he imbibed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, is unknown; but we learn, that in the year 1136, being then a youth, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he studied under several eminent professors, and acquired considerable fame for his application and proficiency in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and particularly in the learned languages. Thence he travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and, during his residence at Rome, was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> favour with Pope Eugenio III. and his successor Adrian IV. After his return to England, he became the intimate friend and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of the famous Thomas Becket, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, whom he attended in his exile, and is said to have been present when that haughty prelate was murdered in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. What preferment he had in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> during this time, does not appear; but in 1176 he was promoted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry II. to the bishopric of Chartres in France, where he died in 1182. This John of Salisbury was really a phenomenon. He was one of the first reformers. refiners of the Greek and Latin languages in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; a classical scholar, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a learned divine, and an elegant Latin poet. He wrote several books; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, his Life of St Thomas of Canterbury, a collection of letters, and Polycraticon. Pope John XXII, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAHORS">Cahors</a>, before called James d'Euze, was well skilled in the civil and canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and was elected pope after the death of Clement V. on the 7th of August 1316. He published the constitutions called Clementines, which were made by his predecessor; and drew up the other constitutions called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRAVAGANTES">Extravagantes</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> being elected emperor, John XXII opposed him in favour of his competitor; which made much noise, and was attended with fatal consequences. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, in 1329, caused the antipope <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de Corbiero, a cordelier, to be elected, who took the name of Nicholas V. and was supported by Michael de Celenne, general of his order; but that antipope was the following year taken and carried to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>, where he begged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of the pope with a rope about his neck, and died in prison two or three years after. Under this pope arose the famous question among the cordeliers, called the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> of the cordeliers; which was, Whether those monks had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the things given them, at the time they were making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them? for example, Whether the bread belonged to them when they were eating it, or to the pope, or to the Roman church? This frivolous question gave great employment to the pope; as well as those which turned upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, form, and stuff, of their habits, whether they ought to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, gray, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; whether the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COWL">cowl</a> ought to be pointed or round, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> or small; whether their robes ought to be full, short, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; of cloth, or of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>, &c. The disputes on all these minute trifles were carried so far between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> brothers, that some of them were burned upon the occasion. He died at Avignon in 1334, aged 90. John, king of England. See England, No 135, 147. John of Fordoun. See Fordoun. John of Gaunt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, a renowned general, father of Henry IV. king of England, died in 1438. John of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, otherwise called Bucold. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>. John Sobieski of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, one of the greatest warriors in the 17th century, was, in 1663, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-marshal of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and, in 1667, grand-general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. His victories obtained over the Tartars and the Turks procured him the crown, to which he was elected in 1674. He was an encourager of arts and sciences, and the protector of learned men. He died in 1696, aged 72. St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, the name of two Christian festivals; one observed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 24th, kept in commemoration of the wonderful circumstances attending the birth of John the Baptist; and the other on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 27th, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of St John the evangelist. St John's Wort. See Hypericum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. John's, St, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the East Indies, and one of the Philippines, east of Mindanao, from which it is separated by a narrow strait. E. Long. 125° 25'. N. Lat. 7° 0'. Johnson, St, an island of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of St Lawrence, having New Scotland on the south and west, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Breton on the east. The British got possession of it when Louisbourg was surrendered to them, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 26, 1758. Johnson, Ben, one of the most considerable dramatic poets of the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, whether we consider the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or the merit of his productions. He was born at Westminster in 1574, and was educated at the public school there under the great Camden. He was descended from a Scottish family; and his father, who lost his estate under <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, dying before our poet was born, and his mother marrying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRICKLAYER">bricklayer</a> for her second husband, Ben was taken from school to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at his father-in-law's trade. Not being captivated with this employment, he went into the Low Countries, and distinguished himself in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity. On his return to England, he entered himself at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; and having killed a person in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>, was condemned, and narrowly escaped execution. After this he turned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>; and Shakespeare is said to have first introduced him to the world, by recommending a play of his to the stage, after it had been rejected. His Alchymist gained him such reputation, that in 1619 he was, at the death of Mr Daniel, made poet-laureate to King James I. and master of arts at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. As we do not find Johnson's economical virtues anywhere recorded, it is the less to be wondered at, that after this we find him petitioning King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, on his accession, to enlarge his father's allowance of 100 merks into pounds; and quickly after we learn that he was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and sick, lodging in an obscure alley; on which occasion it was, that Charles, being prevailed on in his favour, sent him ten guineas; which Ben receiving laid, "His majesty has sent me ten guineas, because I am poor, and live in an alley; go and tell him, that his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> lives in an alley." He died in August 1637, aged 63 years, and was buried in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>. The most complete edition of his works was printed in 1756, in 7 vols 8vo. Johnson, Dr Samuel, who has been styled the brightest ornament of the 18th century, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, on the 18th of September S. S. 1729. His father Michael was a bookseller; and must have had some reputation in the city, as he more than once bore the office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. By what cautious reasoning he reconciled his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> required to be taken by all who occupy such stations, cannot now be known; but it is certain that he was zealously attached to the exiled family, and instilled the same principles into the youthful mind of his son. So much was he in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> in this work, and at so early a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> did he commence it, that when Dr Sacheverel, in his memorable tour through England, came to Litchfield, Mr Johnson carried his son, not then quite three years old, to the cathedral, and placed him on his shoulders, that he might see as well as hear the far-famed preacher. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> prejudices were not the only bad things which young Sam inherited from his father: he derived from the same source a morbid melancholy, which, though it neither depraved his imagination, nor clouded his perspicuity, filled him with dreadful apprehensions of infancy, and rendered him wretched through life. Johnson's life. From his nurse he contracted the *serofula* or king's evil, which made its appearance at a very early period, disfigured a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> naturally well-formed, and deprived him of the sight of one of his eyes. When arrived at a proper age for grammatical instruction, he was placed in the free school of Litchfield, of which one Mr Hunter was then master; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whom his illustrious pupil thought "very severe, and wrong-headedly severe," because he would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> a boy for not answering questions which he could not expect to be asked. He was, however, a skilful teacher; and Johnson, when he stood in the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of learning, was sensible how much he owed to him; for upon being asked how he had acquired so accurate a knowledge of the Latin tongue, he replied, "My master beat me very well; without that, Sir, I should have done nothing." At the age of 15 Johnson was removed from Litchfield to the school of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOURBRIDGE">Stourbridge</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, at which he remained little more than a year, and then returned home, where he stood two years without any settled <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of life or any regular course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. He read, however, a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in a deftful manner, as chance threw books in his way, and as inclination directed him through them; so that when in his 19th year he was entered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> college, Oxford, his mind was stored with a variety of such knowledge as is not often acquired in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, where boys seldom read any books but what are put into their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by their tutors. He had given very early proofs of his poetical genius both in his school exercises and in other occasional compositions: but what is perhaps more remarkable, as it shows that he must have thought much on a subject on which other boys of that age seldom think at all, he had before he was 14 entertained doubts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of revelation. From the melancholy of his temper these would naturally prey upon his spirits, and give him great uneasiness: but they were happily removed by a proper course of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>; for "his studies being honest, ended in conviction. He found that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is true; and what he had learned, he ever afterwards endeavoured to teach."

JOHNSTON

Pages 336-337

Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">ARTHUR</a>, was born at Caskieben, near Aberdeen, the seat of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and probably was educated at Aberdeen, as he was afterwards advanced to the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in that university. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> he chiefly applied himself to was that of physic; and to improve himself in that science, he travelled into foreign parts. He was twice at Rome; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his residence was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, in which university the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.D. was conferred on him in 1610, as appears by a MS. copy of verses in the advocate's library in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. After leaving Padua, he travelled through the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and over Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, England, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and other countries; and at length settled in France; where he met with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause as a Latin poet. He lived there 20 years, and by two wives had 13 children. After 24 years' absence, he returned into Scotland in 1632. It appears by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> books at Edinburgh, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> before that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> about that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In the year following, it is very well known that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. went into Scotland, and made Bishop Laud, then with him, a member of that council; and by this accident, it is probable, that acquaintance began between the doctor and that prelate, which produced his "Psalterium Davidis Paraphrastum Poetica;" for we find that, in the same year, the doctor printed a specimen of his Psalms at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and dedicated them to his lordship. He proceeded to perfect the whole, which took him up four years; and the first edition complete was published at Aberdeen in 1637, and at London the same year. In 1641, Dr Johnston being at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, on a visit to one of his daughters who was married to a divine of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England in that place, was seized with a violent diarrhoea, of which he died in a few days, in the 54th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, not without having seen the beginning of those troubles that proved fatal to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>. He was buried in the place where he died; which gave occasion to the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of his learned friend Wedderburn in his Sapphira on the doctor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: Scotia maga, dole, tanti viduata sepulchro Vatis: is Angligenis contigit altius honos In what year Dr Johnston was made physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> does not appear: it is most likely that the archbishop procured him that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> at his coming into England in 1633, at which time he translated <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s Song into Latin elegiac <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and dedicated it to his majesty. His Psalms were reprinted at Middleburgh, 1642; London, 1657; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, 1661; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> 1706; Edinburgh, by William Lauder, 1739; and last on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the Delphin classics, at London, 1741, 8vo, at the expense of Auditor Benson, who dedicated them to his late majesty, and prefixed to this edition <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of Dr Johnston, with the testimonies of various learned persons. A labouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between the two translations, of Buchanan and Johnston was printed the same year in English, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOIGNY">Joigny</a> in 8vo, entitled, A Prefatory Discourse to Dr John- son's Psalms, &c. and A Conclusion to it. His transla- tions of the Te Deum, Creed, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECALOGUE">Decalogue</a>, &c. were subjoined to the Psalms. His other poetical works are his Epigrams; his Parerga: and his Musae Anglicae, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> commendatory Verses upon persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in church and state at that time.

JOIGNY

Pages 337-337

a town of France, in Champagne, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENS">Sens</a>, with a very handsome castle. It consists of three parishes, and is pleasantly situa- ted on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YONNE">Yonne</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 25'. N. Lat. 47° 56'.

JOINERY

Pages 337-337

the art of working in wood, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of fitting various pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> together. It is called by the French menuiserie, "small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>," to distinguish it from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>, which is employed about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and less curi- ous works.

JOINT

Pages 337-337

in general, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> of two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more things. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body are cal- led by anatomists articulations. See ANATOMY, No. 2. The suppleness to which the joints may be brought by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> practice from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of infancy, is very fur- nishing. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> posture-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> shows us a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of this; but one of the most wonderful in- stances we ever had of it, was in a person of the name of Clark, and famous for it in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of Clark the posture- master. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had found the way, by long prac- tice, to distort many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, of which nobody before had every thought it possible to alter the posi- tion. He had such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> command of his muscles and joints, that he could almost disjoint his whole body; so that he once imposed on the famous Mullens by his distortions, in such a manner, that he refused to undertake his cure: but, to the amaze- ment of the physician, no sooner had he given over his patient, than he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him restore himself to the fi- gure and condition of a proper man, with no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTORTION">distortion</a> about him.

JOINTURE

Pages 337-337

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, generally signifies a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>- ment of lands and tenements, made on a woman in con- sideration of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>.

JOINVILLE

Pages 337-337

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of France, in Champagne, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> magnificent castle. It is situated on the ri- ver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 10'. N. Lat. 48° 22'.

JOISTS

Pages 337-337
or JOISTS, in Architecture, those pieces of timber framed into the girders and summers, on which the boards of the floor are laid. JOKES. See JESTING.

JOLLOXOCHITL

Pages 337-337

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> word, signifying flower of the heart, is the name of a plant which bears a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> beautiful flower, growing in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, where it is much esteemed for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and odour; which lat- ter is so powerful, that a single flower is sufficient to fill a whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> with the most pleasing fragrance.

JONAH

Pages 338-339

JONAH, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Prophecy of Jonah, a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; in which it is related, that Jonah (about 771 B.C.) was ordered to go and prophecy the destruction of the Ninevites, on account of their wickedness. But the prophet, instead of obeying the divine command, embarked for Tarshish; when, a tempest arising, the mariners threw him into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: he was swallowed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fish; and after being three days and nights in his belly, was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Hereupon being sensible of his past danger and surprising deliverance, he betook himself to the journey and embassy to which he was appointed; and arriving at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, he, according to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, boldly laid open their sins and misdeeds, and proclaimed their sudden overthrow: upon which the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and fasting, and a speedy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, happily averted the divine vengeance, and escaped the threatened ruin. Jonah upon this, fearing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for a false prophet, retired to a hill at some distance from the city; where God, by a miracle, condescended to show him the unreasonableness of his discontent.

JONATHAN

Pages 339-339

the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, celebrated in sacred <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for his valour, and his friendship for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Slain in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> 1055 B.C. Jonathan Maccabaeus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Judas, a renowned general of the Jews. He forced Bacchides the Syrian general, who made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Jews, to accept a peace; conquered Demetrius Soter, and afterwards Apollonius, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s general; but, being ensnared by Tryphon, was put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> 144 B.C.

JONES

Pages 339-342

Inigo, a celebrated English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, was the son of a cloth-worker of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and was born in 1572. He was at first put apprentice to a joiner; but early distinguished himself by his inclination to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>, and was particularly taken notice of for his skill in landscape-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. This afterwards recommended him to the favour of William <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>, who sent him abroad with a handsome allowance in order to perfect himself in that branch. He was no sooner at Rome, than he found himself in his proper sphere: he felt that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had not formed him to decorate cabinets, but to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> palaces. He dropt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> and conceived Whitehall. In the state of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the works of Palladio, and learned how beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> may be exerted on a less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an empire. How his abilities distinguished themselves in a spot where they certainly had no opportunity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, we are not told, though it would not be the least curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; certain it is, that, on the strength of his reputation at Venice, Christian IV invited him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and appointed him his architect; but on what buildings he was employed in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, we are yet to learn. James I. found him at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> took him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of her architect to Scotland. He served <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry in the same capacity, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of surveyor-general of the works was granted to him in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that prince, with whom at least all his lamented qualities did not die, Jones travelled once more into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and, afflicted by ripeness of judgment, perfected his taste. To the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between these voyages Mr Walpole is inclined to assign those buildings of Inigo, which are less pure, and border too much upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> style, which one may call <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James's Gothic. Inigo's designs of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> are not Gothic, but have a littleness of parts, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of ornaments, with which the revival of the Grecian taste was encumbered, and which he shook off in his grander designs. The surveyor's place fell, and he returned to England; and, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> was not all he had learned at Rome, with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Roman disinterestedness he gave up the profits of his office, which he found extremely in debt; and prevailed upon the comptroller and paymaster to imitate his example, till the whole arrears were cleared. In 1620, he was employed in a manner very unworthy of his genius: King James set him upon discovering, that is, gulling, who were the founders of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> were all Romanized; consequently, his partiality to his favourite people, which ought rather to have prevented him from charging them with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of barbarous clumsiness, made him conclude it a Roman temple. In the same year Jones was appointed one of the commissioners for the repair of St Paul's; but which was not commenced till the year 1633, when Laud, then bishop of London, laid the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and Inigo the fourth. In the restoration of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, he made two capital faults. He first renewed the sides with very bad Gothic; and then added a Roman portico, magnificent and beautiful indeed, but which had no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> parts that remained, and made his own Gothic appear ten times heavier. He committed the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, thrusting a screen in the Roman or Grecian taste into the middle of that cathedral. Jones indeed was by no means successful when he attempted Gothic. The chapel of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn has none of the characteristics of that architecture. The cloister beneath seems oppressed by the weight of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> above. The authors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Jones place the erecting of the Banqueting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the reign of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>; but it appears, from the accounts of Nicholas Stone, that it was begun in 1619, and finished in two years—a small part of the pile designed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of our kings; but so complete in itself, that it stands a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the most pure and beautiful taste. Several plates of the intended palace at Whitehall have been given; but Mr Walpole thinks, from no finished design. The four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sheets are evidently made up from general hints; nor could such a source of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and taste as the mind of Inigo ever produce so much fancies. The whole fabric, however, was so glorious an idea, that one forgets for a moment (says Mr Walpole), in the regret for its not being executed, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of our liberties, obtained by a melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> that passed before the windows of that very Banqueting-house. In 1623 he was employed at Somerset-house, where a chapel was to be fitted up for the Infanta, the intended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> of the prince. The chapel is still in being. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> to the river, part only of what was designed, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-gate, were erected afterwards on the designs of Inigo, as was the gate at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>-stairs. On the accession of Charles, Jones was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in his posts under both king and queen. His fee as surveyor was £3. 4d. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, with an allowance of £61 a-year for house-rent, besides a clerk, and incidental expenses. What greater rewards he had, are not upon record. During the prosperous state of the king's affairs, the pleasures of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> were carried on with much taste and magnificence. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, painting, music, and architecture, were all called in to make them rational amusements. Mr Walpole is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the celebrated festivals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. were copied from the shows exhibited at Whitehall, in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the most polite court in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Ben Johnson was the laureat; Inigo Jones the inventor of the decorations; Lanier and Farnolco composed the symphonies; the king, the queen, and the young <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, danced in the interludes. We have accounts of many of those entertainments, called masques; they had been introduced by Anne of Denmark. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a> had a folio of the designs for these solemnities, by Inigo's own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, consisting of habits, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a>, scenes, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of these masks was a little interrupted by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> that broke out between the composers, Inigo and Ben, in which whoever was the aggressor, the turbulent temper of Johnson took care to be most in the wrong. The works of Inigo Jones are not scarce; Surgeon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is one of his best works. One of the most admired is the arcade of Covent-garden, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>: "Two structures (says Mr Walpole), of which I want taste to see the beauties. In the arcade there is nothing remarkable; the pilasters are as arrant and homely stripes as any plasterer would make. The barn-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> over the portico of the church strikes my eyes with as little idea of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, as it could do if it covered nothing but a barn. It must be owned, that the defect is not in the architecture, but in the order.—Whoever saw a beautiful Tuscan building? Would the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> have chosen that order for a temple?" The expense of building that church was £500. Ambrosebury in Wiltshire was designed by Jones, but executed by his scholar Webb. Jones was one of the first that observed the same diminution of pilasters as in pillars. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINDSEY">Lindsey</a>-house in Lincoln's-Inn Fields, which he built, owes its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> to this singularity. In 1618, a special <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> was issued to the lord-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, Pembroke, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>, and others, to plant and reduce to uniformity, Lincoln's-Inn Fields, as it shall be drawn by way of map, or ground-plot, by Inigo Jones, surveyor-general of the works. That <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> is laid out with a regard to so trifling a singularity, as to be of the exact dimensions of one of the pyramids: this would have been admired in those ages when the keep at Kenilworth Castle was erected in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-fetter, and the Escorial in the shape of St Laurence's gridiron. Colehill in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, the seat of Sir Matthew Pleydell, built in 1650, and Cobham-hall in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, were Jones's. He was employed to rebuild Castle Ashby, and finished one front: but the civil war interrupted his progress there and at Stoke-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a>-house, now the London Lying-in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, on the east side of Aldergate-street, is a beautiful front. The Grange, the seat of the lord chancellor Henley in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, is entirely of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. It is not a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> house, but by far one of the best proofs of his taste. The hall, which opens to a small vestibule with a cupola, and the staircase adjoining, are beautiful models of the purest and most classic antiquity. The gate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a>-garden at Chelsea, designed by Jones, was purchased by Lord Burlington, and transported to Chilwick. He drew a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for a palace at Newmarket; but not that wretched hovel that stands there at present. One of the most beautiful of his works is the queen's house at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. The first idea of the hospital is said to have been taken from his papers by his scholar Webb. Heriot's hospital in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and the improvements made in his time on Glamis castle in Forfarshire in Scotland, are specimens of the designs of Inigo Jones. Inigo taunted early the misfortunes of his master. He was not only a favourite, but a Roman Catholic: in 1646 he paid £45. for his delinquency and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEQUESTRATION">sequestration</a>. Whether it was before or after this fine, it is uncertain, that he and Stone the mason buried their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> stock in Scotland yard; but an order being published to encourage the informers of such concealments, and four persons being privy to the spot where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was hid, it was taken up, and reburied in Lambeth-marsh. Grief, misfortunes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, put an end to his life at Somerset-house, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 21, 1651. Several of his designs have been published by Mr Kent, Mr Colin Campbell, and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">Ware</a>. He left in MS. some curious notes on Palladio's architecture, which are inserted in an edition of Palladio published in 1714.
