Jones, Sir William, the son of William Jones Esq., an eminent mathematician, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with the great Newton, was born in London on the 28th of September 1746, and received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">Harrow</a> school, under the tuition of Dr Robert Sumner, whom he has celebrated in a eulogium which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably be coeval with time. From Harrow school he went to University <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where the rapidity of his literary acquisitions excited the admiration of all. He travelled through France at the age of 23, taking up his residence for some time at Nice, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and the various forms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, became the favourite objects of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. A wish to relieve his mother from the burden of his education, made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> for a fellowship in his college, but having no immediate prospect of obtaining it, he in 1765 became <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to young Lord Althorp, afterwards Earl Spencer, in which situation he was introduced to the best of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and had also leisure to prosecute the acquisition of knowledge, and the farther cultivation of his intellectual powers, which were objects ever dear to him. He obtained next year, the fellowship he expected, and was thus raised to a state which he could not help viewing as independent. Being at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPA">Spa</a> with his pupil in the year 1767, he employed much of his time in making himself acquainted with the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and in the following year he was requested by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Grafton's under-secretary, to undertake a translation of a Persian MS. of the life of Nadir Shah, into the French language, of which the king of Denmark was anxious. anxious to have a version. This, his first publication, appeared in 1770, with the addition of a treatise on oriental poetry, which was very much admired, on account of the elegance of the French style and the accuracy of the translation. For this excellent publication it appears that he received nothing more than a diploma from his Danish majesty, constituting him a member of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Copenhagen, with a warm recommendation to the notice of his own sovereign. That he might be enabled to gratify his commendable ambition, he now began to think seriously of some profession through life; and, as he had conceived an early predilection for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he made that the object of his choice; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September 1770, he entered at the Temple. Yet the studies of his profession did not prevent him from making those literary advances, in which he took delight, and oriental literature still continued a favourite object. When the life of Zoroaster by Anquetil du Perron made its appearance, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> discourse to which the university of Oxford had been attacked, our author defended it in a pamphlet written with severity and with elegance. In 1772, he published a small volume of poems, being translations from the Asiatic poets, remarkable for the grace and brilliancy of their style; and in 1774 appeared his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> "De Poesi Afiatica," the beauty and purity of the Latin in which it is composed, exciting the admiration of men of literature both at home and abroad. He was called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> in the beginning of 1774, but declined to act in that capacity without a previous knowledge of the actual business of the profession. He was appointed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of bankrupts in 1776, about which period he addressed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Lord Althorpe, in which he beautifully expresses his ardent wish to have constitutional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> established by constitutional means. His translation of the speeches of Iseus, on account of his elegant style, his profound critical and historical knowledge, commanded the admiration of every competent judge. Soon after this his practice at the bar increased with rapidity; but he had little reason to flatter himself with the prospect of advancement in professional <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and dignity, because he was known to be convinced of the injustice of the British cause respecting the American war, which he was at no pains to conceal; and therefore an opponent of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of those who had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of public affairs, had little pretension to look for. In 1780 he became a candidate to succeed to Sir Roger Newdigate as representative in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for the university of Oxford, in which he was respectfully supported; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> sentiments were ill suited to secure him a majority, which made him decline the contest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. He soon after published a pamphlet entitled "An Inquiry into the legal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of suppressing riots, with a constitutional plan of future <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>," recommending the propriety of making every citizen a soldier in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of imminent danger. He next published a translation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> ancient poems of the highest reputation in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, which, with an ode on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Lord Althorpe, procured for him the highest reputation. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on the laws of bailments was also much admired, as was his speech at the London tavern. in defence of a parliamentary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> in 1782. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he drew up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> between a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> and a country <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> on the principles of government, published in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of St Asaph, for which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> was preferred against that clergyman. In a letter to Lord Kenyon, Mr Jones avowed himself to be the author, and asserted the principles it contained to be perfectly agreeable to the British <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; but it appears that he afterwards relaxed considerably in his political ardour. After the resignation of Lord <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, and appointment of Lord Shelburne, Mr Jones was nominated one of the judges in the British territories of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, an appointment which he had long wished for, as it would afford him an opportunity of prosecuting his favourite researches into oriental literature. He was chosen a judge in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1783, and on the 20th of that month the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> was conferred upon him. He arrived at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a> in September, and entered upon his office in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, opening the sessions with a very elegant <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. Here he planned the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of a society similar to the Royal Society of London, many valuable labours and researches of which are already in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the public. He collected materials for a complete digest of the Hindoo and Mahometan laws, which interesting work he did not live to bring to a conclusion. The publication of the "Asiatic Researches" occupied much of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. In 1789 he translated an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> drama called "Sacontala," which has been considered as an interesting curiosity. In 1794 he gave the world his "Ordinances of Menu," a famous Indian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, containing a system of duties both civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of India proving unfavourable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of Lady Jones, obliged her to return to England, whither Sir William soon desirous to follow her. On the 26th of April 1794, he was seized at Calcutta with an inflammation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, which set the powers of medicine at defiance, and on the 27th of the same month put a period to his existence without pain or struggle. It may be fairly asserted that few men have died more respected or regretted, as few have passed a more useful and irreproachable life. The uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his erudition has been displayed in all his writings, and scarcely any subject of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> research escaped his notice. He has scarcely ever been equalled as a linguist, for he is said to have been more or less acquainted with about 28 different languages. Taste and elegance marked all his exertions, and he might have risen as a poet to the very first rank. Great as his knowledge was, his virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> were not inferior. In whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> we think proper to view him as standing in relation to society, he was undoubtedly a pattern worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. As a permanent monument to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, his affectionate lady published his whole finished works in six quarto volumes, in the year 1799; and a marble monument to his memory by the same endearing friend, is placed in the antechamber of University college, Oxford. The East India Company also voted a monument to his memory in St Paul's cathedral, and a statue of him to be sent out to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of his life were published by Lord Teignmouth, and a society... society of gentlemen in Bengal who had been educated at Oxford, subscribed a sum for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> dissertation on his character and merits, by students in that university.

JONK

Pages 342-342
or Jonque, in naval affairs, is a kind of small ship, very common in the East Indies. These vessels are about the size of our fly-boats; and differ in the form of their building, according to the different methods of naval architecture used by the nations to which they belong. Their sails are frequently made of mats, and their anchors are made of wood.

JOPPA

Pages 342-342

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, lying south of Caesarea; and anciently the only port to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, whence all the materials sent from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s temple were brought hither and landed, (2 Chr. ii. 16). It is said to have been built by Japhet, and from him to have taken its name Japho, afterwards moulded into Joppa; and the very heathen geographers speak of it as built before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. It is now called Jaffa, somewhat nearer to its first appellation, and is but in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> condition.

JORDANO

Pages 342-342
LUCCA, an eminent Italian painter, was born at Naples in 1632. He became very early a disciple of Joseph Ribera; but going afterwards to Rome, he attached himself to the manner of Pietro da Cortona, whom he assisted in his great works. Some of his pictures being seen by Charles II. king of Spain, he engaged him in painting the Escorial; in which task he acquitted himself as a great painter. The king showed him a picture of Baffani, expressing his concern that he had not a companion: Lucca painted one so exactly in Baffani's manner, that it was taken for a performance of that master; and for this service he was knighted, and gratified with several honourable and valuable employments. The great works he executed in Spain gave him still greater reputation when he returned to Naples; so that though he was a very quick workman, he could not supply the eager demands of the citizens. No one, not even Titian, ever painted so much as Jordano; and his generosity carried him so far as to present altar-pieces to churches that were not able to purchase them. His labours were rewarded with great riches; which he left to his family, when he died, in 1705.

JOSEPH

Pages 342-342

the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>; memorable for his chastity, and the honours conferred on him at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, &c. He died in 1635 B.C. aged 110.

JOSEPHUS

Pages 342-342

the celebrated historian of the Jews, was of noble birth, by his father Matthias descended from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priests, and by his mother of the blood-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>; he was born A.D. 37, under Caligula, and lived under Domitian. At 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> he betook himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Essenes, and then to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; and having been successful in a journey to Rome, upon his return to Judea he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALILEANS">Galileans</a>. Being taken prisoner by Vespasian, he foretold his coming to the empire, and his own deliverance by his means. He accompanied Titus at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, and wrote his "Wars of the Jews," which Titus ordered to be put in the public library. He afterwards lived at Rome, where he enjoyed the privileges of a Roman citizen, and where the emperors loaded him with favours, and granted him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pensions. Besides the above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he wrote, 1. Twenty books of Jewish antiquities, which he finished under Domitian. 2. Two books against Apion. 3. An elegant discourse on the martyrdom of the Maccabees. 4. His own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. These works are excellently written in Greek.

JOSHUA

Pages 342-344

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, containing a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the wars and transactions of the person whose name it bears. This book may be divided into three parts: the first of which is a history of the conquest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, which begins at the 12th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of it among the tribes; Josiah and the third, comprised in the two last chapters, contains the renewal of the covenant he caused the Israelites to make, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of their victorious leader and governor. The whole comprehends a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of 17, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, of 27 years. Josiah, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Judah, the destroyer of idolatry, and the restorer of the true worship, an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and a valiant general, was slain in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, 699 B.C. Jotapata, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Lower Galilee, distant 40 stadia from Gabara; a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, situated on a rock, walled round, and encompassed on all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, so as not to be seen but by those who came very near. It was with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty taken by Vespasian, being defended by Josephus, who commanded in it; when taken, it was ordered to be razed. Jovian, the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, elected by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, after the death of Julian the apostate, in 363. He at first refused, saying he would not command idolatrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; but, upon an assurance that they would embrace Christianity, he accepted the throne, and immediately shut all the Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and forbade their sacrifices. But he did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to which his merit had raised him; being suffocated in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> by the fumes of a fire that had been made to dry the chamber, in 364, the 33d of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of his reign. See Constantinople, No. 67. Jovius, Paul, in Italian Giovin, a celebrated historian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMO">Como</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the year 1483. As his father died in his infancy, he was educated by his eldest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Benedict Jovius, under whom he became well skilled in classical learning; and then went to Rome, for the sake of enjoying the benefit of the Vatican library. He there wrote his first piece, De pilibus Romanis, which he dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>. He received a pension of 500 crowns for many years from Francis I., king of France, whose favour he secured by his flatteries. But, in the following reign, having disgraced the contabale <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTMORENCY">Montmorency</a>, his name was struck out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of pensioners. Jovius did not suffer his spirits to sink under his misfortune: he had obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation in the learned world by his writings; and having always showed great respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Medicis, on whose praises he had expatiated in his works, he applied to Clement VII. and obtained the bishopric of Nocera. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> piece is his history, which is that of his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> throughout the world, beginning with 1494, and extending to the year 1544. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> business of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. For he formed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of it in the year 1515; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> upon it till his death, which happened at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1552. It is printed in three volumes folio. He is allowed to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> as well as learning: he was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a bright and polished style, and has many curious observations: but being a venal writer, his histories are not much credited. Journal, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-book, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, or account of what passes daily. See Diary. Journal, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> accounts, is a book into which every particular article is posted off the waste-book, and made debtor. This is to be very clearly worded, and fairly engrossed. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOOK_KEEPING">Book-Keeping</a>. Journal, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, a sort of diary, or daily register of the ship's course, winds, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; together with a general account of whatever is material to be remarked in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-voyage. In all sea-journals, the day, or what is called the 24 hours, terminate at noon, because the errors of the dead-reckoning are at that period generally corrected by a solar observation. The daily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> usually contains the state of the weather; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>, increase, or diminution of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and the suitable shifting, reducing, or enlarging the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sail extended; as also the most material incidents of the voyage, and the condition of the ship and her crew; together with the discovery of other ships or fleets, land, shoals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">breakers</a>, soundings, &c. Journal, is also a name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> for weekly essays, newspapers, &c. as the Gray's Inn Journal, the Westminster Journal, &c. Journal, is also used for the titles of several books which come out at stated times, and give abstracts, accounts, &c. of the new books that are published, and the new improvements daily made in arts and sciences; as the Journal de Sciences, Journal de Physique, &c. Journey, a tract of ground passed over in travelling by land; properly as much as may be passed over in one day. Management of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a> on a Journey. See Horse. Journeyman, properly one who works by the day only; but the word is now used for any one who works under a master, either by the day, the year, or the piece. Joy, in Ethics, is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> which is produced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, regarding its object as present, either immediately or in prospect, in reality or imagination. This passion has been found to increase the perspiration and urine of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bodies. Joynery. See Joinery. Ipecacuanha, the root of a plant which is well known by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> as an emetic. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IPHICRATES">Iphicrates</a>, general of the Athenians, had that command conferred upon him at 20 years of age, and became famous for the exactness of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. He made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on the Thracians; restored Seuthes, who was an ally of the Athenians; attacked the Lacedemonians; and, on many other occasions, gave signal proofs of his conduct and courage. Many ingenious repartees have been mentioned of this general: a man of good family with no other merit than his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, reproaching him one day for the meanness of his birth, he replied, "I shall be the first of my <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, and thou the last of thine." He died 380 B.C. Iphigenia, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Agamemnon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYTEMNESTRA">Clytemnestra</a>. When the Greeks going to the Trojan war were detained by contrary winds at Aulis, they were informed by one of the footlakers, that to appease the gods they must sacrifice Iphigenia Agamemnon's daughter to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>. The father, who had provoked the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> by killing her favourite stag, heard this with the greatest horror and indignation; and rather than to shed the blood of his daughter, he commanded one of his heralds, as chief of the Grecian forces, to order all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> to depart each to his respective home. Ulysses and the other generals interfered, and Agamemnon consented to imitate his daughter for the common cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. As Iphigenia was tenderly loved by her mother, the Greeks sent for her on pretence of giving her in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>. Clytemnestra gladly permitted her departure, and Iphigenia came to Aulis. Here she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the bloody preparations for the sacrifice. She implored the forgiveness and protection of her father; but tears and entreaties were unavailing. Calchas took the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and as he was going to strike the fatal blow, Iphigenia suddenly disappeared, and a goat of uncommon size and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> was found in her place for the sacrifice. This supernatural change animated the Greeks, the wind suddenly became favourable, and the combined fleet set sail from Aulis.

JUAN DE FUCA

Pages 418-420

a strait on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, was surveyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Vancouver, and the entrance of which he places in N. Lat. 48. 20. and W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 124. The object of this survey was to discover a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the North Pacific and North Atlantic oceans; but none of the inlets <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> channels in this broken coast was found to extend more than 100 miles to the eastward of the entrance into the strait. Thus it appeared, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> forming the north side of that strait is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, or of an archipelago, extending nearly 100 leagues in length from south-east to north-west; and on the side of this land, most distant from the continent, is situated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOOTKA">Nootka</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. The most peculiar circumstance of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> depth of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, when contrasted with the narrowness of the channels. The people of Juan de Fuca are said to be well versed in the principles of trade, which they carry on in a very fair and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> manner. The commodities most prized by them are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, fire-arms, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>-coats. Their dress, besides skins, are a kind of woollen garments. According to Vancouver, the dogs belonging to this tribe of Indians are numerous, resembling those of Pomerania, though larger in general. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> even in the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> or villages does not exceed 600, and the smallpox is reckoned to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> very fatal among them. Their method of disposing of their dead is singular. "Baskets (says Vancouver) were found suspended on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> trees, each containing the skeleton of a young child, some of which were also small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> boxes filled with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> paste, resembling such as I had seen the natives eat, supposed to be made of the same root: some of these boxes were quite full; others were nearly empty, eaten probably by the mice, squirrels, or birds." Juan, St. de la Frontera, a town of South America, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Chiquito, near the lake Guancho. The territory of this town is inhabited by 20,000 native Americans, who are tributary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and produces a kind of almonds that are very delicate. It is seated at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>, in W. Long. 66. 35. S. Lat. 23. 25. Juan de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>, an island of America, and one of the Caribbees, being 100 miles in length and 50 in breadth. It belongs to the Spaniards; and is full of very high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and extremely fertile valleys, interspersed with woods, and well watered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and rivulets. It produces <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, rum, ginger, corn, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; partly proper to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and partly introduced from Spain. Besides, there are so many cattle, that they often kill them for the sake of the skins alone. Here are a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of uncommon trees, and there is a little gold in the north part of the island. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> said that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is healthy; and yet the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, when he had taken this island, lost most of his men by sickness; and for that reason was forced to abandon it. This happened in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. It is subject to storms and hurricanes, like the rest of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. It lies to the east of Hispaniola, at the distance of 30 miles. Juan de Porto Rico, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of the island of Porto Rico, with a good harbour defended by several forts, and a bishop's see. It is seated on the north coast of the island, in W. Long. 65. 35. N. Lat. 18. 30. Juan Fernandez, an island in the great South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in S. Lat. 33. 40. and W. Long. 78. 30. from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for the buccaneers who annoyed the western coast of the Spanish continent. They were led to resort hither from the multitude of goats which it nourished; to deprive their enemies of which advantage, the Spaniards transported a considerable number of dogs, which increasing greatly, have almost exterminated the goats, who now only find security among the steep mountains in the northern parts, which are inaccessible to their pursuers. There are instances of two men living, at different times, alone on this island for many years; the one a Mafquito <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>; the other Alexander Selkirk, a Scotchman, who was, after five years, taken on board an English ship, which touched here in about 1712, and brought back to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. From the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this recluse, Daniel Defoe is said to have conceived the idea of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the adventures of Robinson Crusoe. This island was very propitious to the remains of Commodore Anson's squadron in 1741, after having been buffeted with tempests, and debilitated by an inevitable scarcity, during a three months' passage round <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>; they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> here three months; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the dying crews, who on their arrival could scarcely with one united effort heave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, were restored to perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. Captain Carteret, in the Swallow, in 1767, having met with many difficulties and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a> in his passage into the South sea, by the straits of Magellan, attempted to make this island in order to recruit the health of his men; but he found it fortified by the Spaniards, and therefore chose rather to proceed to the island of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>. But M. de Bougainville that same year is said to have touched here for refreshments, although in the narrative of the voyage the fact is cautiously suppressed. This island is not quite 15 miles long and about six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; its only safe harbour is on the north side. It is said to have plenty of excellent water, and to abound with a great variety of excellent vegetables highly antiscorbutic; besides which, Commodore Anson sowed a variety of garden-seeds, and planted the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of plums, apricots, and peaches, which he was many years afterwards informed had thriven greatly; and now doubtless form a very valuable addition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions of this spot. Vast shoals of fish of various various kinds frequent this coast, particularly cod of a prodigious size. There are but few birds here, and those few are of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> well known and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Juan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLANCO">Blanco</a>, or White Jack, a Spanish name for platinum. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">Platina</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Juba, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>. He had succeeded his father Hiempal, and he favoured the cause of Pompey against Julius Caesar. He defeated Curio whom Caesar had sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a> he joined his forces to those of Scipio. He was conquered in a battle at Thapsus, and totally abandoned by his subjects. He killed himself with Petreius, who had shared his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> and his adversity, in the year of Rome 707. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> became a Roman province, of which Sallust was the first governor. Juba II, son of the former, was led among the captives to Rome to adorn the triumph of Caesar. His <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> was the source of the greatest honours, and his application to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> procured him more <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> than he would have obtained from the inheritance of a kingdom. He gained the heart of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the courteousness of his manners, and Augustus rewarded his fidelity by giving him in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> Cleopatra the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Antony, and conferring upon him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of king, and making him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all the territories which his father once possessed, in the year of Rome 723. His popularity was so great, that the Mauritanians rewarded his benevolence by making him one of their gods. The Athenians raised him a statue, and the Ethiopians worshipped him as a deity. Juba wrote an history of Rome in Greek, which is often quoted and commended by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Of it only few fragments remain. He also wrote on the history of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and the antiquities of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, chiefly collected from Berolus. Besides these, he composed some treatises upon the drama, Roman antiquities, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, &c. now lost. Jubilee, among the Jews, denotes every fiftieth year; being that following the revolution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> weeks of years; at which time all the slaves were made free, and all lands reverted to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> owners. The jubilees were not regarded after the Babylonish captivity. The word, according to some authors, comes from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> jobel, which signifies fifty; but this must be a mistake, for the Hebrew יובל, jobel does not signify fifty; neither do its letters, taken as cyphers, or according to their numerical powers, make that number; being 10, 6, 2, and 30, that is, 48.—Others say, that jobel signifies a ram, and that the jubilee was thus called, because proclaimed with a ram's horn, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the ram that appeared to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> in the thicket. Maimon chooses to derive the word from jabal, the first inventor of musical instruments, which, for that reason, were called by his name; whence the words jobel and jubilee came to signify the year of deliverance and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a>, because proclaimed with the sound of one of those instruments which at first was no more than the horn of a ram. Others derive jobel from יובל, jabal in hiphil יובל, hobal, which signifies to recall or return; because this year restored all slaves to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of this festival is in Lev. xxv. 8, 17. The learned are divided about the year of jubilee; some maintaining that it was every forty-ninth, and others that it was every fiftieth year. The ground of the former <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is chiefly this, that the forty-ninth year being of course a sabbatical year, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the jubilee had been kept on the fiftieth, the land must have had two sabbaths, or have lain fallow two years, which, without a miracle, would have produced a dearth. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it is alleged, that the Scripture expressly declares for the fiftieth year, Lev. xxv. 19, 11. And besides, if the jubilee and sabbatical year had been the same, there would have been no need of a prohibition to sow, reap, &c. because this kind of labour was prohibited by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the sabbatical year, Lev. xxv. 4, 5. The authors of the Universal History, book i. chap. 7, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> R, endeavour to reconcile these opinions, by observing, that as the jubilee began in the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the civil year, which was the seventh of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>, it might be said to be either the forty-ninth or fiftieth, according as one or other of these computations was followed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the law of the jubilee was to prevent the too great oppressions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, as well as their being liable to perpetual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. By this means a kind of equality was preserved through all the families of Israel, and the distinction of tribes was also preserved, that they might be able, when there was occasion, on the jubilee-year, to prove their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the inheritance of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. It served also, like the Olympiads of the Greeks, and the Lustra of the Romans, for the readier computation of time. The jubilee has also been supposed to be typical of the gospel state and dispensation, described by Isaiah, lxi. ver. 1, 2. in reference to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, as the "acceptable year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>." Jubilee, in a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> solemnity or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, celebrated at Rome, wherein the pope grants a plenary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> to all sinners; at least to as many as visit the churches of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul at Rome. The jubilee was first established by Boniface VII. in 1300, in favour of those who should go <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> limina apostolorum; and it was only to return every hundred years. But the first celebration brought in such store of wealth to Rome, that the Germans called this the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> year; which occasioned Clement VI. in 1343, to reduce the period of the jubilee to fifty years. Urban VI. in 1389, appointed it to be held every thirty-five years, that being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of our Saviour; and Paul II. and Sixtus IV. in 1475, brought it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to every twenty-five, that every person might have the benefit of it once in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Boniface IX. granted the privilege of holding jubilees to several princes and monasteries; for instance, to the monks of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, who had a jubilee every fifty years; when people flocked from all parts to visit the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Thomas à Becket. Jubilees are now become more frequent, and the pope grants them as often as the church or himself have occasion for them. There is usually one at the inauguration of a new pope. To be entitled to the privileges of the jubilee, the bull enjoins fasting, alms, and prayers. It gives the priests a full power to absolve in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, even those otherwise referred to the pope; to make commutations of vows, &c. in which it differs from a plenary indulgence. During the time of jubilees, all other indulgences are suspended. One of our kings, viz. Edward III., caused his birthday to be observed in manner of a jubilee, when he became fifty years of age, in 1362, but never before or after. This he did by releasing prisoners, pardoning all offences except <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, making good laws, and granting many privileges to the people. There are particular jubilees in certain cities, when several of their feasts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>: at Puy en Velay, for instance, when the feast of the Annunciation happens on Good-Friday; and at Lyons when the feast of St John Baptist concurs with the feast of Corpus Christi. In 1649, the Jesuits celebrated a solemn jubilee at Rome; that being the centenary or hundredth year from their institution; and the same ceremony was observed in all their houses throughout the world.

JUCATAN

Pages 420-420
or YUCATAN, a large province of New Spain in North America, which is a peninsula. It is over against the island of Cuba, and contains a large quantity of timber, proper for building ships; as also sugar, caffia, and Indian corn. The original inhabitants are few, they having been very ill used by the Spaniards. Merida is the capital town. It is a flat level country; and is very unhealthy, which may be owing to the frequent inundations.

JUDAH

Pages 420-420

the fourth son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, and father of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the tribes of the Jews, distinguished by his name, and honoured by giving birth to the Messiah, died 1636 B.C. Judah Hakkadosh, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Saint, a rabbi celebrated for his learning and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Antoninus, and was the friend and preceptor of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Leo of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, a rabbi of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, tells us, that Rabbi Judah, who was very rich, collected about 26 years after the destruction of the temple, in a book which he called the Mifnia, the constitutions and traditions of the Jewish magistrates who preceded him. But as this book was short and obscure, two Babylonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RABBIS">rabbis</a>, Rabbina and Afe, collected all the interpretations, disputes, and additions, that had been made until their time upon the Mifnia, and formed the book called the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a> or Gemara; which is preferable to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> Talmud, composed some years before by Rabbi Johanan of Jerusalem. The Mifnia is the text of the Talmud; of which we have a good edition in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> and Latin by Surenhusius, with notes, in 3 vols folio. It were to be wished the fame had been done to the Gemara. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a> of Judah was of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> compared with that of the kingdom of Israel; consisting only of two tribes, Benjamin and Judah: its east boundary, the Jordan; the Mediterranean its west, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the Danites, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except some places recovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, and others taken by the kings of Israel; on the south, its limits seem to have been contracted under Hadad of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> progeny of Edom, (1 Kings xi. 14.) Tribe of Judah, one of the 12 divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> by tribes (Josh. xv.), having Idumea on the south, from the extremity of the Lacus <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASPHALTITES">Asphaltites</a>, also the Wilderness of Zin, Cadebarne, and the brook or river of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; on the east, the said lake; on the west the Mediterranean; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the mouth of the said lake; where it receives the Jordan, Bethfemes, Thinna, quite to Ekron on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

JUDAISM

Pages 420-420

the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> doctrines and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the Jews. Judaism was but a temporary dispensation, and was to give way, at least the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, at the coming of the Messiah. For a complete system of Judaism, see the books of Moses. Judaism was anciently divided into several sects; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> whereof were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>, Sadducees, and Essenes. At present there are two sects among the Jews, viz. the Caraites, who admit of no rule of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> written by Moses; and the Rabbinites, who add to the law the traditions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>.

JUDAS MACCABEUS

Pages 420-420

a celebrated general of the Jews, renowned for his many victories over his enemies, at last slain in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, 261 B.C. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Jews, No. 13. Judas-Tree. See Cercis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JUDE

Pages 420-420

St., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of St James the younger, and son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> (Mat. xiii. 55). He preached in Mepotamia, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, Idumea; and died in Berytus for the confession of Christ. He wrote that epistle which goes under his name, and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of most of the apostles. He was cruelly put to death for reproving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>. Jude, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the General Epistle of Jude, a canonical book of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, written against the heretics, who, by their disorderly lives and impious doctrines, corrupted the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and good morals of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. St Jude draws them in lively colours, as men given up to their passions, full of vanity, conducting themselves by worldly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and not by the spirit of God.

JUDEA

Pages 420-420

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, taken largely, either denotes all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it; and thus it is generally taken in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Rutilius, Jerome, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, and Eusebius, take it for the whole of Palestine. Here we consider it as the third part of it on this side the Jordan, and that the southern part is distinct from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a> and Galilee; under which notion it is often taken, not only in Josephus, but also in the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. It contained four tribes; Judah, Benjamin, Dan, and Simeon, together with Philistia and Idumea; so as to be comprised between Samaria on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea on the south, and to be bounded by the Mediterranean on the west, and by the lake <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASPHALTITES">Asphaltites</a>, with part of Jordan, on the east. Josephus divides it into 11 tetrarchies; Pliny into 10; by which it has a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> than that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned. See PALESTINE.

JUDENBURG

Pages 420-420

a handsome and considerable town of Germany, in the circle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, with a handsome castle; the public buildings with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> are very magnificent. It is seated on the river Meur. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 20. N. Lat. 47. 20.

JUDEX

Pages 420-420

Matthew, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> writers of the Centuries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a>, was born at Tipplewolde in Mifnia, in 1528. He taught <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; but met with many difficulties in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his ministry from party-feuds. He wrote several works, and died in 1564.

JUDGE

Pages 420-422

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, appointed to hear causes, to explain the laws, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. Judges, in Jewish antiquity, certain supreme magistrates who governed the Israelites from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Joshua till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>. These judges resembled the Athenian archons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Roman dictators. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> judges, nity of judge was for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, but not always in uninter- rupted succession. God himself, by some express de- claration of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, regularly appointed the judges: But the Israelites did not always wait for his appoint- ment, but sometimes chose themselves a judge in times of danger. The power of the judges extended to af- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> of peace and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. They were protectors of the laws, defenders of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, avengers of all crimes; but they could make no laws, nor impose any new bur- dens upon the people. They lived without pomp or re- tinue, unless their own fortunes enabled them to do it; for the revenues of their office consisted in voluntary presents from the people. They <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Joshua till the beginning of the reign of Saul, being a space of about 339 years. Judges, for ordinary affairs, civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, were appointed by Moses in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> to terminate differences; in affairs of greater <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, the dif- ferences were referred to the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>'s family, and the judge of the people or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> at that time established. Moses likewise set up two courts in all the cities, one consisting of priests and Levites, to de- termine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> concerning the law and religion; the other consisting of heads of families, to decide in civil matters. Book of Judges, a canonical book of the Old Testa- ment, so called from its relating the state of the Is- raelites under the administration of many illustrious persons who were called judges, from being both the ci- vil and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> governors of the people, and who were raised up by God upon special occasions, after the death of Joshua, till the time of their making a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. In the time of this peculiar polity, there were several remark- able occurrences, which are recorded in this book. It acquaints us with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> impiety of a new genera- tion which sprung up after the death of Joshua; and gives us a short view of the dispensations of heaven to- wards this people, sometimes relieving and delivering them, and at others severely chastising them by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of their enemies. Select Judges (Judices selecti), in Antiquity, were persons summoned by the praetor to give their verdict in criminal matters in the Roman courts, as juries do in ours. No person could be regularly admitted into this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> till he was 25 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The Sortitio Judicum, or impanelling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, was the office of the Judex Questionis, and was performed after both parties were come into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, for each had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to reject or challenge whom they pleased, others being substituted in their room. The number of the Judices selecti varied, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. When the proper number appeared, they were sworn, took their places in the judicellia, and heard the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. Judgement, among logicians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> or ra- ther <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, whereby it compares its i- deas, and perceives their agreement or disagreement. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>; and Logic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. Judgement, in Law, is the sentence pronounced by the court upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> contained in the record. Judgements are of four sorts. First, where the facts are confessed by the parties, and the law determined by the court; as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of judgement upon demurrer: se- condly, where the law is admitted by the parties, and the facts disputed; as in the case of judgement on ver- dict; thirdly, where both the fact and the law arising thereon are admitted by the defendant; which is the judgement case of judgements by confession or default: or, lastly, where the plaintiff is convinced that either fact, or law, or both, are insufficient to support his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and therefore abandons or withdraws his prosecution; which is the case in judgements upon a nonuit or re- traxit. The judgement, though pronounced or awarded by the judges, is not their determination or sentence, but the determination and sentence of the law. It is the conclusion that naturally and regularly follows from the premises of law and fact, which stands thus: A— gainst him who hath rode over my corn, I may recover damages by law: but A hath rode over my corn; therefore I shall recover damages against A. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> proposition be denied, this is a demurrer in law: if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, it is then an issue of fact: but if both be confessed or determined to be right, the conclusion or judgement of the court cannot but follow. Which judgement or conclusion depends not therefore on the arbitrary caprice of the judge, but on the settled and invariable principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. The judgement, in short, is the remedy prescribed by law for the redress of injuries; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> or action is the vehicle or means of administering it. What that remedy may be, is indeed the result of deliberation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> to point out; and therefore the style of the judgement is, not that it is decreed or resolved by the court, for then the judgement might appear to be their own; but, "it is considered," consideratum est per curiam, that the plain- tiff do recover his damages, his debt, his possession, and the like; which implies that the judgement is none of their own; but the act of law, pronounced and de- clared by the court, after due deliberation and inquiry. See Blackft. Comment. iii. 396. Judgement, in criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, is the next stage of prosecution, after Trial, and Conviction are past, in such crimes and misdemeanors as are either too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or too low to be included within the benefit of clergy. For when, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> charge, the Jury have brought in their Verdict guilty in the presence of the prisoner; he is either immediately, or at a convenient time soon after, asked by the court, if he has any thing to offer why judgement should not be awarded against him? And in case the defendant be found guil- ty of a misdemeanor (the trial of which may, and does usually, happen in his absence, after he has once appeared), a capias is awarded and issued, to bring him in to receive his judgement; and if he absconds, he may be prosecuted even to outlawry. But whenever he appears in person, upon either a capital or inferior con- viction, he may at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, as well as at his arraign- ment, offer any exceptions to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> or stay of judgement: as for want of sufficient certainty in setting forth either the person, the time, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, or the offence. And if the objections be valid, the whole proceedings shall be set aside; but the party may be indicted again. And we may take notice, 1. That none of the statutes of jeofails, for amendment of er- rors, extend to indictments or proceedings in criminal cases; and therefore a defective indictment is not aided by a verdict, as defective pleadings in civil cases are. 2. That, in favour of life, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strictness has at all times been observed, in every point of an indictment. Comment. Sir Matthew Hale indeed complains, "that this strict- ness JUDGEMENTS are grown to be a blemish and inconvenience in the law; and the administration thereof: for that more offenders escape by the over-easy <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> given to exceptions in indictments, than by their own innocence; and many times gross murders, burglaries, robberies, and other heinous and crying offences, remain unpunished by these unseemly niceties: to the reproach of the law, to the shame of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, to the encouragement of villany, and to the dishonour of God." And yet, notwithstanding this laudable zeal, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was more tender of life than this truly excellent judge. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> also may be pleaded in arrest of judgement: and it has the same advantage when pleaded here as when pleaded upon ARRAIGNMENT; viz. the saving the ATTAINERD, and, of course, the CORRUPTION OF BLOOD: which nothing can reftore but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, when a pardon is not pleaded till after sentence. And certainly, upon all accounts, when a man hath obtained a pardon, he is in the right to plead it as soon as possible. See PARDON. Praying the benefit of clergy may also be ranked among the motions in arrest of judgement. See Benefit of CLERGY. If all these resources fail, the court must pronounce that judgement which the law hath annexed to the crime. Of these some are capital, which extend to the life of the offender, and consist generally in being hanged by the neck till dead; though in very atrocious crimes other circumstances of terror, pain, or disgrace, are superadded: as, in treasons of all kinds, being drawn or dragged to the place of execution; in high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> affecting the king's person or government, disembowelling alive, beheading, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERING">quartering</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, a public dissection. And in case of any treason committed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, the judgement is, to be burned alive. But the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> has authorized, by a tacit consent, an almost general mitigation of such parts of these judgements as favour of torture or cruelty: a fledge or hurdle being usually allowed to such traitors as are condemned to be drawn; and there being very few instances (and those accidental or by negligence) of any person's being disembowelled or burned, till previously deprived of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> by strangling. Some punishments consist in exile or banishment, by abjuration of the realm, or transportation beyond the seas: others, in loss of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, by perpetual or temporary imprisonment. Some extend to confiscation, by forfeiture of lands, or moveables, or both, or of the profits of lands for life; others induce a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISABILITY">disability</a> of holding offices or employments, being heirs, executors, and the like. Some, though rarely, occasion a mutilation or dismemberment, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or ears: others fix a lasting stigma on the offender, by slitting the nostrils or branding in the hand or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Some are merely pecuniary, by stated or discretionary fines: and, lastly, there are others that consist principally in their ignominy, though most of them are mixed with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of corporeal pain; and these are inflicted chiefly for such crimes as either arise from indigence, or render even opulence disgraceful. Such as whipping, hard labour in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of correction, the pillory, the stocks, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCKING">ducking</a>-stool. Disgusting as this catalogue may seem, it will afford <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to a British reader, and do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the British laws, to compare it with that shocking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of death and torment to be met with in the criminal codes of almost every other nation in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. And it is moreover one of the glories of our law, that the nature, though not always the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or degree, of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> is ascertained for every offence; and that it is not left in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of any judge, nor even of a jury, to alter that judgement which the law has beforehand ordained for every subject alike, without respect of persons. For if judgements were to be the private opinions of the judge, men would then be slaves to their magistrates; and would live in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, without knowing exactly the conditions and obligations which it lays them under. And, besides, as this prevents oppression on the one hand; so, on the other, it stifles all hopes of impunity or mitigation, with which an offender might flatter himself if his punishment depended on the humour and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the court. Whereas, where an established penalty is annexed to crimes, the criminal may read their certain consequence in that law, which ought to be the unvaried rule, as it is the inflexible judge, of his actions. JUDGEMENT OF GOD. See JUDICIOUM DEI.

JUDICATURE

Pages 422-422

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> profession of those who administer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. JUDICATURE is also used to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the jurisdiction of the judge, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> wherein he sits to render justice.

JUDICIA CENTUMVIRALIA

Pages 422-422

in Roman antiquity, were trials before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTUMVIRI">Centumviri</a>, to whom the praetor committed the decision of certain matters of inferior <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, like our justices of peace at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> sessions. During the judicia centumviralia, a spear was stuck up in the forum, to signify that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> was sitting.

JUDICIOUM CALUMNIE

Pages 422-422

was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> brought against the plaintiff for false <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, upon conviction, was ingufo fronsis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branding in the forehead. See INUSTIO.

JUDICIOUM DEI

Pages 422-422

Judgement of God, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> anciently applied to all extraordinary trials of secret crimes; as those by arms, and single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>; and the ordeals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those by fire, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot ploughshares, by plunging the arm in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or the whole body in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water; in hopes God would <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> a miracle, rather than suffer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and innocence to perish. Si super defendere non positis, judicio Dei seil. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> vel ferro, fieret de eo jufitia.—These customs were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> kept up even among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; and they are still in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in some nations. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BATTEL">BATTEL</a>, ORDEAL, &c.—Trials of this sort were usually held in churches in presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, priests, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> judges; after three days fasting, confession, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, and many adjurations and ceremonies described at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> by Du Cange.

JUDICIOUM PARVUM

Pages 422-423

M PARVUM denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s equals, i.e. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> by peers, and of commoners by commoners. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a> it is more than once insisted on as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> bulwark of our liberties, but especially by chap. 29, that no freeman shall be hurt in either his person <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, nisi per legale judicium parium suorum vel per legem terrae. And this was even esteemed in all countries a privilege of the highest and most beneficial <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Judicium JUGICUM Falsi, was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> which lay against the judges for corruption or unjust proceedings.
