JUGICUM Prevaricationis, was an action brought against the prosecutor, after the criminal was acquitted, for suppressing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of, or extenuating his guilt, rather than urging it home, and bringing it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

JUDOIGNE

Pages 423-423

a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Brabant. Near this town the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> gained that signal victory over the French in 1706, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAMILLIES">Ramillies</a>. It is seated on the river Geete, 13 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>; and 16 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>.

JUGERUM

Pages 423-423

in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of 120 Roman feet; its proportion to the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> being as 10,000 to 16,097.

JUGGLERS

Pages 423-423

a kind of people whose profession has not been often deemed either respectable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> useful. Yet Professor Beckmann defends them, and pleads ably the cause of the practitioners of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGERDEMAIN">legerdemain</a>, in the third volume of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Inventions, including rope-dancers, and such as exhibit feats of uncommon strength. He places all these under the general denomination of jugglers; and taking it for granted that every useful employment is full, he contends that there would not be room on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> for all its present inhabitants, did not some of them practise the art of juggling. "The arts, he observes, are not unprofitable, for they afford a comfortable subsistence to those who practice them, which they usually spend upon the spot, and this he considers as a good reason why their stay in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> ought to be encouraged. He is also of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the arts of juggling served no other end than to amuse the most ignorant of our citizens, it is proper that they should be encouraged, for the sake of those who cannot enjoy the more expensive deceptions of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>. They convey instruction in the most acceptable manner, and serve as an antidote to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. We scarcely think, however, that it is innocent to entice the labouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, by useless deceptions, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with their hard-earned pittance to idle vagabonds, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> cannot be comfortable, which is passed amidst scenes of the most grovelling dissipation. Juggling is certainly of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. The deception of breathing out flames was practised by some of the slaves in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> about 150 years before the commencement of the Christian era. It is, however, practised in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times with much greater dexterity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of naphtha, a liquid mineral <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which kindles when it only approaches a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. According to Plutarch, Alexander the Great was astonished and delighted with the secret effects of naphtha, which were exhibited to him at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECBATANA">Ecbatana</a>. Wonder has been excited in modern times by persons who could walk over <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coals or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which is easily done by rendering the skin of the feet callous and insensible, so that the nerves under it are secured from injury. We are told by Beckmann, that the Hippi, who dwelt near Rome, jumped through burning coals; that women were accustomed to walk over burning coals at Caetabala, near the temple dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>; that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of balls and cups is often mentioned in the works of the ancients; and that the various feats of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> exhibited in our circuses palled, in the 13th century, from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to the Byzantine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and thence over all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

JUGLANS

Pages 423-423

the walnut, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 50th order, Amenitaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JUGORA

Pages 423-423

a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Muscovy, depending on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Archangel. It has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>; and is inhabited by a kind of Tartars, who are very <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, and much of the same disposition with the Samoiedes.

JUGULAR

Pages 423-423

among anatomists, is applied to certain veins and glands of the neck. See Anatomy.

JUGULARES

Pages 423-423

in the Linnaean system, is the name of an order <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of fish, the general character of which is, that the ventral fins are placed before the pectoral. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JUGUM

Pages 423-424

an humiliating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted by the victorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> upon their vanquished enemies. It was thus: They set up two spears, and laying a third across, in the form of a gallows, they ordered those who had surrendered themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under this ignominious erection, without arms <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> belts. None suffered Jugurtha suffered this disgrace of falling sub jugo but such as had been obliged to surrender.

JUGURTHA

Pages 424-424

the illegitimate son of Manatbal, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Micipha. Micipha and Manatbal were the sons of Massinissa <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>. Micipha, who had inherited his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, educated his nephew with his two sons Adherbal and Hiempsal; but as he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that the former was of an aspiring disposition, he sent him with a body of troops to the assistance of Scipio, who was besieging Numantia, hoping to lose a youth whose ambition seemed to threaten the tranquillity of his children. His hopes were frustrated; Jugurtha showed himself brave and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and he endeared himself to the Roman general. Micipha appointed him successor to his kingdom with his two sons; but the kindness of the father proved fatal to the children. Jugurtha destroyed Hiempsal, and stripped Adherbal of his possessions, and obliged him to fly to Rome for safety. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> listened to the well-grounded complaints of Adherbal; but Jugurtha's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> prevailed among the senators, and the suppliant monarch, forsaken in his distress, perished by the fancies of his enemy. Cæcilius Metellus was at last sent against Jugurtha; and his firmness and success soon reduced the crafty Numidian, obliging him to fly among his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> neighbours for support. Marius and Sylla succeeded Metellus, and fought with equal success. Jugurtha was at last betrayed by his father-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Bocchus, from whom he claimed assistance; and he was delivered into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Sylla 106 years before the Christian era. He was exposed to the view of the Roman people, and dragged in chains to adorn the triumph of Marius. He was afterwards put in a prison, where he died six days after of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>.

JUICE

Pages 424-426

denotes the sap of vegetables, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the liquors of animals. See ANATOMY, BLOOD, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">PLANTS</a>, SAP, &c. The juices of several plants are expressed to obtain their essential salts, and for several medicinal purposes, with intention either to be used without further <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, or to be made into syrups and extracts. The general method of extracting their juices is, by pounding the plant in a marble <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and then by putting it into a press. Thus is obtained a muddy and green liquor, which generally requires to be clarified, as we shall soon observe. The juices of all plants are not extracted with equal ease. Some plants, even when fresh, contain so little juice, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> must be added while they are pounded, otherwise scarcely any juice would be obtained by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. Other plants which contain a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of juice, furnish by expression but a small quantity of it, because they contain also much mucilage, which renders the juice so viscid that it cannot flow. Water must also be added to these plants to obtain their juice. The juices thus obtained from vegetables by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> method, are not, properly speaking, one of their principles, but rather a collection of all the proximate principles of plants which are soluble in water; such as the faponaceous extractive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, the mucilage, the odoriferous principle, all the saline and saccharine substances; all which are dissolved in the water of the vegetation of the plants. Besides all these matters, the juice contains some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the resinous substance, and the green colouring matter, which in almost all vegetables is of a resinous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. These two latter substances, not being soluble in water, are only interposed between the parts of the other principles which are dissolved in the juice, and consequently disturb its transparency. They nevertheless adhere together in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and so strongly in most juices, that they cannot be separated by filtration alone. When therefore these juices are to be clarified, some previous preparations must be used by which the filtration may be facilitated. Juices which are acid, and not very mucilaginous, are spontaneously clarified by rest and gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. The juices of most antiseptic plants abounding in saline volatile principles, may be disposed to filtration merely by immersion in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water; and as they may be contained in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> bottles, while they are thus heated in a water bath, their saline volatile part, in which their medicinal qualities chiefly consist, may thus be preserved. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">Fermentation</a> is also an effectual method of clarifying juices which are susceptible of it; for all liquors which have fermented, clarify spontaneously after fermentation. But this method is not used to clarify juices, because many of them are susceptible of only an imperfect fermentation, and because the qualities of most of them are injured by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. The method of clarification most generally used, and indispensably necessary for those juices which contain much mucilage, is boiling with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. This matter, which has the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of coagulating in boiling water, and of uniting with mucilage, does accordingly, when added to the juice of plants, unite with and coagulate their mucilage, and separates it from the juice in form of scum, together with the greatest part of the resinous and earthy matters which disturb its transparency. And as any of these resinous matters which may remain in the liquor, after this boiling with the whites of eggs, are no longer retained by the mucilage, they may easily be separated by filtration. The juices, especially before they are clarified, contain almost all the same principles as the plant itself; because in the operation by which they are extracted, no decomposition happens, but every thing remains, as to its nature, in the same state as in the plant. The principles contained in the juice are only separated from the grosser oily, earthy, and resinous parts, which compose the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> matter that remains under the press. These juices, when well prepared, have therefore the same medicinal qualities as the plants from which they are obtained. They must evidently differ from each other as to the nature and proportions of the principles with which they are impregnated, as much as the plants from which they are extracted differ from each other in those respects. Most vegetable juices coagulate when they are exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, whether they are drawn out of the plant by wounds, or naturally run out; though what is called naturally running out, is generally the effect of a wound in the plant, from a sort of tumor, or some other internal cause. Different parts of the same plant yield different juices. The same veins in their course through the different parts of the plant yield juices of Juice. a different appearance. Thus the juice in the root of the cow-parsnip is of a brimstone <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; but in the stalk it is white. Among those juices of vegetables which are clammy and readily coagulate, there are some which readily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> with a whey. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wild lettuce, with the smell of opium, yields the greatest plenty of milky juice of any known British plant. When the stalk is wounded with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, the juice flows out readily like a thick cream, and is white and ropy; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> these wounds are made at the top of the stalks, the juice that flows out of them is dished with a purple tinge, as if cream had been sprinkled over with a few drops of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine. Some little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after letting this out, it becomes much more purple, and thickens; and finally, the thicker part of it separates, and the thin whey sticks at top. The whey or thin part of this separated matter is easily pressed out from the curd by squeezing between the fingers, and the curd <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> then remain white; and on washing with water it becomes like rags. The purple whey (for in this is contained all the colour) soon dries into a purple cake, and may be crumbled between the fingers into a powder of the same colour. The white curd being dried and kept for some time, becomes hard and brittle. It breaks with a thinning surface like resin, and is inflammable; taking fire at a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> all away with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. The same thick part being held over a gentle heat, will draw out into tough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> threads, melting like wax. The purple cake made from the whey is quite different from this; and when held to a candle scarce flames at all, but burns to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> coal. The whole virtue of the plant seems also to consist in this thin part of its juice: for the coagulum or curd, though looking like wax or resin, has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> at all; whereas the purple cake made from the serum is extremely bitter, and of a taste somewhat resembling that of opium. Of the same kind with the wild lettuce are the throatwort, spurge, and many other plants. These are all replete with a milky juice which separates into curds and whey like that already described. But this, though a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nature, is not universal; for there are many plants which yield the like milky juices without any separation ensuing upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. The white juice of the foxglove never separates, but dries into an uniform cake: the common red wild poppy bleeds freely with a milky juice; and the heads or capitules of feed bleed not less freely than the rest of the plant, even after the flower is fallen. This juice, on being received into a shell or other small vessel, soon changes its white to a deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour, and dries into a cake which seems resinous and oily, but no whey separates from it. The tragopogon, or goat's-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, when wounded, bleeds freely a milky juice; it is at first white, but becomes immediately yellow, and then more and more red, till at length it is wholly of a dusky red. It never separates, but dries together into one cake; and is oily and resinous, but of an insipid taste. The great bindweed also bleeds freely a white juice; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, as well as the stalks and leaves, affording this liquor. It is of a sharp taste; and as many of the purging plants are of this class, it would be worth trying whether this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> is not purgative. These juices, as well as the generality of others which bleed from plants, are white like milk; but there are some of other colours. The juice of the great celandine is of a fine yellow colour; it flows from the plant of the thickness of cream, and soon dries into a hard cake, without any whey separating from it. Another yellow juice is yielded by the seed-vessels of the yellow centaury in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, when the seeds are full grown. This is very clammy; it soon hardens altogether into a cake without any whey separating from it. It sticks to the fingers like birdlime, is of the colour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, and will never become harder than soft wax if dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; but if laid in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, it immediately becomes hard like resin. These cakes burn like wax, and emit a very pleasant smell. The great angelica also yields a yellowish juice on being wounded; and this will not harden at all, but if kept several years will still be soft and clammy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> out into threads or half melted resin. Another kind of juices very different from all these, are those of a gummy nature. Some of these remain liquid a long time, and are not to be dried without the assistance of heat; the others very quickly harden of themselves, and are not inflammable. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> of the juice of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a> leaves soon hardens; and is afterwards soluble in common water, and sparkles when put into the flame of a candle. The clusters of the common honeyuckle are full of a liquid gum. This they frequently throw out, and it falls upon the leaves, where it retains its own form. The red hairs of the ros folis are all terminated by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bladders of a thin watery fluid. This is also a liquid gum; it sticks to the fingers, draws out into long threads, and stands the force of the sun all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. In the centre of each of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>-drops there is a small red bladder, which stands immediately on the summit of the red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and contains a purple juice which may be squeezed out of it. The pinguicula, or butterwort, has also a gummy matter on its leaves in much greater quantity than the ros folis. Some plants yield juices which are manifestly of an oily nature. These, when rubbed, are not at all of a clammy nature, but make the fingers glip and slippery, and do not all harden on being exposed to the air. If the stalk of eleocharis be wounded, there flows out an oily juice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> upon a watery one. The stalks of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a> also afford a similar oily liquor swimming upon the other; and in like manner the white mullein, the berries of ivy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, juniper, dog-berry tree, and the fruit of the olive, when wounded, show their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> floating on the watery juice. Some of these oily juices, however, harden into a kind of resin. Our ivy yields such a juice very abundantly; and the juice of the small purple-berried juniper is of the same kind, being hard and fat, and not very gummy. If the bark of the common ivy is wounded in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, there will ooze out a tough and greasy matter of a yellowish colour, which, taken up between the fingers, feels not at all gummy or sticking, but melts in handling into a sort of oil, which in process of time hardens and crusts upon the wounds, and looks like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. It burns with a lasting flame, and smells very strong. The tops of the wild lettuce, and the leaves growing near the tops, if examined with a magnifying glass, show a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small bladders or drops of an oily juice of a brownish colour, hardening into a kind of resin; they are easily wiped off when of any size, and are truly an oily juice a little hardened. It is probable also, that the fine blue flour or powder, called the bloom, upon the surface of our common plums, is no other than such an oily juice exuding from their pores in small particles, and hardening into a sort of resin.

JUJUBE

Pages 426-426

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, the name of a fruit of the pulpy kind, produced on a tree which Linnaeus makes a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of rhamnus. See RHAMNUS. The jujubes have been made a general ingredient in pectoral decoctions; but they are now seldom used on these occasions, and are scarce at all heard of in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to be met with in our shops.

JUL

Pages 426-426
or Jol, a Gothic word signifying a "sumptuous treat;" and particularly applied to a religious festival first among the heathens and afterwards among Christians. By the latter it was given to CHRISTMAS; which is still known under the name of Jul, or Yule, in Denmark, Norway, Iceland, and Sweden; nay, even in the north of Britain, and whence the month of January by the Saxons was styled Giuli, i.e., "the Festival." As this feast had originally been dedicated by our heathen ancestors to the sun, their supreme deity; so the Christians, for the purpose of engaging the minds of their Ethnic (gentile) brethren, ordered it should be celebrated in memory of the birth of Christ; and thus it has been through ages a feast of joy and entertainment. We are indebted to Procopius for the first account of this feast.

JULEP

Pages 426-426

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a medicine composed of some proper liquor and a syrup <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, of extemporaneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, without decoction. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">MATERIA MEDICA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JULIAN

Pages 426-428

the famous Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, styled the Apostate, because he professed the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> before he ascended the throne, but afterwards openly embraced Paganism, and endeavoured to abolish Christianity. He made no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of violence, however, for this purpose; for he knew that violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> had always rendered it more flourishing; he therefore behaved with a polite mildness to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; recalled all who had been banished on account of religion under the reign of Constantius; and undertook to pervert them by his carelessness, and by temporal advantages and mortifications covered over by artful pretences; but he forbade Christians to plead before courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to enjoy any public employments. He even prohibited their teaching polite literature; well knowing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantages they drew from profane authors in their attacks upon Paganism and irreligion. Though he on all occasions showed a sovereign contempt for the Christians, whom he always called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALILEANS">Galileans</a>, yet he was sensible of the advantage they obtained by their virtue and the purity of their manners; and therefore incessantly proposed their example to the Pagan priests. At last, however, when he found that all other methods failed, he gave public employments to the most cruel enemies of the Christians, when the cities in most of the provinces were filled with tumults and seditions, and many of them were put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: Though it has been pleaded by Julian's apologists, that the behaviour of the Christians furnished sufficient pretence for most of his proceedings against them, and the animosities among themselves furnished him with the means; that they were continually prone to sedition, and made a merit of insulting the public worship; and, finally, that they made no scruple of declaring, that want of numbers alone prevented them from engaging in an open rebellion. Historians mention, that Julian attempted to prove the falsehood of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s prediction with respect to the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; and resolved to have that edifice rebuilt by the Jews, about 350 years after its destruction by Titus; but all their endeavours served only the more perfectly to verify what had been foretold by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; for the Jews, who had assembled from all parts to Jerusalem, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> the foundations, flames of fire burst forth and consumed the workmen*. However, the Jews, who were obstinately bent on accomplishing that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, made several attempts; but it is said, that all who endeavoured to lay the foundation perished by these flames, which at last obliged them entirely to abandon the work. Julian being mortally wounded in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with the Persians, it is said, that he then caught in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> some of the blood which flowed from his wound; and throwing it towards heaven, cried, "Thou Galilean hast conquered." But notwithstanding this popular report, Theodoret relates, that Julian discovered a different disposition; and employed his last moments in conversing with Maximus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. He died the following night, aged 32. For a particular account of his reign and exploits, see <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Constantinople, No. 7. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was ever more differently represented by different authors; on which account it is difficult to form a true judgement of his real character. It must, however, be acknowledged, that he was learned, liberal, temperate, brave, vigilant, and a lover of justice; but, on the other hand, he had apostatized to Paganism; was an enemy to the Christian religion; and was, in fact, a persecutor, though not of the most fanatical class. We have several of his discourses or orations; some of his letters; a treatise intitled Misopogon, which is a satire on the inhabitants of Antioch; and some other pieces, all written in an elegant style. They were published in Greek and Latin by Father Petavius in 1632 in quarto; and of which Spanheimius gave a fine edition in folio in 1696. His most famous work was that composed against the Christians, of which there are some fragments in Cyril's refutation of it. JULIAN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">Period</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, a period so called, as being adapted to the Julian year. It is made to commence before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the world. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> advantage lies here, that the same years of the cycles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and indiction, of which three cycles it was made to consist by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger in 1580, belonging to any year of this period, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> together again till after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of 7980 years. There is taken for the first year of this period that which hath the first of the cycle of the sun, the first of the cycle of the moon, and the first of the indiction cycle, and so reckoning on. The first year of the Christian era is always, in our systems Julian systems of chronology, the 4714th of the Julian period. To find what year of the Julian period any given year of Christ answers to: To the given year of Christ add 4713, because so many years of the Julian period were expired A.D. 1; and the sum gives the year of the Julian period fought. On the contrary, having the year of the Julian period given, to find what year of Christ answers thereto: From the year of the Julian period given subtract 4713, and the remainder will be the year fought. Julian, St., a harbour on the south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATAGONIA">Patagonia</a>, in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where ships usually touch that are bound to the South seas. S. Lat. 48. 15. Juliens, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> in the circle of Westphalia, in Germany, seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Maas and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and bounded by Prussian Guelderland on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of Triers on the south, by the electorate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> on the east, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> on the west. It is about 60 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and is a very plentiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, abounding in cattle, corn, and fine meadows, and is well supplied with wood; but it is most remarkable for a fine breed of horses, and woad for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, which is gathered here in abundance. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Juliens, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUREN">Duren</a>, Münster-Eifel, Bedburg, Weselburgh, and Laerlen. It is subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine, with the consent of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. Juliens, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the duchy of Juliens in Westphalia; some think this city was founded by Julius Caesar or Julia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRIPPINA">Agrippina</a>; but this is much questioned by others, because it is not mentioned before Antoninus's Itinerary and Theodosius's Tables. The town is small but well fortified, and neatly built; the houses are of brick, and the streets broad and regular. The citadel is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and very strong, containing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dukes, and a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a>. In the suburbs there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHUSIANS">Carthusians</a>, nobly endowed by several dukes of Juliens. The town is but poorly inhabited, though they have a fine woollen manufacture in this country, and likewise another of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. It was taken by Prince Maurice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a> in 1610, and by the Spaniards in 1622. It is seated on the river Roer, in E. Long. 6. 35. N. Lat. 50. 55. Julio Romano. See Romano. Julius Cæsar. See Cæsar. Julius II. Julian de la Rovere, pope, remarkable for his warlike disposition, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> negotiations: by the latter, he engaged the principal powers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with him against the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, called the league of Cambrai, signed in 1508. The Venetians having purchased peace by the cession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> Romania, Julius turned his arms against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, and appeared in person armed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>-apee, at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRANDOLA">Mirandola</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he took by assault in 1511. But proceeding to excommunicate Louis, the king wisely turned his own weapons against him, by calling a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> at Pifa: at which the pope refusing to appear, was declared to be suspended from the holy see; and Louis, in his turn, excommunicated the pope, who died soon after in 1512. He built the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> at Rome, and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the polite arts. Julius Vicus, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Julius Vicus Nemetes in Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>; situated between the Tres Tabernae and Noviomagus. Now Germerstein, a town of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>, on the west side of the Rhine. E. Long. 8. 15. N. Lat. 49. 12. Julius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>. See Pollux. Iulus, a son of Alcæmus, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVINIUM">Lavinium</a>. In the succession to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>, Æneas Sylvius, the son of Æneas and Lavinia, was preferred to him. He was, however, made chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. Iulus, a genus of insects of the order aptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the year; during which the sun enters the sign Leo. The word is derived from the Latin Julius, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of C. Caesar the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, who was born in it. Mark Antony first gave this month the name July, which before was called Quintilis, as being the fifth month of the year in the old Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> established by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, which began in the month of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. For the same reason, August was called Sextilis; and September, October, November, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, still retain the name of their first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. Quae sequitur, numero turba notata suo. Ovid. Fast. On the 19th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of this month the dog-days are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed to begin; when, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> and Pliny, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> boils, wine turns sour, dogs go mad, the bile is increased and irritated, and all animals decline and languish. July <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">Flowers</a>. See Dianthus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Jumiege, a town of Normandy in France, and in the territory of Caux, with a celebrated Benedictine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, in E. Long. 0. 55. N. Lat. 49. 25. Junci lapidei, the name given by old authors to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of coral, of the tubularia kind, and composed of a congeries of small tubules. See Tubularia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">Juncture</a>, any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> or closing of two bodies. See Joint. Juncture, in Oratory, is a part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, particularly recommended by Quintilian, and denotes such an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>, and syllables, in the connection of words, with regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, as will render the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> most easy and pleasant, and best promote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. Thus the coalition of two vowels, occasioning a hollow and obscure sound, and likewise of some consonants, rendering it harsh and rough, should be avoided; nor should the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> be repeated at the beginning and end of words, because the sound becomes hereby harsh and unpleasant.—The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Æneid is an example of juncture. Arma virumque cano, Trojae qui primus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> ortu. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCUS">Juncus</a>, the rush, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 5th order, Tripetaloidace. See Botany Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, the sixth month of the year, during which the sun enters the sign of Cancer. The word comes Jungerman—from the Latin *junius*, which some derive *à junone*. Ovid, in the 6th of his *Fasti*, makes the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> say, *Junius à nostro nomine nonem habet.* Others rather derive it *à junitoribus*, this being for young people as the month of May was for old ones. *Junius eff juvenum; qui fuit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a> senum.* In this month is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice.

JUNGERMANNIA

Pages 428-428

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of algae, and belonging to the cryptogamia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JUNGLIA

Pages 428-428

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngeneia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JUNIPERUS

Pages 428-428

the juniper tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the coniferae class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 51st order, Coniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

JUNIUS

Pages 428-428

Adrian**, one of the most learned men of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOORN">Hoorn</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in 1511. He travelled into all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and practised physic with reputation in England, where, among other works, he composed a Greek and Latin Lexicon, to which he added above 6,000 words; an Epithalamium on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and *Animadversa et de Coma Commentarius*, which is the most applauded of all his works. He died in 1575. **Junius, Francis**, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a> in 1545, of a noble family, and studied some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Lyons. Bartholomew Ancau, who was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, gave him excellent instructions with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> method of studying. He was remarkable for being <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against all temptations to lewdness; but a libertine so far overpowered him by his fondness, that he made him an atheist; however, he soon returned to his first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; and, adverse as he was to unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, he had no aversion to matrimony, but was married no less than four times. He was employed in public affairs by Henry IV.; and at last was invited to Leyden to be professor of divinity; which employment he discharged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, till he was snatched away by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> in 1602. Du <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">Pin</a> says, he was a learned and judicious critic. He wrote, in conjunction with Emmanuel Tremellius, a Latin version of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. He also published Commentaries on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Holy Scriptures; and many other works, all in Latin. **Junius, Francis**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Francis du Jon, the son of the preceding, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a> in 1589. He at first designed to devote himself to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but after the truce concluded in 1639, he applied himself entirely to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. He came to England in 1620, and lived 30 years in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>'s family. He was greatly esteemed not only for his profound erudition, but also for the purity of his manners; and was passionately fond of the study of the northern languages, that, being informed there were some villages in Friesland where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Saxons was preserved, he went and lived two years in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He returned to England in 1675; and after spending a year at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, retired to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, in order to visit Wolfius, at whose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> he died in 1677. The university of Oxford, to which he bequeathed his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, erected a very handsome monument to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. He wrote, 1. *De Pictura Veterum*, which is admired by all the learned; the best edition of it is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> in 1694. He published the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in English. 2. An explication of the old Gothic manuscript, called the Silver one, because the four Gospels are there written in silver Gothic letters; this was published with notes by Thomas Maredchal or Marthal. 3. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">Harmony</a> of the four Gospels by Tatian, which is still in manuscript. 4. A Glossary in five languages, in which he explains the origin of the Northern languages; published at Oxford in 1745, in folio, by Mr Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>.

JUNK

Pages 428-428

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a name given to any remnants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces of old cable, which is usually cut into small portions, for the purpose of making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, mats, gaskets, femit, &c. **Juno**, in pagan worship, was the sister and wife of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of kingdoms and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>; and also styled the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of heaven; she presided over <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> and childbirth, and was represented as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Rhea. She married Jupiter; but was not the most complaisant wife: for according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, that god was sometimes obliged to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all his authority to keep her in due subjection; and the same author observes, that on her entering into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against him, he punished her by suspending her in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> with two anvils fastened to her feet, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> manacles on her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, while all the other deities looked on without a possibility of helping her. However, her jealousy made her frequently find opportunities of interrupting her husband in the course of his amours; and prompted her to punish with unrelenting fury <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a>, Semele, Io, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>, and the rest of his mistresses. Jupiter himself having conceived without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, Juno, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, conceived Vulcan by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> by touching a flower pointed out to her by the goddess Flora, and Hebe by eating greedily of lettuces. Juno, as the queen of heaven, preferred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> state: her usual attendants were Terror and Boldness, Calor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, and 14 nymphs; but her most faithful attendant was the beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">Iris</a>, or the rainbow. Homer describes her in a chariot adorned with precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of which were of ebony, and which was drawn by horses with reins of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. But the is more <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> painted drawn by peacocks. She was represented in her temple at Corinth, seated on a throne, with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on her head, a pomegranate in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and in the other a sceptre with a cuckoo on its top. This statue was of gold and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>.

JUNONALIA

Pages 428-428

a festival observed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Juno. It was instituted on account of certain prodigies that happened in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and was celebrated by matrons. In the solemnity two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cows were led from the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> through the gate called Carmentalis; and two images of Juno, made of cypresses, were borne in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>. Then marched 27 girls habited in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> robes, singing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>; then came the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMVIRI">decemviri</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-

JUST

Pages 6-6

just apparent. The other paps are seen very distinctly, but all of them inferior in height. Mr Banks and his friends mounted to that, the fourth, and found the height to be 2359 feet; but this is far overtopped by Beinn-an-oir. The stones of this mountain are white, a few red, quartzy, and composed of small grains; but some are brecciated, or filled with crystaline kernels of an amethystine colour. The other stones of the island are, a cinereous slate, veined with red, and used here as a whetstone; a micaceous sandstone; and between the small isles and Arfin, a micaceous quartzy rock stone. On the west side of the island there is an anchoring place called Whitsfarlan; towards the north end is a bay called Dal'gaul; and on the same coast is formed another riding place for vessels among several small islets. Between the north end of Jura and the small isle of Skarba, there is a famous whirlpool, called Cory Bhreacan, from Breacan son to a king of Denmark, who perished in this gulf. His body being cast ashore on the north side of Jura, was buried in a cave, and his grave is still distinguished by a tombstone and altar. In this vortex, which extends about a mile in breadth, the sea begins to boil and ferment with the tide of flood, increasing gradually to a number of whirlpools, which, in the form of pyramids, spout up the water with a great noise, as high as the mast of a small vessel, agitated into such a foam as makes the sea appear white even at the distance of two leagues. About half flood the violence begins to decrease, and continues to do so till about half an hour after high water; then it boils as before, till within an hour of low water, when the smallest fishing boat may cross it without danger. Jura is furnished with many rivulets and springs of excellent water, and the air is remarkably healthy; its salubrity being increased by the high situation, perpetually fanned by breezes. It is, however, but ill peopled; and did not contain above 700 or 800 inhabitants at the time it was visited by Mr Pennant. The number in 1805 has increased to 1100. The women are prolific, and very often bear twins. The inhabitants live to a great age, and are liable to few distempers. Men of 90 can work; and there was living in Pennant's time a woman of 80, who could run down a sheep. The inhabitants are all Protestants, but addicted to some superstitions. The parish is supposed to be the largest in Great Britain, and the duty the most dangerous and troublesome; it consists of Jura, Oranfay, Colonfay, Skarba, and several little isles divided by narrow and dangerous sounds; forming a length of not less than 60 miles; supplied by only one minister and an assistant. The very old clans of Jura are the Macilvays and the Macraines; but it seems to have changed masters more than once. In 1549, Donald of Cantyre, Macguillayne of Doward, Macguillayne of Kinlochbuy, and Macduffie of Colonfay, were the proprietors: Maclean of Mull had also a share in 1586. Mr Campbell of Jura, and Mr Macneil of Colonfay, are now (1807) the only proprietors of this island; but by far the greatest part belongs to the former. Jura is also the name of a chain of mountains in Switzerland, beginning in the canton of Zurich, extending from thence along the Rhine into the canton and bishopric of Baflé, stretching into the canton of Soleure and the principality of Neuchatel, and branching out towards the Pays de Vaud; separating that country from Franche Comté and Burgundy, and continued beyond the Genevan territories as far as the Rhone. Many elevated valleys are formed by different parts of this chain in the country of the Pays de Vaud; among which one of the most remarkable is the valley of the lake of Joux, on the top of that part of the chain named Mont Joux. It contains several populous villages, and is beautifully diversified with wood, arable land, and pasture. It is watered by two lakes; the largest of which is that of Joux already mentioned. This has one shore of a high rock covered with wood; the opposite banks forming a gentle ascent, fertile and well cultivated; behind which is a ridge covered with pines, beech, and oak wood. The smaller lake, named Brenet, is bordered with fine corn fields and villages; and the stream which issues from it is lost in a gulf named Entonnor, or the Funnel, where the people have placed several mills which are turned by the force of the falling current. The river Orbe issues from the other side of the mountain, about two miles from this place; and probably owes its origin to the subterraneous stream just mentioned. The largest lake is supplied by a rivulet which issues from the bottom of a rock, and loses itself in it. The valley contains about 3000 inhabitants, remarkable for their industry. Some are watchmakers; but the greatest number employ themselves in polishing crystals, granites, and marcasites. The country is much infested with bears and wolves. In ascending to this place there is a very extensive prospect of great part of the Pays de Vaud, the lake of Geneva, and that of Neuchatel, which from that high point of view appear to be nearly on a level; though M. de Luc found the latter to be 159 feet above the level of the lake of Geneva. JURATS, Jurati, magistrates in the nature of Aldermen, for the government of several corporations. Thus we meet with the mayor and jurats of Maidstone, Rye, Winchelsea, &c.—So also Jersey has a bailiff and twelve jurats, or sworn assistants, to govern the island. IVREA, an ancient and strong town of Italy, in Piedmont, and capital of Canavese, with a strong fort,

JUSTICE

Pages 6-14

justice in cases of complaint made before him. There are two kinds of jurisdiction, the one ecclesiastical, the other secular. Secular jurisdiction belongs to the king and his justices or delegates. The courts and judges at Westminster have jurisdiction all over England, and are not restrained to any county or place; but all other courts are confined to their particular jurisdictions, which if they exceed, whatever they do is erroneous. There are three sorts of inferior jurisdictions; the first is tenere placita, to hold pleas, and the plaintiff may sue either there or in the king's courts. Another is the cognizance of pleas, where a right is invested in the lord of the franchise to hold pleas: and he is the only person that can take advantage of it, by claiming his franchise. The third sort is an exempt jurisdiction, as where the king grants to some city, that the inhabitants shall be sued within their city, and not elsewhere; though there is no jurisdiction that can withstand a certiorari to the superior courts. Ecclesiastical jurisdiction belongs to bishops and their deputies. Bishops, &c., have two kinds of jurisdiction; the one internal, which is exercised over the conscience in things purely spiritual; and this they are supposed to hold immediately of God. The other is contentious, which is a privilege some princes have given them of terminating disputes between ecclesiastics and laymen. JURISPRUDENCE, the science of what is just or unjust; or the knowledge of laws, rights, customs, statutes, &c., necessary for the administration of justice. See Law. JUROR, JURATOR, in a legal sense, is one of those twenty-four or twelve men who are sworn to deliver truth upon such evidence as shall be given them touching any matter in question. The punishment of petty jurors attainted of giving a verdict contrary to evidence, willingly, is very severe. JURY, a certain number of men sworn to inquire into and try a matter of fact, and to declare the truth upon such evidence as shall appear before them. Juries are, in these kingdoms, the supreme judges in all courts and in all causes in which either the life, property, or reputation, of any man is concerned: this is the distinguishing privilege of every Briton, and one of the most glorious advantages of our constitution; for as every one is tried by his peers, the meanest subject is as safe and as free as the greatest. See the article Trial. Fury Mast, whatever is set up in room of a mast that has been lost in a storm or an engagement, and to which a lesser yard, ropes, and sails, are affixed. JUS CORONÆ. See Hereditary Right, and Succession. Jus Deliberandi, in Scots Law, that right which an heir has by law of deliberating for a certain time whether he will represent his predecessor. Jus Devolutum, in Scots Law, the right of the church, of presenting a minister to a vacant parish, in case the patron shall neglect to use that right within the time limited by law. Jus Marit, in Scots Law, the right the husband acquires to his wife's moveable estate, in virtue of the marriage. Jus Religiae, in Scots Law, the right the wife has in the goods in communion, in case of the previous decease of the husband. Jus Precedentioris, in Scots Law, the preferable right of jurisdiction acquired by a court, in any cause to which other courts are equally competent, by having exercised the first act of jurisdiction. Jus Civile, amongst the Romans, signified no more than the interpretation given by the learned, of the laws of the twelve tables, though the phrase now extends to the whole system of the Roman laws. Jus Civitatis, signifies freedom of the city of Rome, which entitled those persons who had obtained it to most of the privileges of Roman citizens—yet it differs from Jus Quiritum, which extended to all the advantages which a free native of Rome was entitled to—the difference is much the same as betwixt denization and naturalization with us. Jus Honorarium, was a name given to those Roman laws which were made up of edicts of the supreme magistrates, particularly the praetors. Jus Imaginis, was the right of using pictures and statues amongst the Romans, and had some resemblance to the right of bearing a coat of arms amongst us. This honour was allowed to none but those whose ancestors or themselves had borne some curule office, that is, had been Curule Aedile, Censor, Praetor, or Consul. The use of statues, &c., which the Jus Imaginis gave, was the exhibiting them in funeral processions, &c. See IMAGE. Jus Papirianum, was the laws of Romulus, Numa, and other kings of Rome; collected into a body by Sextus Papirius, who lived in the time of Tarquin the Proud; which accounts for the name. Jus Trium Liberorum, was a privilege granted to such persons in the city of Rome as had three children, by which they were exempted from all troublesome offices. The same exemption was granted to any person who lived in other parts of Italy, having four children; and those that lived in the provinces, provided they had five (or as some say seven) children, were entitled to the same immunities. This was good policy, and tended to the population of the empire. For a further account of these privileges, see CHILDREN. Jussica, a genus of plants belonging to the deciduous class; and in the natural method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthemae. See BOTANY Index. JUST, a sportive kind of combat on horseback, man against man, armed with lances. The word is by some derived from the French jouste, of the Latin juxta, because the combatants fought near one another. Salmius derives it from the modern Greek ξυλοφάρα, or rather ξύλον, which is used in this sense by Nicephorus Gregorius. Others derive it from juxta, which in the corrupt age of the Latin tongue was used for this exercise, by reason it was supposed a more just and equal combat than the tournament. The difference between justs and tournaments consists in this, that the latter is the genus, of which the former is only a species. Tournaments included all kinds of military sports and engagements made out of gallantry and diversions; justs were those particular combats where the parties were near each other, and engaged with lance and sword. Add, that the tournament was frequently performed by a number of cavaliers, who fought in a body; the just was a single combat of one man against another.—Though the justs were usually made in tournaments after a general rencontre of all the cavaliers, yet they were sometimes singly, and independent of any tournament. See TOURNAMENT. He who appeared for the first time at a just, forfeited his helm or casque unless he had forfeited before at a tournament. JUSTICE, in a moral sense, is one of the four cardinal virtues, which gives every person his due. Civilians distinguish justice into two kinds: communicative and distributive. The former establishes fair dealing in the mutual commerce between man and man; and includes sincerity in our discourse, and integrity in our dealings. The effect of sincerity is mutual confidence, so necessary among the members of the same community; and this mutual confidence is sustained and preserved by the integrity of our conduct. Distributive justice is that by which the differences of mankind are decided, according to the rules of equity. The former is the justice of private individuals; the latter of princes and magistrates. Fidelity and truth are the foundation of justice. As to be perfectly just is an attribute of the Divine Nature, to be so to the utmost of our ability is the glory of man. The following examples of this virtue are extracted from various authors. 1. Among the several virtues of Ariftides, that for which he was most renowned was justice; because this virtue is of most general use, its benefits extending to a greater number of persons, as it is the foundation, and in a manner the soul, of every public office and employment. Hence it was that Ariftides, though in low circumstances, and of mean extraction, obtained the glorious surname of the ἀριστός; a title, says Plutarch, truly royal, or rather truly divine: but of which princes are seldom ambitious, because generally ignorant of its beauty and excellency. They choose rather to be called the conquerors of cities and the thunderbolts of war, preferring the vain honour of pompous titles, which convey no other idea than violence and slaughter, to the solid glory of those expressive of goodness and virtue. How much Ariftides deserved the title given him, will appear in the following instances; though it ought to be observed, that he acquired it not by one or two particular actions, but by the whole tenor of his conduct. Themistocles having conceived the design of supplanting the Lacedemonians, and of taking the government of Greece out of their hands, in order to put it into those of the Athenians, kept his eye and his thoughts thoughts continually fixed upon that great project; and as he was not very nice or scrupulous in the choice of his measures, whatever tended towards the accomplishing of the end he had in view he looked upon as just and lawful. On a certain day then he declared in a full assembly of the people, that he had a very important design to propose; but that he could not communicate it to the people, because its success required it should be carried on with the greatest secrecy: he therefore desired they would appoint a person to whom he might explain himself upon the matter in question. Ariftides was unanimously fixed upon by the whole assembly, who referred themselves entirely to his opinion of the affair; so great a confidence had they both in his probity and prudence. Themistocles, therefore, having taken him aside, told him that the design he had conceived was to burn the fleet belonging to the rest of the Grecian states, which then lay in a neighbouring port; and by this means Athens would certainly become mistress of all Greece. Ariftides hereupon returned to the assembly, and only declared to them that indeed nothing could be more advantageous to the commonwealth than Themistocles's project, but that at the same time nothing in the world could be more unjust. All the people unanimously ordained that Themistocles should entirely desist from his project. There is not perhaps in all history a fact more worthy of admiration than this. It is not a company of philosophers (to whom it costs nothing to establish fine maxims and sublime notions of morality in the school) who determine on this occasion that the consideration of profit and advantage ought never to prevail in preference to what is honest and just; but the whole people who are highly interested in the proposal made to them, that are convinced it is of the greatest importance to the welfare of the state, and who, however, reject it with unanimous consent, and without a moment's hesitation; and for this only reason, that it is contrary to justice. How black and pernicious, on the other hand, was the design which Themistocles proposed to them, of burning the fleet of their Grecian confederates at a time of entire peace, solely to aggrandize the power of the Athenians! Had he a hundred times the merit ascribed to him, this single action would be sufficient to fully all his glory; for it is the heart, that is to say, integrity and probity, which constitutes and distinguishes true merit. 2. The government of Greece having passed from Sparta to the Athenians, it was thought proper under this new government to lodge in the island of Delos the common treasure of Greece; to fix new regulations with regard to the public money; and to lay such a tax as might be regulated according to the revenue of each city and state, in order that the expenses being equally borne by the several individuals who composed the body of the allies, no one might have reason to murmur. The difficulty was to find a person of so honest and incorrupt a mind, as to discharge faithfully an employment of so delicate and dangerous a kind, the due administration of which so nearly concerned the public welfare. All the allies cast their eyes on Ariftides; accordingly they invested him with full powers, and appointed him to levy a tax on each of them, relying entirely on his wisdom and justice. The citizens had no cause to repent their choice. He presided over the treasury with the fidelity and disinterestedness of a man who looks upon it as a capital crime to embezzle the smallest portion of another's possessions, with the care and activity of a father of a family in the management of his own estate, and with the caution and integrity of a person who considers the public money as sacred. In fine, he succeeded in what is equally difficult and extraordinary, viz. to acquire the love of all in an office in which he who escapes the public odium gains a great point. Such is the glorious character which Seneca gives of a person charged with an employment of almost the same kind, and the noblest eulogium that can be given to such as administer public revenues. It is the exact picture of Ariftides. He discovered so much probity and wisdom in the exercise of this office, that no man complained; and those times were considered ever after as the golden age; that is, the period in which Greece had attained the highest pitch of virtue and happiness. While he was treasurer-general of the republic, he made it appear that his predecessors in that office had cheated the state of vast sums of money, and among the rest Themistocles in particular; for this great man, with all his merit, was not irreproachable on that head; for which reason, when Ariftides came to pass his account, Themistocles raised a mighty faction against him, accused him of having embezzled the public treasure, and prevailed so far as to have him condemned and fined. But the principal inhabitants, and the most virtuous part of the citizens, rising up against unjust a sentence, not only the judgement was reversed and the fine remitted, but he was elected treasurer again for the year ensuing. He then seemed to repent of his former administration; and by showing himself more tractable and indulgent towards others, he found out the secret of pleasing all that plundered the commonwealth; for as he neither reproved them nor narrowly inspected their accounts, all these plunderers, grown fat with spoil and rapine, now extolled Ariftides to the skies. It would have been easy for him, as we perceive, to have enriched himself in a post of that nature, which seems, as it were, to invite a man to it by the many favourable opportunities it lays in his way; especially as he had to do with officers, who for their part were intent upon nothing but robbing the public, and would have been ready to conceal the frauds of the treasurer their master, upon condition he did them the same favour. These very officers now made interest with the people to have him continued a third year in the same employment: but when the time of election was come, just as they were on the point of electing Ariftides unanimously, he rose up, and warmly reproved the Athenian people: "What (says he), when I managed your treasure with all the fidelity and diligence an honest man is capable of, I met with the most cruel treatment, and the most mortifying returns; and now that I have abandoned it to the mercy of these robbers of the republic, I am an admirable man and the best of citizens! I cannot help declaring to you, that I am more ashamed of the honour you do me this day, than I was of the condemnation you passed against me this time twelve months; and with grief I find that it is more glorious Justice, with us to be complaisant to knaves than to save the treasures of the republic." By this declaration he silenced the public plunderers and gained the esteem of all good men. 3. In the Universal History we meet with the following remarkable instance of a scrupulous regard to justice in a Persian king named Nouchirvan. Having been out hunting, and desirous of eating some of the venison in the field, several of his attendants went to a neighbouring village and took away a quantity of salt to season it. The king suspecting how they had acted, ordered that they should immediately go and pay for it. Then turning to his attendants, he said, "This is a small matter in itself, but a great one as it regards me: for a king ought ever to be just, because he is an example to his subjects; and if he swerves in trifles, they will become dissolute. If I cannot make all my people just in the smallest things, I can at least show them it is possible to be so." These examples, to which many more might be added, are highly pleasing to a sagacious and virtuous mind; but the sensual and brutal part of mankind, who regard only the present moment, who see no objects but those which fall under the cognizance of the corporeal eye, and estimate the merit of every action by the gain which it produces, have always considered justice and utility as independent of each other. They put utility in the balance against honesty every day; and never fail to incline the beam in favour of the former, if the supposed advantage is thought to be considerable. They have no regard to justice but as they reckon to gain by it, or at least not to lose; and are always ready to desert it when it exposes them to any danger or threatens them with any loss. From this disposition of mind proceeds that avidity of wealth and that habitual fraud which perpetually embroil civil society: from this fatal source arises that deluge of iniquity which has overflowed the world; from this preference of interest to honesty proceed every unjust litigation and every act of violence.
